stories.title: B.C. MLA Ian Paton questioned by Mounties over allegation Conservatives offered him a job if he’d step down
stories.summary: Investigation comes as two more MLAs leave the B.C. Conservative caucus
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
A former B.C. Conservative says he was questioned by Mounties Wednesday over his allegation that he was offered an inducement to give up his seat so leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay could run, an accusation Ms. Findlay rejected as being part of a baseless and escalating political attack.

Ian Paton, who left caucus Aug. 24 and now represents Delta South as an independent, said he was interviewed by two Mounties for one hour at their Surrey headquarters on Wednesday morning.

“I told them that I got the phone call on June 30th, asking if I would step down for Kerry-Lynne, that there would be a job for me at the party level as an agriculture advisor and I would get paid the same remuneration I’m getting as an MLA,” Mr. Paton told The Globe and Mail in an interview.

The police investigation and Ms. Findlay’s denial come as two more sitting members of B.C.’s Official Opposition – Donegal Wilson and Scott McInnis – quit the caucus , bringing the total number of departures to nine since Aug. 14. Chris Delaney, Ms. Findlay’s chief of staff, also resigned Wednesday.

Since Ms. Findlay took over in May, the Conservatives have been rocked by a succession of controversies involving her inner circle, the departures of senior staff and a mass exodus of MLAs, all citing issues with her leadership. The turmoil unfolds as the embattled leader campaigns for her own seat in a Sept. 26 by-election.

“What we are seeing is a co-ordinated political attack designed to sidetrack our campaign at the very moment we are taking our message directly to the people of Abbotsford-Mission,” Ms. Findlay said in a media statement. She has not responded to interview requests from The Globe and Mail.

Mr. Paton said he was approached to give up his seat by Mr. Delaney and that remuneration for the new job would be about $122,000.

Mr. Paton said that he somewhat expected that Ms. Findlay would want his seat, given that she had previously served as an MP for Delta-Richmond East, which included the area now represented by Mr. Paton provincially, and that people might remember her.

He was unaware that the offer could amount to a criminal offence until police called him in for questioning, he said.

“I had no idea that, you know, maybe I should have written things down or recorded the conversation,” Mr. Paton said.

It is illegal under the Criminal Code to offer a legislator any kind of reward, advantage or benefit to resign from office, punishable by up to five years imprisonment.

Mr. Paton said he is aware of two other defectors who have been questioned by police for the same reason.

Ms. Findlay rejected the allegations and said they were part of a co-ordinated political attack designed to derail her campaign.

“I categorically reject any suggestion that I engaged in illegal or unethical conduct,” she said in a statement.

An audio recording that circulated online last week captured Ms. Findlay telling caucus members that if an MLA were to give up their seat, “I could give them a role as a senior advisor in their same portfolio.” Mr. Paton, who was in attendance, confirmed the authenticity of the recording to The Globe.

Ms. Findlay said in a social media post that while she was “unable to determine authenticity” of the recording, it contained “normal political discussions that respect the boundaries of the law and ethics.”

Prince George-Valemount MLA Rosalyn Bird, who left the Conservative caucus on Aug. 25 , confirmed to The Globe that Ms. Findlay had asked her to give up her seat. She declined to comment on whether she had been questioned by police.

Ms. Bird said she quit the party for several reasons, including staffing changes, a lack of communication and the recent allegations. (Operations director Apollo Chung was fired Aug. 26 after audio recordings circulated on X purportedly capturing a staffer plotting to monetize the office and fundraise “so we can steal everything.” Ms. Findlay gave no reason for his termination and has not confirmed the authenticity of the recordings.)

Ms. Bird said she has serious concerns regarding the leadership and is saddened by what is happening to the party.

“This was a movement a lot of people worked very hard to build [and] came very close to making government,” she said. “To see it eroding at this point, with the challenges we have here in the province, is disappointing and a little scary, to be honest.”

No reason was given for Mr. Delaney’s resignation. Ms. Findlay on Wednesday named Reann Gasper – who had been serving as deputy chief of staff since vacating her seat as Abbotsford-Mission MLA to allow Ms. Findlay to run – as Mr. Delaney’s replacement.

Ms. Wilson, MLA for Boundary-Similkameen and Mr. McInnis, MLA for Columbia River-Revelstoke became the latest members to leave the caucus, both cited issues with Ms. Findlay’s leadership.

Ms. Wilson said that, when Ms. Findlay became leader in late May, she promised herself she would give her three months to show caucus how she would lead.

“Three months later, I have my answer,” Ms. Wilson said in a statement. “I never imagined things could go this wrong, this quickly.”

Mr. McInnis, meanwhile, cited a litany of issues that have caused him growing concern, including the firing of competent and experienced staff, ethical questions involving Ms. Findlay’s senior team, reported connections to Alberta separatism and matters that now involve the RCMP.

“At the same time, the party has increasingly become an exclusive private club more concerned with ideological bona fides than building the broad coalition required to serve British Columbians and form government,” Mr. McInnis said.

stories.title: ‘Dream come true’: Easton Cowan reflects on rookie year while preparing for upcoming season
stories.summary: The line to meet Easton Cowan wrapped all the way around the exterior of the clubhouse at Caradoc Sands Golf Club in Strathroy, Ont.
stories.content:
Easton Cowan poses with the Calder Cup trophy at Caradoc Sands Golf Club in Strathroy, Ont. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

The line to meet Easton Cowan wrapped all the way around the exterior of the clubhouse at Caradoc Sands Golf Club in Strathroy, Ont.

Fans arrived as early as 7:15 a.m. to be at the front of the line for the meet and greet with the local hockey hero.

He brought the Calder Cup trophy and a pair of championship rings from the London Knights.

He was expected to sign autographs from noon to 2 p.m. but the response was so overwhelming he stayed for an extra hour.

“This community has done a lot for me and it will always have a special place in my heart,” said Cowan.

Maple Leafs Rangers Hockey Toronto Maple Leafs' Easton Cowan (53) skates towards his team's bench after scoring a goal during the second period of an NHL hockey game against the New York Rangers Thursday, March 5, 2026, in New York. (Source: Frank Franklin II/The Associated Press)

“I’m just super glad I could bring the cup here today and some rings from London for the fans to take pictures with.”

After a rookie season which saw him score 11 goals in 66 games with the Toronto Maple Leafs, he was loaned to the American Hockey League affiliate Toronto Marlies.

He scored eight times helping the Marlies win the Calder Cup trophy.

“Obviously playing for your hometown team is something special,” said Cowan.

“Growing up a Leafs fan and then winning a cup with their farm team was something special. I’ll never forget it.”

Toronto Marlies' Easton Cowan Toronto Marlies' Easton Cowan (53) reacts after assisting a goal by his teammate Benoit-Olivier Groulx (29) against Chicago Wolves goaltender Cayden Primeau (30) during second period in Game 5 of the AHL Calder Cup Final in Toronto on Friday, June 19, 2026. (Source: Arlyn McAdorey/The Canadian Press)

This summer he spent time meeting fans, working out on and off the ice and playing a lot of golf. He’s now heading back to Toronto to prepare for his sophomore season.

“Camp starts on the 16th, so just getting down a couple of weeks early, skating with the guys, meeting the new guys and just gelling with the boys again,” he said.

Depth charts have him pencilled in as a second- or third-line winger this season. However, he’s taking nothing for granted.

“You’re never guaranteed a spot,” said Cowan.

“You got to go there and work hard and earn your spot. So that’s what I’m willing to do and just excited to start playing hockey again. Last season dream come true”.

He’s hoping the next trophy he’ll be bringing home for a meet and greet will be the Stanley Cup.

“That’s the one I really want,” said Cowan.

“Looking forward to the challenge to get there and excited to get started.”

A Calgary aid worker is helping deliver emergency assistance in Nepal as international relief efforts ramp up following the devastating earthquake that struck the country last week.

Darren Tosh, a response manager with Samaritan’s Purse Canada, travelled to Nepal two days after the disaster to help coordinate aid deliveries to communities affected by the quake.

“We have to move quickly because these people have nothing. There’s absolutely nothing out there,” Tosh told Global News from Nepal.

Early Wednesday, a Samaritan’s Purse aircraft carrying 40 tonnes of relief supplies from southern Alberta arrived in Kathmandu, joining aid teams and military personnel from several countries responding to the crisis.

“The Korean government showed up, then Samaritan’s Purse and the 767, followed by the Australian Army. The Americans also showed up,” Tosh said.

While aid is flowing into the capital, reaching the hardest-hit communities remains a challenge. Tosh said the areas most severely affected are about a four-hour drive from Kathmandu, while some remote villages remain inaccessible by road.

“We’ll end up helicoptering what we can into these other remote areas that don’t have road access,” he said. “Right now it looks like there’s about 3,000 households that still remain inaccessible.”

The disaster is also being felt deeply in Calgary, home to tens of thousands of people with ties to Nepal.

For members of the Nepalese Community Society of Calgary, the past week has been marked by uncertainty as they await news from relatives and friends in the disaster zone.

Ghanendra “Ray” Neupane said community members have been sharing updates and supporting one another as reports continue to emerge from Nepal.

“I have a very good friend of mine whose uncle and aunt are still missing,” Neupane said. “I was reaching out to him yesterday only asking if there was any update. He said there’s almost no hope.”

Despite the devastation, both aid workers and community leaders say Nepal has demonstrated resilience in the face of previous disasters, including the major earthquake that struck the country a decade ago.

“This is a country that has only just got on its feet after having the massive earthquake that shook the country 10 years ago,” Tosh said.

He added that relief teams are focused not only on providing supplies but also on supporting affected families.

“We want to bring hope to these families,” Tosh said.

Neupane said the Nepalese community remains confident the country will recover again.

“We are united together when we are in need, so we are resilient,” he said.

Canadians looking to support relief efforts can donate through organizations such as Samaritan’s Purse and the Canadian Red Cross, or connect with local Nepalese community groups.

Goderich Salt Festival sign in September 2025. (file)

Goderich is going to get “salty” this long weekend.

The third annual Goderich Salt Festival runs Thursday through Sunday, in Goderich.

There will be special markets, food, music, tours, and events, with a “salted” theme.

Salt was first discovered in Goderich in 1865, by accident. The town is now home to the World’s Largest Salt mine, 500 metres under Goderich, and stretching far out into Lake Huron, and along the Lake Huron shoreline.

stories.title: Londoner honours her dog’s memory by pushing for newly proposed dangerous dog bylaw
stories.summary: London is considering giving its pet licensing by-law more teeth, with greater consequences for the owners of dogs declared “dangerous”.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London is considering giving its pet licensing by-law more teeth, with greater consequences for the owners of dogs declared “dangerous”.

Next week, the Community and Protective Services (Caps) Committee will consider a staff report that proposes modernizing the Dog Licensing and Control Bylaw by strengthening city hall’s response to dogs that pose a risk to public safety.

“Butch would want me to give a voice to all of the dogs that were taken and all of the people that were hurt,” said Debbie Morris, whose 13-year-old Chihuahua named Butch was killed during an unprovoked attack by her neighbour’s dog in April, 2025.

“I didn’t have time to react. My neighbour’s dog picked him up and killed him instantly,” Morris recalls, fighting back tears. “It was really tough. I had a lot of nightmares and Ptsd for a long time trying to figure out what I could have done differently.”

Morris launched an online petition calling for city hall to strengthen its response to dangerous dogs.

Responding to a subsequent direction from city council last summer, city staff are proposing several enhancements to the current bylaw and enforcement protocol.

The changes would include defining what constitutes “dangerous acts” and “dangerous dogs”.

Based on the severity and frequency of incidents, a graduated response would begin with a written warning for an initial (non-severe) act.

Subsequent dangerous acts, or a severe first act, would result in a Dangerous Dog Order to Comply.

The staff report recommends, “An Order to Comply would impose lifetime requirements, including a city-supplied warning sign, muzzling, leash restraint, a dangerous dog tag, microchipping and behavioural training. A public registry would identify the dog’s location using only the first three characters of the owner’s postal code.”

Not obeying the order would result in a fine.

Exemptions would apply if it’s determined that a dog acted in self defence.

“My concern is primarily responsible dog ownership because there’s been an influx of the number of dogs people are buying in the last six years,” Morris explains.

She says bringing London’s policies in line with some other Ontario municipalities like Waterloo, would be a fitting tribute to Butch.

“It started as a personal journey for me, and then I noticed there were others speaking up,” she said. “As soon as I brought it up, there were other people speaking up saying their dog was killed by a dog, or they were attacked.”

The Caps Committee will consider the proposed changes to the bylaw on Tuesday.

If endorsed by council, a subsequent report detailing implementation, resourcing, and cost will be completed in spring 2027.

stories.title: Nova Scotia energy minister resigns over offensive rap lyrics
stories.summary: Marco MacLeod resigned after weeks of meeting with women’s groups over songs critics say are hateful and violent toward women
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Nova Scotia’s energy minister has resigned from cabinet over misogynistic rap lyrics he wrote before entering politics.

The premier’s office says Marco MacLeod resigned Wednesday night after weeks of meeting with women’s advocacy groups over songs he published in 2013.

Critics said the lyrics are hateful toward women and violent and called for MacLeod’s resignation.

Premier Tim Houston says MacLeod has expressed regret for publishing the songs and feels his actions have become a distraction for the government.

MacLeod entered public office when he won a provincial byelection in May 2024 and kept his seat in a general election later that year.

The premier’s office says MacLeod will continue to represent Pictou West in the legislature while Houston will take over the energy portfolio.

stories.title: Hilroy’s classic back-to-school notebook features flawed map of Canada
stories.summary: Cover’s omission of Newfoundland and Cape Breton sparks second national geography scandal in less than a week, infuriating provincial leaders
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
The Hilroy notebook, with its iconic map of Canada on the cover, has been a back-to-school staple for generations. But in what’s become the second Canadian geography scandal in less than a week, Hilroy and its American parent company are under fire for lopping off parts of Atlantic Canada.

Hilroy said a printing error caused Newfoundland and Cape Breton, N.S., to be left off the map shown on the covers of its glossy notebooks. The company has apologized, and said it has stopped distributing the notebooks and plans to correct the map.

But the gaffe landed at a particularly sore time for Canadians, incensing provincial political leaders and sharpening anti-American tensions during a trade war with the U.S. Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump signed an order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, and followed that up with social-media posts criticizing Canada. He, and others in his orbit, have also repeatedly questioned Canada’s sovereignty, suggesting the country should become the 51st state.

The map mishap sparked outrage on social media, with some users linking Hilroy’s blunder to Mr. Trump.

“Who drew the map for Hilroy – Donald Trump?” wrote one poster on social media.

Others pointed out that the Hilroy notebook cover also appears to be missing the Haida Gwaii islands off the coast of British Columbia.

A spokesperson said the company is aware and addressing that omission as part of its “correction plan.”

Hilroy’s cartographical error also riled East Coast politicians, who condemned the notebook cover in their own social media posts.

“You can leave Newfoundland off an exercise book, but you can’t erase us,” Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham wrote on Wednesday (the map did not omit Labrador). “Hilroy will never take away our identity, our history, or our place on the map.”

In a statement to The Globe and Mail, Mr. Wakeham added that it’s disheartening to see such a historically beloved Canadian brand overlook a vital part of our nation’s geography.

Hilroy’s ubiquitous back-to-school notebooks have been on the market for more than 100 years. The company, founded in downtown Toronto in 1918, was acquired by U.S.-based Acco Brands Corp. in 2012.

Hilroy produces 14 million notebooks annually and still manufactures some of its products in Mississauga, Ont. Copies of the lined 40-page notebooks with the flawed map viewed by The Globe had a copyright date of 2025 and said they were made in China.

Acco Brands said the faulty exercise books first hit the market last year.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston also reacted strongly to the map error, calling it “unacceptable” and directing his Education Minister, Brendan Maguire, to send the makers of Hilroy notebooks a map of Canada that includes Cape Breton and Newfoundland.

In a letter to Hilroy Canada’s vice-president, culture and administrative services, Lori Conley, which was shared with The Globe, Mr. Maguire wrote: “I understand Canada is a big country. There are provinces, territories, islands and, apparently, some places that can be surprisingly difficult to locate. Cape Breton, however, is fairly easy to find.”

Mr. Maguire went on to describe Cape Breton’s historical and economic contributions, finishing with a nod to the trade tensions.

“At a time of global uncertainty, Canadian pride matters. So does making sure every part of our country is represented. That includes Cape Breton (and our friends in Newfoundland and Labrador).”

Nova Scotia Opposition Leader Claudia Chender had a more succinct way of putting it in her social media post: “Time for Hilroy to go back to school.”

Hilroy’s scribblers are widely distributed at large retailers such as Staples and Walmart.

At a busy Walmart in Halifax, where throngs of parents and children were shopping for back-to-school supplies on Wednesday, there were multiple boxes of the gem-toned pink, blue, turquoise and purple notebooks with the erroneous map on display at the front of the store.

In a social media post, Hilroy Canada thanked those who spotted the mistake.

“Getting it wrong stings,” said a company post on Instagram. “A production error left Newfoundland and Cape Breton off the map on our glossy cover design. That’s our mistake, and we’re sorry.”

Hilroy Canada said anyone who wants a replacement or refund should reach out via its website.

With a report from Canadian Press

stories.title: Rona in St. Thomas closed following break and enter
stories.summary: Police are investigating a break and enter at a Rona store on Edward Street in St. Thomas.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
Police are investigating a break and enter at a Rona store on Edward Street in St. Thomas.

A source with Rona who wished to remain anonymous told CTV News that thieves entered the store through a hatch in the roof and made their way down to the offices.

We’ve learned they left out the back door with a safe while leaving their tools behind.

Police have not confirmed those details.

stories.title: ‘We’re still in this’: Trauma still fresh in Tumbler Ridge ahead of return to school
stories.summary: Seven months after the mass shooting that devastated a small northeastern B.C. community, residents say they there is still a sense of shock, and as if no time has passed at all.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Seven months after the mass shooting that devastated a small northeastern B.C. community, residents say they there is still a sense of shock, and as if no time has passed at all.

“As soon as you leave town, you get it,” said Lydia Mannion, a mother of two. “You really realize that other people’s lives have continued and things have (stood) still in Tumbler. We’re still in this.”

For some directly impacted by the shooting, Mannion said, moving on with life in the months since has been like going through the motions.

“I’ve had a couple friends who said that they’re going to their counselling, they’re going to their activities, whatever it is, but they just feel it’s still kind of numb,” she said.

Tumbler Ridge B.C. shooting Lydia Mannion, a mother of two based out of Tumbler Ridge, B.C. (CTV News)

For Mannion, one of the clearest signs of the passage of time since the Feb. 20 shooting that left nine dead, and what has changed in a physical sense, is the deconstruction of the high school where much of the massacre took place.

“It really changes the sightline of downtown, because you could see the entrance to the college and the school from basically anywhere. If you’re at the grocery store, at some of the restaurants, the library,” she said.

Mannion said she doesn’t expect the community will ever completely move on from the shooting. In the short term, she said, the process is being complicated by the return to school, as feelings of excitement are followed by fear.

“It’s just really realizing, like, ‘oh, school’s starting!’ And then, ‘oh, is it safe?’ It’s just sort of in the back (of your mind).”

Some students will also not be returning to the classroom, with some transitioning to home learning or other arrangements, Mannion said.

Tumbler Ridge B.C. shooting Seven months after the mass shooting that devastated a small northeastern B.C. community, residents say they there is still a sense of shock. (CTV News)

B.C. Premier David Eby announced in May that a replacement school would be built in the community “as quickly as possible.”

The federal and provincial governments have together pledged $200 million toward construction of the new school and upgrades to the community’s health centre.

The community is also continuing to rally around and do what they can to provide long-term support to victims, their families and others affected by the shooting. A fundraiser and benefit concert planned for Saturday is part of that effort.

Also top of mind are the dozens of lawsuits being filed in California against OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, by teachers and students who survived the shooting and families of victims.

New lawsuits filed against OpenAI following Tumbler Ridge mass shooting

The lawsuits allege OpenAI was negligent in failing to report concerns about the shooter’s ChatGPT activity to police. OpenAI has acknowledged the account was flagged before the shooting, but said its leadership did not forward the concerns to authorities.

OpenAI has disputed allegations the decision was made with its image, not safety, in mind.

“It’s completely untrue to say that the people at the centre of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play,” the company said in a statement.

The legal action is unfolding thousands of kilometres from Tumbler Ridge, but Mannion said she backs the victims and their families “100 per cent.”

“They’re going to need support for their whole lives with this,” she said. “Those companies need to be held accountable.”

stories.title: Damaging storms sweep across Ontario causing flooding, power outages in Toronto area
stories.summary: Weather office issues multiple emergency alerts as police responded to multiple reports of downed power lines and hail pummelled neighbourhoods in the north
stories.author: Sharif Hassan
stories.content:
Severe storms cut across the Greater Toronto Area late Wednesday afternoon, causing widespread power outages, localized flooding and serious damage to a major concert venue as an intense weather system brought torrential rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado to wide swaths of southern Ontario.

The weather office issued multiple emergency alerts for extreme weather in parts of the GTA as skies darkened to almost nighttime levels over the city’s downtown and hail pummelled neighbourhoods further north.

Rogers Stadium, a 50,000-capacity music venue in the city’s north end, sustained “significant damage” in the storm, Live Nation Canada said in a statement.

“Fortunately, no one was injured during today’s extreme weather event,” the venue operator said late Wednesday. “We are currently assessing the extent of the damage.”

Video footage circulating on social media shows collapsed framing and torn off coverings on stadium grounds.

Severe storms cut across Ontario, causing flooding and power outages in the Toronto area.

The Canadian Press

Subway service was suspended on a stretch of one of Toronto’s main lines during the afternoon and evening rush hours due to flooding, as police responded to multiple reports of fallen trees and downed power lines across the city. The sound of emergency alerts rang out inside Toronto subway train cars held up by flooding at multiple stations.

Under one overpass in the downtown core, at least two partially submerged vehicles were abandoned in the floodwater Wednesday evening as police cordoned off the area. Toronto police also issued a hazard alert on social media about flooding on the Don Valley Parkway, a major city artery.

Long stretches of Yonge Street in midtown Toronto were flooded, with waves breaking over curbs and covering sidewalks in inches of water.

Outside the city, there were reports of damaged buildings, including a destroyed roof in Brampton, Ont.

Toronto Hydro said approximately 65,000 customers were without power as of Wednesday evening.

“We are responding to reported hazards, including downed power lines and damaged electrical equipment, while co-ordinating restoration efforts across the city,” the utility said in a social media post.

“Given the scale of the storm and the number of outages, restoration efforts May take time and vary by location,” it said.

The storm caused numerous flight delays at Toronto’s Pearson airport.

“Passengers are encouraged to check their flight status directly with their airline before travelling to the airport,” it said in a post on X.

The Salt-N-Pepa concert at the outdoor RBC Amphitheatre in Toronto was also postponed due to severe weather.

Videos from across the region shared on social media showed large hail pummelling cars in parking lots, flooding transit stations and sending people running for cover.

A severe weather alert stretched from near Sarnia east to Peterborough and north to Barrie, with areas such as Windsor and parts of cottage country under a yellow watch earlier in the day.

Environment Canada said hard-hit areas could see torrential downpours, ping pong-sized hail and wind gusts up to 110 kilometres an hour.

The primary concern was the possibility for damaging winds and torrential rains.

The storm came after parts of Ontario were lit up with lightning strikes and inundated by heavy rains by passing storms Wednesday morning.

stories.title: Tornado watch lifted for London and Middlesex County, power outages remain across the region
stories.summary: Tornado watch lifted for London and Middlesex County, power outages remain across the region CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 11:01 AM | Last Updated: 10 hours ago
Thousands left without power in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties
A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.
Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.
Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines , according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.
Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.
The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.
A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.
It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.
Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."
One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.
"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.
The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.
Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.
People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.
The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.
The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.
It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.
A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the
Middlesex-London Health Unit website .
There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.
It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.
Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.
Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.
Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines , according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.
Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.
The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.
A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.
It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.
Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."
One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.
"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.
The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.
What to do if a tornado warning is issued
Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.
People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.
The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.
Storms come amid ongoing heat event
The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.
It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.
A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the
Middlesex-London Health Unit website .
There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.
It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.
Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

stories.title: Staffer injured in Columbia Icefield all-terrain vehicle rollover
stories.summary: A Pursuit staff member was conducting an operational maintenance check on the Ice Odyssey all-terrain tour vehicle when the rollover happened at the Columbia Icefield.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
A man was injured on the job after a tour vehicle rolled down a hill on the Columbia Icefield , about 120 kilometres south of Jasper, Alta.

RCMP and Pursuit, the company that runs the bus tours, said the man was the only one involved and no one else was on the all-terrain vehicle when the rollover happened around 11 a.m. Tuesday.

An Ice Odyssey tour vehicle operated by a Pursuit team member was conducting an operational maintenance check when the rollover happened, the company said.

Pursuit’s Canadian chief operating officer Stuart Back said the vehicle rolled backwards and down off the road.

The employee was taken to hospital with unknown injuries and is now recovering.

“He’s actually just been just been released from hospital, which is great news, positive sign,” Back said. “May require further care but is on the mend, so to speak, having just been released.”

The all-terrain Ice Odyssey vehicles — also known as “Fat Trucks” —are built to traverse the Athabasca Glacier at the icefield, which straddles the Alberta-British Columbia boundary.

The investigation has been handed over to Alberta’s Occupational Health and Safety department.

Pursuit cancelled tours, but said they would resume Thursday but said Ice Odyssey tours will remain unavailable until September 8, at the earliest.

“We are gathering facts about the incident and carefully reviewing the circumstances with the applicable authorities. We will not speculate about the cause while that work is underway,” Back said.

Affected customers were offered refunds for their glacier tours or the opportunity to rebook, it added.

The Columbia Icefield Skywalk, which operates separately from the glacier experience, remains open.

Back in 2020, three people died and 14 were seriously injured when a different vehicle, an Ice Explorer bus, lost control and rolled in what a judge later determined to be caused by a “catastrophic braking issue.”

CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 11:01 AM | Last Updated: 4 hours ago

Thousands left without power in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties

A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.

Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.

Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines , according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.

Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.

The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.

A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.

It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.

Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."

One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.

"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.

The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.

Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.

People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.

The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.

The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.

It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.

A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the

Middlesex-London Health Unit website .

There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.

It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.

Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

stories.title: 20.2% property tax increase required if Calgary funds all 2027 budget requests
stories.summary: The figures were included in a number of confidential, preliminary budget documents obtained by Global News after being presented to Calgary city council earlier this summer.
stories.author: Adam MacVicar
stories.content:
Preliminary budget documents obtained by Global News show the slew of funding requests from city departments under consideration by Calgary city council could result in a significant, double-digit property tax increase next year.

The confidential documents, which were presented to city council during a closed session meeting on July 28, indicate property tax revenue would need to increase by 20.2 per cent in 2027 to fund an additional $510 million in operating spending required to cover a number of budget requests from various city departments and partners.

Those funding requests, if approved, would also result in hikes over the ensuing years: 8.5 per cent property tax increase in 2028, a nine per cent increase in 2029 and an 8.9 per cent increase in 2030; the final year of this council’s four-year budget.

It remains unclear how significant an impact those property tax increases could have on monthly bills.

“It is important to recognize the significant gap between funding requests and available funding,” administration said in a cover report as part of the preliminary budget documents.

According to a slide deck presented to council during the closed session, the city has additional funding capacity of just $139 million for the various budget requests without the need to increase property taxes in 2027.

However, property taxes would need to rise 5.4 per cent next year just to maintain services.

2:01 Questions over property taxes as City of Calgary officials craft next 4-year budget

Council spent much of the July 28 meeting reviewing more than 107 requests for funding increases from various departments, including Calgary Transit, Mobility, the Calgary Fire Department and the Calgary Police Service.

Get expert insights, Q&A on markets, housing, inflation, and personal finance information delivered to you every Saturday.

The report warned there is “a high likelihood” that funding requests will continue to exceed available financial capacity “if not sufficiently addressed through prioritization, scaling or reducing requests.”

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas told reporters Wednesday it was premature to speculate what the property tax increase will be and any figures “floating around” would be the total of all the requests in front of council.

“We’re going to consider everybody’s asks, but we’re going to be funnling that down specifically for essential infrastructure, specifically for public safety, and the investments to be able to catch up particularly in those areas that will save money in the long run,” Farkas said.

“Just because you ask for something, doesn’t mean you get it.”

Global News has learned city councillors were provided workbooks to rank and prioritize the budget requests in front of them, in which many aren’t expected to make it into the finalized four-year spending plan.

City councillors have already directed administration to refine the preliminary property tax increases after a narrow 8-7 vote following the July 28 meeting.

1:59 Affordability remains top of mind for many Calgarians

Although the council direction was confidential, it was included in the slew of documents obtained by Global News.

As part of that direction, administration will brief council on an updated review of the four-year budget that proposes a 15 per cent property tax increase next year, followed by a 12.5 per cent increase in 2028, a nine per cent jump in 2029 and a six per cent increase in 2030.

Couns. Rob Ward, Landon Johnston, Mike Jamieson, Dan McLean, Andre Chabot, Kim Tyers and Jennifer Wyness voted against.

Johnston, who represents Ward 14, told Global News he believes city council will need to cut up to $300 million from the preliminary spending to deliver a property tax increase Calgarians would deem acceptable.

“We’re always asking taxpayers to tighten the belt, now is the time for council to tighten the belt,” he said.

“There’s going to be some tough choices, but as long as we fund our police, fund our fire, fund our roads, fund our water, Calgarians will be happy with that.”

In a statement to Global News, a city spokesperson said work continues on the four-year budget with a focus on “the services and infrastructure Calgarians expect and rely on every day.

“Council provided funding guidance that administration requires to refine and prioritize budget requests that help form the creation of the budget document,” the statement read.

“These are not approved or final numbers and do not represent the tax change on an individual property owner.”

Spending on infrastructure is also expected to be cornerstone of the upcoming four-year budget, with the preliminary documents indicating around $21 billion in capital spending needs between next year and 2030.

“At present, known financial capacity does not exist to fund all needs,” the confidential report warned, with $13 billion of net new financial capacity for capital infrastructure spending.

The report notes that figure is “approximately three times” the financial capacity for new infrastructure spending in the previous four-year budget.

Following further refinements in September, the proposed four-year budget is expected to be released to the public on Nov. 10, with budget deliberations to begin on Nov. 23.

stories.title: Lambton County alerts staff to prepare for arrival of AI data centres
stories.summary: The mayor of Sarnia is pushing Lambton County to set a clear platform for the anticipated arrival of AI Data Centres.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
The mayor of Sarnia is pushing Lambton County to set a clear platform for the anticipated arrival of AI Data Centres.

“Right now, we’re flying blind, without radar,” said Mike Bradley in an interview with CTV News London.

Bradley is calling for staff to review the potential impact of data centres on water, power, the environment and municipal infrastructure.

On the other side of the coin, he wants a better understanding of how the centres could create, and potentially cost jobs.

“And I think that’s why we’re all grappling with jobs versus the other impacts that could actually cut jobs in our communities. That’s what this is all about, just let’s understand what we’re dealing with, which is a difficult question,” he conceded.

Lambton County is already part of the rapidly evolving data centre push, including an AI advanced manufacturing education site at Lambton College.

Additionally, this past spring, MPP Bob Bailey was quoted in various local media suggesting that representatives from a data centre had reached out to him directly.

But with large volumes of water, and several hundred megawatts of power needed to supply a large data centre, opposition exists.

Aerial of data centre Aerial of data centre. (file)

However, at the county council level, Bradley’s motion received unanimous support without comment.

“And I’m not arguing the merits either way,” he stated. “I just think we need a better understanding of what we can do, what we should do, and what we shouldn’t do.”

There are examples for Lambton County to look to across the country.

In one case, Bell Canada Enterprises (BCE), the owner of CTV, is preparing to build a $1.7 billion data centre in Saskatchewan.

BCE contends it will generate $12 billion in economic value and create more 1600 permanent, construction and spinoff jobs.

Yet, the project faces opposition from environmentalists and nearby residents.

It is a scenario likely to repeat in Lambton once a data centre is announced, but Bradley argues having a plan will give Lambton the edge.

“We May be innovative and do some different things that others are not doing with AI data centres. It’s evolving very quickly, this part of the economy.”

Council has directed staff to have the report completed by early 2027.

stories.title: Ontario student accused in U.S. of taking airport photos for Chinese official
stories.summary: Chris Mathers, a former RCMP officer who runs a private crime and risk consulting firm, said it's common practice for Chinese state security to try to recruit people online.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
An Ontario university student has been arrested in the United States after allegedly taking photos at two airports at the request of someone he believed to be a Chinese government official.

In an affidavit filed in Michigan court, an FBI agent said Weiheng Zeng, a Chinese citizen studying at the University of Waterloo, was initially flagged by authorities in connection with an incident at Chicago’s O’Hare airport in April.

The agent said a man was seen taking photos, climbing a forklift and trying to open locked trailers at a FedEx facility at the airport on April 21, about 10 days after Zeng drove into the U.S. via the Ambassador Bridge.

Zeng was later linked to a car that was at the facility during the incident, a dark blue minivan with Ontario licence plates, the affidavit said.

When Zeng tried to drive into the U.S. again with the same minivan on Aug. 23, the student was pulled aside for a series of interviews first with border agents and later with the FBI in its counter-intelligence investigation.

Zeng gave conflicting accounts over the course of the interviews, the agent said. The document said he has been charged with making false statements.

At first, Zeng gave few details about his trip to Chicago in April, saying only that he took photos of planes, the affidavit said. He had told customs officers at the time that he was going to visit his sister, it said.

When agents reviewed his phone, they found multiple photos of aircraft and military planes, as well as photos of Zeng and others in tactical clothes holding rifle-style firearms, the court document said.

Zeng said he took photos of model aircraft for a flight radar website, and that the guns in the photos were airsoft guns, which shoot pellets rather than bullets, the agent said. He also denied having any kind of military training.

During a second interview with border agents, Zeng said he took photos of planes landing at O’Hare from a public parking lot, the affidavit said. Later, he said he went to a FedEx facility and climbed a forklift to take pictures.

The university student said he had also previously trespassed at a FedEx facility at Toronto’s Pearson airport but had been caught, the agent said.

In a third interview, Zeng said a Chinese contact had reached out to him on a website for aviation spotters and assigned him specific planes to photograph, giving him the planes’ tail numbers and paying $20 to $30 per photo, it said.

He told border agents the Chinese contact mailed him SIM cards to use for their communications. Zeng said he would later destroy the SIM cards and delete the conversations as well as the photos, the agent said.

He admitted he’d gone to O’Hare to take photos of American planes for the Chinese contact, who he suspected was connected to the Chinese Communist Party, the agent said.

Zeng’s story continued evolve during his interview with the FBI, according to the affidavit.

The Chinese contact was an aviation enthusiast who was interested in photos of rare planes for “research,” Zeng allegedly told the FBI.

Zeng said he took photos of a specific American United plane at O’Hare in April because it had a temporary paint job that made photos “highly desired,” and went to the FedEx facility to take photos of an MD11 that was rare due to its age, the agent said.

After more questioning, however, Zeng admitted he wasn’t taking photos of specific planes, the agent alleged. Rather, that was the cover story provided by the Chinese contact, who was actually interested in information on transportation logistics and wanted photos of particular locations around airports, the affidavit said.

Zeng also told the FBI the Chinese contact had sent him a photo of a badge as well as videos of scenes that only security officials could access, then used a function to recall the messages, the document said.

The Chinese contact asked Zeng for “help” after the pair had been messaging daily for three months starting in October or November 2024, the student allegedly told the FBI. Zeng said he agreed because he thought it was “cool,” the affidavit said.

Zeng said he received a new SIM card every few months and destroyed the previous one, the document said. He added he would send the photos through the phone and then delete them, and got paid through transfers to a Bank of China account, it said. He never took the phone with him to the U.S.

Though he was asked to go to locations in Orlando and Las Vegas, Zeng told the FBI he only accepted the O’Hare and Pearson assignments, the document said. He was only able to take photos of the exterior of the FedEx facility at Pearson, it said.

When FBI agents looked into the forum where Zeng said he’d met the Chinese contact, they found it didn’t exist, the agent said.

The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

Chris Mathers, a former RCMP officer who now runs a private crime and risk consulting firm in Toronto, said it’s common practice for Chinese state security to try to recruit people online.

“They cruise around these online forums and … try and attract individuals that might be able to do some work for them,” he said.

The kinds of assignments described in the court document sound like a test run to see whether someone can be cultivated as a source, Mathers said.

As for the information allegedly collected, while basic, it could nonetheless be valuable in light of tensions between China and the U.S. over Taiwan, he said.

The Americans May not have the logistical capability to get more equipment to Taiwan at the moment given their involvement in the Middle East and would likely have to use civilian transport on some occasions, he said.

Knowing more about the baseline situation at freight facilities might help government officials detect any unusual movement of equipment, Mathers added.

“The Chinese technique of intelligence gathering is to hoover up everything. Train schedules, phone books, a restaurant menu — they just hoover it all up and then they parse through it and pick out what might be of value now or in the future,” he said.

“It’s rather nebulous, obviously, but that’s just the espionage world.”

stories.title: Invading Canada would be ‘preposterous,’ U.S. commander says at Indo-Pacific military meeting
stories.summary: Admiral Samuel Paparo dismissed question about hypothetical military action but added, ‘I follow the orders of the president’
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
The commander of the United States Indo-Pacific Command dismissed a question about whether he would obey orders to launch military action against Canada, saying the country is a close ally and the scenario was “preposterous.”

The commander, Admiral Samuel Paparo, sputtered with disbelief while responding to the question from a reporter Wednesday morning in Victoria, where a conference of the chiefs of defence for the Indo-Pacific moved into its third and final day.

The question was “needlessly emotional,” Adm. Paparo said, but he added, “I follow the orders of the president.”

“Will you ask me, please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?” he said.

Standing beside him unflinchingly at the press conference was General Jennie Carignan, chief of defence staff for Canada, who reiterated her point made earlier this week about the separation between Canada and the U.S.’s military-to-military relationship, versus its political relationship, especially in the context of the conference.

“We are really here to have the conversation that needs to be had on Indo-Pacific security,” she said.

The two senior military officials are this year’s co-hosts for the annual conference that’s held in rotating locations across the Indo-Pacific. The 2026 edition brought together 29 countries to discuss topics such as multilateral co-operation, artificial intelligence and defence industrial bases.

Adm. Paparo called Canada an “indispensable partner,” highlighting the two countries’ collaboration in the Indo-Pacific and through North American Aerospace Defense Command.

He added, ON the topic of defence procurement, that “there’s no demand on the United States’ part that Canada procures U.S. equipment.” It’s a sovereign decision for Canada, he said.

However, Adm. Paparo’s remarks come after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down last month, with reports of the U.S. pressuring Canada to follow through on its purchase of American fighter jets as part of negotiations.

Adm. Paparo maintained that militaries across the Indo-Pacific are “designed to remain apolitical and ruthlessly focused on the facts of the geography.”

The deterrence of conflict in the region has been a theme at this year’s conference. Gen. Carignan said Canada’s persistent presence in the Indo-Pacific region is a growing priority for the country, with the goal of promoting deterrence. “If we are not present, then there can be miscalculation as part of being away from the theatre.”

A delegation from China was also in attendance at the event this year. Prime Minister Mark Carney formed a new strategic partnership between Canada and China earlier this year during the first visit to the country by a Canadian prime minister since 2017.

Gen. Carignan said she didn’t have any bilateral meetings planned with China at the conference but pending further conversations, that could change.

“There is a clear demand from the government to recalibrate and realign our relationship with China,” she said in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the military committee for the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, also attended the conference in Victoria, where he said he met with officials from several countries including India, China, Singapore and Sri Lanka.

Prior to his meeting with General Yang Zhibin, China’s commander of the eastern theatre, he told The Globe he planned to emphasize that Nato was not at the conference to assert its presence, but rather to have an open dialogue about confrontation in the region.

Nato currently has four Indo-Pacific partners: Australia, Japan, the Republic of Korea and New Zealand. Adm. Cavo Dragone said no other countries in the region have requested partnership status at this time but they are welcome to do so.

Canada has taken several steps over the past few years to increase its own work within the Indo-Pacific, including the release of a region-specific strategy in 2022 and the appointment of an inaugural senior military representative to the Indo-Pacific earlier this year.

Lieutenant-General Derek Macaulay has been busy the past few months after stepping into this new role, meeting with other senior military leaders and defence officials in countries such as Japan, New Zealand, Australia, Vietnam and Malaysia. He said Canada’s contribution to the region goes well beyond military equipment and into other efforts such as training.

“It’s not just about ships. It’s not about just planes. It’s about training to a point of English lessons, from a military perspective,” Lt.-Gen. Macaulay said.

The three-day conference concludes Wednesday, and a separate defence industry event is planned for Thursday, Gen. Carignan said, to “highlight Canadian industrial strength, encourage international partnership and reinforce our collective efforts to transform innovation into warfighting advantage.”

stories.title: Turtles to be released into wild in Exeter Thursday
stories.summary: Tiny turtles will be released into the wild near Exeter Thursday. The 11th annual turtle release event happens Thursday, Sept. 3 at the Morrison Dam Conservation Area, east of Exeter.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Turtle release event in Exeter in August 2024. (Scott Miller/CTV News London)

Tiny turtles will be released into the wild near Exeter Thursday.

The 11th annual turtle release event happens Thursday, Sept. 3 at the Morrison Dam Conservation Area, east of Exeter.

Turtle hatchlings will be released into the Morrison Dam every 20 minutes, from 1:20 p.m. to 4 p.m.

Hundreds turn out each year to witness the event, and learn more about turtles who aren’t yet endangered, but face many threats largely from humans.

Turtle release event Exeter Turtle release event in Exeter in August 2024. (Scott Miller/CTV News London)

Staff collected the turtle eggs at the water’s edge earlier this summer. Many of them wouldn’t survive without saving the eggs, organizers said.

The event is organized by the Ausable Bayfield Conservation Authority and the Huron Stewardship Council.

Organizers say people can help turtles by creating and enhancing habitat on their properties, helping turtles cross the road in the direction they are heading, when it is safe to do so, and working with their local municipalities and communities to erect turtle crossing signs and build safe passages.

stories.title: Tornado watch issued for London and eastern Middlesex County as severe storm approaches
stories.summary: Tornado watch issued for London and eastern Middlesex County as severe storm approaches CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 11:01 AM | Last Updated: 10 hours ago
Thousands left without power in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties
A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.
Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.
Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines , according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.
Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.
The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.
A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.
It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.
Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."
One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.
"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.
The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.
Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.
People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.
The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.
The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.
It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.
A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the
Middlesex-London Health Unit website .
There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.
It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.
Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

stories.title: Man convicted of manslaughter, not murder, in Vancouver Starbucks stabbing
stories.summary: Vancouver - A man has been found guilty of manslaughter but not guilty of murder in the killing outside a Vancouver coffee shop of a father who was pushing his daughter in a stroller just before he was stabbed to death.
stories.author: Ashley Joannou The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A man has been found guilty of manslaughter but cleared of murder in the 2023 stabbing outside a Vancouver coffee shop of a father who whose death was captured on video and shared widely online.

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Kathleen Ker told a courtroom Wednesday that after looking at the cumulative factors that contributed to the death of Paul Schmidt outside the Starbucks where he was stabbed six times, she could not be certain that Inderdeep Singh Gosal had the intent required for a second-degree murder conviction.

stories.title: London area under tornado watch, winds could top 110 km/h
stories.summary: Environment Canada warns of possible large hail, torrential downpours and significant damage.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
More than 1,000 London Hydro customers lost power Wednesday evening as branches came down on power lines and a fallen tree blocked Empress Avenue amid severe weather across the region.

London Hydro said 1,083 customers in central and west London were affected by the outage. The utility said branches on a power line were causing the outage, while more of the same tree had fallen and was blocking Empress Avenue.

Crews were on site and London Hydro asked people to avoid the area while work continued to restore power.

The utility initially estimated power would be restored by 12:30 a.m. Thursday, but later moved that estimate up to 10:30 p.m. Wednesday.

London Hydro advised motorists to treat affected traffic lights as four-way stops.

By 6:54 p.m., Environment Canada had London, Parkhill and eastern Middlesex County under a yellow-level severe thunderstorm watch, warning of strong wind gusts up to 90 km/h, nickel- to toonie-sized hail and torrential downpours.

The agency said thunderstorms could persist through Wednesday night into Thursday morning, potentially bringing a significant rainfall threat.

“Local utility outages are possible. Damage to roofs, fences, branches or soft shelters is possible. There is a risk of injury,” Environment Canada said in the alert.
