stories.title: Apple changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for U.S. users of Maps app
stories.summary: Google rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order
stories.author: Shannon Proudfoot
stories.content:
Apple Aapl-Q has relabelled Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for U.S. users of its Maps app, following competitor Google days after President Donald Trump ordered a new name for the body of water amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

As of Wednesday morning, Apple Maps displayed “Lake America” for U.S. users looking at the lake that sits between the state of New York and Canada’s Ontario province. Users outside of the U.S. still saw the Lake Ontario name.

Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Earlier this week, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told Fox that Trump had reached out to the company “directly” about the change.

Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

The President declared the new “Lake America” name last week — marking one of the latest provocations during his trade war with Canada that is now hiking tariffs on both sides of the border. His executive order on Friday directed the Interior Department to update the lake’s name in the U.S. geographic naming service.

Google Maps rolled out the change over the weekend, citing Trump’s order and its already-established practice of using names assigned by the U.S. Geographic Names Information System (or Gnis).

“People using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement on Saturday, reiterating that such updates “follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

Trump cannot force Canada to also change the name of Lake Ontario. And America’s northern neighbors quickly panned the idea.

“It’s Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever,” Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media Friday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also rejected the move last week, invoking the lake’s Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both the Canadian Confederation and U.S. Declaration of Independence.

This isn’t the first time Trump has moved to rename water spanning beyond U.S. borders. Last year, Trump ordered that the Gulf of Mexico be renamed the Gulf of America — and both Apple and Google later updated the name on their maps in the U.S.

But not all map providers have followed suit. MapQuest, in particular, has declared it won’t be changing Lake Ontario’s label — and gave users the option to name the lake “whatever you want” through a separate online tool. Both the Lake Ontario and Gulf of Mexico names still appear as default on its platform.

MapQuest, owned by California company System1, has reported a surge of downloads recently. On Wednesday, MapQuest topped the charts of free apps with new downloads in both the U.S. and Canada on Apple’s App Store.

stories.title: Carney's 'hydronym' moment is behind a cheeky campaign to raise awareness about Lake Ontario
stories.summary: Carney's 'hydronym' moment is behind a cheeky campaign to raise awareness about Lake Ontario CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: 21 hours ago
Proceeds from apparel sales to support awareness, environmental advocacy for Great Lake
A new fundraising campaign builds off Prime Minister Mark Carney's use of the word "hydronym" to raise awareness and environmental protections for Lake Ontario.

London, Ont., apparel company Branded By Collins has created T-shirts emblazoned with the phrase, "My hydronyms are Lake & Ontario." A portion of the sales proceeds go to Swim Drink Fish Canada, a Toronto-based, national charity that connects people with the lake, and works to keep it safe and clean.
"This is an opportunity where for the first time in a generation, we're seeing people talk about Lake Ontario and take pride in it," said Gregary Ford, the charity's vice-president and waterkeeper.

The idea came about after U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America, as the two countries traded social media jabs over trade talks that broke down last month.

Carney responded to Trump's renaming idea with a social media statement , which read in part, "We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always."

Hydronym is the proper name for a body of water. The internet was abuzz with Carney's use of the word. Many people, including Swim Drink Fish Canada's Ford, who lives in Dundas in Hamilton on the lake's Western tip, admitted they had to search for its meaning.

"I did have to look it up just with everybody else, and I'm a bit embarrassed to admit that because I work in water," he said. "But it is a beautiful and wonderfully nerdy word that I think captured people's attention to the idea of a name and what it represents."

Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is between Ontario and New York. Its name comes from the Huron-Wendat word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters." The province, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Carney said on social media that the name is more than 400 years old, and predates Canada and the U.S. as countries.
Political leaders in both countries have condemned Trump's executive order.
On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a sign in Winona that said "Lake Ontario, now and always." Some U.S. politicians, both Republicans and Democrats, have also denounced the renaming.
Branded By Collins created the T-shirts after the public relations firm Curious Public reached out to managing partner Steve Ryall with the idea.

"Funny enough, I was riding a bicycle in Toronto, going right by Lake Ontario, when I got the phone call, so it was interesting timing," Ryall said. "It's fun to be a part of something like this. We’re definitely proud Canadians, so we're excited to support the initiative."
He said the majority of the company's customers are in Canada, so it hasn't directly been impacted by U.S. tariffs, but added that many people buying the products have been affected.

"Everybody's affected by it one way or another. And so hopefully [the trade situation] goes well for everybody involved, and things settle down between the two countries soon because I think it's an important relationship on so many levels."

"hydronym" campaign started out with just hats, but has since grown to T-shirts, sweaters and hoodies that come in black, red and white. Ten dollars from the sale of each item, ranging from $30 to $50, go to the non-profit. Its efforts include sharing real-time water quality data and advocating for the lake.
Gregary Ford said he works closely with the

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the New York State Department of Environment and Conservation. He admitted an executive order makes things challenging on a day-to-day basis because U.S. federal employees have to refer to it as Lake America, but he said has received support from his American counterparts.

However, Ford said, the tensions have reignited Canadian pride and more people are interested in learning about the lake's Indigenous origins, its connection to the other Great Lakes and how Lake Ontario can better be protected.

"This is obviously a deflection from trade negotiations and ongoing discourse between federal leaders on both sides of the border, but it's also an opportunity to feel proud about our heritage in water and our history with Indigenous place naming," said Ford.
"People are learning more not just about new terms like hydronyms, but also new concepts and ways of bettering our relationship with the lake that is in our backyard."
Ford said the lake is under stress from a variety of sources, including climate change, invasive species, microplastics and others, so this campaign is one way to encourage action.

Ford said the lake is under stress from a variety of sources, including climate change, invasive species, microplastics and others, so this campaign is one way to encourage action.

stories.title: Couche-Tard reports slowing U.S. sales growth as it pushes ahead with takeover of Poland’s Zabka
stories.summary: ‘Progress in a business like ours is measured over years, not quarters,’ CEO Alex Miller told analysts on a call
stories.author: Nicolas Van Praet
stories.content:
Canadian convenience store operator Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. ATD-T tallied a fifth straight quarter of same-store sales growth in the United States over the summer, maintaining positive momentum in its biggest market as it works to expand its footprint in Europe with an US$8.7-billion deal for Polish retailer Zabka Group SA.

The Laval, Que.-based company, which owns the Circle K chain, on Tuesday published results for the first quarter of the company’s fiscal 2027, which ended July 19. It included a 1.7-per-cent year-over-year increase in merchandise sales at comparable U.S. stores. Energy drinks and nicotine products performed particularly well, and the company is taking market share from rivals in key segments, it said.

The sales increase in the U.S. wasn’t as strong as in previous quarters. Analysts had warned that a sequential slowdown was coming based on the recent performance of some competitors, such as ARKO and Murphy USA.

“Progress in a business like ours is measured over years, not quarters,” Couche-Tard chief executive officer Alex Miller told analysts on a call Wednesday morning. “We’re encouraged by the start to fiscal 2027, and we’re seeing evidence that our strategy is resonating with customers and strengthening the business.”

Over all, net profit came in at US$828.5-million or US$0.90 per diluted share on total revenue of US$21.7-billion for the period, improving on the US$782.5-million during the same quarter last year, Couche-Tard said in a release after market close. The company reports in U.S. dollars.

On an adjusted basis, net earnings were US$827-million or US$0.90 per share. That’s roughly in line with the US$0.89 analysts were expecting. The company sold less gasoline over all but boosted its fuel gross margin in the U.S. and Canada.

After a solid trajectory of profit growth over the past two decades, Couche-Tard’s business has come under pressure more recently as consumers slash their spending to deal with higher levels of debt as well as inflation. Global conflict, including in the Middle East, has added to those worries and industry observers are analyzing whether it will lead to any lasting change in consumer behaviour.

Mr. Miller and his team are trying to make Circle K’s offerings more attractive in response, launching meal deals priced from US$3 to US$6 in the United States and offering rebates on gasoline on certain days in a bid to build customer loyalty. The company has said it expects it can generate year-over-year adjusted earnings-per-share growth of 10 per cent or more from fiscal 2026 through 2030.

While the 15-per-cent EPS growth for the latest quarter is higher than that, the deceleration of U.S. merchandise same-store sales growth “may raise questions” about the health of the American consumer, Stifel analyst Martin Landry said in a research note. Still, the company is outperforming many of its rivals in this environment, according to Desjardins analyst Chris Li.

Mr. Miller said consumers continue to spend but they’re being more targeted and intentional in their spending choices. One big change is that items located in the centre of stores, such as salty snacks, are falling in popularity, a fact Mr. Miller attributes in part to the growth of GLP-1 weight management drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy.

Couche-Tard announced in late July that it is making a multibillion-dollar takeover play for Poland’s Zabka, widening its footprint in Europe with a major push in one of the continent’s fastest-growing economies. Owners of about 57 per cent of Zabka stock are backing the deal and have signed agreements to tender their shares, Couche-Tard said.

The purchase still needs approval by European, Polish and Romanian regulators, including clearance by the European Commission under the European Union’s Foreign Subsidies Regulation.

It would be the Canadian company’s biggest acquisition to date, further cementing its position in a key part of the world against global rival 7-Eleven. It would also be a unique acquisition as Couche-Tard takes control of a dominant, technology-powered retailer that could transform the way Circle K operates in other countries. Couche-Tard could scale up Zabka’s AI-driven shopping application, for example, or use Zabka’s experience with cashier-less stores to roll out more autonomous sites in North America.

Couche-Tard has since launched a voluntary tender offer for Zabka at a price of 32 Polish zloty or about US$8.48 a share. That’s a premium of about 9.4 per cent from Zabka’s closing stock price the day before the offer was announced.

Analyst Janusz Pieta at mBank is among those who have argued that Couche-Tard’s offer is too low, raising the possibility that there could be shareholder pressure for better terms. But Couche-Tard’s chief financial officer Filipe Da Silva told The Globe and Mail it’s “already very attractive.”

stories.title: Bank of Canada holds key rate at 2.25 per cent once again
stories.summary: Monetary policymakers at the Bank of Canada use the policy rate to keep a lid on inflation and support economic growth when prices are contained.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

The Bank of Canada held its benchmark interest rate steady again on Wednesday as new U.S. tariffs and the ongoing war in Iran cloud the central bank’s outlook.

The Bank of Canada’s policy rate remains at 2.25 per cent after a seventh straight hold. The move was widely expected by economists.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said in prepared remarks that the persistence of the Middle East conflict has increased inflationary risks as global energy prices continue to float higher.

A re-escalation in the trade dispute with the United States meanwhile threatens Canada’s burgeoning economic rebound, he said. That renewed uncertainty might lead businesses to delay investment and hiring decisions until the trade picture crystalizes.

“Monetary policy cannot offset the effects of tariffs or influence global energy prices. What we can do is ensure global developments don’t jeopardize price stability in Canada,” Macklem said.

Monetary policymakers at the Bank of Canada use the policy rate to keep a lid on inflation and support economic growth when prices are contained.

Inflation rose to three per cent in July after the Iran war drove a volatile period for gas prices over the spring and summer.

Economic growth, meanwhile, has shown signs of rebounding after stagnating for much of the last year. The economy surged with 3.3 per cent annualized growth in the second quarter, though few analysts expect that same pace continued into the current quarter.

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods on Aug. 22. Macklem said the Bank of Canada doesn’t expect a “large direct impact” on the economy from the new duties, though targeted sectors could be hit hard.

Canada is planning a slate of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods starting Sept. 8.

Heading into the latest wave of tariffs, Macklem said exports were on the rise and there were signs businesses were adapting to trade restrictions.

“Overall, the data reaffirm our view of a broadening recovery,” he said.

Because the economy was evolving broadly in line with the bank’s forecasts, governing council opted to keep the policy rate unchanged, Macklem said.

But he said there could be future adjustments depending on where the economy and inflation go from here.

“Governing council will assess the sustainability of the economic rebound and the outlook for inflation, and is prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed,” Macklem said.

stories.title: American cruise ship passengers visiting Canada offer their views on the trade war
stories.summary: Two massive cruise ships were docked in Halifax Harbour on Tuesday - the Holland America Line’s Zuiderdam and Princess Cruises’ Sapphire Princess. Both vessels delivered thousands of Americans to the Nova Scotia capital for a brief visit.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Two massive cruise ships were docked in Halifax Harbour on Tuesday -- the Holland America Line’s Zuiderdam and Princess Cruises’ Sapphire Princess. Both vessels delivered thousands of Americans to the Nova Scotia capital for a brief visit.

“It is nice, very nice,” said Gary Charland from Palm Springs, Calif., who admitted the trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. were on his mind as he prepared for his trip to Canada. “It is difficult to tune it out.”

Some American tourists, citing the sensitivity of the trade war, preferred not to give their names for privacy purposes.

One tourist visiting from Colorado said she was a repeat customer. The trade war did not alter her vacation plans nor dampen her enthusiasm for her neighbours to the north.

“I like Canada, I especially like Halifax and I guess all of the gobbledygook doesn’t really seem to bother me,” she said, as she referred to the recent cross-border dialogue surrounding tariffs.

As for who is to blame for the tariff tensions between the two countries, a tourist from Florida pointed the finger at Canada, a country he said has protectionist tariffs that are bad for his home country’s economy.

“It is the same as what’s been going on the other way,” he said. “It’s OK if the Canadians charge tariffs, but it’s not OK if the Americans do?”

A woman from Nevada came here to see the sites and enjoy our country’s temperatures.

“It is 30 degrees cooler here, which is a big bonus, there is a lot of natural beauty in Canada, and you cannot just deny the majesty of creation when you’re in this area,” she said.

Her husband also had a blunt message for both the U.S. president and the Canadian prime minister.

“Those guys need to chill out,” he said.

It should be noted that most Americans interviewed by CTV News gushed about how much they like Canada and Canadians.

“We very much enjoy coming to Canada,” said Charland. “We very much feel that Canadians are not only our neighbours, but also our partners.”

That’s a common opinion, according to Halifax-based tourism operator Sean Buckland, who pointed out American visitation is up this year in Halifax by roughly 13 per cent, largely because of two factors.

“There is no question that Americans are taking advantage of the exchange rate and the increased value of the American dollar,” said Buckland, who is the owner and CEO of Ambassatours Gray Line tour company. “And the hospitality because we hear time and time again what a welcoming city and destination, we are.”

A steady influx of American visitors coming to Canada comes at a time when Canadians are choosing to avoid travelling to the U.S.in increasing numbers because of their displeasure over the ongoing trade tensions.

Charles Bartholomew, also from Palm Springs, used his visit to Halifax to urge Canadians to give his country a second chance.

“Canadians are very welcome and we want them to come back,” said Bartholomew.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting survivors sue OpenAI, alleging negligence
stories.summary: Lawsuits name CEO Sam Altman and allege the company withheld potentially life-saving information about the shooter’s violent chat history
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
A U.S. law firm representing survivors of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is filing 30 lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging the tech giant was negligent in not reporting the shooter’s chat history to police in an effort to help prevent the attack.

Three new lawsuits, filed Wednesday in U.S. federal court in California, name OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and accuse the company of having a double standard when it comes to safety. The firm intends to file 30 in total.

The suits, one for each plaintiff, allege the company notified law enforcement immediately about threats against its own staff but allegedly withheld potentially life-saving information about the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s violent chat history before the shooting.

The suits also allege ChatGPT was allowed to continue chats with users on violent subjects in order to boost engagement, which allegedly facilitated the chats that allowed the shooter to plan her attack.

Jesse Van Rootselaar, 18, killed eight people in the northern B.C. community in February before killing herself in one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. Before entering the town’s school, she killed her mother and 11-year-old half-brother in their family home.

The 30 new lawsuits add to seven others launched in April on behalf of victims who were killed. The new lawsuits claim the company knew the shooter posed a significant threat, but allegedly avoided alerting police before the attack because doing so would force the company to create an internal system for reporting other violent users to the authorities.

That, in turn, the lawsuits allege, would expose the threat its signature product routinely poses to human life, which could complicate a coming initial public offering that could be worth a trillion dollars.

The allegations have not been proven in court.

Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer for the plaintiffs, said it’s critical these cases get to a trial quickly because that could force the company to reveal the conversations the shooter had with ChatGPT, which he alleged would show how dangerous the chatbot can be.

“These cases have to get to a jury soon, not just for our clients but for public safety,” Mr. Edelson said.

In an e-mailed statement, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, disputed the claims, saying the company’s intelligence and investigations team members, who report to him, work diligently to balance public safety with user privacy in what can be “really difficult and complex situations.”

“That judgement is not infallible, but it is always rooted in looking out for this balance for people,” Mr. Kwon’s statement said.

“It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the centre of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.”

The plaintiffs in the new lawsuits include one student who survived after being shot in the chest, and 29 other students and school staff who witnessed the violence at close range.

One of them is a 13-year-old boy identified as A.C., who, after watching the shooter kill his classmates and shoot a teacher in the face, survived by pretending to be dead among the bodies of his murdered classmates, the statement of claim says.

Another is Deidre Rushlow, a Grade 7 teacher who locked her classroom door and hid students under her desk. The shooter then circled around to the back door and fired into the classroom. Bullets struck the wall around Ms. Rushlow’s and her students’ heads, according to the statement of claim.

Mr. Edelson said interviewing so many survivors drove home for him the deep emotional crater the attack has left on the small northern mining community. “They watched their fellow students get shot at and, in some cases, die in front of them. It basically was a scene out of a war.”

According to the statements of claim, OpenAI has two different threat analysis and security teams. The intelligence and investigations team, the lawsuits claim, is responsible for reviewing and assessing automatically flagged user content and developing responses, up to and including notifying law enforcement about potential threats to public safety.

That team reports to the company’s Global Affairs team, the lawsuits allege, which is responsible for managing the company’s public reputation, including deciding when to issue notices about potential threats from ChatGPT users.

The lawsuits allege Global Affairs stymied the intelligence and investigation team’s requests to notify law enforcement about the Tumbler Ridge shooter’s violent ChatGPT history.

According to the lawsuits, a second internal group – the corporate security team – handles threats made against OpenAI staff and has the power to act on safety and security threats immediately, without considering reputational repercussions.

The lawsuits allege that’s what OpenAI did in November, 2025, when it learned of an individual who had “expressed interest in physically harming” its employees.

The corporate security team immediately notified San Francisco police, warned employees and locked down offices, despite there being no imminent threat, the lawsuits allege.

OpenAI did not respond to The Globe and Mail’s questions about its corporate security team or the alleged November incident.

San Francisco Police did not confirm whether it received any reports about threats to OpenAI staff last November.

While it has historically been challenging to bring lawsuits against tech companies such as OpenAI, Mr. Edelson said the legal landscape is shifting, pointing to the US$17-billion settlement Meta agreed to last week over claims brought against it by numerous U.S. states that its social media products are addictive and unsafe, allegations Meta denied.

“I think that [these cases] would have been really challenging to bring 10 years ago, but the law is a lot clearer now,” Mr. Edelson said.

stories.title: Cost of living, fuel has Couche-Tard customers cutting back on snacks
stories.summary: The convenience store chain's chief executive Alex Miller says shoppers are being more deliberate about their purchases as the cost of living and fuel rises.
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

Pocketbook pressures are encouraging some Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. customers to ditch buying snack foods.

The convenience store chain’s chief executive Alex Miller says shoppers are being more deliberate about their purchases as the cost of living and fuel rises.

He says their cautious spending is pushing sales of packaged carbonated soft drinks, salty snacks and sweets to lower-than-usual levels.

To cope with the shift in consumer behaviour, Miller says Couche-Tard is reallocating shelf space, refining its product assortment and tweaking its promotions to better suit demand.

Miller’s remarks came a day after Couche-Tard revealed its net earnings attributable to shareholders were US$828.5 million in its first quarter, up from US$782.5 million during the same period last year.

The Laval, Que.-based company, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, reported revenues of US$21.7 billion, rising from US$17.3 billion a year earlier.

stories.title: From street names to product boycotts, Canadians are severing ties with U.S. amid trade dispute
stories.summary: Trump’s latest actions have triggered a renewed surge of anger and patriotism in a country better known for being easygoing
stories.author: Maria Cheng
stories.content:
For more than 20 years, Diane Hosker has lived on Trump Avenue in Ottawa’s leafy west end, a neighbourhood with New York City -themed street names including Central Park, Bloomingdale Street and Gotham Private.

Hosker was never a fan of the name, which was chosen when U.S. President Donald Trump was known primarily as a Manhattan real estate developer. Now, amid the worsening trade war and escalating verbal threats, the city council is moving to rename it.

Trump’s latest actions– imposing new tariffs on goods from Canada and signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” – have triggered a renewed surge of anger and patriotism in a country better known for being easygoing.

Some Canadians have boycotted U.S. products and stopped travelling south of the border since Trump returned to office in early 2025, but his renewed attacks on Canada are prompting what May be a more permanent rupture between two longtime allies. From street names to supply chains to vacation bookings, Canadians are severing everyday ties in ways that could outlast the current trade dispute.

“[Trump] is just the king of chaos and destroying everything and nothing good ever comes out of this man,” Hosker told Reuters. “I just don’t like the way he makes fun of Canada,” she said, adding that she finds it embarrassing to tell people she lives on a street named after Trump.

Ottawa City Councillor Riley Brockington said he is taking steps to rename Trump Avenue, but that it could take up to a year, as it involves research, a consultation process and help for residents to adjust their documents when the change happens.

Some lighthearted suggestions, from members of the public, include Taco, a reference to “Trump Always Chickens Out,” or naming the street after former U.S. President Barack Obama.

“Street names in Canada’s capital are named after people of honor and integrity and [who] work in partnership, in this case, with Canada,” Brockington said. “[Trump] does not meet any of those standards.”

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

Amid the worsening trade war and escalating verbal threats, the Ottawa city council is moving to rename Trump Avenue in Ottawa’s leafy west end.

An Abacus Data poll released last week found that more than 70 per cent of Canadians support Prime Minister Mark Carney’s decision to suspend trade talks with the U.S., despite the likelihood of job losses and economic uncertainty. Meanwhile, a Reuters/Ipsos poll showed only 20 per cent of Americans support the tariffs on Canadian goods and even fewer agree with renaming the lake.

Some dual citizens are deepening their ties to Canada.

Sara Seager, a Canadian-American astrophysicist who left MIT, is moving to Toronto after being recruited by the University of Toronto under the Carney government’s push to attract top academics from abroad.

Seager said that when she renewed her Canadian passport she explained to the officials working there why she was moving home.

“I explained how Prime Minister Carney is giving over a billion dollars to recruit top talent from all over, but especially Canadians, to come home to help Canada become more sovereign from the U.S. in technology, trade and defence,” she said. “The amount of Canadian pride in that row of passport offices was heart-melting.”

Ashley Chapman, chief operating officer of Chapman’s Ice Cream, a family-owned Canadian company, said his company has pivoted away from using U.S. ingredients since Trump levelled the first round of tariffs against Canada last year. By mid-2027, Chapman said, the company aims to cut its use of U.S. ingredients by 70 per cent.

“We’ve got years left of Trump in power and we need to figure out how we insulate ourselves,” he said. In recent months, Chapman said the company has severed ties with nine long-standing U.S. suppliers and is sourcing ingredients like almonds and cherries from Australia and Chile.

Chapman has also pledged not to raise prices during the trade war, even if his profit margins take a hit.

“That is a price I’m willing to pay, to say that we will not be bullied and we will not be treated like this by what used to be our closest ally and friend,” he said.

Dave Samojlenko, a 53-year-old programmer in Ottawa, said he’s cancelled subscriptions to U.S. streaming services like Netflix and sworn off visiting the U.S. while Trump remains in office.

“We’re an independent nation and we should stand up for ourselves,” he said. “I haven’t travelled [to the U.S.] since this last administration came in and I probably won’t until at least they’re gone and probably long after.”

Visits to the United States declined by 10.6 per cent in the first three months of the year from a year earlier, official data shows, and spending on travel to the U.S. fell 13.6 per cent to $5-billion as domestic tourism grew.

Megan Woodward, a travel agent based in Edmonton, confirmed she had seen a further shift since the latest round of tariff threats.

“We’re not getting bookings to the U.S. anymore, and [Canadians] are very vocal about where they want to spend their money. If we recommend a U.S. vacation, a lot of people are very much against that. They want to keep their dollars in Canada or are very happy to spend them in Europe,” Woodward said.

stories.title: Federal gas tax cut extended until January 2027
stories.summary: The federal government has extended its excise tax cut on gasoline and diesel until Jan. 31, 2027, the finance minister announced.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Patricia D'Cunha

Posted September 2, 2026 9:32 am.

Last Updated September 2, 2026 2:23 pm.

The federal government has extended its excise tax cut on gasoline and diesel until Jan. 31, 2027, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced on Wednesday.

CityNews had learned earlier in the day that the federal government would be extending the gas tax break but Champagne confirmed it during a press conference in Ottawa on Wednesday afternoon.

“It’s about making life more affordable. … Many Canadians are concerned by the price of rent, the price of food [and] the price of gas,” the finance minister said.

He also said from Feb. 1 to March 31, 2027, the fuel excise tax will return to half its regular rate and then fully resume on April 1.

The tax break, which saves Canadians 10 cents per litre on regular gasoline and four cents on a litre of diesel, was set to end the day after Labour Day. However, there were calls to extend it beyond that date.

Back in April, the federal government announced a suspension of the fuel excise tax on gasoline and diesel when the war in Iran caused global fuel prices to spike.

stories.title: Maritime farmers hit by major drought last summer say they’re on the road to recovery
stories.summary: A year after a severe drought left farms hurting across the East Coast, some Maritime growers say they’re on the road to recovery.
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

A year after a severe drought left farms hurting across the East Coast, some Maritime growers say they’re on the road to recovery.

A mix of rainfall and sunny conditions across the region has helped a number of crops regain their footing, some farmers say. But there are still signs of damage from the hot and dry summer of 2025.

Danny Dill, a giant pumpkin grower and owner of Howard Dill Enterprises, in Windsor, N.S., said it’s hard to describe the severity of what happened last year.

“It was a historic drought. Never seen nothing like it in my lifetime. I’m in my 60s now, and some of the people that are in their 90s saying they’ve never seen nothing like it,” he said in a recent interview.

Scientists say climate change is responsible for more frequent and more intense storms, droughts, floods and fires. It’s a new reality that farmers like Dill may be experiencing on the ground.

Dill said last fall he had no choice but to turn away pumpkin customers due to a shortage of stock, but this year he’ll be able to accommodate all their orders.

“The pumpkins are coming on, because we’ve had some good, timely rains this year,” he said.

However, Dill said their large pumpkin varieties are smaller than they would typically be at this time of year, and he wonders if last year’s drought has played a role in that.

“Maybe it’s something to do with that drought, the moisture level in the soil,” he said.

Trevor Hadwen, an agroclimate specialist with Agriculture Canada, said last year’s drought was significant in a region that doesn’t typically experience prolonged dry conditions.

The federal department said Nova Scotia, eastern Newfoundland, southeastern New Brunswick and portions of Prince Edward Island were all under severe drought conditions last August.

“We see significant rainfall throughout the region each year, so when we look at how dry it was last year, certainly an anomaly in the climate cycle,” he said in a recent interview.

Patrick O’Neil, Executive Director of the Wild Blueberry Association of North America, which represents Canadian growers and producers, said that last year’s drought was “devastating.”

“We saw almost no rain in July and oppressive heat in New Brunswick. Some farmers weren’t even allowed to harvest during peak season because of fire bans and restrictions,” O’Neil said in a recent interview.

Wildfires also burned in Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick last summer, prompting some provincial governments to implement restrictions on activity.

In a summary of climate change impacts on farming published in 2020, Agriculture Canada said rising temperatures and extreme weather would affect the industry across the country.

It also said the Atlantic region would likely experience a range of impacts, including extended drought patterns that may put pressure on yields and water availability, as well as milder winters that could have an impact on pests and diseases. It also said the area is at risk to rising sea level, storm surges and erosion.

Scientists say that humans are contributing to climate change primarily through the burning of fossil fuels and land-use changes.

Dill said he first began to notice the impacts of climate change on his farm about 15 years ago, but over the past five years there’s been a sharp increase in extreme weather conditions, with flooding, storms, wildfires and drought.

“I knew the shift, the gradual change in the seasons, just because (I’ve) always been working with the land … But in the last five years, the dramatic weather events, there’s just no words to describe it,” he said.

It’s a shift that has caused some anxiety for Dill and other farmers in the region.

Jordan Eyamie, the manager of Webster Farms Ltd. in Cambridge, N.S., which harvests strawberries, raspberries, rhubarb and dry beans, said “morale wise, there was definitely the fear that this might happen again.”

Last year’s drought caused the loss of about 20 per cent of their yield and affected the growth and flowering of some of their plants that are producing this year, she said, but the frequent rain provided some relief.

“Watering beans is very, very expensive because it uses a lot of fuel,” she said, adding that this year they were able to rely mostly on rain to keep the beans healthy.

“I was touring the beans today and they all look pretty good,” Eyamie said.

For wild blueberries, O’Neil said the plants that are now producing experienced stress during last year’s drought, because the berries are harvested on a two-year cycle.

“The plants overall were healthy, but they just didn’t grow out around the outskirts, new growth just didn’t make it … But the crop is doing very well, all things considered,” he said.

Hadwen said the dry heat resulted in water supply shortages that meant many producers struggled with crop yield. “From tree fruits, to berries, to potatoes, to traditional grains,” all felt the impact.

“When you talk to producers, I’m sure they’re going to tell you that going into this season, they were very concerned for another repeat,” Hadwen said.

Some of those concerns started to lift in May, when rain fell consistently throughout the entire region, replenishing lakes, reservoirs and adding moisture to the soil.

Hadwen said while it’s too early to assess the success of yields this season, he would expect to see a fairly slow recovery.

“It wasn’t a typical wet year, it was up and down, wet and dry. So depending on when those rains came … depending on the critical periods there are for individual crops, some crops may have done really well and recovered quite quickly with those rains,” while others may not have, he said.

Hadwen added that some areas still experienced drier-than-normal conditions, particularly the Northumberland Shore area in northern mainland Nova Scotia.

stories.title: Ditch the Manhattan. Drink the Toronto instead
stories.summary: For those who want to drink patriotically without leaning on a Caesar
stories.author: Sarah Efron
stories.content:
It’s the perfect drink for Canadians during the trade war with the United States.

Instead of a Manhattan (named after the Trumpian borough) or an Old Fashioned (traditionally made with American Bourbon), a similar cocktail called the Toronto can serve as a Canadian alternative if you want a bit of patriotism in your glass.

The Toronto is a lesser-known classic cocktail made with Fernet-Branca, a bitter Italian liqueur known as a bartender favourite. It also contains simple syrup, Angostura bitters and rye whisky. Canadian varieties are currently being used, of course, given the lack of availability of American whiskey in most provinces. The orange garnish and zest lift up this intense drink, giving it a bright, fruity edge.

Like many classic cocktails, the Toronto has hazy origins, but it’s believed it was a popular drink in its namesake Ontario city in the 1920s.

Jamie Boudreau, a Canadian who owns and operates the Seattle cocktail bar Canon, says he discovered the Toronto while doing research in vintage cocktail books. He wrote about the drink in a 2006 blog post , and says the recipe then began to spread to fellow “cocktail nerds.”

The Toronto is only listed occasionally on bar menus, but bartenders with classic cocktail skills are often able to make it upon request. Customers who request it tend to be people curious about the name, or those with cocktail knowledge who aren’t afraid of a drink with a strong punch.

“It’s not an easy, bright cocktail, like a Margarita. It’s an earthy, slow sipper,” says Helena Kosikova, owner of E.L. Ruddy , a Toronto bar that serves the drink. “It’s a good cocktail for pondering hard decisions.”

While it’s not officially on the menu at Henrietta Lane, another Toronto bar, co-owner Josh Colleran makes it occasionally by request. “It’s nicely balanced. Rye whisky tends to be drier, and it has a slight spiciness and astringency to it, and that is offset by the small amount of simple syrup. Then there’s a small amount of Fernet-Branca, which gives it depth and bitterness. Everything sits nicely together.”

Colleran serves his own variation on the Toronto called the Corktown , which uses rye steeped with bitter and sweet oranges, as well as cardamom syrup.

There are other Canadian and Canadian-themed cocktails – Boudreau’s research has unearthed drinks such as the Vancouver, the Habitant (referencing Quebec’s historic farmers) and Hotel Georgia (a drink from the storied Vancouver hotel). And of course there’s the Caesar, a spicy Canadian oddity made with vodka, clam juice and tomato juice.

While all of them allow Canadians to tap into their patriotism, it’s perhaps the Toronto – thanks to its potency – that can most help Canucks forget about their current troubles, at least until the next morning.

¼ oz of Fernet-Branca

¼ oz of simple syrup

2 dashes of Angostura bitters

2 oz of rye whisky (could be Alberta Premium or Lot 40)

In a mixing glass full of ice, stir the combined ingredients until very cold. Strain into a chilled coupe. Garnish with orange peel and drop in the zest.

stories.title: Canadian families still waiting for answers 1 week after Nepal disaster
stories.summary: The flooding on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,100 people and left roughly 4,400 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

Neeral Patel sent well-wishes to her cousin on his birthday last Wednesday, but she never heard back.

Her cousin Ishan Patel was in Nepal at the time, not far from the border with China, where a devastating flash flood ripped through the valley that same day.

She’s calling for a wider international response to help in rescue efforts as the days tick by with no word on her cousin or the three family members he was travelling with.

“We want to give a lot of hope. But with each passing day, it’s just getting chipped away, and time is of the essence,” said Patel, who lives in Toronto.

Ishan Patel was travelling with his wife, Akanksha Patel, both dual Canadian-U. S. citizens, along with his mother, Shilpa Patel, and father-in-law, Umesh Patel, who are Canadian, she said.

The four were on a long-planned pilgrimage to Mount Kaliash ahead of Ishan Patel starting a new job as an orthopedic surgeon, after finishing his fellowship in July, said Neeral Patel.

“It was kind of the big holy beginnings to his new career.”

The flooding on Aug. 26 killed more than 1,100 people and left roughly 4,400 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.

The scale of the disaster is hampering rescue efforts, as landslides and destroyed roads have cut off remote areas.

Rescuers were also racing to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand has said 30 Canadians and permanent residents are among the missing — a number that may change as the government gets more information.

With so many still unaccounted for, Neeral Patel said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any relatives come up.

She said two family members have also travelled to Kathmandu to look in hospitals and anywhere else they can find answers, but the roads up to the flood-hit area are closed.

Making the wait even harder is that they know where to search, she said, because her cousin’s phone pinged from a spot a short distance from Hotel Kailash, where they had breakfast last Wednesday.

“This is why we’re urging everyone to please, in the right area, search as much as you can, because we’re coming up to a week’s time and still no news,” she said.

Ottawa said Monday it has 10 government officials on the ground in Nepal to support Canadians affected by the flooding and help locate the missing.

Patel said Global Affairs told her family about the team being sent but they’re still holding out hope for a bigger response.

“There should be a global effort, everyone work together to try to bring our family members home.”

stories.title: Ottawa set to extend the pause on federal fuel excise tax: source
stories.summary: A planned renewal of the federal excise tax on fuel that was to kick in after Labour Day will be paused, Canada's finance minister is to announce Wednesday afternoon.
stories.author: David Akin
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Wednesday that the current pause on the federal excise tax on gasoline and diesel will be extended until next February.

The extension was first reported by Radio-Canada and confirmed by Global News’ sources Wednesday morning.

The federal excise tax on gasoline was 10 cents a litre and the tax on diesel was four cents a litre but those taxes were suspended in April. The suspension was to have ended on Sept. 8.

Now, with fuel prices pushing higher because of renewed hostilities in the Iran war , the government will extend that suspension.

“Canadians did not cause these global challenges, it’s very clear. But they are feeling the consequences,” Champagne told reporters Wednesday.

“This is real relief right now. Relief for families that are commuting to work … driving their children to activities or managing the cost of everyday life, these savings add up.”

Champagne said the fuel excise tax suspension will remain in place until the end of January 2027, before returning to half its regular rate for the following two months. The tax will be fully restored on April 1.

The federal Conservatives have had an ongoing social media campaign to “Scrap Carney’s Labour Day Gas Tax Hike” for several weeks and renewed that campaign with a fresh round of posts on Wednesday morning.

stories.title: Canadian Tire, Tim Hortons launch loyalty partnership allowing Triangle members to earn on select Tims purchases
stories.summary: Tie-up is a bid by legacy brands to snag incremental share in an oversaturated loyalty market, retail analyst says
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. CTC-T and Tim Hortons are hoping to perk up their customer bases by linking their loyalty programs.

Under a partnership launched between the home goods retailer and café giant Wednesday, customers who link their Triangle and Tims Rewards accounts will earn between 2 and 5 per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

The arrangement is meant to draw Tims customers to Canadian Tire and vice versa.

Right now, 53 per cent of Triangle Rewards customers are enrolled in both loyalty programs. Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.

By uniting, “both Triangle Rewards will grow and Tim Hortons reward members will grow,” Darryl Jenkins, Canadian Tire’s executive vice-president and chief development officer, said in an interview.

How much Canadian Tire money shoppers earn will depend on whether they use a Triangle credit card to pay and what they buy.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.

The arrangement came about organically, Jenkins and Hope Bagozzi, Tims’ chief marketing officer, said.

Canadian Tire and Tims executives sit on many of the same boards, often network with one another and their companies sponsor many of the same events, so it made sense for them to explore if they could boost the reach of their loyalty programs together.

“Wouldn’t it be great to add more value together?” was the thinking, Bagozzi recalled.

But Liza Amlani, principal and co-founder of the Retail Strategy Group, suspects “this is less about customer delight and more about two legacy brands scrambling for incremental share in an oversaturated loyalty market.”

“Canadians are already juggling too many programs, and unless the value proposition is simple, transparent and genuinely rewarding, this risks becoming just another corporate tie-up that benefits the brands more than the shoppers,” she said in an e-mail when the partnership was teased last September .

Canadian Tire first announced the partnership almost a year ago but waited until Wednesday to launch it and reveal how it will work.

The year in between both milestones was spent ensuring the mechanics of the partnership will work on a technical level.

Jenkins said it was by chance that it’s launching “at a really interesting time” – just after the U.S. hit Canada with a fresh round of tariffs and as Canada prepares to implement its own round of retaliatory levies in September.

“We certainly didn’t plan it this way,” he said.

stories.title: Elections Alberta receives 225,000 requests for referendum mail-in ballots
stories.summary: Special mail-in ballots for Alberta’s 10-question referendum next month started going out the door Tuesday
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Special mail-in ballots for Alberta’s 10-question referendum next month started going out the door Tuesday, Elections Alberta said.

The agency said those who have previously registered for a special ballot will soon start receiving their packages in the mail or they can pick them up in person.

Spokesperson Maia-Lys Hanrahan said Elections Alberta received 225,000 requests to date for mail-in ballots. The special ballots are designed to allow those who may not be able to go to the polls in person on Oct. 19 the opportunity to still submit their votes.

The agency said in a news release later Tuesday that the total number of requests to date is more than triple the nearly 60,000 special ballots that were requested for the province’s last general election in 2023.

Among the questions Premier Danielle Smith’s government is putting voters is one on whether Albertans want to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating from Canada.

Albertans will also be asked five questions around the province taking more control over immigration and four on constitutional reform.

The elections agency says Albertans have until Oct. 9 to apply for a mail-in ballot and that the ballots must be received by Elections Alberta no later than Oct. 16.

The referendum is shaping up to be a massive undertaking for Elections Alberta, which has said it will need to hire at least 60,000 workers to hold the vote.

Ms. Hanrahan said that since it launched its hiring spree in June, it has received more than 35,000 applications.

“Elections Alberta will continue to seek election officers right up until voting for the referendum,” she said.

She also said the agency is specifically seeking election officers for a number of rural areas, including Medicine Hat, about 300 kilometres southeast of Calgary, and Athabasca, which is about 150 km north of Edmonton.

Ms. Hanrahan added that they were seeking applications “all across northern Alberta.”

She said Elections Alberta was coming up with a new hiring process specifically designed for groups of people, such as “your hockey team, community group, choir, or even the group chat” and that more details would be available soon.

The agency is also bringing in help from other provincial election organizations, a practice it says is normal for all major voting events.

Ms. Hanrahan didn’t provide a number but said a small group of professionals from across the country will be providing relief for Elections Alberta’s fewer than 50 permanent staff come voting day.

“This assistance will allow us to cover shift-work spanning the 60 consecutive hour period from the beginning of election day through to the end of the count,” she said.

stories.title: Women take the reins in family-friendly condo project
stories.summary: Reina, at 689 The Queensway in Toronto, features larger-than-average units and is thoughtful with storage options
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
In the booming, consumer-happy year of 1955, auto maker Dodge introduced the “La Femme,” billed as the “first and only car designed for Your Majesty, the modern American woman.” An option package offered on the Royal Lancer model, the La Femme came in one colour: pink, with interiors of pink jacquard fabric peppered with little rosebuds. For ease of driveability, everything that could be powered – steering, brakes, windows – was. And each purchaser was gifted with a lipstick case, cigarette lighter and case, compact, and a change purse. If that weren’t enough, Dodge threw in a raincoat, rain hat and umbrella that matched the car’s upholstery.

Sales were terrible. In an era when a popular model could sell in the hundreds of thousands, Dodge sold 1,500 La Femmes over two model years before quietly putting it out of its misery. Calling the move “pinkwashing” in a 2020 article for Hagerty, Benjamin Hunting wrote that “no amount of mansplaining its accessorized virtues via complementary advertising was enough” to “appeal to a woman’s wants and needs.”

Thank goodness we’ve come a long way since then, or 689 The Queensway would be dressed in pink brick, come with preselected ‘feminine’ furniture, and have a beauty salon as an amenity. Likely Canada’s first condominium to be led, designed and engineered entirely by women, “Reina” doesn’t outwardly flaunt its femininity. Rather, it quietly reveals itself to be more sensitive to the needs of families, more thoughtful when it comes to storage, and feels a little safer in semipublic spaces.

The idea for Reina came from Taya Cook, executive vice-president at Urban Capital. She’d seen an article profiling some “condo kings” says architect Lisa Spensieri at BDP Quadrangle, “and she wanted to represent the women, so she had this idea that she pitched to Urban Capital.”

After the idea was accepted, Ms. Cook and Spotlight Development president Sherry Larjani assembled an all-woman consulting team, which quickly found kinship with Ms. Spensieri and Heather Rolleston at BDP Quadrangle: “They liked our ideas,” confirms Ms. Spensieri. “[The building] takes up a whole block, it’s a rather large massing, and one of the things we said was that we wanted the building to touch the ground lightly, like a high heel, and that really struck a chord with the client.”

But what should go inside? For that, the team took to the streets and held a community design workshop, which attracted almost 200 participants.

“What do we want this building to have – this community – because we really saw this as a community,” says Ms. Spensieri. “The event was a lot of fun, I sat at a table and asked questions, and we had sticky notes, and we got a lot of good information.”

So, as built, Reina (Spanish for “Queen”) features larger-than-average units, a much higher percentage of two- and three-bedroom units, and, on the ground floor, three intergenerational units: “They’re bought as one unit, but there are two doors to the exterior and connected with one door on the interior … the second unit is smaller, but it has a bathroom and a kitchenette,” says Ms. Spensieri. “It’s good for when your kids are coming back from university and they have their own place next door.”

Amenities are family-focused as well: stroller-parking on residential floors; soundproof music rooms (for listening parties or if there’s a young clarinet player in the family); yoga room; crafting room; a glassed-in, daycare room to park toddlers with a picture book while mom uses the gym across the hall (with full view of her little one); a large dog-washing room; and, after a consultation with a group of Girl Guides, a “snack shack” equipped with a vending machine and tables.

There is ample exterior lighting for safety, and, behind the building, a gated, 6,500-square-foot garden with barbecues, benches, lounge chairs and a communal table. Out here, the U-shaped, curvy, white-brick building almost seems to give residents a reassuring hug.

“I was driving in the neighbourhood, and it was the tag line for this place that caught me,” says resident (and single mother of two teenage boys) Justine Nolasco. “‘Designed by women, developed by women, made for everyone’… but people think I live in an all-woman community,” she says with a laugh. “We’ve got families [and] we’ve got empty-nesters.”

And while Ms. Nolasco’s three-bedroom, two-bath unit is notable for its large kitchen, curved balcony, lovely herringbone floors and a good-sized primary bedroom with a walk-in closet, it’s the storage area around her upright laundry pair that gets her most excited.

“I call it my basement,” she says, opening the door. “This is amazing; the fact that some condos just have [space for the machines] and not the room on the sides. I put these [shelves] in, and I just throw everything in here. My kids will ask for something, and I’ll say: ‘It’s in the basement.’”

“The units aren’t shoe boxes,” adds Ms. Spensieri. “We’re not struggling to find millimetres of space … we’re not fighting to cram one more unit in on the floor plan; it’s just about making the units better.” And because BDP Quadrangle used their in-house interiors team, amenities spaces are generous, logical and colourful.

And well used, says Ms. Nolasco: “When I bought this place, my youngest was eight, and then when we moved in he was 12 or 13 … but my teenagers use the gym in here, and they bring their friends all the time.”

A calm oasis on a busy thoroughfare – widened in the 1950s to make room for all those chrome-laden Dodges, Chevys and Fords – Reina is a game-changer that’s long overdue.

Amenities are family-focused as well: stroller-parking on residential floors; soundproof music rooms (for listening parties or if there’s a young clarinet player in the family); yoga room; crafting room; a glassed-in, daycare room to park toddlers with a picture book while mom uses the gym across the hall (with full view of her little one); a large dog-washing room; and, after a consultation with a group of Girl Guides, a “snack shack” equipped with a vending machine and tables.

There is ample exterior lighting for safety, and, behind the building, a gated, 6,500-square-foot garden with barbecues, benches, lounge chairs and a communal table. Out here, the U-shaped, curvy, white-brick building almost seems to give residents a reassuring hug.

“I was driving in the neighbourhood, and it was the tag line for this place that caught me,” says resident (and single mother of two teenage boys) Justine Nolasco. “‘Designed by women, developed by women, made for everyone’… but people think I live in an all-woman community,” she says with a laugh. “We’ve got families [and] we’ve got empty-nesters.”

And while Ms. Nolasco’s three-bedroom, two-bath unit is notable for its large kitchen, curved balcony, lovely herringbone floors and a good-sized primary bedroom with a walk-in closet, it’s the storage area around her upright laundry pair that gets her most excited.

“I call it my basement,” she says, opening the door. “This is amazing; the fact that some condos just have [space for the machines] and not the room on the sides. I put these [shelves] in, and I just throw everything in here. My kids will ask for something, and I’ll say: ‘It’s in the basement.’”

“The units aren’t shoe boxes,” adds Ms. Spensieri. “We’re not struggling to find millimetres of space … we’re not fighting to cram one more unit in on the floor plan; it’s just about making the units better.” And because BDP Quadrangle used their in-house interiors team, amenities spaces are generous, logical and colourful.

And well used, says Ms. Nolasco: “When I bought this place, my youngest was eight, and then when we moved in he was 12 or 13 … but my teenagers use the gym in here, and they bring their friends all the time.”
A calm oasis on a busy thoroughfare – widened in the 1950s to make room for all those chrome-laden Dodges, Chevys and Fords – Reina is a game-changer that’s long overdue.

content_blocks.text: In the booming, consumer-happy year of 1955, auto maker Dodge introduced the “La Femme,” billed as the “first and only car designed for Your Majesty, the modern American woman.” An option package offered on the Royal Lancer model, the La Femme came in one colour: pink, with interiors of pink jacquard fabric peppered with little rosebuds. For ease of driveability, everything that could be powered – steering, brakes, windows – was. And each purchaser was gifted with a lipstick case, cigarette lighter and case, compact, and a change purse. If that weren’t enough, Dodge threw in a raincoat, rain hat and umbrella that matched the car’s upholstery.

stories.title: Have you seen Cole Rioux? London man still missing after failing to arrive at work
stories.summary: London Police are releasing new information in their search for 19-year-old Cole Rioux, who was reported missing by his family.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
London Police are releasing new information in their search for 19-year-old Cole Rioux, who was reported missing by his family.

Rioux was last seen at about 3:40 a.m. on Aug. 27 in the area of High Street and Moore Street.

On Tuesday, family and friends were gathered at the family’s home as his mother Marla Rioux spoke to CTV News.

“I last saw him on Friday morning, when he was on his way to work. We gave each other great big long hugs and he left,” she explained. “He left the house in a very big hurry. He didn’t have his phone on him, he didn’t show up to work, which is very unlike him.”

On Tuesday, London police provided additional details about the car Cole could be driving.

Cole Rioux car Pictures of the black 2001 Volkswagen Jetta driven by Cole Rioux when he was last seen (supplied)

“Cole is believed to be driving a 2001 Volkswagen Jetta with Ontario license plate Avxm 279,” a news release reads.

Cole’s mother describes some of the car’s distinctive features, “It’s a very old, black, 2001 Volkswagen Jetta 1.8 turbo. He has customized the front grille so you don’t see a Volkswagen emblem at the front of the car. It also has a very customized exhaust. It’s got a distinctive sound if you hear it driving. Its loud.”

Martha says her son was excited about his welding job, so his family became alarmed when he didn’t show up for his shift on Friday.

Fighting back tears, she has a message for her son, “We just want him to know that we’re all here for him. We love him. We just want to know that he’s okay.”

Cole is described as white man, approximately 5-foot-8, 155 pounds, with a slim build, blue eyes, and light brown buzz cut hair.

He was last seen wearing a black t-shirt, with pink or green shorts.

Anyone with information is asked to contact London Police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477).

stories.title: Three bidders for designer home in Ottawa’s west end
stories.summary: The two-storey house was designed in 1988 by Barry Hobin, a former president of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
30 Castlethorpe Cres., Ottawa

Asking price: $1.05-million (June, 2026)

Selling price: $1.05-million (June, 2026)

Taxes: $7,507 (2025)

Days on the market: Five

Listing agent: Raymond Chin, Coldwell Banker First Ottawa Realty

The owners of this four-bedroom house were in a hurry to sell after zeroing in on another property they wanted to buy this summer. They had their home professionally staged to make a strong first impression on potential buyers around the first weekend in June.

“The rule of thumb is, any buyer that’s really motivated and looking in this area will come out as soon as possible,” agent Raymond Chin said.

“A lot more people would be available during the weekend, so we timed [the launch] closer to the weekend.”

By Monday, three guests were jockeying for ownership of the home, two kilometres from Algonquin College and College Square mall. One buyer, matching the sellers’ full asking price of $1.05-million, made the best case.

“We priced it at market value,” Mr. Chin said.

“It’s on a great, quiet crescent, which is always very desirable.”

This two-storey house, designed in 1988 by Barry Hobin, a former president of the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada, has 1,916 square feet of living space, including classic living and dining areas, and an open-concept family room with a gas fireplace and cathedral ceilings.

The updated, eat-in kitchen has an island, sliding doors to a south-facing deck and a second exit closer to the double garage on the 42- by 112-foot lot.

All three bathrooms have been renovated, including a four-piece, primary ensuite upstairs.

There are additional recreation areas in the basement.

“The architecture is a little unique to the area, which attracted a lot of people,” Mr. Chin said.

“The home was meticulously maintained, and you can sense that throughout the home.”

stories.title: Police investigating murder of employee of ex-MP Raj Grewal, who's accused of fraud
stories.summary: Multiple lawsuits and the Law Society of Ontario accuse Grewal and others of fraud, misappropriation of client funds and other wrongdoing.
stories.author: Tom Blackwell
stories.content:
The recent cross-examination of a witness in a lawsuit against the ex-Liberal member raised the fact that an employee was shot dead eight months ago

Litigation over millions in alleged financial misconduct by former MP and lawyer Raj Grewal and his colleagues has brought to the fore a more chilling backdrop to the saga — a shocking murder of a Grewal associate and shootings at his home.

stories.title: Are the B.C. Conservatives in free fall?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses what led up to the latest events for the Conservative Party of British Columbia and what comes next.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted September 2, 2026 8:15 am.

Things are not going well for the Conservative Party of British Columbia. Following Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s win as leader earlier this summer after the ousting of John Rustad, there have been questions as to whether or not she is too far right for British Columbians. Since then, seven Conservative MLAs have decided their answer was ‘yes,’ leaving the party to sit as independents, citing a lack of faith in Findlay’s leadership.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Mo Amir, host of This is VANCOLOUR , about what led up to these latest events, what the seven newly independent MLAs plan on doing now, and whether or not Findlay can survive the losses.

stories.title: Tumbler Ridge shooting survivors among 30 new plaintiffs suing OpenAI
stories.summary: Thirty new plaintiffs have joined legal action tied to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting, expanding the case against OpenAI and Sam Altman to 37 claims.
stories.author: Catherine Urquhart
stories.content:
If you get Global News from Instagram or Facebook - that will be changing. Find out how you can still connect with us .

Warning: This story contains content that may be disturbing to some readers. Discretion is advised.

An additional 30 lawsuits have been filed in California in connection with the deadly school shooting in Tumbler Ridge , B.C. that shook the country nearly seven months ago.

This brings the total to 37 claims against OpenAI and founder Sam Altman related to the mass shooting.

Eight people were killed by 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, who shot their mother and step-brother, then opened fire at a school in Tumbler Ridge Feb. 10.

In February, OpenAI confirmed that an account connected with Van Rootelsar was identified the previous June and was subsequently banned for violating the usage policy.

The company considered referring the account to law enforcement but determined the account activity did not meet the threshold for referring a user to law enforcement because it did not involve an imminent and credible risk or planning of serious physical harm to others.

The 30 new plaintiffs are educators, a principal and students, including a 13-year-old referred to as ‘A.C.,’ who was trapped in the library.

Court documents filed on behalf of teacher Deidre Rushlow claim, “When the gunfire started, she locked her classroom door and pulled the students who remained beneath her desk… The shooter reached her classroom, found the door locked, and fired shotgun blasts through the front door… From under that desk, Deidre called the library to check on the students… EA Shannda Aviugana-Durand and several of those students were killed in that library.”

Another claim states “16-year-old D.I. was sitting in his science classroom when the gunfire started. He heard shots in the hallway and the screams of terrified children, and then bullets began tearing through the classroom door. His teacher ordered D.I. and the other students to hide under their desks. D.I. heard a blood-curdling scream just outside the classroom, followed by more gunfire, and then gunfire in the library next door.

Moments later, the teacher left the room and returned carrying a younger student who had been shot and gravely wounded. D.I. watched as blood poured from the wounded student’s body and spread across the classroom floor. After a few minutes, the teacher moved the injured student, D.I., and D.I.’s classmates into a small storage closet that shared a wall with the library. They remained packed tightly together in the closet, watching as the teacher administered first aid to the injured student. D.I. will never forget the moment the teacher covered her body with his jacket after her breathing slowed to a gurgle and then stopped.”

Lawyer John Rice represents the victims.

“We want full disclosure of the chat logs between the shooter and ChatGPT from the beginning up until the date of the mass shooting,” he told Global News. “We also want full disclosure of all the internal chain of command documents relating to the identification as the shooter as a credible threat, the recommendation to report the shooter to Canadian authorities and the decision to not make that phone call.”

Chicago-based lawyer Jay Edelson is part of the cross-border legal team representing the victims. In April he told Global News “we’ll be asking the jury to send a strong message to OpenAI that it can’t make a decision to put profits over the lives of little kids and it’s hard to imagine that we won’t ask for at least a billion dollars.”

The civil allegations against OpenAI and Altman include:

Negligence

Negligent Entrustment

Aiding and Abetting a Mass Shooting

Strict Product Liability

Negligent Infliction of Emotional Distress.

“Probably most importantly for these families, they want to prevent another Tumbler Ridge and so this lawsuit is seeking specific injunctive relief from a California court to compel corporate changes at OpenAI,” said Rice.

None of the allegations have been tested in court. OpenAI and Altman have not yet filed statements of defence responding to the latest claims.

OpenAI claims it has strengthened safeguards, including how it assesses and escalates potential threats of violence.

In a statement provided to Global News in April , an OpenAI spokesperson said: “The events in Tumbler Ridge are a tragedy. We have a zero-tolerance policy for using our tools to assist in committing violence. As we shared with Canadian officials, we have already strengthened our safeguards, including improving how ChatGPT responds to signs of distress, connecting people with local support and mental health resources, strengthening how we assess and escalate potential threats of violence, and improving detection of repeat policy violators.”

All 37 lawsuits are requesting trials by jury.

With files from Amy Judd

stories.title: Hot Docs restructures leadership team to ‘future-proof’ arts organization
stories.summary: Hot Docs carried a deficit of about $180,000 for the fiscal year ending May 2025 according to CRA filings, a marked reduction from 2023 deficit
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
A year and a half after taking over Toronto’s beleaguered Hot Docs festival and year-round cinema, executive director Diana Sanchez has been promoted to president of the organization as part of a series of internal shifts that leaders hope will “future-proof” the organization.

On Wednesday, Hot Docs announced that in addition to Sanchez’s new role, the institution has hired Canadian arts administrator Mara Gourd-Mercado, currently the head of industry and training at Copenhagen’s doc festival, CPH: DOX, to take over the position of executive director. At the same time, a new structure has been put in place for the board of directors. Julie Bristow, founder of the television development firm Catalyst, will now serve as chair of the board, with filmmaker Aaron Zeghers taking on the role of vice-chair.

“The shorthand is that Mara is going to be thinking about today, and I’m going to be thinking about tomorrow,” Sanchez said in an interview. “We’re a 365-day organization and we have the flagship festival and our industry forum, but we also have our cinema, our Docs for Schools program, Doc Soups, our foundation and production funds. We’re trying to future-proof the organization, to come up with a structure that addresses the day-to-day issues but also think about multiyear initiatives.”

Sanchez, a two-decade veteran of the Toronto International Film Festival, joined Hot Docs as executive director in the spring of 2025 after a string of significant financial and structural challenges, including an exodus of festival programmers, the 2024 departure of president Marie Nelson, and the temporary shuttering of the organization’s flagship Bloor Street West cinema.

This past spring’s 33rd edition of the Hot Docs festival, once the largest celebration of nonfiction filmmaking in North America, delivered a 14 per cent increase in single-ticket revenue compared with the year before, as well as a three per cent increase in festival attendance.

“We’ve made a lot of gains over the past year and a half, but I saw a clear need for someone to come in to serve the documentary community,” Sanchez said. “And then I have the ability to think three years ahead, five years ahead.”

Gourd-Mercado, who prior to her work in Copenhagen served as the executive director of the Montreal International Documentary Festival and executive director of the Academy of Canadian Cinema & Television’s Quebec division, will also focus on boosting the festival’s Hot Docs Forum and industry programming, which had been slimmed down over the past two editions.

“As long as I’ve worked in documentaries, the industry has been in a crisis. And this one is a really tough one,” said Gourd-Mercado, who will be relocating to Toronto in the fall. “We’re seeing more and more people who made a living in documentaries now having it as a side job. It’s really important for us to be responsible in the way we imagine the activities and programs that we can offer the industry.”

With the restructuring, four positions have been consolidated or eliminated.

“These are hard decisions. But looking at the organization and what we used to deliver is very different from what we’re delivering today and what we want to deliver in the future,” said Sanchez. “So we had to align the structure for now, for the present and the future.”

According to the most recent financial information filed with the Canada Revenue Agency, Hot Docs carried a deficit of about $180,000 for the fiscal year ending May, 2025 – though that was a marked reduction from the $2-million deficit the organization carried at the end of its 2023 fiscal year.

“We have renewed momentum,” Sanchez said. “We have renewed interest from our donors, we’ve tripled our Founder Circle memberships, we’ve had an increased audience at the festival, our screening series are going very well.”

“We haven’t even announced programming for Doc Soup, and we’ve sold 200 packages at this point,” added Sanchez. “What’s very different from a year ago is that while everyone then wanted us to thrive and rally, we now have even more people in the room interested in what Hot Docs is doing.”

In terms of growth, Sanchez is cautious about the size of the forthcoming 2027 festival’s programming. This year’s slate featured 115 titles (80 features, 35 shorts), smaller than the festival’s supersized 2023 edition, which screened 214 films.

“Each film has to have a reason to be in the festival. We want to serve each film well. I want to lean into a strategy around each title, and deliver a highly curated festival and market,” Sanchez said.

“These are early days with the festival, but the kind of growth we’re looking for is impact and relevance. Let’s focus on serving our audiences.”
