“We haven’t even announced programming for Doc Soup, and we’ve sold 200 packages at this point,” added Sanchez. “What’s very different from a year ago is that while everyone then wanted us to thrive and rally, we now have even more people in the room interested in what Hot Docs is doing.”

In terms of growth, Sanchez is cautious about the size of the forthcoming 2027 festival’s programming. This year’s slate featured 115 titles (80 features, 35 shorts), smaller than the festival’s supersized 2023 edition, which screened 214 films.

“Each film has to have a reason to be in the festival. We want to serve each film well. I want to lean into a strategy around each title, and deliver a highly curated festival and market,” Sanchez said.
“These are early days with the festival, but the kind of growth we’re looking for is impact and relevance. Let’s focus on serving our audiences.”

stories.title: Toronto couple turns their backyard into a sleek, two-bedroom garden suite
stories.summary: The pair downsized while their daughter’s family moved into the larger main house
stories.author: Olivia Grandy
stories.content:
For years, former school principal Bill Harrison and former teacher Mary Hamawaki regularly hosted staff parties in their large Danforth backyard in Toronto’s east end. They always looked at the space with an eye for what it could become.

But the couple’s vision of building a small extra home in their backyard encountered a snag: Such garden suites were illegal in Toronto. At least they were until February, 2022, when the city approved zoning amendments that made detached backyard units an option, following the embrace of back-alley laneway houses in 2018.

Now retired, Mr. Harrison, 69, and Ms. Hamawaki, 72, spent about a year on the project, replacing their two-car garage with a much swankier arrangement. The renovation allowed them to give their adult daughter, Caitlin Harrison, who grew up on the property, their full-sized home while they moved in to the garden suite in May, 2025.

Caitlin’s husband, Mitch Bates, runs a ramen restaurant nearby. Meanwhile, the couple’s two daughters are growing up in a home with a family history dating back to 1991, when their grandparents bought the two-storey house.

“That’s what drove us to this: Being able to give them a house in a great part of the city that they could live in, and also being close to us,” Mr. Harrison said.

That motivation led the couple to approach Toronto-based Lanescape Architecture and Construction. After also considering modular homes from other companies, built with low, sloped ceilings to fit within city bylaws (to avoid blocking neighbours’ sunlight), the couple was sold on the design firm’s garden suite with a sunken bedroom layout.

Lanescape, one of the companies in Toronto that caters to the garden suite and laneway home market, said multigenerational living is a common use case for its designs. Building costs run between about $400 to $550 per square foot, Lanescape’s director of business development, Daniel Mansubi, said.

The suite’s walkout basement and slanted roof on the main floor “gave us these fabulous cathedral ceilings,” Mr. Harrison said. Within their 1,100-square-foot space, the couple has two bedrooms, 1½ bathrooms and an open-concept living space with a bounty of sunlight.

For finishings, the pair opted for modern and low-maintenance details including a waterfall quartz countertop, an abundance of built-in storage and a slatted wood support wall on the main floor that lets light through.

“We’re a little older, but we want to make sure that somebody else, when we’re gone, still finds the place appealing,” Ms. Hamawaki said. The couple also made sure that the dimensions of the stairs could eventually accommodate a lift.

Outside, they selected a dark exterior for its dramatic look against greenery and to keep cleaning minimal. Even with the garden suite, there is still plenty of remaining outdoor space, including grassy areas and patios for both residences. Garden suites in the city must also have a clear, not-too-long path from the street to ensure fire and emergency access .

A grey stone walkway connects the main house to the garden suite. Like many families, the older couple leans on the younger generation for help when needed, such as with computer challenges or when booking vacations, Mr. Harrison said.

For a period during construction, the couple and their daughter’s family all lived together in the main house. At the time, one granddaughter was a newborn baby.

Mr. Harrison recalled the mess and noise of sharing the home during the construction. They even had a portable toilet on their front lawn. “I remember we decorated it at Christmas. We wrapped some tinsel around,” Mr. Harrison said.

Now through the chaos, the couple is enjoying the more compact residence because it takes less work to maintain.

“We’ve built a small house that works so much better for us,” Mr. Harrison said. Though, Ms. Hamawaki added, “it’s not that small.”

stories.title: After 399 days on the market, price cuts help find a buyer for lakefront condo in Toronto
stories.summary: Most recent price drop coaxed three past visitors into purchase talks for the 2,000-square-foot unit
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
99 Harbour Square, No. 613, Toronto

Asking price: $2,598,000 (July, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $2,798,000 (May, 2026); $2,998,000 (January, 2026); $3,098,000 (October, 2025); $3,145,000 (September, 2025); $3,295,000 (June, 2025)

Selling price: $2.45-million (July, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $1.2-million (December, 2012); $695,000 (May, 2002); $650,000 (June, 2000); $500,000 (June, 1992)

Taxes: $8,709 (2026)

Days on the market: Seven

Property days on market: 399

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

There are a small number of two-storey units in the podium of this high-rise next to the Jack Layton Ferry Terminal. Each one has a terrace and unobstructed views over Toronto Harbour. The last one sold more than 10 years ago, making it a challenge to correctly price this one. Agent Christopher Bibby settled on a price under $3.3-million last summer, but slowly wound it back over the 399 days it took to find a buyer.

“It’s overlooking the lake, has two terraces and parking,” Mr. Bibby said. “It was a very unique space that just took one buyer to appreciate how special it was.

“You just don’t know who’s out there and what they’re willing to pay.”

The most recent price drop – to roughly $2.6-million in July – coaxed three past visitors into purchase talks for the 2,000-square-foot unit. The best offer hit $2.45-million.

“Nothing has gone over $1,000 per square foot in the building, but we got $1,225 per square foot,” Mr. Bibby said.

“We did exceptionally well.”

What they got

This roughly 35-year-old unit has one terrace off the living room and a second terrace off the two bedrooms upstairs.

In 2022, the unit was redesigned, complete with an enclosed den, a modern kitchen and a dining area by a fireplace.

There are three bathrooms, including two with heated flooring and a laundry room upstairs.

The unit is on the same floor as its storage locker and its parking spot in the above-grade garage.

Monthly fees of $2,506 include utilities, cable concierge and use of building amenities, which include indoor and outdoor pools.

“The owners took everything back to the walls, nothing about the original suite really remains,” Mr. Bibby said.

“All the materials were top-of-the-line.”

stories.title: Toronto-area home buyers adjust to the new normal
stories.summary: Initial shock of threatened tariffs in early 2025 did unnerve buyers for a time, but many threats were rolled back, real estate broker says
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
The traditional end-of-summer lull in the Southern Ontario real estate market is well-timed this year: buyers and sellers have some time to absorb the shock of upheaval in the trade war between Canada and the United States .

The fall market typically kicks off a week or so after Labour Day when families have their back-to-school routines in place.

Real estate agents in Toronto and surrounding cities are hoping that the fragile recovery in sales will maintain traction as they launch new properties on the market in the coming weeks.

Some potential buyers may be rattled by renewed uncertainty surrounding the economic outlook, market watchers say, but overall, they don’t expect the shock waves of failed negotiations and retaliatory tariffs to reverberate as strongly as the initial jolt after U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House early in 2025.

Patrick Rocca, broker with Bosley Real Estate, recently represented buyers who pushed ahead with plans to bid on a property in Leaside on the date set for reviewing offers, which just happened to fall on the same day the U.S. President signed an executive order changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Six bidders competed for the semi-detached house listed with an asking price of $1.299-million. After a couple of rounds of bidding, Mr. Rocca’s clients secured the property with an offer about $150,000 above asking.

A few days before trade negotiations broke down between the two countries, Mr. Rocca drew five offers for a semi-detached house in East York with an asking price just under $1.2-million.

The house at 27 Mountnoel Ave. sold approximately $200,000 above asking. The renovated property near Danforth and Greenwood avenues has an attractive location close to a parkette, he said.

Mr. Rocca decided to list in August instead of September because the timing worked for the sellers and there were few rival listings.

“Why not? There was less competition,” said Mr. Rocca. “If the price is right, and it shows well, it will sell.”

Mr. Rocca has been fielding calls for the last couple of weeks from homeowners gearing up to list in the fall. So far, none have decided to hold off because of the failed trade talks, but some are wondering if they will fetch more money next spring.

Mr. Rocca said there’s no reason at the moment to expect prices will rebound in early 2027. A significant recovery in prices could take years, in his opinion.

Mr. Rocca points out that the market has wobbled in the past, but it pushed through the COVID-19 pandemic and the initial jolt of Donald Trump’s return to the White House.

Still, if the trade conflict intensifies, the economy may worsen.

“In 2027, we could have a real problem,” he said. We had kind of adapted to the ‘not normal’. Now you’ve got a completely different game with added pressures.”

Mr. Rocca worries about the outlook for jobs in auto manufacturing hubs such as Oshawa, Oakville and Windsor, but he expects Toronto’s diversified employment landscape to remain more stable.

Still, struggling businesses in this city may suffer, he said, and he sees more “power of sale” properties listed by lenders every day.

Mr. Rocca notes that the initial shock of threatened tariffs in early 2025 did unnerve buyers for a time, but many threats were rolled back.

“This is more serious in terms of economic impact,” he said of tariffs and counter-tariffs.

If sellers do want to list, he advises them to price sharply.

“If you have a product and you’re selling, you’d better be realistic,” he said. “Most of the people I’m talking to are listening.

Matthew Regan, broker with Re/Max Escarpment Realty, believes that consumer sentiment is more positive in 2026 in markets west of Toronto, where he does much of his business.

He is fielding fewer questions from anxious buyers and sellers compared with last year, when the United States increased and implemented tariffs on specific imports from Canada.

“In April of 2025, that was the talk at the kitchen table,” he said. “We’ve been toughened up over the past 16 months.”

Mr. Regan said sales have remained steady through August. In most parts of Oakville, Mississauga and Burlington, the strategy of setting an asking price with room for negotiation will not attract buyers, he said.

“You used to price with wiggle room. Not any more. The name of the game today is to get it priced right so you will receive an offer.”

He adds that buyers have also adjusted their mindset: “ridiculously low” offers are not landing as frequently.

“There is more equilibrium. Buyers are no longer trying to steal the house.”

Mr. Regan and his partner at Re/Max Escarpment, real estate agent Alex Irish, have listed a lakefront three-bedroom house with an asking price of $6.975-million.

The house with rare riparian rights on Lake Ontario had lingered on the market for two years because no buyer was willing to take on the significant overhaul the building needed, Mr. Regan said.

Mr. Regan and Ms. Irish purchased the property at 21 Second St. in Oakville last year and revamped the home with downsizers in mind.

House hunters have booked two to three showings a week, he said, which is considered high activity in that price bracket.

Mr. Regan has received calls from New York and Naples, Fla., where one buyer is planning to sell their U.S. property and return to Canada.

The broker adds that some buyers at the high end may look at the trade uncertainty and try to take advantage of the jitters in order to move up to a more expensive property.

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert with Rates.ca, saw a pickup in buyers seeking a preapproved mortgage in August so they can go house hunting after a lengthy stretch on the sidelines.

The more hesitant buyers – or those in hard-hit industries – will likely pull back now that the trade war has flared up again, he said, but the serious house hunters will follow through.

“Many buyers are engaged – they’re just waiting for the right listing.”

Mr. Tran does expect many of those house hunters to tighten their budgets, however, and the properties they are willing to consider may shift too.

The federal government’s planned counter-tariffs on U.S. imports include a 25 per cent levy on major appliances, for example, which may encourage buyers to set aside more of their cash for a new refrigerator, stove or washing machine.

In Mr. Tran’s view, reining in spending is prudent.

“That’s what I would advise my buyers.”

Air conditioners, furnaces and water heaters also face added cost pressures.

Some buyers may favour move-in ready properties with new appliances and HVAC equipment over those with models that need to be replaced, Mr. Tran said.

“All of that is going to cost more. That’s something buyers are going to have to consider.”

The trade upheaval may influence borrowers’ decisions at mortgage renewal time as well, Mr. Tran said. Even before the latest fight, he was seeing an increase in clients who are refinancing when the time comes to renew a mortgage.

In the face of higher rates, Mr. Tran said, some homeowners are setting their amortization period back to 25 years, for example, which allows them to lower monthly payments.

He has also seen an uptick in homeowners setting up a home equity line of credit in case they need some extra cash down the road.

“They are setting up a HELOC while they are employed. They won’t be able to qualify if they lose their job.”

stories.title: Sudbury, Ontario’s mining capital, unshaken by Ford’s threat to cut off U.S. critical minerals supply
stories.summary: Strategic importance of nickel to U.S. manufacturing and city’s economic diversification seen as buffers against trade-war fallout
stories.author: Elissa Mendes
stories.content:
With each development in U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada, many Ontario cities have received news of tariffs on Canadian goods with panic and devastation for their local industries.

A Hamilton official last year warned that tariffs in the steel town could spell “the end of the industry” and thousands of jobs lost.

In Oshawa, autoworkers already mourning the steady decline of the industry feared for their ability to put food on the table.

But even as Ontario Premier Doug Ford has threatened to cut off the flow of critical minerals to the United States in response to the latest round of Trump’s tariffs, the province’s mining capital appears unshaken, minimizing trade fears as it doubles down on getting its product to other markets.

Sudbury Mayor Paul Lefebvre says he is 'confident' the U.S. won't impose tariffs on Canadian nickel.

The Canadian Press

Paul Lefebvre, the Mayor of Greater Sudbury, said the city is largely sheltered from the trade war compared to other municipalities because nickel and copper – its two key exports – are not subject to tariffs. The city is only feeling indirect effects from some suppliers, he said, so he’s not overly worried about the United States.

“They need our nickel to continue,” Lefebvre said in an interview. “They would just be hurting themselves.” He added, “We’re confident that the U.S. will not want to impose tariffs on us.”

Critical minerals have become increasingly important to American national security and manufacturing. The Pentagon has sought more secure supplies of minerals used in military aircraft, missiles, munitions and electronics as the U.S. tries to curtail its reliance on China, which dominates the mining and processing of multiple strategically important minerals.

The U.S. only has one operational nickel mine, in Michigan, and the nickel extracted there is processed in Sudbury, the mayor said with a laugh.

Ontario produced the largest share of the 125,364 tonnes of nickel in concentrate dug out from Canadian mines in 2024, according to official figures.

Natural Resources Canada also reported that 98,199 tonnes of unwrought nickel valued at $2.4-billion were exported in 2024. By volume, 43 per cent of these exports went to the United States, followed by 15 per cent to the Netherlands.

The versatile metal known for its strength and ability to withstand extreme temperatures has long been Sudbury’s claim to fame. The Big Nickel, a nine-metre tall replica of a Canadian five-cent coin, is one of the best known tourist attractions in the area.

After the United States imposed 50-per-cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods last month, Ford said all forms of retaliation, including cutting off electricity supply to U.S. states and shutting down the flow of critical minerals, were on the table should Trump continue to target Canadian industries.

Though Lefebvre said “it’s always concerning” to hear threats about cutting off critical mineral exports to the U.S., he approves of Ford’s strategy. The mayor said he supports the premier leveraging critical minerals to rid the country of tariffs, but believes the local economy must be taken into consideration.

“The uncertainty that (Trump) has created in North America has really shied away a lot of investments,” he said, such as a Sudbury delegation’s trip to Japan and South Korea that was soured by Trump imposing tariffs on the two Asian countries.

The mayor added that Sudbury has not been in any talks with American officials, and he declined an invitation to a conference in the U.S. because of the trade war.

“We don’t have any relationship with them,” Lefebvre said.

Ford did not reference his earlier threat directed at the U.S. when he was in Sudbury last week but rather called the industry a “heartbeat of the north and an engine of our economy.”

The premier was touring an expansion at Glencore Canada’s Craig Mine, where the existing mine shaft was deepened to gain access to nickel and copper ore. Ford donned an orange hard hat and a high-visibility suit before descending deep into the hot, cavernous mine.

He said the project reinforces the province’s position as “a global supplier of high-class nickel the world needs.”

“And guess who else needs it?” Ford said. “President Trump needs it desperately.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says everything is on the table, including surcharges on electricity the province sends to several American states, amid the escalating U.S.-Canada trade war. Ford called U.S. President Donald Trump a 'loser' in his response to the latest tariff threats.

Despite the rhetoric, Marie Litalien, president of the Greater Sudbury Chamber of Commerce, said “it’s business as usual” for the municipality, which is used to weathering economic ups and downs.

Questions about tariff ramifications are hanging over some small- and medium-sized businesses, she said, but the community is focused on attracting investment and strengthening their international relationships.

The politics of Ford’s threat to cut the U.S. off from critical minerals is “not really of any consequence to us,” she said, adding the government should keep putting funding toward Canadian infrastructure.

Because Sudbury is a global mining centre, “I have no doubt that we’re prepared to deal with any short-term and long-term effects in this,” she said.

Sadequl Islam, an economics professor at Sudbury’s Laurentian University, said there are lessons for flailing Ontario municipalities.

Relying heavily on one industry – such as Sault Ste. Marie’s dependence on steel – is risky, Islam said, and other communities could learn from Sudbury’s diversification. For example, it’s had success boosting its financial services sector on top of its position as a mining powerhouse.

Size also matters in Sudbury’s case, he said, as it is the largest municipality in the province by land area, and it could benefit from the mayor’s push for a special economic zone designation.

Lefebvre, who is seeking re-election this fall, said his push for the designation is a unique ask, but argued Sudbury contributes more to the province’s economy than many other municipalities and deserves infrastructure support.

“We are an economic zone that is very special in our country,” he said. “Nobody else has this around the world.”

David Robinson, a retired professor of resource and environmental economics at Laurentian, also said Sudbury stands to suffer much less than the rest of the country.

Robinson also doubts the U.S. would ever impose tariffs on nickel, pointing out that the metal is necessary for vehicles made by billionaire Elon Musk’s Tesla, and Musk is an on-again-off-again ally of the president. And if tariffs on nickel were to be imposed, much of the effects would be offset by adjustments in international markets, Robinson said, and the U.S. would simply be raising prices for their own manufacturers.

“We can do without American wine and whiskey,” he said, but the U.S. can’t do without the goods that go into production processes, from nickel and uranium to potash and timber.

He, too, believes Ford’s threat to cut off critical minerals was a smart play.

“What happens if you choked all those goods off?” Robinson said. “Suddenly, you’ve got a baseball bat instead of a pencil to fight with.”

stories.title: Canadian families still waiting for answers a week after deadly flash flood in Nepal
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand has said 30 Canadians and permanent residents are among the missing – a number that May change
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Neeral Patel sent well-wishes to her cousin on his birthday last Wednesday, but she never heard back.

Her cousin Ishan Patel was in Nepal at the time, not far from the border with China, where a devastating flash flood ripped through the valley that same day.

She’s calling for a wider international response to help in rescue efforts as the days tick by with no word on her cousin or the three family members he was travelling with.

Ishan Patel was travelling with his wife, Akanksha Patel, both dual Canadian-U. S. citizens, along with his mother, Shilpa Patel, and father-in-law, Umesh Patel, who are Canadian, she said.

The four were on a long-planned pilgrimage to Mount Kaliash ahead of Ishan Patel starting a new job as an orthopedic surgeon, after finishing his fellowship in July, said Neeral Patel.

“It was kind of the big holy beginnings to his new career.”

The flooding on Aug. 26 killed at least 1,118 people and left more than 3,900 missing after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said 324 foreign nationals have been rescued, while about 590 from 39 countries remain unaccounted for.

Ottawa had said 30 Canadians and permanent residents were among the missing. Later Wednesday, it reported that one Canadian citizen was safe, and the tally was changed to 29.

“The individual was unreachable due to communication outages and established contact yesterday,” Anita Anand, Canada’s foreign affairs minister, said in statement.

In Kathmandu, police have buried dozens of unidentified bodies in trenches because there are too many to keep or identify individually.

The scale of the disaster is hampering rescue efforts, as landslides and destroyed roads have cut off remote areas.

Rescuers were also racing to reach hundreds of hydropower workers trapped in tunnels.

With so many still unaccounted for, Neeral Patel said family members have been left scouring the internet, looking on Nepal police sites and missing identity sites to see if the names of any relatives come up.

She said two family members have also travelled to Kathmandu to look in hospitals and anywhere else they can find answers, but the roads up to the flood-hit area are closed.

Making the wait even harder is that they know where to search, she said, because her cousin’s phone pinged from a spot a short distance from Hotel Kailash, where they had breakfast last Wednesday.

“This is why we’re urging everyone to please, in the right area, search as much as you can, because we’re coming up to a week’s time and still no news,” she said.

Anand said search teams in China and Nepal are using a range of specialized tools and technologies including drones, helicopters, search dogs and other advanced equipment as the ground search continues.

She added that Canada would be sending more than 18,000 emergency items from Canadian Red Cross stockpiles, including blankets and buckets, to the area in addition to the $5 million Ottawa has already pledged in humanitarian aid.

“We have a 10-person team on the ground in Nepal. I am in continuous touch with my colleague, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal, and we will leave no stone unturned to help Canadians in need.”

Patel said Global Affairs told her family about the team being sent but they’re still holding out hope for a bigger response.

“There should be a global effort, everyone work together to try to bring our family members home.”

stories.title: September kicks off with extreme heat warning issued for London area
stories.summary: September kicks off with extreme heat warning issued for London area CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 2, 2026 11:01 AM | Last Updated: 14 hours ago
Thousands left without power in parts of Huron, Lambton and Perth counties
A tornado watch has been dropped for London and Middlesex County following a busy afternoon of severe weather across southwestern Ontario.

A severe thunderstorm watch and yellow heat warning remained in place for the London area as of 8 p.m. A yellow severe thunderstorm warning was also active for St. Thomas and Elgin County and areas between London and Chatham-Kent.
Thousands of people were left without power in Huron, Lambton, Oxford and Perth counties after a major storm that crossed Lake Huron from Michigan battered the region around 5 p.m.
Nearly 5,000 were offline in the Grand Bend and Lambton Shores areas, while nearly 3,500 were without power near Goderich, in Ashfield-Colborne-Wawanosh, Central Huron and North Huron.

Several roads in the region have also been impacted by fallen trees and downed power lines , according to Ontario Provincial Police, including Highway 8 from Clinton to Road 140, Highway 23 near Road 165, and Perth Line 55 from Highway 23 to Road 166.
Power had been expected to return to most areas by 7:30 or 7:45 p.m., but remained out as of 8 p.m., according to the Hydro One outage map. Roughly 2,000 people were also impacted near Woodstock.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.
The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.
A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.
It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.
Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."
One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.
"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.
The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.
Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.
People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.
The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.
The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.
It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.
A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the
Middlesex-London Health Unit website .
There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.
It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.
Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

In London, a small branch on a power line along Empress Avenue knocked out power to residents in Blackfriars and West London, according to London Hydro , who estimated power would be restored by 10:30 p.m.

The storm system triggered a red thunderstorm warning for areas north of London into Midwestern Ontario, and along the Lake Huron shoreline from Ipperwash to Goderich.

A red tornado warning had also been issued for the Clinton area, Mitchell, Seaforth and Vanastra, but was lifted as the storm moved eastward at 75 km/h to 100 km/h, according to Environment Canada.

It's unclear whether a downburst or tornado occurred, and no significant damage has been reported so far.

Environment Canada initially issued an orange-level tornado watch at 4:25 p.m. ET, warning that conditions were favourable for the development of thunderstorms that could produce a tornado with significant winds, large hail and torrential rain.

Severe weather meteorologist Rob Kuhn said the greatest risk was expected between 4 p.m. and 8 p.m. ET, with the potential for torrential rain, large hail and damaging wind gusts.

"These thunderstorms could pack quite a punch," said Kuhn early in the day. "There is also a risk of an isolated tornado system through late this afternoon to early this evening, so it's got the potential to be a very active day."

One thunderstorm moved quickly through London around 2 p.m., bringing heavy rain and hail to some areas.

"The black cloud came over, and all of a sudden golf ball-sized hail stones were coming down," said Matt Goldsmith, who was working on a home in east London at the time.

The hail dented Goldsmith's truck but quickly stopped, he said, with the sun back out by the time he finished his lunch. More rain, however, would be on the way.

Environment Canada urges people to continue monitoring weather alerts and forecasts.

If a tornado warning is issued for an area, officials say people should go indoors immediately and move to a room on the lowest floor, away from outside walls and windows. A basement, bathroom, stairwell or interior closet can provide shelter.

People in mobile homes, vehicles, tents, trailers or other temporary or free-standing shelters should move to a strong building if possible.

The agency says people should take cover immediately if they hear a roaring sound, see a funnel cloud or swirling debris near the ground, or see threatening weather approaching.

The tornado watch comes amid an ongoing extreme heat warning for the London area.

Wednesday's daytime high was expected to reach 32 C, with the humidex making it feel closer to 41. The Middlesex-London Health Unit is reminding people to take precautions in the heat, including drinking plenty of water, limiting time outdoors, seeking shade and avoiding strenuous physical activity.

It also warns people never to leave children or pets in parked cars.

A full list of recommendations to avoid heat-related illness and other resources is available on the

Middlesex-London Health Unit website .

There won't be much relief overnight, with the temperature expected to fall only to 19 C. Environment Canada says there will continue to be a risk of thunderstorms late into Wednesday night.

It will be mainly cloudy Thursday, with a 40 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, a risk of a thunderstorm and a high of 27 C, feeling more like 35.

Friday will be cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a high of 26 C. Saturday will be cloudy, with a high of 24 C.

stories.title: Pentagon defends Hegseth's controversial post about Canadian cadet program
stories.summary: The Pentagon is standing behind a controversial social media post by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about a Canadian cadet program as the Trump administration continues to denigrate Canada’s Armed Forces.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WASHINGTON -- The Pentagon is standing behind a controversial social media post by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth about a Canadian cadet program as the Trump administration continues to denigrate Canada’s Armed Forces.

Hegseth on Monday posted an image from the Cadet Training Centre in Vernon, B.C., depicting two young women in uniform with the caption “this is real” alongside a Canadian flag.

The online response to Hegseth’s post was filled with remarks belittling the physical appearance of the cadets but it also triggered massive backlash from Canadians.

Some people posted that it was unfair for Hegseth to target the youth program in an attempt to disparage the Canadian Armed Forces and others criticized the U.S. defence secretary for body-shaming women serving in the cadet program.

Asked about the backlash Tuesday, Pentagon deputy press secretary Jacob Bliss said, “The X post speaks for itself.”

Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Tuesday that comments from Trump administration officials maligning Canada’s military were “beneath their office.”

B.C. Premier David Eby said Hegseth’s post and the Pentagon’s defence of it were an embarrassment.

“It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” Eby said.

He cited an ongoing military conference in Victoria, which includes U.S. representatives, as an example of the importance of co-operation during “unstable times.”

The post comes amid increased tensions between Canada and the United States after trade talks broke down last month.

The Trump administration hit Canada with 50 per cent tariffs on an array of goods in August, with both countries blaming the other for adding last-minute changes during negotiations.

Canada is set to implement its retaliatory duties next week.

Trump has spent the weeks since talks were frozen incessantly targeting Canada in his public remarks and social media posts. Last week, he signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” in his latest effort to agitate America’s northern neighbour.

Many in Trump’s team have turned their insults to Canada’s military. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday told CNBC the U.S. isn’t at war with Canada.

“What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?” Bessent said.

The week prior, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy claimed on Fox News that Canada “doesn’t have a military.”

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis responded to Hegseth’s post on Monday saying “cadets do great work, and are not members of the military.” He added that “158 members of the Canadian military gave their lives in Afghanistan after your country was attacked.”

“Canada and the U.S. have a great history of fighting together for freedom and justice. It’s history worth remembering,” Genuis said.

The Army Cadet League of Canada condemned the online harassment and mockery of cadets and their achievements.

“Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the league said about Hegseth’s remarks in a statement.

It said the league “stands firmly behind cadets, adult staff, volunteers, and officers who dedicate their time to building stronger communities and developing the next generation of Canadian leaders.”

The national, community-based cadet program is for youth aged 12 to 18. A federal government website says the program provides “opportunities for youth to gain valuable knowledge and skills that build confidence and help pave the way in a transition to adulthood.”

🇨🇦 (this is real) pic.twitter.com/Ucx2FNdi1q — Pete Hegseth (@PeteHegseth) September 1, 2026

It’s not clear how exactly the cadet training program’s Instagram account -- which had 1,821 followers as of Tuesday morning -- came onto Hegseth’s radar. Bliss, who works in the office of the assistant to the secretary of war for public affairs, did not respond to questions about how the defence secretary became aware of it.

The post comes as Hegseth is facing immense pressure domestically from an unpopular and escalating war with Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, depleting stockpiles of munitions and the departure of top military figures during his tenure.

In the latest series of shakeups of military leadership, on Monday Army Secretary Dan Driscoll handed in his resignation following widely reported tensions with Hegseth.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

By Kelly Geraldine Malone

With files from Chuck Chiang and Nono Shen in Vancouver and The Associated Press

stories.title: The weak link in Canada’s ambitions
stories.summary: The breakdown of the Second Narrows bridge in B.C. highlights the fragility of this country’s window to the Pacific
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
It is hard to imagine a piece of infrastructure more vital to the national economy than the Second Narrows Bridge over the Burrard Inlet in British Columbia’s Lower Mainland – the only rail crossing connecting two halves of the Port of Vancouver.

It is a critical link connecting the Canadian economy to markets across the world, but it is also a weak link.

In February, the 57-year-old bridge got stuck in the down position for four days, blocking the passage of commercial ships. The breakdown practically ground the port to a standstill.

On the south side of the bridge, nestled against the downtown core of the city, is the port’s container terminals and cruise terminal, among others. Serviced by the bridge on the north side of the port are terminals that ship out critical Canadian commodities such as potash, grain, sulphur, forestry products, and steel.

The bridge must rise for the large cargo vessels servicing the petroleum marine terminals east of the crossing. While crews worked to fix the problem, trains were also restricted from crossing and unloading in terminals on the other side of the bridge.

This standstill at Canada’s port happened days before the closing of a critical global shipping channel: the Strait of Hormuz. As the war in the Middle East kicked off, backlogged in the Port of Vancouver were mountains of the kinds of critical resources the world most needed. Trans Mountain Corp. (TMX) has the capacity to fill up 30 oil tankers from its Port of Vancouver marine terminal every month. In February, it loaded and shipped 17 tankers, just over half of its total capacity.

This moment is representative of not just the weaknesses of a single port, but also the broader failings of the Canadian economy. The problems facing this bridge have been well known for decades (like, say, the overdependence of the Canadian economy on the U.S. market). But for years, that problem has been kicked down the road, rather than undertaking necessary but unglamorous work (again, an unfortunate parallel with the national economy). And that neglect came back to bite at a most inopportune time, this past February in Vancouver, and the past year, nationwide.

The Port of Vancouver is a representation of what Canada can offer the world. Everyday $1-billion worth of the nation’s riches pass through it: Atlantic lobster, Quebec aluminum, Saskatchewan potash and grain, Albertan energy and B.C. lumber.

The bridge is the key to achieving federal promises of doubling non-U.S. exports within the decade. It will also be essential should Ottawa successfully invigorate a resource industry that will depend upon the reliable flow of goods in and out of this port.

Yet considering the significance of this bridge, it receives little attention.

Some work is happening with regards to dredging the inlet beneath the bridge. In June, the port authority gained all regulatory authorizations required to dig into the shallow sides of the channel leading up to the bridge. It means that the vessels passing underneath, such as those calling at Westridge Marine Terminal, can sink deeper into the water. They will be able to load more cargo.

This a small change – the plan is to dredge an area of two hectares to a depth averaging 1.3 metres below the seabed – and yet it still took over one year to get regulatory approval. It will be at least 2027 until work is completed (depending on when construction begins).

But timeline of this project is not what makes it problematic. It is the fact that this is the only project happening with regards to the narrow stretch of Pacific water that severs the Port of Vancouver in half.

This crossing will still need to lift for vessels passing below, stalling traffic on either side. And should we see a predictable repeat of the closing that happened in February, a slightly deeper seabed won’t matter much. The Port of Vancouver is at the mercy of one weak link in its chain; a new link must be forged.

Ottawa wants to expand Canada’s resources sector, increase exports to Asia and send a message to the world that this country is open for business. Dealing with the chokepoint of the Second Narrows, at long last, will be a test of the government’s seriousness.

Editor’s note: This article has been updated to clarify that the Vancouver port authority plans to dredge a two-hectare area to a depth averaging 1.3 metres below the Burrard Inlet's seabed.

The problems facing this bridge have been well known for decades (like, say, the overdependence of the Canadian economy on the U.S. market). But for years, that problem has been kicked down the road, rather than undertaking necessary but unglamorous work (again, an unfortunate parallel with the national economy). And that neglect came back to bite at a most inopportune time, this past February in Vancouver, and the past year, nationwide.

stories.title: Business Brief: The road to rate change is paved with protectionism
stories.summary: Forecasting the Bank of Canada beyond today’s rate decision
stories.author: Matt Lundy
stories.content:
Good morning. The Bank of Canada is widely expected to hold rates steady at 2.25 per cent today, as it has all year. The more relevant question is whether the next move is up or down – and on what timeline. Keep scrolling for the details to consider for your calendar.

Trade: Canada is willing to return to the negotiating table once the U.S. changes its tone and can “stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said.

Labour: Unifor began contract talks with Stellantis , vowing to fight for the Brampton assembly plant’s future, while securing production volumes at factories in Windsor and Toronto.

Streaming: JioHotstar, one of India’s largest streaming services, launches in Canada today with offerings ranging from reality TV shows to Bollywood movies.

Hi, I’m Matt Lundy, economics editor at The Globe. The Bank of Canada will make its next interest-rate decision on Wednesday morning. Don’t expect any fireworks. Regardless, there will be plenty to unpack.

Investors have certainly cast their vote: Lending rates will be much higher by next summer. As of Tuesday, swaps markets were pricing in one quarter-point rate hike by January and three by July, according to Bloomberg data. Those would take the central bank’s benchmark interest rate to 3 per cent.

But there’s a difference between expectations and reality. Investors have been quick to predict a rate-hike cycle that, as of yet, hasn’t materialized. In the spring, for instance, swaps markets were pricing in a rate hike for today, on account of inflationary pressures stemming from the Middle East war.

Economists on Bay Street have overwhelmingly projected rates to hold steady this year – so far they’ve been proven correct – as the Bank of Canada weighs the stagflationary risks posed by protectionism.

Still, market watchers will be closely parsing Governor Tiff Macklem’s comments for how the central bank is thinking about this new phase of the Canada-U.S. trade war.

Trade comments

Canada is around 18 months into a trade war with the United States that, as early as next week, could ratchet up further, with Ottawa set to impose countertariffs on some American goods. The U.S. has threatened to retaliate against Canada’s retaliation, adding even more uncertainty to the near-term outlook.

The trade war is a tricky situation for the BoC, because these barriers constrain economic growth (a reason to cut rates) while also raising prices (a reason to hike rates). And as Macklem has stressed before, monetary policy can only help the country so much.

“The Bank of Canada hasn’t recently outlined a playbook for dealing with both upside inflation risks and downside growth risks,” Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins Securities, said in a recent client note. “At a time when the nation’s economy is under assault, it could be argued that monetary policy needs to row in the same direction as fiscal policy,” he added, meaning lower lending rates to support the economy.

“But taking a step back, the Bank of Canada’s inflation mandate dictates that monetary policy respond to price pressures ahead of growth concerns when the two are in conflict.”

If Canada imposes countertariffs on Sept. 8, as currently planned, that would likely give a modest lift to the overall inflation rate. This was observed last year, when Ottawa retaliated against the early rounds of American tariffs on Canadian products.

This year, the added risk is that consumers are facing major pain at gas stations, given the trickle of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate pushed above US$90 a barrel yesterday on renewed fighting between the U.S. and Iran.

The conflict is having a big effect on consumer prices . Canada’s headline inflation rate hit 3 per cent in July, the top end of the BoC’s target range. (While the central bank’s inflation target is 2 per cent, it has some wiggle room on either side, so that it doesn’t overreact to temporary factors affecting prices.) Core measures of inflation, which strip out volatile price movements, are more in line with the bank’s target, suggesting inflation isn’t overly worrisome.

That could prove fleeting, on account of a U.S.-Iran war and a U.S.-Canada trade war that aren’t relenting. In all likelihood, the BoC will need to stand by and see how those situations develop. But again, Macklem’s comments will be under the microscope for any clues on the rate path.

No Canadian-listed ETF tracks the MSCI World Equal Weighted Index, but there are some other options, which have their own pros and cons. Equal-weight indexes tend to outperform, but can also lag over extended periods. Investment reporter Andrew Galbraith answers a reader question: How can I buy an equal-weighted global ETF?

I won’t pretend I’m a deep tech expert, but I’m pretty good at picking out people who have a chance of being great entrepreneurs, and she just struck me that way. — Daniel Debow, angel investor and ex-Shopify Inc. executive

Olivia Leng, 21, is a piano teacher, a powerlifter and an entrepreneur with an ambitious goal: invent a high-performance superconducting material that would make quantum computers more commercially viable. Her tech startup, Meissner, just scored millions in funding from prominent financiers, Sean Silcoff reports .

Feeling: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says Russia’s presence at a G20 meeting hosted by the U.S. has made many countries uncomfortable .

Taste: Patrons of Schwartz’s Deli, the Montreal smoked-meat institution, love the locally brewed black cherry soda that replaced an American offering on the restaurant’s menu.

After the bell: We’re watching for earnings reports expected from Broadcom Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.

Global markets fell as fresh U.S. airstrikes ​on Iran pushed oil prices to five-week highs, ‌stoking inflation concerns and extending a global bond sell-off .

Wall Street futures in the red after major North American markets closed down yesterday. TSX futures followed sentiment lower.

Overseas, the pan-European STOXX 600 was down 0.57 per cent in morning trading. Britain’s FTSE 100 fell 0.56 per cent, Germany’s DAX dropped 0.77 per cent and France’s CAC 40 gave back 0.62 per cent.

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei closed 2.85 per cent lower, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.07 per cent.

The Canadian dollar traded at 71.73 U.S. cents.

stories.title: Tiff 2026: The 15 buzziest movies you can’t miss at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival
stories.summary: The Globe’s most anticipated films include a Palme d’Or winner, Korea’s submission at the Academy Awards and a satirical Brian Mulroney documentary
stories.author: Barry Hertz, Johanna Schneller, Brad Wheeler, Radheyan Simonpillai
stories.content:
Even though corporate mergers, the threat of AI and myriad other crises loom in the background of the film industry, the promise of a new edition of the Toronto International Film Festival tends to erase any doom and gloom for the time being.

But with almost 300 titles to choose from at the 51st annual edition of TIFF, ticket-buyers need all the help they can get to know where to focus their attention and which movies to keep on their radar after the festival ends. To that end, The Globe and Mail has been busy digging through this year’s slate to bring you our most anticipated TIFF 2026 prospects.

An absurdist comedy pitched as the abandoned love child of Nathan Fielder, John Wilson, and alt-comedy pioneers Tim & Eric (whose company Abso Lutely Productions helped birth this vision into the world), the second feature from experimental comic Matt Barats promises to simultaneously enthrall and bewilder Midnight Madness audiences.

Japanese director Takashi Miike has made more movies than you’ve likely had meals, so his batting average can be a bit wobbly. But this spiritual sequel to Abel Ferrara’s 1992 cult classic (which itself was followed up by the narratively unrelated 2009 Werner Herzog film Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans ) has the potential to deliver the best kind of gonzo Miike cinema, akin to his Dead or Alive trilogy. Following a tough Tokyo cop (Shun Oguri) as he hunts down a crazed killer alongside FBI agent (Lily James), the film promises more neon than the eye could possibly handle.

Arriving in Toronto after winning the Palme d’Or in Cannes this spring, Cristian Mungiu’s morality play might be the most effective drama of the festival . Like the Romanian director’s Graduation , R.M.N. , and 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days (the latter of which won Cannes’ Palme d’Or in 2007), Fjord is a thorny look at societal taboos and the splintering of the family unit. But the director takes a more stomach-twisting approach than even his most loyal admirers are used to, aided by excellent performances from Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve.

September, 1989, National Theatre, London. Daniel-Day Lewis, mid- Hamlet , breaks down in tears and leaves the stage, never to return. Enter Ian Charleson, the Scottish actor famous for playing the priest “running for God” in Chariots of Fire . Unbeknownst to everyone except his director, Charleson is dying of AIDS-related complications, yet he delivers a handful of incandescent performances, confronting mortality in character and in life.

When he dies in January, 1990, eight weeks after his final performance, his obituary includes his real cause of death, the first British celebrity to do so. I have huge hopes that a film about a moment this indelible will be incredible, especially with Andrew Scott, an acclaimed Hamlet himself, playing Charleson, and Olivia Colman as a doctor desperate to beat back the raging HIV epidemic.

With her 2022 film Slash/Back , the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.

With In the Heart of the South , Innuksuk turns her camera on another alien landscape: the Toronto art world. Anna Lambe ( North of North ) stars as Yura, an up-and-comer whose latest piece recalls a traumatic story from her Inuk youth. But things begin to unravel when someone from that story, her friend Sesi (Zorga Qaunaq), roars back into her life. Innuksuk is sharply insightful about the way Canada’s South perceives – and co-opts – its North, but she embeds her observations organically in character and story. This one looks like smart, twisty fun.

“Go in there, read, sing, kill.” That’s the mandate for Misty Green (Rosalind Eleazar), an Emmy-winning actress who blew up her career, but may have a second chance. That is, if this audition goes well, and she can overcome her own stubborn independence, and deal with her unpredictable brother (Daniel Kaluuya) and problematic ex (Adam Driver) – not to mention the racism, sexism and classism that Hollywood pretends it doesn’t have.

I’ve just realized that all three of my picks this year are about outsiders struggling to make art in worlds that don’t welcome them. It’s crucial to see that in films, because they are still a potent deliverer of our cultural mythologies. Chris Rock – who wrote, produced and stars here, as well as directed – appears to have made it to the top. I can’t wait to see what raw truths he exposes about all it takes to get there.

So much of the excitement around Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is predicated on what it is not. As in, it’s not Blade . Or rather, it’s not the Blade movie that star Mahershala Ali and writer and director Bassam Tariq were set to make for Marvel, before that reboot fell apart. The duo walked away from that disaster and made what looks like the furthest thing from a Marvel movie: an intimate and melancholic crime thriller that cites Islamic scripture in its title. Ali stars as a hitman struggling to raise kids on his own after his wife’s sudden death. He gets to wield a blade. That’s really all we wanted.

It’s been eight years since Lee Chang-dong’s last movie (2018’s Burning ) and another eight years since the one before that (2010’s Poetry ). I’d like to think Korea’s master dramatist has been giving us the time to recuperate. His films have been soul-shaking portraits of people coping with unimaginable loss, unbearable guilt or unspeakable anger – sometimes all at once.

Chang-dong’s latest, which is Korea’s submission for the international prize at the Academy Awards, is about the intense, close-quarters relationship between two couples, one a pair of documentary filmmakers, and the other their subject. That’s a vague premise, I know. But I didn’t need to be told any of that to be sold.

Last year’s TIFF had Chandler Levack’s sophomore film, the semi-autobiographical Mile End Kicks , in which she mined her own past life as a Toronto freelance arts and culture writer who moves to Montreal and finds herself in the era before #MeToo. This year, Alexandra Pechman, another former freelance writer, whose byline appeared in the pages of Vogue and The New York Times, is premiering Magazine at the festival.

Her movie looks back at the same era but at a New Yorker-like magazine. Two movies don’t make a trend, but I’m interested in seeing this become one. I’m curious to see my contemporaries revisit a moment I sort of witnessed and open my eyes to the things I missed.

Director Ira Sachs’s story about a New York artist dying of AIDS in the 1980s is a story close to the director’s own heart, as the filmmaker himself moved to New York during the peak of the AIDS crisis in the late 1980s. The Man I Love , starring Rami Malek, is a portrait of a man still driven to create – in this case, to perform the lead in an adaptation of a piece by Quebec playwright Michel Tremblay – in spite of a terminal diagnosis. Sachs, who last directed 2023’s Passages , has a deft hand with intimacy, longing and loss. The Man I Love promises to centre the artist, not his illness, while never forgetting the crisis that devastated so many like Malek’s character in real life.

The double-barrelled threat of climate change and a hot real estate market meet in Piedmont in this documentary that looks at the past, present and unsure future of three winemaking families in the region. The Northern Italian area is a stunning backdrop to a narrative that looks at whether the next generation of Piedmontese winemakers are willing to inherit the family business, or if they would rather accept a tempting offer from a foreign real estate investor to relieve them of an uncertain future.

Our Lady Peace may not be the nineties Canadian alt-rock band with the biggest hits, the most memorable singles or the most staying power. But don’t tell any of that to the titular OLP superfan Gail. Directed by Michael Maxxis, the documentary follows Gail as she, in turn, follows the band across the country on their 30th anniversary tour. Gail is middle-aged, unapologetic in her devotion to the band and, interestingly, American, making this film not only a compelling cultural curiosity, but a timely case study in the unifying cross-border power of Cancon.

Documentarian Sean Menard, who previously explored made-in-Canada phenomena Vince Carter (2017’s The Carter Effect ) and MuchMusic (2023’s 299 Queen Street West ) now delivers a portrait of iconic marathoner Terry Fox. I do hope the title is not a riff on Forrest Gump ’s “run, Forrest, run” meme.

In case anyone wonders which A-list drummers may have been considered as fill-ins for the late Neil Peart on the current comeback tour by Canadian prog-rockers Rush, this rock doc features performance sequences with Stewart Copeland, Danny Carey, Chad Smith and Gavin Harrison sitting in with the band’s Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson.

Do not complain after the festival that you didn’t go to a screening of Matthew Rankin’s far-out, satirical documentary on Canada’s 18th prime minister. As Brian Mulroney said to John Turner, you had an option.

content_blocks.text: When he dies in January, 1990, eight weeks after his final performance, his obituary includes his real cause of death, the first British celebrity to do so. I have huge hopes that a film about a moment this indelible will be incredible, especially with Andrew Scott, an acclaimed Hamlet himself, playing Charleson, and Olivia Colman as a doctor desperate to beat back the raging HIV epidemic.

content_blocks.text: In the Heart of the South
content_blocks.html: In the Heart of the South

content_blocks.caption: Zorga Qaunaq and Anna Lambe in In the Heart of the South. TIFF/Supplied

content_blocks.text: With her 2022 film Slash/Back , the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.
content_blocks.html: With her 2022 film Slash/Back, the Igloolik-born director Nyla Innuksuk delivered a miracle: a rollicking, ambitious, teen-girl sci-fi, shot entirely in Pangnirtung, Nunavut, with largely non-professional actors on a ungirut (shoestring) budget.

content_blocks.text: With In the Heart of the South , Innuksuk turns her camera on another alien landscape: the Toronto art world. Anna Lambe ( North of North ) stars as Yura, an up-and-comer whose latest piece recalls a traumatic story from her Inuk youth. But things begin to unravel when someone from that story, her friend Sesi (Zorga Qaunaq), roars back into her life. Innuksuk is sharply insightful about the way Canada’s South perceives – and co-opts – its North, but she embeds her observations organically in character and story. This one looks like smart, twisty fun.

content_blocks.text: Misty Green
content_blocks.html: Misty Green

content_blocks.caption: Misty Green stars Rosalind Eleazar as an actress looking for a second chance. Merrick Morton/Supplied

content_blocks.text: “Go in there, read, sing, kill.” That’s the mandate for Misty Green (Rosalind Eleazar), an Emmy-winning actress who blew up her career, but may have a second chance. That is, if this audition goes well, and she can overcome her own stubborn independence, and deal with her unpredictable brother (Daniel Kaluuya) and problematic ex (Adam Driver) – not to mention the racism, sexism and classism that Hollywood pretends it doesn’t have.

content_blocks.text: I’ve just realized that all three of my picks this year are about outsiders struggling to make art in worlds that don’t welcome them. It’s crucial to see that in films, because they are still a potent deliverer of our cultural mythologies. Chris Rock – who wrote, produced and stars here, as well as directed – appears to have made it to the top. I can’t wait to see what raw truths he exposes about all it takes to get there.

content_blocks.text: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
content_blocks.html: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

content_blocks.text: So much of the excitement around Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother is predicated on what it is not. As in, it’s not Blade . Or rather, it’s not the Blade movie that star Mahershala Ali and writer and director Bassam Tariq were set to make for Marvel, before that reboot fell apart. The duo walked away from that disaster and made what looks like the furthest thing from a Marvel movie: an intimate and melancholic crime thriller that cites Islamic scripture in its title. Ali stars as a hitman struggling to raise kids on his own after his wife’s sudden death. He gets to wield a blade. That’s really all we wanted.

content_blocks.caption: Possible Love comes to Toronto eight years after Lee Chang-dong's last drama. Netflix/Supplied

content_blocks.text: It’s been eight years since Lee Chang-dong’s last movie (2018’s Burning ) and another eight years since the one before that (2010’s Poetry ). I’d like to think Korea’s master dramatist has been giving us the time to recuperate. His films have been soul-shaking portraits of people coping with unimaginable loss, unbearable guilt or unspeakable anger – sometimes all at once.

content_blocks.text: Last year’s TIFF had Chandler Levack’s sophomore film, the semi-autobiographical Mile End Kicks , in which she mined her own past life as a Toronto freelance arts and culture writer who moves to Montreal and finds herself in the era before #MeToo. This year, Alexandra Pechman, another former freelance writer, whose byline appeared in the pages of Vogue and The New York Times, is premiering Magazine at the festival.

content_blocks.text: The Man I Love
content_blocks.html: The Man I Love

content_blocks.caption: The Man I Love stars Rami Malek as a man driven to create while dying during the AIDS crisis. TIFF/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Director Ira Sachs’s story about a New York artist dying of AIDS in the 1980s is a story close to the director’s own heart, as the filmmaker himself moved to New York during the peak of the AIDS crisis in the late 1980s. The Man I Love , starring Rami Malek, is a portrait of a man still driven to create – in this case, to perform the lead in an adaptation of a piece by Quebec playwright Michel Tremblay – in spite of a terminal diagnosis. Sachs, who last directed 2023’s Passages , has a deft hand with intimacy, longing and loss. The Man I Love promises to centre the artist, not his illness, while never forgetting the crisis that devastated so many like Malek’s character in real life.

content_blocks.text: Low Lies the Land
content_blocks.html: Low Lies the Land

content_blocks.caption: Low Lies The Land looks at three Italian winemaking families in Piedmont. TIFF/Supplied

content_blocks.text: The double-barrelled threat of climate change and a hot real estate market meet in Piedmont in this documentary that looks at the past, present and unsure future of three winemaking families in the region. The Northern Italian area is a stunning backdrop to a narrative that looks at whether the next generation of Piedmontese winemakers are willing to inherit the family business, or if they would rather accept a tempting offer from a foreign real estate investor to relieve them of an uncertain future.

content_blocks.text: Gail
content_blocks.html: Gail

content_blocks.caption: Gail follows a superfan of Canadian band Our Lady Peace. TIFF/Supplied

content_blocks.text: Our Lady Peace may not be the nineties Canadian alt-rock band with the biggest hits, the most memorable singles or the most staying power. But don’t tell any of that to the titular OLP superfan Gail. Directed by Michael Maxxis, the documentary follows Gail as she, in turn, follows the band across the country on their 30th anniversary tour. Gail is middle-aged, unapologetic in her devotion to the band and, interestingly, American, making this film not only a compelling cultural curiosity, but a timely case study in the unifying cross-border power of Cancon.

stories.title: Inside the world’s most accessible circus at Toronto’s CNE
stories.summary: A performance championing disabled artists and accessibility features broadens spectators’ horizons
stories.author: Graham Isador, Photography by Laura Proctor
stories.content:
Inside one of the world’s most accessible circuses, making its Canadian debut at Toronto’s CNE

Omnium Circus is widely considered one of the world’s most accessible stage shows. This week, its flagship act I’M POSSIBLE is on at the Canadian National Exhibition in Toronto.

With access accommodations built into the performance and several disabled entertainers championed on each bill, the show is a celebration of access culture and a space where audiences with disabilities are both welcomed and encouraged.

“Our access is integral to the production, as opposed to a retrofitted afterthought,” said Lisa B. Lewis , the Omnium founder. To make I’M POSSIBLE accessible to all audience members, the circus features sensory-first design (think house lights on at a low level), ASL translation, audio description devices and captioning when available.

On a practical level, that allows patrons with disabilities to engage with the show in a setting that feels more comfortable than a traditional circus. The venue and the entertainers can also introduce the concept of accessible performance to people who may not have engaged with it before.

“What Omnium does is different because we focus on the things that unite all of us and the human spirit that we all share, rather than focusing on just physical things that make us different,” said Ms. Lewis.

Attendees can expect acrobatics, music, and a few whimsical surprises at the show. Headlining the performances in Toronto is deaf ringmaster Malik Paris . Before joining the circus, Mr. Paris had worked as an actor and performance artist, but Omnium was a new opportunity to share his talents.

“This is the first time I’ve ever been in a leading role in a performance piece, especially one that tours all over,” Mr. Paris told The Globe via e-mail.

“Even though I am the first Deaf ringmaster, it doesn’t feel like a ‘first,’ it feels like a ‘finally.’ I’ve been here the whole time, but now, finally, I’m able to show the world what Deaf performers like me can do.”

Since its first live show in 2021, the organization has performed for more than 143,000 spectators across the United States.

The Canadian debut features one local performer, juggler and free-standing ladder acrobat: Abebe Erigete. While Mr. Erigete does not have a disability, the Omnium team believes his talent and story speak to the overall values of the company.

“Abebe trained in circus arts in Ethiopia, and has performed all over the world. One of his goals is to create a circus and dance show exploring the struggles of migration,” said Dan Lyon, the show’s Canadian producer and a trustee with the Circus Historical Society . “Abebe fits perfectly with the ethos of Omnium, which celebrates the achievements of talented people from all backgrounds.”

The feedback from patrons, both with and without disabilities, has been overwhelmingly positive, Ms. Lewis and Mr. Paris said.

They’ve received numerous letters from parents expressing thanks for the show, sharing stories about how Omnium has offered a safe environment for their kids to engage with new artistic practices and encouraging them to think differently about disability in general.

“In the middle of the circus, after seeing one of our artists flip his wheelchair over his head, a young [wheelchair user] screamed out, ‘Mom, I told you I could do more than the doctor said I could!’” said Ms. Lewis.

That kind of response is a major reason why the creative team wanted to make a different kind of circus. It’s a magical environment where people can open their minds to new ideas.

“[Omnium] allows audiences to experience the circus in a way that meets them where they are, which is so neat,” wrote Mr. Paris.

“And for many kids and families, this may be their first exposure to ASL, as well as a fully bilingual show like this. That kind of representation is much-needed across the entertainment industry.”

stories.title: Canadian Tire and Tim Hortons launch partnership to boost loyalty programs
stories.summary: Toronto — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. and Tim Hortons are hoping to perk up their customer bases by linking their loyalty programs.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Posted September 2, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated September 2, 2026 1:28 pm.

TORONTO — Canadian Tire Corp. Ltd. and Tim Hortons are hoping to perk up their customer bases by linking their loyalty programs.

Under a partnership launched between the home goods retailer and café giant Wednesday, customers who link their Triangle and Tims Rewards accounts will earn between two and five per cent in Canadian Tire money in addition to Tims points on select Tims purchases.

The arrangement is meant to draw Tims customers to Canadian Tire and vice versa.

Right now, 53 per cent of Triangle Rewards customers are enrolled in both loyalty programs. Canadian Tire has about 12 million Triangle Rewards members and 1,600 locations across its banners. Tims counts eight million loyalty program users and 4,000 restaurants in Canada.

By uniting, “both Triangle Rewards will grow and Tim Hortons reward members will grow,” Darryl Jenkins, Canadian Tire’s executive vice-president and chief development officer, said in an interview.

How much Canadian Tire money shoppers earn will depend on whether they use a Triangle credit card to pay and what they buy.

Canadian Tire money can be redeemed for savings on purchases at the retailer as well as its other banners, including SportChek, Mark’s and Party City. Tims points can be used to purchase food and beverages at the chain.

The arrangement came about organically, Jenkins and Hope Bagozzi, Tims’ chief marketing officer, said.

Canadian Tire and Tims executives sit on many of the same boards, often network with one another and their companies sponsor many of the same events, so it made sense for them to explore if they could boost the reach of their loyalty programs together.

“Wouldn’t it be great to add more value together?” was the thinking, Bagozzi recalled.

But Liza Amlani, principal and co-founder of the Retail Strategy Group, suspects “this is less about customer delight and more about two legacy brands scrambling for incremental share in an oversaturated loyalty market.”

“Canadians are already juggling too many programs, and unless the value proposition is simple, transparent and genuinely rewarding, this risks becoming just another corporate tie-up that benefits the brands more than the shoppers,” she said in an email when the partnership was teased last September.

Canadian Tire first announced the partnership almost a year ago but waited until Wednesday to launch it and reveal how it will work.

The year in between both milestones was spent ensuring the mechanics of the partnership will work on a technical level.

Jenkins said it was by chance that it’s launching “at a really interesting time” — just after the U.S. hit Canada with a fresh round of tariffs and as Canada prepares to implement its own round of retaliatory levies in September.

“We certainly didn’t plan it this way,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 2, 2026.

stories.title: Williams strikes out 13, leads Guardians to 6-1 win over Blue Jays
stories.summary: Williams struck out the side in the seventh and fanned five of his last six. It was his 10th double-digit strikeout game this season.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Tom Withers, The Associated Press

Posted September 2, 2026 5:27 am.

Gavin Williams struck out a career-high 13 and allowed just two singles in seven innings, leading the Cleveland Guardians to a 6-1 win on Tuesday night over the Toronto Blue Jays in a matchup of teams in the thick of the AL wild-card race.

Patrick Bailey, rookie Angel Genao and Angel Martinez all hit two-run homers for the Guardians, who are 11-4 since Aug. 12. Cleveland came in with a slim lead for the third wild-card spot.

Williams (13-7) began September by dominating the Blue Jays, allowing one unearned run. The right-hander, who was coming off a shaky outing last week, didn’t give up a hit until the fourth.

Williams struck out the side in the seventh and fanned five of his last six. It was his 10th double-digit strikeout game this season.

Hunter Gaddis and Matt Festa pitched an inning apiece to finish the three-hitter.

Bailey put the Guardians up 2-1 in the fifth with his eighth homer. Martinez led off with a walk, and one out later, Bailey drove a 3-1 pitch from Spencer Arighetti (7-8) into the left-field bleachers.

Pinch-hitting for fellow rookie Travis Bazzana in the seventh, Genao made it 4-1 with a 426-foot blast over the wall in left. Martinez opened with a single before Genao connected for his second homer since debuting on Aug. 5.

Martinez hit his 14th homer in the eighth.

Toronto got some help in scoring its only run off Williams in the fifth.

Rookie Kazuma Okamoto singled and went to third when Guardians catcher Bailey threw wildly into center on a steal. Williams then uncorked a wild pitch, allowing Okamoto to come home.
