Jordan Jullian had her heart set on attending the final regular season Calgary Flames’ game at the Saddledome.
Despite setting an alarm and waiting in a queue for 30 minutes before single-game tickets went on sale Monday, Jullian was out of luck.
“I was one minute in (and) all the tickets were sold,” she told Global News.
“I was actually in shock. I refreshed it a few times. I’m like, no way, this is like the Era’s Tour all over again.”
The upcoming 2026-2027 NHL season will be the Flames’ last at the Saddledome, which was built in 1983. The Flames will call the brand-new Scotia Place home the following season.

The $1.2 billion facility, located on the corner of 12 Avenue and Olympic Way S.E., is expected to seat 18,400 people for hockey games and up to 20,000 for concerts. It also includes a 1,000-seat community arena, indoor and outdoor plaza and a 450-stall parkade.
Steve Edgar, director of game operations and strategy for the Calgary Sports and Entertainment Corporation, said demand for the regular-season finale was always going to be high.
“It’s not just about one game. We’ve got so many great opportunities here for fans to come in (and) share their stories with us,” he said.
Resale tickets are already popping up on third-party websites. Prices range from $500 to nearly $1,500, and one expert warns scammers could be preying on buyers seeking high-demand tickets.
“It’s creating that emotion, that urgency and that demand,” said Julie Matthews, a consumer protection expert.
“It makes people maybe do a little bit less research than maybe they normally would.”
Unless the Flames make the NHL playoffs, its final game at the Saddledome — and its last game of the regular season — will be played on April 10 against the Vancouver Canucks.
– with files from Global News’ Craig Momney

stories.title: Woman randomly stabs 2 people in New York City’s Times Square, killing 1, then is killed by police
stories.summary: A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
NEW York — A woman randomly stabbed two people in New York City’s Times Square on Monday, killing one woman, and then was fatally shot by police, according to officials.

The shooting happened just before 4:30 p.m. next to a New York Police Department substation, just outside One Times Square, the building that hosts the city’s annual New Year’s Eve ball drop celebration. It is one of the most heavily touristed and policed spots in all of New York.

The 49-year-old woman from Queens pulled out two knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man who had just come out of the subway station and was waiting to cross the street with his wife, striking him in the abdomen, Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said at a news conference.

Seconds later, the woman stabbed a 32-year-old woman also in the abdomen, Tisch said. Both victims were taken to the hospital. The woman died and the man is in stable condition, according to police.

Police didn’t say if the victims were tourists visiting the city or residents.

Videos posted on social media show a group of at least 10 officers gathered around the woman, who was holding two large kitchen knives.

Officers tried to convince the woman to drop the knives for several minutes before using a Taser, Tisch said. The woman told them: “I’m not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you,” according to Tisch.

The video shows the Taser not incapacitating her and the woman walking quickly toward the officers while waving the knives in front of her.

Two officers then shot the woman, according to police. In the video posted by bystanders, the woman fell to the ground, where an officer handcuffed her. Officers rolled her onto her back and rendered first aid.

“This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world,” Tisch said.

The woman has a “documented mental health history with the Nypd,” which include incidents in 2018 and 2019 but no arrest history with the department, Tisch said. She didn’t provide additional details.

Police are investigating. Tisch said there was no evidence suggesting it was a terrorist attack.

The names of the victims have not been released until next of kin are notified, according to police.

“We know that those families’ lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Both Mamdani and Tisch praised the officers, saying more people could have been hurt or killed if not for their actions.

The Nypd temporarily closed part of 7th Avenue and warned the public to stay away from the area. Police tape cordoned off the area as a large group of law enforcement officers worked nearby.

Violent crime has fallen sharply in New York City so far this year, with homicides down 24 per cent and on pace to potentially hit their lowest level in decades. But this is the second killing this year in Times Square. A man was fatally stabbed in the same area in May.

Hallie Golden, The Associated Press

stories.title: Rick Campanelli reveals personal battle with past gambling addiction in ‘Tempted’ memoir
stories.summary: With his autobiography, "Tempted: My Story," Breakfast Television reporter Rick Campanelli opened up about his own life.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Posted September 1, 2026 9:53 am.

It’s been just over 30 years since a contest entry with MuchMusic would forever change Rick Campanelli’s life and make “Rick the Temp” a beloved household name.

The media personality’s storied career in the entertainment industry, which included co-hosting ET Canada, granted him VIP access to interview the biggest stars like Britney Spears, George Clooney and Jay-Z, to name a few.

With his autobiography, Tempted: My Story, co-authored by Canadian author John Meyer, hitting the shelves on Tuesday, the Breakfast Television reporter opened up about his own life. Described by the publisher as a “bombshell memoir” and a “cautionary tale,” the book reveals secret personal battles and hard lessons learned behind the scenes.

Rick Campanelli released his memoir, “Tempted: My Story,” on Sept. 1, 2026. (Photo credit: Instagram/Rick Campanelli)

On Breakfast Television on Tuesday, Campanelli spoke out his personal battle with a previous gambling addiction that almost tore his life apart.

Campanelli said his addiction stemmed from the high he received from entering the winning contests as a young person.

“I loved entering contests back in the day. I would enter any contest that I came across, whether it was winning a stuffed bunny for a colouring contest, winning a contest at a grocery store that sent me away to visit an NHL hockey team. I just loved winning. And it wasn’t about the prize as much as about just winning, being that person,” he explained.

stories.title: MP Cathay Wagantall officially becomes 10th MP to resign this year
stories.summary: Saskatchewan Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall officially resigned from the House of Commons on Monday, making her the 10th MP to step down this year. Wagantall announced in June that she would resign at the end of August. She said she originally planned on finishing her term but did not offer a reason for her exit […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall rises during question period in the House of Commons on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, ON Friday, June 6, 2025. THE Canadian Press/Spencer Colby The Canadian Press

By David Baxter, The Canadian Press

Posted September 1, 2026 9:49 am.

Last Updated September 1, 2026 11:12 am.

Saskatchewan Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall officially resigned from the House of Commons on Monday, making her the 10th MP to step down this year.

Wagantall announced in June that she would resign at the end of August.

She said she originally planned on finishing her term but did not offer a reason for her exit as member of Parliament for Yorkton—Melville, a riding she’d represented since 2015.

Ontario Conservative Larry Brock is also expected to resign this month. After representing Brantford—Brandt South—Six Nations since 2021, he now plans to go back to his old job as a Crown prosecutor.

The House of Commons is set to return on Sept. 21 with three new Liberal MPs elected in Monday’s byelections, all of which were triggered by resignations.

On Monday, the Liberals held on to two seats previously represented by former cabinet ministers Jonathan Wilkinson and Nate Erskine-Smith.

Wilkinson stepped down for a diplomatic appointment as Canada’s ambassador to the European Union.

Erskine-Smith planned to run for the Ontario Liberal leadership but that plan ended when he lost a nomination contest to run for the provincial party in a byelection in Toronto. He is now seeking a seat on Toronto’s city council.

Former Quebec Conservative Richard Martel’s seat of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord is now in Liberal hands after Monday’s byelection. Martel left the House to take a Senate appointment in July.

The year of resignations began with former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland’s official departure in January, initially to take an economic advisory position with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. She began a job as CEO of the Rhodes Trust on July 1.

Former cabinet minister Bill Blair then left his Toronto seat for a posting as high commissioner in the U.K. His posting was announced in February and his term began in March.

Both Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay and the Ndp’s Alexandre Boulerice stepped down to run in Quebec’s election, which is set for Oct. 5.

Toronto Liberal Shaun Chen resigned his seat last month after he said a car crash last year made it too difficult for him to commute to Ottawa. He is now running for city council in Toronto.

And former Liberal cabinet minister Steven Guilbeault officially vacated his Montreal seat on Friday. Guilbeault has been vocal in his opposition to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s policies on the environment and energy since quitting cabinet last November.

Elections Canada estimates each byelection costs around $2 million but notes that those costs tend to be higher in places like Toronto, where facility rentals and advertising cost more.

stories.title: Tornado touches down in southwestern Manitoba, leaves trail of damage
stories.summary: A late-summer storm brought a tornado to a southwestern Manitoba community.
stories.author: Kayla Rosen
paragraphs: A tornado tore through a southwestern Manitoba community Sunday evening, downing trees, snapping power lines and tearing the roof off a local business.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (Eccc) confirmed the tornado struck Elkhorn, a small community about 15 kilometres east of the Saskatchewan border, around 6:30 p.m. Sunday. The agency said it received a report about the tornado through the RCMP, along with a number of tips from the public on social media.

Eccc said two more tornadoes were confirmed in southeastern Saskatchewan near the Manitoba border as part of the same weather system. Several severe thunderstorms moved through the region, bringing heavy rain and large hail along with the twisters.

Pat Siemens, whose barn was heavily damaged in the storm, called it “an emotional evening.” She said her hay shed was also destroyed, but that she considers herself fortunate her house and her animals came through unharmed.
Area resident Michelle Martens said her family took shelter in the basement as the storm bore down on their home.
“We [saw] a shelf coming, and I got everybody to go downstairs,” Martens said. “It was here in seconds … and we all went down to the basement and hid. And it was really loud.”
Martens said the ordeal lasted roughly 10 to 15 minutes before her family emerged to survey the damage. Driving through the community afterward, Martens said the destruction was widespread.
“There’s lots of trees, lots of trees down, lots of power lines that are just snapped off and trees over houses,” she said. She added that part of the roof was torn off a building at the local Co-op.
As of Monday afternoon, Martens said her home was still without power, though crews had just cleared a fallen tree from a neighbouring property.
“They actually just finished getting that tree off the neighbour’s house, so now we can actually get it hooked up,” she said.

The storm system also dumped significant rainfall across several Manitoba communities. According to 48-hour rainfall totals recorded up to 8 a.m. Monday, Eccc said Kola received 80.5 millimetres, Minitonas received 71.7 millimetres and San Clara received 71.6 millimetres.
CTV News previously reported that the storm was caused by a cold front combining with an unseasonably warm atmosphere.
The Northern Tornadoes Project, a research initiative based at Western University, will also investigate the storm in the coming days to help determine its strength and track.
With files from CTV’s Danton Unger

Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to schedule another six by-elections for the coming months.
Liberal MP Steven Guilbeault officially resigned his Montreal seat on Friday, according to the House of Commons website.
The MP for Laurier—Sainte-Marie has said he’s leaving government on a matter of principle because the party’s direction on energy and the environment changed under Carney’s leadership.
Ottawa dropped the consumer carbon tax and endorsed building new pipelines out of Alberta.
Conservative MP Cathay Wagantall was also expected to officially resign this week after announcing her plans in June.
Wagantall, a Saskatchewan MP since 2015, announced her resignation this summer after originally saying she planned to stick around until the next election.
Nelson Pohl will run under the Conservative banner in her Yorkton-Melville riding in the next election.
Guilbeault and Wagantall are just the latest MPs to exit the Commons in recent months.
Two MPs stepped down this summer to run in Quebec’s provincial election.

Bloc Québécois MP Simon-Pierre Savard-Tremblay resigned on June 19 to run for the Parti Québécois, while Alexandre Boulerice resigned his Rosemont—La Petite-Patrie seat on Aug. 25 to run for Québec solidaire.
Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock has announced plans to step down on Sept. 18 to return to the Crown prosecutor’s office in Brantford, Ont.
Ontario Liberal Shaun Chen resigned as a member of Parliament on Aug. 15, attributing his exit to injuries he sustained in a car crash last fall that led to significant health issues.
The prime minister must call a by-election after a seat becomes vacant, but he has a window of 11 to 180 days in which to do so. The election period must last from 36 to 50 days.
The Liberals also swept three April by-elections earlier this year — two in the GTA and one in Quebec.
The Toronto-area races were called to replace former cabinet ministers Chrystia Freeland and Bill Blair.

The April byelection in Quebec’s Terrebonne riding was called after the Supreme Court of Canada nullified the riding’s result from the general election over a clerical error on the return address for some mail-in ballots.

stories.title: U.N. food agency halves West Bank aid because of funding shortages, warns new cuts May be needed
stories.summary: The United Nations’ food agency said Tuesday it is halving food assistance in the Israeli-occupied West Bank because of severe funding shortages and warned it May be forced to make further cuts in Gaza, where it supports 1.5 million people.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content: Rome — The United Nations’ food agency said Tuesday it is halving food assistance in the Israeli-occupied West Bank because of severe funding shortages and warned it May be forced to make further cuts in Gaza, where it supports 1.5 million people. The U.N. World Food Program said it will reduce assistance in the West Bank from 400,000 people to 200,000 beginning this month. In Gaza, it reduced the value of cash assistance by 40 per cent for 375,000 people in July and said additional cuts will be unavoidable unless it secures new funding. “In Gaza we’ve already had to start reducing the amount of cash that we’re giving to around 75,000 families,” Claire Nevill, WFP spokesperson for the Palestinian territories, told The Associated Press on Tuesday. “Now, the same is happening for Wfp’s West Bank operation.” WFP said it urgently needs an additional $386 million over the next six months to assist an estimated 2 million food-insecure people across Gaza and the West Bank. “All of this pressure has been building in terms of the economic downturn coupled with increasing settler violence and incursions on land, people sort of losing access to their livestock and agricultural land, which has also now had an impact on people’s food security,” Nevill said. “So just as the situation is getting worse and we should be scaling up to meet these needs, we’re unfortunately having to scale back and effectively halve the amount of people that we can reach because of the lack of funding,” she added. The world’s leading authority on food insecurity, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, said in July the situation in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in parts of the Palestinian territory last year, but warned conditions were still at crisis levels. Also in July, the WFP cautioned that funding shortages and what it described as donor fatigue could force deeper reductions in Gaza and said it needed more than $420 million to sustain operations in Gaza and the West Bank through the end of the year. Humanitarian conditions remain severe In the West Bank, WFP estimated in its Tuesday report that 900,000 people are food insecure. The agency said increased violence, displacement and economic deterioration have disrupted livelihoods and deepened hunger, while food needs have more than doubled since 2023. “Families who were once thriving and earning a living from their land are now unable to afford enough food,” Shaun Hughes, Wfp’s country director, said in a statement Tuesday. He added the agency was being forced to prioritize the most vulnerable households while cutting assistance to others despite widespread need. According to Wfp’s latest food security analysis, 76 per cent of households in the West Bank have experienced a significant decline in income. One-third cannot afford a nutritious diet, while food and fuel prices remain among the highest in the Middle East. Rural communities and the southern West Bank are among the hardest hit, the agency said. Humanitarian conditions also remain severe in Gaza. According to recent U.N. figures from aid agencies, about one in five families ate only one meal a day, while half reported running out of food entirely at least once in the previous month. Aid agencies say cash shortages and soaring food prices have made it increasingly difficult for families to obtain basic necessities. According to WFP, three-quarters of households in Gaza had difficulty accessing markets in August. The U.N. and its partners recently collected hundreds of pallets of food, fuel and other supplies through the Kerem Shalom crossing and distributed food parcels and wheat flour to more than 600,000 people during the August aid cycle. Despite a ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, ongoing hostilities and security restrictions continue to hamper movement and recovery efforts, according to U.N. agencies. The U.N. says more than 2 million people have been displaced during the war and that much of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, including homes, hospitals, schools and water facilities, has been damaged or destroyed. Giada Zampano And Silvia Stellacci, The Associated Press

stories.title: Descartes Systems Group acquires U.S.-company Extensiv for $120-million
stories.summary: Deal follows Descartes’ purchase of Tai Software last month for $100-million
stories.content:
Logistics software company Descartes Systems Group DSG-T has acquired Extensiv, a U.S. provider of warehouse management and fulfilment software, for US$120-million.

Descartes says the deal for the California-based firm expands its warehouse and inventory management capabilities.

Extensiv provides warehouse management and fulfilment systems for third-party logistics providers.

Scott Sangster, general manager, logistics services providers at Descartes, says the combination will enable companies to expand their offerings and grow operations with a single technology provider.

The acquisition follows a deal by Descartes announced last month to buy Tai Software for about US$100-million.

California-based Tai provides AI-powered transportation management services for freight brokers.

stories.title: Liberals won more than 50% of the vote in all three Aug. 31 byelections
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Liberals won more than 50 per cent of the vote in all three of Monday's byelections, holding two seats and picking up an additional Quebec riding from the Conservatives.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Posted September 1, 2026 9:17 am.

Last Updated September 1, 2026 3:39 pm.

Ottawa — In the final hours of byelection voting on Monday, Conservative candidate Jim Syrbos made one last appeal to the people of Beaches-East York: send a clear message to Ottawa and to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government.

But that was not the message Carney received after the votes were counted in all three ridings up for grabs.

“The message from Canadians, I think, is clear. They’ve given their support — more than 50 per cent in each of these ridings — to the government’s plan and I think that’s because Canadians are united and Canadians are ready,” Carney said on Tuesday in Ottawa.

“We’ve been buying Canadian, we’ve been visiting Canada, we have been reinforcing our strength here at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad. That’s been the plan of the government since the start.”

The Liberals swept three byelections on Monday by a wide margin. In Toronto’s Beaches-East York and in North Vancouver-Capilano, the governing party was widely expected to sail to victory.

Carney’s former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley held the Vancouver seat with 58.6 per cent of the vote, and constituency worker Tanveer Shahnawaz comfortably kept Beaches-East York in Liberal hands with 55.7 per cent of the vote.

The NDP made some progress in the Toronto riding, where candidate Shannon Devine took 25.8 per cent of the vote on Monday night — up from the 6.9 per cent she earned in last year’s general election.

Many expected Chicoutimi-Le Fjord to be a different story. In April 2025, the popular Conservative Richard Martel eked out his fourth election win by just three percentage points, with the Bloc Québécois and Liberal candidates separated by only a handful of votes.

Dairy farmer Daniel Gobeil won 51.3 per cent of the vote for the Liberals in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord on Monday — about 18 points ahead of the Bloc candidate Caroline Dubé.

“This is something that sends a strong message about the strength of the Liberals in Quebec right now, and also about how people are concerned about the trade war,” said Daniel Béland, a professor of political science at McGill University.

The province has been hit hard by U.S. tariffs targeting key industries such as aluminum, forestry and supply-managed dairy.

The Conservative vote collapsed in the Quebec riding on Monday, with Régis Gaudreault finishing almost 39 points behind Gobeil.

“It looks very bad for the Conservatives, and again, it will feed all this debate about the future of Pierre Poilievre as leader of the Conservative Party of Canada,” said Béland, who is also director of the McGill Institute for the Study of Canada.

The Conservative leader had not made any public comment on the byelection results as of Monday afternoon.

Questions have been asked about Poilievre’s future as leader since the April 2025 election.

He propelled the Tories to a 20-point lead in national polls in late 2024, pushed Justin Trudeau out of the Prime Minister’s Office and forced Carney to scrap the unpopular consumer carbon price as soon as he took over as Liberal leader.

But the Conservative camp struggled to adjust to the seismic political shift caused by U.S. President Donald Trump’s continuous threats against Canadian sovereignty and the resulting spike in both patriotism and anger north of the border.

Poilievre lost his longtime Ottawa-area seat in the election. He spent that spring watching from the sidelines as caucus members sought to poke holes in Carney’s credibility in Parliament, and spent the summer campaigning in a safe Conservative riding in rural Alberta.

By fall, with the leader back in his House of Commons seat, the Conservatives seemed more settled — until, one by one, four MPs walked across the aisle to join Carney’s government.

A trio of byelection wins last April secured for the Liberals the majority status they’d failed to lock up a year earlier.

Gobeil will add one more vote to the Liberal ranks, provided the Liberals don’t lose ground in any of the byelections set to come in the next several months.

There are five more vacancies already waiting to be filled — one in Ontario, one in Saskatchewan and three in Quebec. A sixth is expected later this month when Conservative Larry Brock steps down from his Ontario riding, which he said would happen Sept. 18.

Carney has not yet set dates for any of these races.

Béland said while byelections tend to focus more on local issues, he expects that won’t be the case with the upcoming votes.

“The evolution of that trade debate and Canada-U.S. relations and how Mark Carney is handling the situation will also affect the outcome,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie and David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: School boards across Canada cancel, tweak field trips
stories.summary: Thousands of students across Canada's school trip plans have been cancelled or tweaked for this school year for various reasons, including global conflicts and uncertainty.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A globe sits in a Peck Elementary School classroom Friday, Feb. 1, 2013, in Chicago. (AP Photo/Charles Rex Arbogast)

Edmonton — Zoe Cogger says two trips to the United States were going to be the highlight of her senior year in high school.

The 16-year-old was set to go with fellow Edmonton students to the National High School Dance Festival in Pittsburgh and to Spokane, Wash., for the annual Bloomsday Run.

But the trips are no more.

Edmonton Public Schools has cancelled all international excursions for the school year, including to Thailand, France, the United Kingdom, Costa Rica and Portugal.

“I was pretty sad when I found out,” Cogger said.

Cogger is among thousands of students across Canada whose school trip plans have been cancelled or tweaked for this school year for various reasons, including global conflicts and uncertainty.

Supt. Rob Thompson with the Edmonton public board said in a letter to parents in June that a recent field trip had students come face to face with civil unrest. The board didn’t specify what country the students were in.

“Couple this with reported global fuel shortages, recently reported public health concerns and ongoing military conflict, which introduces further unpredictability and risk to international travel,” Thompson said.

He added that he doesn’t take the cancellations lightly and that the board would reassess its decision before the 2027-28 school year.

The Vancouver School Board and the Calgary Catholic School District both said they’re approving field trips on a case-by-case basis.

“We are operating within an evolving global context and are carefully considering a range of factors in our review processes,” the Vancouver board said in an email.

Last year, the public Calgary Board of Education cancelled all international trips while it reviewed policies on how trips are planned and students prepare for the rigours of international travel. It said recently that trips have resumed for this year.

In Winnipeg, the Louis Riel School Board has cancelled trips to the United States since last October, after Ottawa posted a travel advisory warning Canadians that the U.S. government is no longer accepting gender markers.

The Winnipeg School Division said it’s allowing school trips -- but not to the United States.

“Travel to other international destinations May still be considered if it supports student learning or business operations,” spokesperson Jillian Recksiedler said in an email.

Public boards in Toronto and Saskatoon say none of their trips have been cancelled.

Some experts say school trip changes are understandable.

“We live in really complex times and international trips are a complex thing to pull off,” said Maren Aukerman, an education professor at the University of Calgary.

“The other side is it is a real loss. There’s lots of research that compares virtual field trips with real field trips and, not surprisingly, you cannot replace being in a different place, exploring a different culture.”

Aukerman said some schools are choosing instead to plan trips within Canada.

Wayne Smith, a hospitality and tourism professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said the cost of living has made it more difficult for parents to sign up their children for trips.

Planning trips has also become complicated, he said. With Canada’s population growth, teachers are seeing students with more diverse citizenship statuses.

“I know in Toronto, for example, the amount of paperwork (teachers) have to file to do a class trip is pretty phenomenal,” he said.

“It’s just got really complicated over the last few years, and especially since the vast majority of the trips are south of the border.”

Aukerman said that the trade war has complicated travel to the United States.

Edmonton high school student Nyla Ahmadzai said she isn’t going on any international school trips this year. But she spent all last year helping friends raise money for their planned excursions.

“They did bottle drives, sold chocolates, candies, even posting on social media, asking family members for donations and stuff,” she said. “I had a friend clean cars.

“Now it’s taken away from them, and it’s really, really frustrating.”

Cogger said she had hoped Edmonton Public Schools would consider trips on a case-by-case basis instead of cancelling them altogether.

“It’s better to find a way to make it work because these experiences are a high school experience.”

But there’s an upside.

Cogger said her school is planning a run in Jasper National Park instead of the one in Washington, and she’s not upset.

“I’m glad that they were able to find a replacement.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 1, 2026.

Fakiha Baig, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Loblaw increases the number of new stores planned for 2026
stories.summary: New locations are part of $2.4-billion in planned capital spending this year
stories.author: Tony Keller
stories.content:
Loblaw Cos. Ltd. L-T is increasing the number of new stores it plans to open this year.

The company behind Loblaws and Shoppers Drug Mart said Tuesday it now expects to open about 75 new locations this year, up from earlier plans for about 70.

Loblaw chief executive Per Bank says Canadians are being thoughtful about every dollar they spend.

“We see that in how they shop our stores, the brands they choose, and how they use our loyalty and e-commerce solutions,” Bank said in a statement.

“We have a significant investment program underway, and we’re putting that capital behind the parts of our business that meets the needs of Canadians. That includes accelerating our network expansion efforts to reach more customers, faster.”

Loblaw has opened 38 new grocery stores and pharmacies in Canada, including 21 grocery stores and 17 Shoppers Drug Mart locations, so far this year.

The new stores are part of $2.4-billion in planned capital spending for 2026, the second year of the company’s five-year plan to invest $10-billion in Canada by 2030.

Loblaw said it has spent about half of the total for 2026 so far, with plans for the remaining money to include accelerating the opening of new stores, renovating existing locations and continuing to develop new store formats and concepts.

Bank said the company has been happy with how its new stores are performing.

“As they mature, we’re seeing strong double-digit same- store sales growth. That gives us confidence in our expansion strategy and in continuing to invest behind the formats customers are choosing,” he said.

Loblaw’s grocery expansion has been focused on its No Frills and Maxi banners.

Grocers have been expanding their discount footprint across Canada since 2023 as shoppers have been grappling with food inflation coming out of the pandemic.

Meanwhile, pharmacy and health-care services have been projected to grow significantly, partly led by sales of generic weight-loss drugs.

The federal government has 10 officials on the ground in Nepal to support Canadians affected by flooding , Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Monday.
“Our priority is to locate Canadians and permanent residents and confirm their safety while offering support wherever and whenever possible,” she said.
Flash flooding killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
Anand said on social media on Saturday that one Canadian who was previously unaccounted for had been found safe.
She said Monday that 30 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing, a number she says may change as the government gets more information.

“We recognize with empathy the profound impact that this situation is having on families and communities across our country,” said Anand. “We remain in direct contact with all affected families through designated points of contact within each family and through a collective meeting with them today.”
The federal government has said it will provide $5 million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal.

Global Affairs Canada said in a statement Monday that officials are engaging with trekking companies, hospitals, local police, rescue centres, airlines and other Canadian travel industry partners to gather information, establish contact and help account for affected Canadians.
The department said the deputy high commissioner of Canada to India is one of the 10 officials in Kathmandu.

“Canadian officials are working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, as well as international partners including the Five Eyes, France, Japan, Italy and Singapore, to share information and support efforts to locate and assist Canadians,” said Global Affairs Canada.

The department said the RCMP has deployed a liaison officer to Nepal to offer assistance and help determine needs for on-the-ground support. It said the RCMP is also engaged through the INTERPOL network and has offered support with forensic equipment and expertise.

Canada’s travel advice for Nepal and China was updated Monday to advise against non-essential travel to affected areas due to the damage caused by severe flash flooding and mudslides and the ongoing risk of further flooding.

stories.title: On-duty OPP officer driving drunk 3x legal limit pleads guilty, fined $3,000
stories.summary: A veteran provincial police officer charged with driving drunk on the job pleads guilty.
stories.author: Mike Arsalides
paragraphs: A veteran provincial police officer charged with driving drunk on the job earlier this year in Midland, Ont., has taken a plea deal.

Suspended with pay since January, Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) officer Christopher Prout has pleaded guilty to driving with more than three times the legal limit of alcohol in his system while on duty in a police cruiser with a gun on his hip.

The court heard, as part of an Agreed Statement of Facts read by the Crown, Prout had been drinking at home and drove to work in his police cruiser for a performance review at the Southern Georgian Bay OPP detachment, when officers in the meeting room smelled alcohol on him.
Prout failed a breath test and provided two samples that produced readings of nearly 260 mg of alcohol in 100 ml of blood.
The defence noted Prout did not show signs of impairment, saying he was shocked by the readings, and that he felt “essentially sober” that day.
His lawyer told the court Prout, 40, who has been a police officer in Midland for 17 years, was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (Ptsd) and substance-use disorder.
According to the defence, his Ptsd was the result of years of dedicated service while experiencing trauma as a police officer.
The defence noted Prout hit “rock bottom” while dealing with mental health struggles and a family history of alcoholism as issues in his personal life affected his performance at work.

The defence said Prout had not sought help for his issues before being charged Jan. 15 and has since taken accountability through counselling and two months at the Homewood medically supervised addiction treatment centre as he continues to receive outpatient care and counselling while maintaining his sobriety.
Prout addressed the court, saying he was embarrassed and that he hurt his platoon and hates and regrets what he did.
He vowed “it will never happen again.”
“Alcohol is not an issue anymore,” Prout told the court, adding he is working hard to move forward.
Following a joint submission by the defence and a Crown attorney brought in from Newmarket to handle the case, the judge handed Prout a $3,000 fine and two-year driving ban.
Justice Edward Prutschi told Prout it was sheer dumb luck and divine intervention that his actions didn’t result in a crash that killed himself or others out on the road.
Along with being placed on probation for two years, Prout could now face further discipline under the Police Services Act.

In a statement issued to CTV News on Tuesday, the OPP said it “is aware of an OPP member pleading guilty on Aug, 28, 2026, to one count of Over 80 contrary to section 320.14 of the Criminal Code from an incident that occurred on Jan. 15, 2026.”
Provincial police said any questions related to the court process and outcome should be directed to the Ministry of the Attorney General.
“The OPP Professional Standards Unit launched a parallel investigation into the matter, relevant to the Community Safety and Policing Act ,” the law enforcement agency said.
“That investigation has now concluded and is being referred to the Ontario Police Arbitration and Adjudication Commission to determine final penalty.”
“At this time, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment,” OPP said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is overhauling the leadership of the federal agency responsible for attracting foreign investment just weeks before a high-profile summit aimed at doing just that.
Carney announced Monday that Dominic Barton , the former Canadian ambassador to China and a well-known name in corporate Canada, will chair the board of directors for Invest in Canada.
Much of Barton’s career was spent at McKinsey and Co., a global consultancy firm. Barton is also the chair of mining giant Rio Tinto and LeapFrog Investments.

In 2016, Barton was named chair of the Liberal government’s economic advisory council under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau . Among the recommendations in the council’s report was one calling for the creation of Invest in Canada, an agency tasked with attracting foreign direct investment.

Barton steered Canada through a turbulent diplomatic period with China between 2019 and 2021. Upon Barton’s resignation in 2021, Trudeau credited him with helping to secure the release of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor , two Canadians detained in China during the deep diplomatic schism.
Barton will serve as chair for a three-year term on a part-time basis. Outgoing chair Karl Tabbakh will remain on the board of Invest in Canada to support the transition.

Gurinder Grewal, founder and managing partner of MEM Growth Partners, becomes chief executive of Invest in Canada. In a release, Carney touted Grewal’s experience with “putting capital to work” in the energy, industrial, infrastructure and technology sectors.

The shakeup at Invest in Canada comes two weeks before Carney’s inaugural investment summit in Toronto, where he’ll assemble foreign investors and the heads of major domestic funds to pitch them on Canadian projects.
Carney said in a statement that Barton and Grewal have the expertise to help Canada capitalize on its strengths “with new investors.”
“Under their leadership, Invest in Canada will catalyze billions in new investments into Canada to build a stronger, more independent, more resilient Canadian economy for all,” he said.
Grewal replaces outgoing CEO Laurel Broten , a former Ontario cabinet minister under former Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty .

Dominic LeBlanc , the minister responsible for the federal investment agency, announced on social media that he would accept Broten’s resignation as of Sept. 1. She leaves the role almost four years into what’s usually a five-year term.
No explanation was given Monday for Broten’s early exit. Spokespeople for LeBlanc’s office and the Privy Council Office did not answer questions about her departure.
Carney praised Tabbakh for his service as Invest in Canada’s chair but did not mention Broten in his statement.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office deferred comment on Broten’s resignation, citing LeBlanc’s statement on Monday. In it, the minister thanked Broten for her years of service and wished her well in her future endeavours.

A source familiar with planning September’s investment summit who was not authorized to speak publicly said that Invest in Canada’s contributions have been largely limited to a few staff members pulled into logistics for the event.

The source said staff within the Prime Minister’s Office and other government departments have largely been spearheading the summit, alongside the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on social media Monday that Carney has appointed the “ultimate Liberal powerbroker to head up the government’s corporate welfare agency.”

“Dominic Barton is the man who ran McKinsey while the firm profited from helping Purdue Pharma ‘supercharge’ the opioid crisis; who chaired Trudeau’s economic advisory council while McKinsey’s federal contracts exploded thirty-fold to over $200m, contracts the Auditor General later found broke the rules,” he said. “Now he will help insiders get billions in handouts, bailouts, and carve outs, paid for by you.”

Poilievre added that Barton “was the man at McKinsey who cozied up to the Communist government in Beijing, even working with state-owned companies that violated international law and he refused to condemn the Uyghur genocide.”
“The Liberal Club gets rich making everyone else poor,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is overhauling the leadership of the federal agency responsible for attracting foreign investment just weeks before a high-profile summit aimed at doing just that.

Carney announced Monday that Dominic Barton , the former Canadian ambassador to China and a well-known name in corporate Canada, will chair the board of directors for Invest in Canada.

Much of Barton’s career was spent at McKinsey and Co., a global consultancy firm. Barton is also the chair of mining giant Rio Tinto and LeapFrog Investments.

In 2016, Barton was named chair of the Liberal government’s economic advisory council under Prime Minister Justin Trudeau . Among the recommendations in the council’s report was one calling for the creation of Invest in Canada, an agency tasked with attracting foreign direct investment.

Barton steered Canada through a turbulent diplomatic period with China between 2019 and 2021. Upon Barton’s resignation in 2021, Trudeau credited him with helping to secure the release of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor , two Canadians detained in China during the deep diplomatic schism.

Barton will serve as chair for a three-year term on a part-time basis. Outgoing chair Karl Tabbakh will remain on the board of Invest in Canada to support the transition.

Gurinder Grewal, founder and managing partner of MEM Growth Partners, becomes chief executive of Invest in Canada. In a release, Carney touted Grewal’s experience with “putting capital to work” in the energy, industrial, infrastructure and technology sectors.

The shakeup at Invest in Canada comes two weeks before Carney’s inaugural investment summit in Toronto, where he’ll assemble foreign investors and the heads of major domestic funds to pitch them on Canadian projects.

Carney said in a statement that Barton and Grewal have the expertise to help Canada capitalize on its strengths “with new investors.”

“Under their leadership, Invest in Canada will catalyze billions in new investments into Canada to build a stronger, more independent, more resilient Canadian economy for all,” he said.

Grewal replaces outgoing CEO Laurel Broten , a former Ontario cabinet minister under former Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty .

Dominic LeBlanc , the minister responsible for the federal investment agency, announced on social media that he would accept Broten’s resignation as of Sept. 1. She leaves the role almost four years into what’s usually a five-year term.

No explanation was given Monday for Broten’s early exit. Spokespeople for LeBlanc’s office and the Privy Council Office did not answer questions about her departure.

Carney praised Tabbakh for his service as Invest in Canada’s chair but did not mention Broten in his statement.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office deferred comment on Broten’s resignation, citing LeBlanc’s statement on Monday. In it, the minister thanked Broten for her years of service and wished her well in her future endeavours.

A source familiar with planning September’s investment summit who was not authorized to speak publicly said that Invest in Canada’s contributions have been largely limited to a few staff members pulled into logistics for the event.

The source said staff within the Prime Minister’s Office and other government departments have largely been spearheading the summit, alongside the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on social media Monday that Carney has appointed the “ultimate Liberal powerbroker to head up the government’s corporate welfare agency.”

“Dominic Barton is the man who ran McKinsey while the firm profited from helping Purdue Pharma ‘supercharge’ the opioid crisis; who chaired Trudeau’s economic advisory council while McKinsey’s federal contracts exploded thirty-fold to over $200m, contracts the Auditor General later found broke the rules,” he said. “Now he will help insiders get billions in handouts, bailouts, and carve outs, paid for by you.”

Poilievre added that Barton “was the man at McKinsey who cozied up to the Communist government in Beijing, even working with state-owned companies that violated international law and he refused to condemn the Uyghur genocide.”

“The Liberal Club gets rich making everyone else poor,” he said.

Special mail-in ballots for Alberta’s 10-question referendum next month started going out the door Tuesday, Elections Alberta said.
The agency said those who have previously registered for a special ballot will soon start receiving their packages in the mail or they can pick them up in person.

Spokesperson Maia-Lys Hanrahan said Elections Alberta received 225,000 requests to date for mail-in ballots. The special ballots are designed to allow those who may not be able to go to the polls in person on Oct. 19 the opportunity to still submit their votes.
Among the questions Premier Danielle Smith’s government is putting voters is one on whether Albertans want to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on separating from Canada.
Albertans will also be asked five questions around the province taking more control over immigration and four on constitutional reform.
The elections agency says Albertans have until Oct. 9 to apply for a mail-in ballot and that the ballots must be received by Elections Alberta no later than Oct. 16.
The referendum is shaping up to be a massive undertaking for Elections Alberta, which has said it will need to hire at least 60,000 workers to hold the vote.
Hanrahan said that since it launched its hiring spree in June, it has received more than 35,000 applications.

“Elections Alberta will continue to seek election officers right up until voting for the referendum.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Elections Alberta will continue to seek election officers right up until voting for the referendum."

She also said the agency is specifically seeking election officers for a number of rural areas, including Medicine Hat, about 300 kilometres southeast of Calgary, and Athabasca, which is about 150 kilometres north of Edmonton.
Hanrahan added that they were seeking applications “all across northern Alberta.”

She said Elections Alberta was coming up with a new hiring process specifically designed for groups of people, such as “your hockey team, community group, choir, or even the group chat” and that more details would be available soon.
The agency is also bringing in help from other provincial election organizations, a practice it says is normal for all major voting events.
Hanrahan didn’t provide a number but said a small group of professionals from across the country will be providing relief for Elections Alberta’s fewer than 50 permanent staff come voting day.
“This assistance will allow us to cover shift-work spanning the 60 consecutive hour period from the beginning of election day through to the end of the count,” she said.

Food and household goods companies in Canada say they’re seeing a surge in demand as Canadians prioritize shopping local amid the ongoing trade dispute.
Despite the strain of higher prices at the grocery store, they say many shoppers across the country are going out of their way to buy Canadian-made products.
Kathleen Chapman, president of aVenco Ltd., says the Bowmanville, Ont., supplier of parchment paper has been slammed by U.S. tariffs.

The company, whose customer base was nearly 40 per cent in the U.S., was initially affected by U.S. tariffs on European goods as it sources raw parchment paper in France, and now it faces an additional 50 per cent tariff because its product is prepared and converted in Canada.

But she says Canadians have reached out to offer support and order directly from the company, sending its direct-to-consumer orders from about 20 in the last two years to hundreds in the week since new U.S. tariffs came into effect.
Chapman says consumers are moving faster than retailers, with many stores slow to respond to shifting demand with more shelf space for Canadian items.

stories.title: Schwartz’s Deli in Montreal opts for local black cherry soda as U.S. tariffs bite – and customers won’t look back
stories.summary: Cott has stopped producing black cherry soda in Canada in part due to aluminum tariffs, prompting the popular deli to choose a made-in-Quebec alternative
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
On a typical summer day at Schwartz’s Deli, in Montreal, there’s a lineup at the door as tourists and locals wait to get their smoked-meat sandwich.

But now, something has changed.

For decades, customers would be able to order a can of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda alongside their sandwich.

While Cott’s used to be a local brand, it was bought out in 2018 by a multinational beverage company, Refresco, which said it has stopped production of the drink in Canada.

The supply change has prompted the iconic smoked-meat deli to to turn to a local made-in-Quebec alternative, Fleischer’s Original Black Cherry Soda.

At Schwartz's Deli in Montreal, the traditional Cott’s black cherry soda customers have drank for decades has disappeared after falling victim to tariffs, and been replaced by a local alternative.

The Canadian Press

This comes as a growing cohort of businesses embrace a Buy Canadian mantra in a landscape disrupted by tariffs and the trade war with the United States.

And some customers at the Montreal landmark smoked-meat shop seem to be enthusiastic about the newest item on the menu.

“It’s always good to support locally,” said Liam Keenan, who was visiting from Toronto and getting ready to tackle the classic Schwartz’s trio: smoked-meat sandwich, pickle, and black cherry soda.

Keenan had been to Schwartz’s once before. He said he noticed the canned drink looked different this time, but that it still tasted great.

Originally, Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was made in Montreal. It had been part of Schwartz’s history since its early years, almost a century ago.

“People appreciated (it) being local and different and a little sweet, with the spices from the smoked meat,” Frank Silva, Schwartz’s general manager, said in a recent interview. “People got hooked on it, so people come here for a smoked meat sandwich and a black cherry. That was always the case.”

But Silva said the canned version of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was discontinued by the manufacturer, in part because of American tariffs on aluminum.

“It was very popular here, but I don’t think they sold to too many other places. So when the cost for aluminum went up, they decided to eliminate black cherry in a can,” Silva said, from behind the counter of the crowded deli, between two smoked-meat sandwich orders.

A 2023 change in the provincial recycling system, which implemented a 10-cent deposit for canned drinks, May also have played a role in the end of Cott’s Canadian production, he said.

Soft-drink producer Refresco declined The Canadian Press’s interview request, but confirmed they stopped manufacturing Cott products in Canada.

After the supply ran out in March, Silva said he was happy to make the switch to Fleischer’s.

A can of Fleischer’s black cherry soda costs around twice as much as Cott’s did, but because of its bigger size, many customers share it, said Silva.

“It’s a bigger can, and it’s local, it’s Canadian, so people are really getting into it,” he said.

A few tables over, Ann Thinghuus and her two children were sharing a can of Fleischer’s to go along with their smoked-meat.

“It works really well with the sandwich, it’s super refreshing, and we did notice that there’s a Canadian flag on the can, so we’re pretty happy about that too,” said Thinghuus, who is from Vancouver.

She said supporting a Canadian business was a big plus, “especially with what’s going on” in the past few weeks.

Montreal-born brewer Victor Lukoshius owns a facility that produces beer and the Fleischer’s soda in St-Hyacinthe, east of the city.

Lukoshius set out to create a new version of the cherry-flavoured soft drink two years ago, when he heard Cott’s might be ending its production.

“I grew up just like everybody else, drinking black cherry as we’re eating smoked meat sandwiches,” he said. “We wanted to take on the challenge of producing something for the smoked meat, the delis, the Jewish delis, the hotdog places, to maintain and keep that tradition.”

Lukoshius sources his ingredients locally and the cans are printed in Montreal. He said Fleischer’s isn’t sheltered from tariffs and inflation, but that he is willing to shoulder some extra costs to keep black cherry soda flowing.

“We’re biting the bullet, we are paying more for it. We have smaller production, but I think we’re doing well,” he said.

Saibal Ray, a professor of operations management at McGill University, said tariffs placed on aluminum have affected the beverage industry even though their main goal was to target the aerospace industry, auto manufacturing and appliances.

Cans can represent up to a third of the cost of producing a soda, said Ray, who has expertise in supply chain management.

He explained that since most cans are produced in the United States using Canadian aluminum, they are tariffed at least twice. So Ray said it’s not surprising that niche products like black cherry soda would be swallowed up.

“It’s a very small margin business,” he said. “When the price increases by that much, most of your margin goes away, and then only the very large volume (products) can play a role.”

At Schwartz’s, the numbers show that customers’ thirst for black cherry soda remains strong. Silva said his new supplier is now trying to keep up with their orders of 12-can cases.

“This morning, I ordered 100 cases, and he only had 87,” said Silva. “I just spoke to him, he’s trying to get me some more.”

Whatever happens with trade negotiations and tariffs, Silva doesn’t plan on going back.

Even if the cans of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda return, he said customers would stick with the made-in-Quebec can of Fleischer’s.

The supply change has prompted the iconic smoked-meat deli to to turn to a local made-in-Quebec alternative, Fleischer’s Original Black Cherry Soda.
At Schwartz's Deli in Montreal, the traditional Cott’s black cherry soda customers have drank for decades has disappeared after falling victim to tariffs, and been replaced by a local alternative.
The Canadian Press
This comes as a growing cohort of businesses embrace a Buy Canadian mantra in a landscape disrupted by tariffs and the trade war with the United States.
And some customers at the Montreal landmark smoked-meat shop seem to be enthusiastic about the newest item on the menu.
“It’s always good to support locally,” said Liam Keenan, who was visiting from Toronto and getting ready to tackle the classic Schwartz’s trio: smoked-meat sandwich, pickle, and black cherry soda.
Keenan had been to Schwartz’s once before. He said he noticed the canned drink looked different this time, but that it still tasted great.
Originally, Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was made in Montreal. It had been part of Schwartz’s history since its early years, almost a century ago.

“People appreciated (it) being local and different and a little sweet, with the spices from the smoked meat,” Frank Silva, Schwartz’s general manager, said in a recent interview. “People got hooked on it, so people come here for a smoked meat sandwich and a black cherry. That was always the case.”
But Silva said the canned version of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was discontinued by the manufacturer, in part because of American tariffs on aluminum.

“It was very popular here, but I don’t think they sold to too many other places. So when the cost for aluminum went up, they decided to eliminate black cherry in a can,” Silva said, from behind the counter of the crowded deli, between two smoked-meat sandwich orders.
A 2023 change in the provincial recycling system, which implemented a 10-cent deposit for canned drinks, May also have played a role in the end of Cott’s Canadian production, he said.
Soft-drink producer Refresco declined The Canadian Press’s interview request, but confirmed they stopped manufacturing Cott products in Canada.
After the supply ran out in March, Silva said he was happy to make the switch to Fleischer’s.
A can of Fleischer’s black cherry soda costs around twice as much as Cott’s did, but because of its bigger size, many customers share it, said Silva.
“It’s a bigger can, and it’s local, it’s Canadian, so people are really getting into it,” he said.
A few tables over, Ann Thinghuus and her two children were sharing a can of Fleischer’s to go along with their smoked-meat.

“It works really well with the sandwich, it’s super refreshing, and we did notice that there’s a Canadian flag on the can, so we’re pretty happy about that too,” said Thinghuus, who is from Vancouver.
She said supporting a Canadian business was a big plus, “especially with what’s going on” in the past few weeks.
Montreal-born brewer Victor Lukoshius owns a facility that produces beer and the Fleischer’s soda in St-Hyacinthe, east of the city.
Lukoshius set out to create a new version of the cherry-flavoured soft drink two years ago, when he heard Cott’s might be ending its production.

“I grew up just like everybody else, drinking black cherry as we’re eating smoked meat sandwiches,” he said. “We wanted to take on the challenge of producing something for the smoked meat, the delis, the Jewish delis, the hotdog places, to maintain and keep that tradition.”

Lukoshius sources his ingredients locally and the cans are printed in Montreal. He said Fleischer’s isn’t sheltered from tariffs and inflation, but that he is willing to shoulder some extra costs to keep black cherry soda flowing.
“We’re biting the bullet, we are paying more for it. We have smaller production, but I think we’re doing well,” he said.

Saibal Ray, a professor of operations management at McGill University, said tariffs placed on aluminum have affected the beverage industry even though their main goal was to target the aerospace industry, auto manufacturing and appliances.
Cans can represent up to a third of the cost of producing a soda, said Ray, who has expertise in supply chain management.

He explained that since most cans are produced in the United States using Canadian aluminum, they are tariffed at least twice. So Ray said it’s not surprising that niche products like black cherry soda would be swallowed up.
“It’s a very small margin business,” he said. “When the price increases by that much, most of your margin goes away, and then only the very large volume (products) can play a role.”
At Schwartz’s, the numbers show that customers’ thirst for black cherry soda remains strong. Silva said his new supplier is now trying to keep up with their orders of 12-can cases.
“This morning, I ordered 100 cases, and he only had 87,” said Silva. “I just spoke to him, he’s trying to get me some more.”
Whatever happens with trade negotiations and tariffs, Silva doesn’t plan on going back.
Even if the cans of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda return, he said customers would stick with the made-in-Quebec can of Fleischer’s.

On a typical summer day at Schwartz’s Deli, in Montreal, there’s a lineup at the door as tourists and locals wait to get their smoked-meat sandwich.
But now, something has changed.
For decades, customers would be able to order a can of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda alongside their sandwich.
While Cott’s used to be a local brand, it was bought out in 2018 by a multinational beverage company, Refresco, which said it has stopped production of the drink in Canada.
The supply change has prompted the iconic smoked-meat deli to to turn to a local made-in-Quebec alternative, Fleischer’s Original Black Cherry Soda.
This comes as a growing cohort of businesses embrace a Buy Canadian mantra in a landscape disrupted by tariffs and the trade war with the United States.
And some customers at the Montreal landmark smoked-meat shop seem to be enthusiastic about the newest item on the menu.
“It’s always good to support locally,” said Liam Keenan, who was visiting from Toronto and getting ready to tackle the classic Schwartz’s trio: smoked-meat sandwich, pickle, and black cherry soda.
Keenan had been to Schwartz’s once before. He said he noticed the canned drink looked different this time, but that it still tasted great.
Originally, Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was made in Montreal. It had been part of Schwartz’s history since its early years, almost a century ago.

“People appreciated (it) being local and different and a little sweet, with the spices from the smoked meat,” Frank Silva, Schwartz’s general manager, said in a recent interview. “People got hooked on it, so people come here for a smoked meat sandwich and a black cherry. That was always the case.”
But Silva said the canned version of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was discontinued by the manufacturer, in part because of American tariffs on aluminum.

“It was very popular here, but I don’t think they sold to too many other places. So when the cost for aluminum went up, they decided to eliminate black cherry in a can,” Silva said, from behind the counter of the crowded deli, between two smoked-meat sandwich orders.
A 2023 change in the provincial recycling system, which implemented a 10-cent deposit for canned drinks, may also have played a role in the end of Cott’s Canadian production, he said.
Soft-drink producer Refresco declined The Canadian Press’s interview request, but confirmed they stopped manufacturing Cott products in Canada.
After the supply ran out in March, Silva said he was happy to make the switch to Fleischer’s.
A can of Fleischer’s black cherry soda costs around twice as much as Cott’s did, but because of its bigger size, many customers share it, said Silva.
“It’s a bigger can, and it’s local, it’s Canadian, so people are really getting into it,” he said.
A few tables over, Ann Thinghuus and her two children were sharing a can of Fleischer’s to go along with their smoked-meat.

“It works really well with the sandwich, it’s super refreshing, and we did notice that there’s a Canadian flag on the can, so we’re pretty happy about that too,” said Thinghuus, who is from Vancouver.
She said supporting a Canadian business was a big plus, “especially with what’s going on” in the past few weeks.
Montreal-born brewer Victor Lukoshius owns a facility that produces beer and the Fleischer’s soda in St-Hyacinthe, east of the city.
Lukoshius set out to create a new version of the cherry-flavoured soft drink two years ago, when he heard Cott’s might be ending its production.

“I grew up just like everybody else, drinking black cherry as we’re eating smoked meat sandwiches,” he said. “We wanted to take on the challenge of producing something for the smoked meat, the delis, the Jewish delis, the hotdog places, to maintain and keep that tradition.”

Lukoshius sources his ingredients locally and the cans are printed in Montreal. He said Fleischer’s isn’t sheltered from tariffs and inflation, but that he is willing to shoulder some extra costs to keep black cherry soda flowing.
“We’re biting the bullet, we are paying more for it. We have smaller production, but I think we’re doing well,” he said.

Saibal Ray, a professor of operations management at McGill University, said tariffs placed on aluminum have affected the beverage industry even though their main goal was to target the aerospace industry, auto manufacturing and appliances.
Cans can represent up to a third of the cost of producing a soda, said Ray, who has expertise in supply chain management.

He explained that since most cans are produced in the United States using Canadian aluminum, they are tariffed at least twice. So Ray said it’s not surprising that niche products like black cherry soda would be swallowed up.
“It’s a very small margin business,” he said. “When the price increases by that much, most of your margin goes away, and then only the very large volume (products) can play a role.”
At Schwartz’s, the numbers show that customers’ thirst for black cherry soda remains strong. Silva said his new supplier is now trying to keep up with their orders of 12-can cases.
“This morning, I ordered 100 cases, and he only had 87,” said Silva. “I just spoke to him, he’s trying to get me some more.”
Whatever happens with trade negotiations and tariffs, Silva doesn’t plan on going back.
Even if the cans of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda return, he said customers would stick with the made-in-Quebec can of Fleischer’s.

This comes as a growing cohort of businesses embrace a Buy Canadian mantra in a landscape disrupted by tariffs and the trade war with the United States.

And some customers at the Montreal landmark smoked-meat shop seem to be enthusiastic about the newest item on the menu.

“It’s always good to support locally,” said Liam Keenan, who was visiting from Toronto and getting ready to tackle the classic Schwartz’s trio: smoked-meat sandwich, pickle, and black cherry soda.

Keenan had been to Schwartz’s once before. He said he noticed the canned drink looked different this time, but that it still tasted great.

Originally, Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was made in Montreal. It had been part of Schwartz’s history since its early years, almost a century ago.

“People appreciated (it) being local and different and a little sweet, with the spices from the smoked meat,” Frank Silva, Schwartz’s general manager, said in a recent interview. “People got hooked on it, so people come here for a smoked meat sandwich and a black cherry. That was always the case.”

But Silva said the canned version of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda was discontinued by the manufacturer, in part because of American tariffs on aluminum.

“It was very popular here, but I don’t think they sold to too many other places. So when the cost for aluminum went up, they decided to eliminate black cherry in a can,” Silva said, from behind the counter of the crowded deli, between two smoked-meat sandwich orders.

A 2023 change in the provincial recycling system, which implemented a 10-cent deposit for canned drinks, may also have played a role in the end of Cott’s Canadian production, he said.

Soft-drink producer Refresco declined The Canadian Press’s interview request, but confirmed they stopped manufacturing Cott products in Canada.

After the supply ran out in March, Silva said he was happy to make the switch to Fleischer’s.

A can of Fleischer’s black cherry soda costs around twice as much as Cott’s did, but because of its bigger size, many customers share it, said Silva.

“It’s a bigger can, and it’s local, it’s Canadian, so people are really getting into it,” he said.

A few tables over, Ann Thinghuus and her two children were sharing a can of Fleischer’s to go along with their smoked-meat.

“It works really well with the sandwich, it’s super refreshing, and we did notice that there’s a Canadian flag on the can, so we’re pretty happy about that too,” said Thinghuus, who is from Vancouver.

She said supporting a Canadian business was a big plus, “especially with what’s going on” in the past few weeks.

Montreal-born brewer Victor Lukoshius owns a facility that produces beer and the Fleischer’s soda in St-Hyacinthe, east of the city.

Lukoshius set out to create a new version of the cherry-flavoured soft drink two years ago, when he heard Cott’s might be ending its production.

“I grew up just like everybody else, drinking black cherry as we’re eating smoked meat sandwiches,” he said. “We wanted to take on the challenge of producing something for the smoked meat, the delis, the Jewish delis, the hotdog places, to maintain and keep that tradition.”

Lukoshius sources his ingredients locally and the cans are printed in Montreal. He said Fleischer’s isn’t sheltered from tariffs and inflation, but that he is willing to shoulder some extra costs to keep black cherry soda flowing.

“We’re biting the bullet, we are paying more for it. We have smaller production, but I think we’re doing well,” he said.

Saibal Ray, a professor of operations management at McGill University, said tariffs placed on aluminum have affected the beverage industry even though their main goal was to target the aerospace industry, auto manufacturing and appliances.

Cans can represent up to a third of the cost of producing a soda, said Ray, who has expertise in supply chain management.

He explained that since most cans are produced in the United States using Canadian aluminum, they are tariffed at least twice. So Ray said it’s not surprising that niche products like black cherry soda would be swallowed up.

“It’s a very small margin business,” he said. “When the price increases by that much, most of your margin goes away, and then only the very large volume (products) can play a role.”

At Schwartz’s, the numbers show that customers’ thirst for black cherry soda remains strong. Silva said his new supplier is now trying to keep up with their orders of 12-can cases.

“This morning, I ordered 100 cases, and he only had 87,” said Silva. “I just spoke to him, he’s trying to get me some more.”

Whatever happens with trade negotiations and tariffs, Silva doesn’t plan on going back.

Even if the cans of Cott’s Black Cherry Soda return, he said customers would stick with the made-in-Quebec can of Fleischer’s.

stories.title: New foreign investment in Mexico stalls as companies fret over Usmca uncertainty
stories.summary: The uncertainty is deterring new investments and prompting some companies already in Mexico to proactively look elsewhere. More than a dozen business leaders told Reuters that they are reconsidering their investment plans, in some cases drawing up proposals to pull out of Mexico and relocate to Asia.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content: When Randy Carr opened a factory in central Mexico in 2005, he was drawn by the country’s low wages and free-trade agreement with the United States. Over the next 20 years, the plant, which produces embroidered patches and custom emblems, grew into an 800-worker operation. But in 2025, after U.S. President Donald Trump began threatening tariffs on Mexico and Canada, Carr quickly moved to diversify. He set his sights on the Dominican Republic. “It all started with the February decision to hit Mexico and Canada with 25 per cent tariffs,” he said. “The writing was on the wall.” Mexico has so far largely escaped the heaviest of Trump’s sweeping tariffs that have fueled a bitter trade dispute with Canada and other U.S. allies. But Trump has repeatedly attacked the U.S.-Mexico-Canada free trade pact known as Usmca, and in July Washington declined to renew it, instead opting for annual reviews, leaving companies unsure what tariff regime they May face from one year to the next. The uncertainty is deterring new investments and prompting some companies already in Mexico to proactively look elsewhere. More than a dozen business leaders told Reuters that they are reconsidering their investment plans, in some cases drawing up proposals to pull out of Mexico and relocate to Asia. Compounding their concerns is Mexico’s sweeping 2024 judicial reform, which replaced appointed judges with elected ones, unsettling companies worried about the rule of law. NEW Investment Wobbles Executives from three auto parts companies, all based in the central state of Aguascalientes, told Reuters they are considering leaving Mexico and relocating to Vietnam, whose auto parts industry has expanded rapidly over the past decade with the arrival of Japanese, Korean, and European automakers. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal business considerations. Two other executives from multinational companies told Reuters they were reassessing their projects in Mexico and had entered a “wait-and-see” phase while the future of the trade pact became clearer. “If we are going to have a constant renegotiation until July of next year, let’s just turn off the lights, close the doors and go invest somewhere else because that’s just pure uncertainty,” said Pedro Casas, CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico, which represents more than 1,450 companies in the U.S. and Mexico. The Usmca trade pact is essential for Mexico’s economy: some 80 per cent of all Mexican exports go to the U.S. and nearly 89 per cent of that daily $1.5 billion worth of goods fall under the treaty’s umbrella. Overall foreign direct investment in Mexico hit a record high of nearly $35 billion in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary numbers. But almost all of that came from reinvested earnings, with just 7.8 per cent representing new investments. Preliminary data shows new foreign investment fell 13 per cent in the first half of 2026 from a year earlier — a sign that Mexico May be struggling to attract fresh capital. Greenfield investment in Mexico, a measure of foreign spending on new factories and warehouses, fell by nearly half to $24 billion in 2025 from the previous year, according to the latest figures available from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development. “If you are already in Mexico and have a plant, investing in machinery and equipment to produce more makes sense,” said Carlos Serrano, chief economist at Bbva Mexico. “But if you are a new firm, and you see all this uncertainty, not only with Usmca but also the judicial system, you will not build a new plant.” Growing Exports Mexico’s President Claudia Sheinbaum has maintained that the country’s economy remains resilient despite the trade tensions with the United States. She has championed what she calls “Plan Mexico,” an ambitious strategy that seeks to revitalize manufacturing in Mexico and boost domestic industries. Mexico’s economy grew 1.4 per cent in the second quarter, its fastest pace since early 2022. Much of that strength has come from exports of computers, servers and other AI-related data-processing equipment to the U.S., highlighting Mexico’s continued dependence on its neighbor to the north and their free trade agreement. While that’s a boon for Mexico’s economy, it has driven the U.S. trade deficit with Mexico to record levels — which could backfire politically, given Trump’s stated mission of reducing trade imbalances with friend and foe alike. Mexico’s central bank, in its August quarterly report, said exports are expected to expand moderately in the near future, noting that the terms of the Usmca are still in effect. But, it noted, “the lack of a definitive resolution regarding its future remains an adverse factor for investment decisions.” Carr’s business, World Emblem, opened its new plant in the Dominican Republic in June and currently employs about 25 people, with plans to hire more. The lower costs and generous tax incentives offset the 10 per cent U.S. tariff on imports from the country, he said. Simultaneously, Carr plans to shrink the company’s 800-employee footprint in Mexico by half through attrition. “It’s a hedge,” he said. “We just have too much at stake right now in Mexico.” (Reporting by Diego Oré and Emily Green, Editing by Rosalba O’Brien)
