stories.title: Alvinston Arena Floor Fund almost halfway to goal after help from London Knights exhibition game
stories.summary: The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze. The facility, built in 1977, is reaching its end of life with critical repairs needed to the rink floor and refrigeration room.

With pinholes in the pipes, the municipality needed to be proactive when it came to the only ice surface in the community.

“It would be shut down for a couple of weeks if you have a major catastrophe,” said Dave Ferguson, mayor of Brooke-Alvinston.

“If that’s the middle of February or hitting a playoff time, it’s going to just wreck everything. So, when you can plan ahead and the ice came in, the cement came in and the boards on budget and on time. That is phenomenal for the small community,” said Ferguson.

Brooke-Alvinston Arena The new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena is starting to freeze after being installed recently. Critical repairs were need to the rink as it approaches 50 years (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

Work began on the arena floor project back in May and continues to progress.

“The quotes came back at $1.1 million,” said Ferguson. “The grant from Ontario (Ontario community Sport and Recreation Infrastructure Fund) is half of 2 million, so we could get up to $1 million of grant money matched dollar for dollar. This was cost effective when the tenders came in and when you’re able to include the boards in it, the total project would be about $1.5 million. Half from the government, half from the township.”

With roads and bridges to pay for, the Municipality did not want to include the repair costs on the tax bill of the 2,350 residents.

They started the Alvinston Arena Floor Fund (Aaff) immediately and with sponsors, and private donors included, they are making a significant dent in the goal.

Brooke-Alvinston Arena Jill Joris (left), fundraising manager for the Municipality of Brooke-Alvinston and mayor Dave Ferguson (right) stand on the new cement floor at the community arena. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

“We’re at about $450,000 so far,” said Jill Joris, fundraising manager for Brooke-Alvinston. “Our goal is $1 million. We have some deals in the works as well, so hopefully those will pan out.”

A major boost came this weekend when the London Knights approached the Municipality about hosting an exhibition game to help raise money for the Aaff.

With the arena under construction, the neighbouring community of Watford allowed them to host the game free of charge.

London Knights exhibition game The London Knights and Erie Otters played an OHL exhibition game in Watford, Ont. to help neighbouring community Brooke-Alvinston install a new arena floor. (Source: Alvinston Arena Floor Fund)

The 650 tickets were snapped up quickly with the game being played in the hometown of Knights forward, Evan Van Gorp.

“Everywhere I went I just knew pretty much everybody because of the small town,” said Mike Van Gorp, Evan’s father.

“Everybody was coming up and talking to me and Melissa and the atmosphere was just great.”

One reason the game was so exciting was to see that calibre of play in a small venue.

“Everyone is so close to the ice and it is a very small ice surface,” said Mike.

“A lot of the comments were, ‘I can’t believe how fast it is’ and how ‘great the players are and how skilled they are to make decisions in such a small rink like that’. It was pretty cool.”

Brooke-Alvinston Arena Ice is starting to form on the new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

With help from Sarnia-Lambton Tourism, additional fan-friendly activities were held around the arena hours prior to puck drop.

“There were tons of fans in the stands,” said Joris.

“We had a few at the watch party as well. There were a silent auction and raffle and the donations for that were incredible. My heart grew three sizes that day.”

Small-town arenas are not just skating and hockey. They host the fall fair, baseball and even the rodeo. The hope is that the donations from the Aaff will prolong the life of the building for generations.

“We replaced the cement and we’re going to do the boards next spring,” said Ferguson.

“The ice pad and the boards will be all freshly redone by this time in 2027.”

With roads and bridges to pay for, the Municipality did not want to include the repair costs on the tax bill of the 2,350 residents.
They started the Alvinston Arena Floor Fund (Aaff) immediately and with sponsors, and private donors included, they are making a significant dent in the goal.

Brooke-Alvinston Arena Jill Joris (left), fundraising manager for the Municipality of Brooke-Alvinston and mayor Dave Ferguson (right) stand on the new cement floor at the community arena. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)
“We’re at about $450,000 so far,” said Jill Joris, fundraising manager for Brooke-Alvinston. “Our goal is $1 million. We have some deals in the works as well, so hopefully those will pan out.”
A major boost came this weekend when the London Knights approached the Municipality about hosting an exhibition game to help raise money for the Aaff.
With the arena under construction, the neighbouring community of Watford allowed them to host the game free of charge.

London Knights exhibition game The London Knights and Erie Otters played an OHL exhibition game in Watford, Ont. to help neighbouring community Brooke-Alvinston install a new arena floor. (Source: Alvinston Arena Floor Fund)
The 650 tickets were snapped up quickly with the game being played in the hometown of Knights forward, Evan Van Gorp.
“Everywhere I went I just knew pretty much everybody because of the small town,” said Mike Van Gorp, Evan’s father.
“Everybody was coming up and talking to me and Melissa and the atmosphere was just great.”
One reason the game was so exciting was to see that calibre of play in a small venue.
“Everyone is so close to the ice and it is a very small ice surface,” said Mike.
“A lot of the comments were, ‘I can’t believe how fast it is’ and how ‘great the players are and how skilled they are to make decisions in such a small rink like that’. It was pretty cool.”
Brooke-Alvinston Arena Ice is starting to form on the new cement floor at the Brooke-Alvinston Arena. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)
With help from Sarnia-Lambton Tourism, additional fan-friendly activities were held around the arena hours prior to puck drop.
“There were tons of fans in the stands,” said Joris.
“We had a few at the watch party as well. There were a silent auction and raffle and the donations for that were incredible. My heart grew three sizes that day.”

Small-town arenas are not just skating and hockey. They host the fall fair, baseball and even the rodeo. The hope is that the donations from the Aaff will prolong the life of the building for generations.
“We replaced the cement and we’re going to do the boards next spring,” said Ferguson.
“The ice pad and the boards will be all freshly redone by this time in 2027.”

stories.title: Community gathers to remember, educate, and advocate amidst growing pushback against harm reduction
stories.summary: Workers on the frontlines of the addiction crisis in St. Thomas marked the 25th annual International Overdose Awareness Day on Monday, calling for continued compassion and evidence-informed support as they face increasing societal pushback against their work.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Workers on the frontlines of the addiction crisis in St. Thomas marked the 25th annual International Overdose Awareness Day on Monday, calling for continued compassion and evidence-informed support as they face increasing societal pushback against their work.

The day, observed globally, highlighted the persistent need for awareness and action with the 2026 theme, “25 Years On. Still Needed,” underscoring the ongoing impact of overdose on individuals, families, and communities worldwide.

Amanda Zielinski, chair of Nameless Harm Reduction and Outreach Services, expressed concern over a growing climate where harm reduction strategies, safe consumption sites, and unconditional support for people who use drugs are misconstrued as “enabling”.

“I think people see harm reduction specifically as enabling,” Zielinski stated. She noted that society often views support services as the root cause of issues linked to addiction and poverty, rather than a vital lifeline.

However, Zielinski emphasized that turning a blind eye to the crisis is not a solution. “Drug use is still happening. There’s people still overdosing every day. And this gives us an opportunity to put the education out there and to make sure that their voices are still heard,” she said.

In just the past couple of months, three individuals have died from overdose in St. Thomas, underscoring the urgency.

Amanda Zielinski Amanda Zielinski addresses those gathered for the 2026 International Oversdose Awareness Day in St. Thomas.

Shawn Fisher, a member of St. Thomas Addicts Sharing Hope (STASH), who helped raise the banner honouring the day, shared his personal journey. After losing his job at the Ford plant, Fisher struggled with alcohol and later drugs but says he is now clean, crediting community support programs. “They do work. You got to let the programs work and you got to put in your work yourself,” he advised.

The Elgin Crisis and Withdrawal Management Program in St. Thomas, which operates with seven beds, also voiced worries.

Staff there fear that moves such as the closure of safe consumption sites, like the one in London, will place immense pressure on their team and exacerbate stress on emergency services.

Allison Dale, co-ordinator for the Elgin Crisis and Withdrawal Management Program, countered the “enabling” narrative. “Safe consumption sites are the least enabling thing ever. Nobody chooses to use fentanyl just because they want to, and because they’re able to.” She explained that these sites offer a safe space helping to keep needles off the streets and preventing fatal overdoses.

The Elgin Mental Health, Substance Use, and Addiction Coalition (EMHSUAC), alongside The Nameless, STASH, and other partners, organized local events. The coalition’s statement, “The City of St. Thomas and Elgin County Unite for International Overdose Awareness Day 2026: 25 Years On. Still Needed,” highlighted that while the day uses the term “overdose,” many deaths are linked to a “toxic and unpredictable drug supply” with unexpected contaminants leading some to use terms like “drug poisoning”.

A community gathering was held in the garden area of Indwell The Station on Talbot Street. The event featured local resource organizations, memorial activities, and opportunities for reflection, alongside a free community BBQ to foster connection and learning. STASH members were present, sharing perspectives to reduce stigma and promote hope.

stories.title: Cardinal Marc Ouellet wins lawsuit against woman who accused him of sexual misconduct
stories.summary: Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet has won his civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Quebec Cardinal Marc Ouellet has won his civil defamation suit against a woman who accused him of sexual misconduct as part of a class-action lawsuit.

Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ruled that Paméla Groleau’s accusations against Ouellet are unfounded and ordered her to pay him $100,000.

“The court finds that the allegations describing the four events cited by Ms. Groleau in the context of the class action are false,” he wrote in a decision released Monday.

Groleau had accused Ouellet of touching her without consent on three occasions between 2008 and 2010, while she was training or working as a lay pastoral agent for the church.

She also said she felt “hunted” by him at a fourth event, during which Ouellet moved across a room to come sit down next to her.

Castonguay noted in his judgment that Groleau changed her story several times, including eventually saying that she only considered one of the alleged interactions to be a sexual assault.

“Her allegations are unfounded to a point that, strategically, she decided to downgrade the three first events,” the judge wrote.

Groleau testified in court to the incidents involving Ouellet that she felt were inappropriate, which all took place at church gatherings with other people present.

The final alleged incident came in 2010, at an event celebrating a priest’s ordination, when Groleau said Ouellet slid his hand down her back to the top of her buttocks and left them there for “several seconds.”

Castonguay concluded that her testimony “was neither credible nor reliable.”

The allegations first surfaced in 2022 as part of a wider class-action lawsuit against the archdiocese of Quebec and dozens of its clergy or lay members.

In response to being named in the class action, Ouellet launched a $100,000 defamation countersuit against Groleau, alleging that she damaged his reputation, honour and dignity.

The judge said the damage to Ouellet “is amplified by the chosen vehicle, meaning that of a class action aimed principally at religious pedophiles, thereby equating Cardinal Ouellet, in the eyes of the ‘ordinary citizen,’ with that group of individuals.”

Quebec Superior Court approved a $31.5-million out-of-court settlement for the class action earlier this month.

In 2013, Ouellet was touted as a front-runner to replace former pope Benedict XVI, a role that went to former pope Francis. Ouellet headed the powerful Dicastery for Bishops, the Vatican office that oversees the selection of new bishops, from 2010 until his retirement in 2023.

The news that he had been named in a class action created a media firestorm.

The trial also heard from two other women who testified to having interactions with Ouellet that they felt were inappropriate. Castonguay ruled that their testimony was not pertinent to the question of whether Groleau had defamed Ouellet.

He also concluded that Ouellet was “not the author of the gestures” described by one of the two women.

The woman had testified that Ouellet had come up behind her and allegedly rubbed his pelvis against her behind as she prepared items for a mass in Montreal in 1992, but Castonguay said the evidence showed that the cardinal was not the person officiating masses at the time.

Castonguay said the true impact of the allegations on Ouellet “is difficult to quantify,” and awarded him the $100,000 he’d been seeking.

Ouellet has promised to donate the damages he’s awarded to organizations fighting against sexual abuse experienced by Indigenous people in Canada.

Lawyers for Groleau did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ouellet’s lawyers said in a statement they were pleased the court had recognized he had suffered an injustice that would result in him getting compensation.

“This judgment reaffirms a fundamental principle: even in the context of judicial proceedings, serious allegations must be based on accurate and relevant facts and advanced with the rigour required by their gravity,” said lawyer Dominique Ménard, in the statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Morgan Lowrie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Cambridge teen turns childhood lemonade stand into licensed business
stories.summary: What started as a lemonade stand built by a three-year-old and her mother has grown into a fully licensed food business in Cambridge.
stories.author: Hannah Schmidt
paragraphs: What started as a lemonade stand built by a three-year-old and her mother has grown into a fully licensed food business in Cambridge, Ont.
Alexis Oliveira, 14, officially registered Lemon Squeeze & Sweets after adding mini pancakes and refreshers to her menu.
“I love meeting people. I love being social,” she told CTV News. “It’s just fun because I get to make drinks and pancakes.”

The business began in 2016 as a simple lemonade stand outside the family’s home in Brantford. It became a summer tradition, with Alexis and her two younger siblings occasionally selling lemonade, cookies and popcorn.
She decided to take the idea further following an incident in May.

Alexis was selling mini pancakes at a citywide garage sale. Her mother, Jody Cowen, said that’s when the family received a visit from bylaw officers after someone complained that Alexis was serving food to the public.
The family contacted the City of Cambridge’s business centre and learned what was required to operate legally.

“We didn’t really know what was all required because we’ve done the lemonade stand for so many years without any issues,” Cowen explained. “Bylaw did some research, and he said everything was okay. But we decided just to register it, make sure she had insurance, and everything became legal after that.”
Alexis completed a food-handler course, and the business is now registered, insured and approved by public health.
The family also rebuilt the stand and Alexis renamed it Lemon Squeeze & Sweets.

“She’s a hard worker, she’s determined, she’s kind, she’s energetic. She’s a people person,” Cowen explained. “She’s grown so much from being the three-year-old little girl that we started this journey with, and it’s just amazing to see her continue with it.”
Alexis said the best part is making her customers happy.
“I love seeing people smile, and it’s really enjoyable.”
The teen has also used the business as a vehicle to give back to the community, including raising money for a children’s book author and hosting a community cleanup.
Lemon Squeeze & Sweets has made appearances at local markets and private bookings.

Alexis and her mother are also scheduled to bring the stand back to Forbes Park in Cambridge for Cruise and Craft Fest on Sept. 19. The following weekend, the stand will be in Galt for the Great Dog Day event.
For Alexis, the business remains as much about the people as the products.
“I love doing it with my mom,” she said. “She makes it funnier with all her jokes and stuff.”
“It honestly gives me goosebumps. Her visions of what she wants it to be is really exciting for me. I wish I could be that little girl,” Cowen said, laughing.

stories.title: Montreal woman searches for cat last seen at Toronto Pearson airport
stories.summary: A Montreal woman says her cat escaped at Toronto Pearson airport and has not been found more than two weeks later.

A Montreal woman is pleading for help finding her cat after the animal disappeared during a journey from Jordan to Canada more than two weeks ago.
Abir Batikhi says her seven-year-old cat, Caramel, was one of four cats travelling with her on a non-stop flight from Jordan on Aug. 17.
The Montreal resident says all four animals were secured in cages before departure. She however says that when she arrived in Montreal and collected the animals, one cage was empty.
“I received the four cages. One cat was missing,” Batikhi said.

After making inquiries, Batikhi says she was told Caramel had been seen in the cargo hold when the aircraft arrived at Toronto Pearson International Airport, where the flight stopped before continuing to Montreal.
She says airport officials informed her the cat escaped onto the airport ramp area near Terminal 3 and ran toward gates 29 and 30.
“That was the last reported sighting,” she said.
Since then, Batikhi has turned to social media in an effort to locate the missing pet.
“I post in all the groups on Facebook. Animal lovers, employees. I post a lot in Montreal and Toronto,” she said.
Batikhi, who has cared for Caramel since the cat was born, fears the animal may be hiding and struggling to survive.
“Because she’s scared, she will be hiding, starved. I don’t want her to die from starvation,” she said.
The animal shelter volunteer says she has been in contact with airport authorities repeatedly but remains frustrated that the cat has not been found.
“Please, I really want to know why they haven’t been able to trap her,” she said.
A spokesperson for Toronto Pearson said wildlife crews have been conducting daily sweeps of the airport grounds, setting humane live-capture traps and notifying ground crews to watch for the animal.
Dacia Rohlehr, CEO of pet transportation company Paws En Route, says incidents involving escaped animals during air travel are uncommon.
“There are about four million pets that travel annually, and out of those four million pets, about 0.01 per cent experience an issue,” Rohlehr said.
She says strict regulations are in place to reduce the risk of animals escaping during transport, including requirements that kennel doors be secured.
“The gate and the door have a zip tie and that is well secured as well, because you don’t want that to open during flight,” Rohlehr said.

Batikhi says the cages were secured with zip ties before departure from Jordan and inspected before the flight. She says she does not know whether Caramel escaped during the flight or after the aircraft landed.
“I just need to bring back my cat,” she said.

stories.title: UAE intercepts an Iranian drone, and other news from the Middle East
stories.summary: An Iranian drone was intercepted early Monday over the United Arab Emirates’ territorial waters, the Defense Ministry said.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
An Iranian drone was intercepted early Monday over the United Arab Emirates’ territorial waters, the Defense Ministry said. The attack followed an exchange of Ffire between Iran and the United States over the weekend, which was the first significant military action in the war for more than a month.

Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here .

Iranian drone intercepted on way toward UAE

Iran fired a drone at the United Arab Emirates on Monday, which the Uae’s Defense Ministry said was intercepted over its territorial waters.

After more than a month with no significant fighting, the U.S. attacked rocket launchers on an Iranian island on Sunday, saying they were preparing to launch mines into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, all of which were intercepted.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that his country wasn’t seeking war, but that “we will respond decisively to aggressors.” The UAE called the attack a “dangerous escalation” from Iran.

Tanker struck by 3 projectiles in strait but no casualties

A tanker was struck by three unknown projectiles 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said late Monday.

The operations center said the tanker reported being struck while transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz. No casualties were reported and the Mtoc said the incident was being investigated.

Israeli airstrike kills at least 5 Palestinians in Gaza City

Israeli airstrikes on Monday killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza City, hospital officials said.

One strike hit the entrance of a residential building near the city’s municipal park, killing two, according to Shifa Hospital, which received the casualties. Two other Palestinians were critically wounded, the hospital said.

A second strike hit a vehicle in the city’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, killing three, the hospital said.

The deaths were the latest among Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire deal reached in October attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and Hamas.

Leaders of China, Russia and India gather as counterweight to the U.S.

The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.

The summit includes Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Pezeshkian was scheduled to meet with Putin on the sidelines on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was set to host meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in North Carolina on Monday and Tuesday, as Washington pressures other countries to help economically isolate Iran.

U.S. approves sale of multipurpose helicopters to Iraq

The Trump administration approved the sale of multiple-purpose helicopters worth US$800 million to the government of Iraq despite concerns that Iraqi authorities are not doing enough to clamp down on Iranian-affiliated militias.

The State Department said Monday it had given the green light for the sale of an unspecified number of Bell 412EPX and Bell 407M helicopters along with related equipment, including weaponry.

The choppers can be used for personnel and cargo transport but can also be converted into attack aircraft.

Israel signs multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece

Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece on Monday, the largest between the two Mediterranean countries, as Israeli defence exports soar.

Israel’s Defense Ministry said the 3 billion-euro ($3.5 billion) defence export deal, dubbed Achilles Shield, is one of the country’s largest and includes a multilayered air defense system for Greece using Israeli technology.

The agreement comes as Israeli weapons exports have reached record highs with more than $19 billion last year, a 30 per cent increase from 2024, according to official data. That is despite widespread criticism of Israel’s conduct in its wars in Gaza, with the Hezbollah militant group and with Iran.

Iraq rejects proposal to keep some forces from U.S.-led coalition

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi rejected a proposal to keep some forces from a U.S.-led coalition in Iraq after Sept. 30, when the mission is supposed to end, state media reported.

Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told The Associated Press by phone that the U.S.-led coalition had offered to leave a number of its advisers in Iraq beyond Sept. 30 if the Iraqi government wanted them to remain.

U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a presence in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. The remaining troops are supposed to leave within the next month.

Countries welcome to join three-nation defence pact

Countries are welcome to join the defence pact signed by Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Monday.

The three countries agreed to a defence alliance on Aug. 7 that would treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Fidan said the Mecca Defense Alliance would be willing to accept new members following the first meeting between high-level officials from the current member states.

Egypt has been touted as a potential member for the alliance of Muslim-majority states and Fidan promised close collaboration with “friendly countries.”

While the alliance is intended to reinforce collective defence in a way similar to Nato’s Article 5, members have stressed that it is not aimed against any specific foe.

Lebanon asks for Greek help to bring peace with Israel

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun is asking for Greece’s help in implementing an agreement to end the war with Israel.

During meetings on Monday in Athens, Aoun told Greek President Constantine Tassoulas and Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis that Lebanon has been through long wars and “its people are tired.”

He suggested that Greece has good relations with both Lebanon and Israel, and could help facilitate an end to decades of war.

Iraqi court sentences man in freelance journalist’s kidnapping

An Iraqi court sentenced a man to 15 years in prison after convicting him of taking part in the kidnapping of U.S. journalist Shelly Kittleson in Baghdad in March.

The Central Criminal Court in Baghdad sentenced Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazim under Iraq’s anti-terrorism law.

Kittleson, a freelance journalist based in Rome who works with several American and European media outlets, was kidnapped by the Kataib Hezbollah militia in Baghdad on March 31 and released after about a week in captivity.

Vance says Trump’s AI post threatening Iran is ‘a message’

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said President Donald Trump was “sending a message” with an AI video posted on social media over the weekend that featured a stylized imaginary attack on Iran’s Kharg Island, which is key to its oil exports and which Trump has repeatedly threatened.

Vance said that the president “would be the first to say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s sending a message to the Iranians.”

Despite Vance’s comment, Trump makes virtually all of his announcements on military action and most other matters on his social media account.

The Central Criminal Court in Baghdad sentenced Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazim under Iraq’s anti-terrorism law.

Kittleson, a freelance journalist based in Rome who works with several American and European media outlets, was kidnapped by the Kataib Hezbollah militia in Baghdad on March 31 and released after about a week in captivity.
Vance says Trump’s AI post threatening Iran is ‘a message’

U.S. Vice President JD Vance said President Donald Trump was “sending a message” with an AI video posted on social media over the weekend that featured a stylized imaginary attack on Iran’s Kharg Island, which is key to its oil exports and which Trump has repeatedly threatened.
Vance said that the president “would be the first to say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s sending a message to the Iranians.”
Despite Vance’s comment, Trump makes virtually all of his announcements on military action and most other matters on his social media account.

content_blocks.text: An Iranian drone was intercepted early Monday over the United Arab Emirates’ territorial waters, the Defense Ministry said. The attack followed an exchange of Ffire between Iran and the United States over the weekend, which was the first significant military action in the war for more than a month.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here .
Iranian drone intercepted on way toward UAE
Iran fired a drone at the United Arab Emirates on Monday, which the Uae’s Defense Ministry said was intercepted over its territorial waters.

After more than a month with no significant fighting, the U.S. attacked rocket launchers on an Iranian island on Sunday, saying they were preparing to launch mines into the Strait of Hormuz. Iran responded by launching missiles at U.S. sites in Jordan, all of which were intercepted.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that his country wasn’t seeking war, but that “we will respond decisively to aggressors.” The UAE called the attack a “dangerous escalation” from Iran.
Tanker struck by 3 projectiles in strait but no casualties
A tanker was struck by three unknown projectiles 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center said late Monday.
The operations center said the tanker reported being struck while transiting out of the Strait of Hormuz. No casualties were reported and the Mtoc said the incident was being investigated.
Israeli airstrike kills at least 5 Palestinians in Gaza City
Israeli airstrikes on Monday killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza City, hospital officials said.

One strike hit the entrance of a residential building near the city’s municipal park, killing two, according to Shifa Hospital, which received the casualties. Two other Palestinians were critically wounded, the hospital said.
A second strike hit a vehicle in the city’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood, killing three, the hospital said.
The deaths were the latest among Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire deal reached in October attempted to halt a more than two-year war between Israel and Hamas.
Leaders of China, Russia and India gather as counterweight to the U.S.

The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.
The summit includes Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Pezeshkian was scheduled to meet with Putin on the sidelines on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was set to host meetings of the Group of 20 finance ministers in North Carolina on Monday and Tuesday, as Washington pressures other countries to help economically isolate Iran.
U.S. approves sale of multipurpose helicopters to Iraq

The Trump administration approved the sale of multiple-purpose helicopters worth US$800 million to the government of Iraq despite concerns that Iraqi authorities are not doing enough to clamp down on Iranian-affiliated militias.
The State Department said Monday it had given the green light for the sale of an unspecified number of Bell 412EPX and Bell 407M helicopters along with related equipment, including weaponry.
The choppers can be used for personnel and cargo transport but can also be converted into attack aircraft.
Israel signs multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece
Israel signed a multibillion-dollar weapons deal with Greece on Monday, the largest between the two Mediterranean countries, as Israeli defence exports soar.

Israel’s Defense Ministry said the 3 billion-euro ($3.5 billion) defence export deal, dubbed Achilles Shield, is one of the country’s largest and includes a multilayered air defense system for Greece using Israeli technology.

The agreement comes as Israeli weapons exports have reached record highs with more than $19 billion last year, a 30 per cent increase from 2024, according to official data. That is despite widespread criticism of Israel’s conduct in its wars in Gaza, with the Hezbollah militant group and with Iran.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi rejected a proposal to keep some forces from a U.S.-led coalition in Iraq after Sept. 30, when the mission is supposed to end, state media reported.

Government spokesperson Haider al-Aboudi told The Associated Press by phone that the U.S.-led coalition had offered to leave a number of its advisers in Iraq beyond Sept. 30 if the Iraqi government wanted them to remain.

U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a presence in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. The remaining troops are supposed to leave within the next month.

Countries are welcome to join the defence pact signed by Turkiye, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Monday.

The three countries agreed to a defence alliance on Aug. 7 that would treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Fidan said the Mecca Defense Alliance would be willing to accept new members following the first meeting between high-level officials from the current member states.
Egypt has been touted as a potential member for the alliance of Muslim-majority states and Fidan promised close collaboration with “friendly countries.”
While the alliance is intended to reinforce collective defence in a way similar to Nato’s Article 5, members have stressed that it is not aimed against any specific foe.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun is asking for Greece’s help in implementing an agreement to end the war with Israel.
During meetings on Monday in Athens, Aoun told Greek President Constantine Tassoulas and Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis that Lebanon has been through long wars and “its people are tired.”
He suggested that Greece has good relations with both Lebanon and Israel, and could help facilitate an end to decades of war.

stories.title: For the first time in six years, the Port of Churchill shipped Canadian grain to Europe
stories.summary: Prairie grain is once again being shipped out of Churchill in northern Manitoba. Approximately 30,000 tonnes of Canadian durum wheat, supplied by Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods, is being loaded at the Port of Churchill and will be shipped to customers in Europe this week.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Churchill, MAN. – Prairie grain is once again being shipped out of Churchill in northern Manitoba. Approximately 30,000 tonnes of Canadian durum wheat, supplied by Saskatchewan-based AGT Foods, is being loaded at the Port of Churchill and will be shipped to customers in Europe this week.

This marks the first shipment through the Port of Churchill since 2020, and is the first of three grain shipments expected out of the port this season, which will send more than 100,000 tonnes of grain to Europe. “Seeing Prairie grain once again moving through the Port of Churchill to European markets is an important milestone for Manitoba agriculture,” said Manitoba Agricultural Minister Ron Kostyshyn.

“Our producers need more ways to reach customers around the world, and Churchill provides an important northern gateway that can help diversify our trade, strengthen our supply chains and create new opportunities for Manitoba and Western Canadian agriculture.” Grain shipments to the port were halted in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the failing rail line, which has now been largely completed.

Chris Avery from Arctic Gateway Group (AGG), which owns and operates the port, says this will be the most diversified shipping season in the port’s history. “We’re very much open for business,” he said. “We’re once again a strategic asset to Canada, but that set of commodities is a mix of commodities.

It’s critical minerals, potash, Arctic resupply. It’s many other goods as well.” Another vessel is set to arrive at the port this week, which will load zinc-concentrate and the first-ever shipment of potash, mined in Manitoba, by Potash and Agri Development Corporation of Manitoba (Padcom).

Avery says AGG is also loading another resupply vessel this season destined for Nunavut, which he says shows how important of a role the port can play for the Arctic. Churchill Mayor Mike Spence hopes resurfacing grain shipments out of the port will help play a bigger role in Canada’s economic strategy, but says Indigenous voices are needed at the table.

“It’s time that we play and take a role in shaping where we need to go,” he said. “There is still much more work ahead, including building up our presence as a supply base for the Canadian Arctic, but this season is showing the potential of this Indigenous and community-owned trade corridor to diversify Canadian trade and connect northern and Western Canada with new markets.” Churchill is building global connections and AGG has also been working to strengthen international partnerships, recently signing an agreement with Port of Antwerp-Bruges International in Belgium, one of the world’s largest cargo-shipping hubs.

‘Getting grain back is huge’ Longtime Churchill resident Joe Stover, who previously worked a decade at the port, says he is delighted to see grain being shipped out of the port again. “With Churchill being in many conversations over the last couple of years, this is a chance to prove that we are indeed a crucial asset for Canada going forward,” said Stover.

“I have always believed in Churchill, and I have always believed the location services industry. It is about time Churchill finally realizes its potential.” Stover has worked the last number of years in tourism and has seen quiet rail lines and empty grain elevators.

He believes the return of grain will change that. “To see grain back after all these years just feels right,” he said. Renewed interest Interest in revitalizing the port has increased in recent years as Canada works to diversify its global trade markets and lessen its dependence on the U.S.

The port was shut down by its previous owner, U.S.-based OmniTrax, in 2016. It was then sold to the current operator, AGG, in 2018. Earlier this year, Ottawa said it’s considering a major expansion of the Port of Churchill that would transform the northern Manitoba facility into a year-round, multi-commodity trade hub.

“At a time when the United States has fundamentally changed all of its trading relationships, we are focused on what we can control,” said Rebecca Chartrand, who is the federal minister of Northern and Arctic affairs. “The return of grain exports is another example of what this northern corridor can deliver as we strengthen and diversify Canada’s trade infrastructure.” Currently, the shipping season out of Churchill is around four months, but new studies show year-round shipping is possible from the Port of Churchill.

A recent report by the University of Manitoba, Fednav Ltd. and the Arctic Research Foundation, say advances in marine technology and declining sea ice due to climate change mean shipping can be greatly expanded from the current four-month window.

It shows waterways could be navigated year-round by icebreakers costing between $100 million and $410 million, rather than the billions of dollars it would cost for more heavy-duty ships. Ottawa said that upgrading the port is still of significant interest, but the plan needs more development.

“We know that there is needed investment and infrastructure to build up the port and those are things that are under review right now,” Chartrand said. Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said earlier this year that Ottawa had indicated it wants to see liquefied natural gas shipped from Churchill by 2030, or federal support for a larger port expansion could be reconsidered.

The federal government has set a target of increasing Canada’s LNG production capacity to 50 million tonnes annually by 2030 and says it is working with provincial, territorial, and Indigenous partners to reach that goal.

stories.title: U.S. plan to develop Venezuelan oil adds urgency to Canada’s export diversification
stories.summary: Trump had said over the weekend that the deal puts Opec and Canada ‘on notice’
stories.author: Sophia Bertuzzi, Jeffrey Jones
paragraphs: A fractured trade relationship with the United States and potential surge in oil production in Venezuela could add urgency to Canada’s push to expand and diversify its energy exports.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on the weekend that he had struck a deal to take majority control of Venezuela’s oil reserves, noting on social media that the deal puts the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and Canada “ on notice .”

Though the details are still unclear, a flood of Venezuelan crude making its way to the U.S. market currently seems like a far-off proposition, and one fraught with risks. Venezuela is an OPEC member.
Still, the deal underscores the importance of Canada further reducing reliance on its dominant southern market – a years-long quest, analysts say.
That would require spending billions more dollars expanding pipeline capacity to the country’s coasts.

The recently expanded Trans Mountain system is currently the only pipeline network in Canada that transports Alberta crude oil to the West Coast, where it can be shipped overseas and sold at a premium to North American prices.

Before the expansion came online in May, 2024, Canada shipped about 97 per cent of its crude to the U.S. Since then, non-U.S. crude oil exports have steadily climbed from about 3 per cent to 15 per cent.

Residents in Cabimas, a historic petroleum hub on Lake Maracaibo, have long lived next to wells, pipelines and oil terminals, witnessing first hand the environmental fallout of Venezuela’s collapsing oil industry.
The Associated Press

In the month of June, non-U.S. crude oil exports jumped nearly 27 per cent year over year, according to Statistics Canada’s latest energy statistics . More recently, that demand has been bolstered by Asian refineries scrambling to replace Persian Gulf crude as the Iran War effectively halted the flow of one-fifth of the world’s supply.

“If you are a big importer of oil, you’re seeing what’s going on in Iran, and you also saw what happened during the initial phase of the war in Ukraine. Those disruptions in global supply can hurt your economy very quickly,” Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in an interview.

“A lot of those countries are trying to find new suppliers, partly to substitute for what they’re losing through the Iranian war, but also to ensure to have the optionality later on if there’s further disruption,” he added.

On Friday, Calgary-based Trans Mountain announced its network moved an average of 840,000 barrels of oil each day, running at 94 per cent of capacity during the second quarter of the year ending June 30th. Two-thirds of that was shipped to Asian refineries.

Canada and its energy industry have benefitted significantly from improved market access after the Trans Mountain expansion, but long-term competitiveness depends on being able to supply different markets rather than being captive to one, according to a TD Cowen report on Monday.
The report noted that Mr. Trump announced the Venezuelan oil deal a month before Ottawa’s Oct. 1 target for listing Alberta’s proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline as a project of national importance.

In July, the federal and Alberta governments announced Trans Mountain would take the lead on building and operating the one-million-barrel-a-day pipeline , running along roughly the same route as its existing system. The project is expected to cost up to $44-billion.

For now, Trans Mountain is in the process of making operational improvements that will boost the current pipeline’s capacity to 1.2-million barrels a day by the end of 2028, chief executive officer Mark Maki told The Globe and Mail.
In the meantime, Canada will continue to export about 4.5-million barrels a day to the U.S.
“We still don’t have the capacity to rotate fully away from the U.S.,” Mr. St-Arnaud said.
Shipping to Asia-Pacific markets is more profitable for Canadian oil producers, as exports are priced against the global Brent crude benchmark, which on Monday was trading at US$88 a barrel.

At home, Alberta producers sell to Canadian and U.S. refineries at the Western Canada Select price, which has recently been selling for a deeper discount to the North American West Texas Intermediate benchmark – as much as US$18.54 a barrel less than WTI as of Monday, compared with about US$12.50 a year ago.

The wider price spread could mean that Canadian oil shippers have filled up available space on the Trans Mountain Pipeline faster than expected when its expansion was completed in 2024, according to TD Cowen.
The lesson from the Venezuelan announcement is that market advantages are not guaranteed to last, the bank said.
With a report from Andrew Willis

A fractured trade relationship with the United States and potential surge in oil production in Venezuela could add urgency to Canada’s push to expand and diversify its energy exports.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced on the weekend that he had struck a deal to take majority control of Venezuela’s oil reserves, noting on social media that the deal puts the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and Canada “ on notice .”

Though the details are still unclear, a flood of Venezuelan crude making its way to the U.S. market currently seems like a far-off proposition, and one fraught with risks. Venezuela is an OPEC member.

Still, the deal underscores the importance of Canada further reducing reliance on its dominant southern market – a years-long quest, analysts say.

That would require spending billions more dollars expanding pipeline capacity to the country’s coasts.

The recently expanded Trans Mountain system is currently the only pipeline network in Canada that transports Alberta crude oil to the West Coast, where it can be shipped overseas and sold at a premium to North American prices.

Before the expansion came online in May, 2024, Canada shipped about 97 per cent of its crude to the U.S. Since then, non-U.S. crude oil exports have steadily climbed from about 3 per cent to 15 per cent.

Residents in Cabimas, a historic petroleum hub on Lake Maracaibo, have long lived next to wells, pipelines and oil terminals, witnessing first hand the environmental fallout of Venezuela’s collapsing oil industry.

The Associated Press

In the month of June, non-U.S. crude oil exports jumped nearly 27 per cent year over year, according to Statistics Canada’s latest energy statistics . More recently, that demand has been bolstered by Asian refineries scrambling to replace Persian Gulf crude as the Iran War effectively halted the flow of one-fifth of the world’s supply.

“If you are a big importer of oil, you’re seeing what’s going on in Iran, and you also saw what happened during the initial phase of the war in Ukraine. Those disruptions in global supply can hurt your economy very quickly,” Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union, said in an interview.

“A lot of those countries are trying to find new suppliers, partly to substitute for what they’re losing through the Iranian war, but also to ensure to have the optionality later on if there’s further disruption,” he added.

On Friday, Calgary-based Trans Mountain announced its network moved an average of 840,000 barrels of oil each day, running at 94 per cent of capacity during the second quarter of the year ending June 30th. Two-thirds of that was shipped to Asian refineries.

Canada and its energy industry have benefitted significantly from improved market access after the Trans Mountain expansion, but long-term competitiveness depends on being able to supply different markets rather than being captive to one, according to a TD Cowen report on Monday.

The report noted that Mr. Trump announced the Venezuelan oil deal a month before Ottawa’s Oct. 1 target for listing Alberta’s proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline as a project of national importance.

In July, the federal and Alberta governments announced Trans Mountain would take the lead on building and operating the one-million-barrel-a-day pipeline , running along roughly the same route as its existing system. The project is expected to cost up to $44-billion.

For now, Trans Mountain is in the process of making operational improvements that will boost the current pipeline’s capacity to 1.2-million barrels a day by the end of 2028, chief executive officer Mark Maki told The Globe and Mail.

In the meantime, Canada will continue to export about 4.5-million barrels a day to the U.S.

“We still don’t have the capacity to rotate fully away from the U.S.,” Mr. St-Arnaud said.

Shipping to Asia-Pacific markets is more profitable for Canadian oil producers, as exports are priced against the global Brent crude benchmark, which on Monday was trading at US$88 a barrel.

At home, Alberta producers sell to Canadian and U.S. refineries at the Western Canada Select price, which has recently been selling for a deeper discount to the North American West Texas Intermediate benchmark – as much as US$18.54 a barrel less than WTI as of Monday, compared with about US$12.50 a year ago.

The wider price spread could mean that Canadian oil shippers have filled up available space on the Trans Mountain Pipeline faster than expected when its expansion was completed in 2024, according to TD Cowen.

The lesson from the Venezuelan announcement is that market advantages are not guaranteed to last, the bank said.

With a report from Andrew Willis

Where pallets of food and supplies should be stacked high instead sit row after row of empty warehouse shelves.
Food banks across Alberta are sounding the alarm as some of their inventories reach dangerously low levels, making the organizations increasingly anxious as the holiday season approaches.
“This is the first time that we’ve encountered this level of scarcity within our warehouse,” said Darryl Burry, executive director of Food Banks Alberta.

The shelves at Food Banks Alberta are typically stocked with pallets upon pallets of donated products, piling all the way up to the roof of the warehouse. But right now, those same aisles are largely bare because of increased demand.
“Our goal here is to receive the donations of products that come from many corporate sponsors and supporters, and then we distribute that out to our network of food banks,” Burry said.

“Unfortunately, this month we have not received the same volume of donations and support as we normally would.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Unfortunately, this month we have not received the same volume of donations and support as we normally would."

The organization’s warehouse supplies 112 member food banks across the province. When a local food bank needs extra support, they place an order with Food Banks Alberta, who subsequently ships out the needed items.
In 2025, the association distributed 3.36 million pounds of food province-wide.
Demand increased so much this year, it distributed nearly 90 per cent of its total 2025 volume in the first six months of this year alone — with the busiest months still to come.
In August, the volume sent out ran 32.8 per cent higher than in August 2025.
Food Banks Alberta says statistics provided by Food Bank Canada’s 2025 HungerCount show Alberta recorded more than 210,000 average monthly food bank visits — a nearly 22 per cent jump from 2024.

“Most of the people walking through our members’ doors are working people and families trying to make ends meet,” Burry said. “They are our neighbours, our co-workers and the children sitting beside our children at school.
“Nobody in this province should have to choose between rent and groceries.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "Nobody in this province should have to choose between rent and groceries."
While the 2026 HungerCount numbers won’t be released until October, projections indicate there’s been yet another significant jump in those accessing food banks in Alberta.
When it comes to this summer, Burry says they have shipped more food out faster than donations came in.
“We’ve got about 350 pallets worth of product that we are short for the coming month of September,” Burry said.
Food Banks Alberta isn’t the only group noticing unprecedented demand; so is Edmonton’s Food Bank.
The organization supports more than 43,000 people monthly through its hamper program and the need is growing.

“We’re seeing higher levels of demand, and that can be in part for a large variety of reasons. However, we’re always trying to match that community demand as well,” said Haley Grinder, communications and media coordinator with Edmonton’s Food Bank.
“It does seem like this is a very, very difficult year for Albertans.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It does seem like this is a very, very difficult year for Albertans."
The food bank says when demand outpaces supply, like it’s on track to do again this year, they have to spend some of their own funding to keep up and inflation makes it even harder.

“Last year, Edmonton’s Food Bank spent $3.9 million on food purchases. We anticipate being higher than that — approximately $2 million more on food purchases — just to offset the lack of donations and our buying power,” Grinder said.

“2026 obviously has been a year of immense challenges, there’s no doubt about that. Inflation, everything that’s going on in the world right now that has that trickle-down effect, and we’re definitely feeling that — so every little bit counts.”
As we head into the busiest season of the year for food banks in the province, they’re hoping for some additional help from Albertans.
“This is the first time that we’ve encountered this level of scarcity within our warehouse,” Burry said.

“It’s going to become a huge challenge as food banks want to make their orders, and we simply don’t have the product to be able to provide them.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It's going to become a huge challenge as food banks want to make their orders, and we simply don't have the product to be able to provide them."

stories.title: Government officials are in Nepal to support search for missing Canadians, Anand says
stories.summary: Floods killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
The federal government has 10 officials on the ground in Nepal to support Canadians affected by flooding, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said Monday.

In a statement posted on social media, Anand said the officials, which include a member of the RCMP, are working to locate missing Canadians and support affected families.

“Our priority is to locate Canadians and permanent residents and confirm their safety while offering support wherever and whenever possible,” she said.

Flash flooding killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

Anand said on social media on Saturday that one Canadian who was previously unaccounted for had been found safe.

She said Monday that 30 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing, a number she says May change as the government gets more information.

“We recognize with empathy the profound impact that this situation is having on families and communities across our country,” said Anand. “We remain in direct contact with all affected families through designated points of contact within each family and through a collective meeting with them today.”

The federal government has said it will provide $5-million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal.

Global Affairs Canada said in a statement Monday that officials are engaging with trekking companies, hospitals, local police, rescue centres, airlines and other Canadian travel industry partners to gather information, establish contact and help account for affected Canadians.

The department said the deputy high commissioner of Canada to India is one of the 10 officials in Kathmandu.

“Canadian officials are working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, as well as international partners including the Five Eyes, France, Japan, Italy and Singapore, to share information and support efforts to locate and assist Canadians,” said Global Affairs Canada.

The department said the RCMP has deployed a liaison officer to Nepal to offer assistance and help determine needs for on-the-ground support. It said the RCMP is also engaged through the Interpol network and has offered support with forensic equipment and expertise.

Canada’s travel advice for Nepal and China was updated Monday to advise against non-essential travel to affected areas due to the damage caused by severe flash flooding and mudslides and the ongoing risk of further flooding.

“Our priority is to locate Canadians and permanent residents and confirm their safety while offering support wherever and whenever possible,” she said.
Flash flooding killed some 800 people and left roughly 3,000 missing, after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.
Anand said on social media on Saturday that one Canadian who was previously unaccounted for had been found safe.
She said Monday that 30 Canadians and permanent residents remain missing, a number she says May change as the government gets more information.

“We recognize with empathy the profound impact that this situation is having on families and communities across our country,” said Anand. “We remain in direct contact with all affected families through designated points of contact within each family and through a collective meeting with them today.”
The federal government has said it will provide $5-million in urgent humanitarian aid to support Nepal.

Global Affairs Canada said in a statement Monday that officials are engaging with trekking companies, hospitals, local police, rescue centres, airlines and other Canadian travel industry partners to gather information, establish contact and help account for affected Canadians.
The department said the deputy high commissioner of Canada to India is one of the 10 officials in Kathmandu.

“Canadian officials are working closely with Nepalese and Chinese counterparts, as well as international partners including the Five Eyes, France, Japan, Italy and Singapore, to share information and support efforts to locate and assist Canadians,” said Global Affairs Canada.

The department said the RCMP has deployed a liaison officer to Nepal to offer assistance and help determine needs for on-the-ground support. It said the RCMP is also engaged through the Interpol network and has offered support with forensic equipment and expertise.

Canada’s travel advice for Nepal and China was updated Monday to advise against non-essential travel to affected areas due to the damage caused by severe flash flooding and mudslides and the ongoing risk of further flooding.

stories.title: U.S. Supreme Court lets White House continue construction on Trump’s US$400M ballroom
stories.summary: A divided U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the White House to continue construction on a US$400 million ballroom project as lawsuits play out, a win for U.S. President Donald Trump as he flexes unprecedented executive power and remakes the capital in his image.
stories.author: The Associated Press
paragraphs: Washington — A divided U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed the White House to continue construction on a US$400 million ballroom project as lawsuits play out, a win for U.S. President Donald Trump as he flexes unprecedented executive power and remakes the capital in his image.
The apparent 5-4 decision replaces a temporary order issued earlier this month, shortly before a court-ordered halt would have gone into effect.

That temporary order was signed by Chief Justice John Roberts, assigned to handle appeals from the capital. But he publicly disagreed with the latest decision, writing a strong dissent that said the project is likely unlawful because it hasn’t been approved by Congress.
“Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers,” Roberts wrote. The court’s three liberal-leaning justices agreed.
The majority, ON the other hand, found the National Trust for Historic Preservation likely did not have the legal right to challenge the project.

The unsigned order pointed to government arguments that the ballroom would address national security concerns by shielding a planned underground military installation and offering a more secure structure for large events than the tents currently used.
By contrast, “the only harm the Trust claims is the offense one of its members will suffer from having to view a structure of the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ the government intends,” it states.

Trump applauded the decision, writing in a social media post, “I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat.”

The majority’s order did not directly decide the legality of the project, and the suit will return to lower courts. Documents filed in the case, though, say that key portions of the project could be complete within months — a quick timeline compared with a typical legal case.

The trust’s president and CEO, Brent Leggs, said the group was disappointed with the decision but pleased with Roberts’ dissent. “This is not the final decision on the merits of our case and does not resolve our fundamental argument — that each President is a temporary steward of the People’s House and does not have the unilateral authority to demolish and redesign it without the approval of Congress,” he said in a statement.
The Trump administration asked the justices to intervene after federal courts found the project must halt because it didn’t have congressional approval.

The lawsuit from the trust argued that Trump has no unilateral authority to undertake the work, which has included demolishing the East Wing. The group’s lawyers accused the White House of trying to “outrun the courts” by accelerating construction.
In lower courts, the administration has argued that the president has total authority to renovate the White House and other federal buildings.
The trust and the four dissenters, however, note that federal law prohibits the construction of any structure on federal parks or public grounds in D.C. “without express authority of Congress.”
The trust and its members, meanwhile, are “deeply committed to the preservation of historic American buildings,” bolstering their legal right to sue, Roberts wrote.
Trump on Monday called the lawsuit “baseless.”
“When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of,” he wrote.

The administration has said crews are working 20 hours a day on the planned 90,000-square-foot (8,400-square-metre) ballroom. The framework is expected to be completed in November and much of the facade done by April, with full completion slated for August 2028, according to court documents.

U.S. District Judge Richard Leon ordered a stop to aboveground construction of the planned ballroom in April, though the order would allow work on bunkers and military installations below ground to continue. Leon was nominated by President George W. Bush, a Republican.

The ruling was suspended but later upheld by a divided appeals court panel. Two judges appointed by Democratic presidents found the project was for Congress to decide and “not a matter for Executive self-help.” A third judge, appointed by Trump, found that the preservationist group that challenged the project had no legal right to sue.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer also made that argument to the justices and said the decision halting the work was “extraordinary and unlawful.” He said the completion of the project was “vitally required by national security.” National security was not an initial focus when Trump announced the work he said would be funded by private donations.
The administration has scored a series of other victories on the high court’s emergency docket, though the justices have ruled against some of the president’s signature policies after fuller review.
By Lindsay Whitehurst
Associated Press writer Michael Kunzelman contributed to this story.

stories.title: Police charge disbarred Brampton lawyer in alleged $4.5-million mortgage fraud
stories.summary: A disbarred Brampton lawyer has been charged in connection with a $4.5-million mortgage and cheque fraud, and police say there May be additional victims.
stories.author: Phil Tsekouras
paragraphs: A disbarred Brampton, Ont., lawyer has been charged in connection with a $4.5-million mortgage and cheque fraud, and police say there May be additional victims.
Investigators began looking into Pawanjeet Singh Mann the month after his legal licence was revoked by the Law Society Tribunal of Ontario in July 2025.
The tribunal had found that Mann, who operated the PJ Mann Law Professional Corporation, knowingly participated in a mortgage fraud scheme in late 2019.

Investigators revealed that, between June and July 2025, they received “multiple” complaints alleging that Mann had engaged in fraudulent activity. They said Mann “orchestrated” four separate mortgage and cheque fraud schemes, resulting in approximately $4.3 million in losses to the victims.

Mann was arrested on Aug. 21 and charged with four counts each of fraud over $5,000 and possession of property obtained by crime. He’s also charged with three counts of criminal breach of trust and two counts of uttering forged documents.

“These allegations represent a profound breach of trust by an individual entrusted with significant financial responsibility,” Peel Regional Police Deputy Chief Nick Milinovich said in a news release issued Monday.

“When that trust is exploited for personal gain, the impact on victims extends far beyond financial loss — it affects their daily lives, their sense of security, and their confidence in the systems meant to protect them. Peel Regional Police will relentlessly pursue those who prey on members of our community. No profession, title, or status places anyone above the law.”
Police are asking anyone who May have been victimized by Mann to contact their Fraud Bureau at 905-453-2121, ext. 3335.

stories.title: Bank of Canada set to grapple with renewed trade war pressures in rate decision
stories.summary: The Bank of Canada finds itself in a familiar dilemma this week as the escalating trade war with the United States casts an uncertain light over Wednesday’s interest rate decision.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: The Bank of Canada finds itself in a familiar dilemma this week as the escalating trade war with the United States casts an uncertain light over Wednesday’s interest rate decision.
The central bank has kept its benchmark rate on hold at 2.25 per cent for nearly a year now.

Before trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart earlier this month, economists and financial markets alike had widely expected the Bank of Canada would stick to the sidelines for the rest of the year and into 2027.
Recent tariff volleys have changed the economic context.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly five per cent of Canadian exports and Canada plans to retaliate with its own counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8. U.S. President Donald Trump has also threatened steeper levies on autos and auto parts starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca
Most economists still believe the Bank of Canada will stick to the status quo as it tries to get a sense of how prices and the economy react to a re-escalating trade war.
“The bank has been always hesitant to make a move on rates that they might have to retrace later, because things are so uncertain,” said Tony Stillo, director of Canada economics at Oxford Economics.
Financial market odds for a seventh straight hold in the policy rate stood at about 94 per cent as of Monday morning, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Over the spring, Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem routinely said that if the energy price shock tied to the war in Iran started to show signs of spreading beyond gas pumps, the central bank might be forced to step in with consecutive interest rate hikes to keep inflation tamed.
He similarly warned that any tightening of trade restrictions between Canada and the U.S. might push monetary policymakers to instead ease the policy rate.
Fresh gross domestic product data from Statistics Canada on Friday showed the economy grew at its fastest pace in more than three years in the second quarter following a year of little growth.
But most forecasts, including the Bank of Canada’s outlook, expect that pace to slow somewhat in the second half of the year.

“I don’t want to overemphasize the negativity, because it is possible that both sides could de-escalate in the months ahead. But I think we do have to brace for a tough spell for a little while here,” BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in an interview.
He said it’s still possible the Canadian and U.S. trade teams reconvene to avoid further escalation in the weeks ahead.

But absent a return to the negotiating table, Porter said he’s expecting the third quarter of the year to look much like the early days of the trade war in 2025, when a lack of clarity about tariffs weighed heavily on business activity.

While Stillo believes the tariff measures themselves aren’t enough to sink the economy into a recession, he said it’s the uncertainty around the long-term trading relationship with the U.S. that might put a chill on growth.

Inflation, meanwhile, has fluctuated sharply in response to gas price volatility. The annual inflation rate has since settled at three per cent as of July, and the central bank’s preferred core inflation metrics have remained well-behaved.

Even if the Bank of Canada does assume Canadian jobs or output will take a hit from the latest U.S. tariffs and associated uncertainty, Stillo said monetary policymakers can’t afford to take their eyes off the Middle East war.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on a range of U.S. goods could also add to inflationary pressures, though Stillo said it’s not clear whether those costs would necessarily get passed on to consumers as businesses grapple with a weak demand environment.
In Oxford Economics’ baseline forecast, Canada’s economy continues to grow through to next year, though a few tenths of a percentage point lower than the pace before the latest round of tariffs.
Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca
In that scenario, Stillo said he expects the Bank of Canada would hold its policy rate steady through 2027.
But if the central bank starts to see later this year that the economic slowdown is more pronounced, he said a drop in the policy rate by as much as half a percentage point could be in the cards.
While monetary policymakers aren’t expected to rush to cut rates on Wednesday, Stillo said he expects Macklem will lean against market expectations for a return to rate hikes.
“We think there’s an easing bias that’s going to be signalled, because they will look at potentially lowering rates if the economy performs, let’s say, weaker than we expect,” Stillo said.
Porter said that, absent the new tariff headwinds, the strong second-quarter GDP data would have made the case that rate hikes could be on the horizon.
But like Stillo, Porter said he expects the central bank will signal a bias for easing on Wednesday as threats to growth outweigh the risks of resurgent inflation.
“The trade battle really does darken the growth outlook. Unless that’s resolved, I think that’s really what they’ve got to focus on, first and foremost,” Porter said.
Craig Lord, The Canadian Press
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

The Bank of Canada finds itself in a familiar dilemma this week as the escalating trade war with the United States casts an uncertain light over Wednesday’s interest rate decision.

The central bank has kept its benchmark rate on hold at 2.25 per cent for nearly a year now.

Before trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart earlier this month, economists and financial markets alike had widely expected the Bank of Canada would stick to the sidelines for the rest of the year and into 2027.

Recent tariff volleys have changed the economic context.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly five per cent of Canadian exports and Canada plans to retaliate with its own counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8. U.S. President Donald Trump has also threatened steeper levies on autos and auto parts starting Jan. 1, 2027.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Most economists still believe the Bank of Canada will stick to the status quo as it tries to get a sense of how prices and the economy react to a re-escalating trade war.

“The bank has been always hesitant to make a move on rates that they might have to retrace later, because things are so uncertain,” said Tony Stillo, director of Canada economics at Oxford Economics.

Financial market odds for a seventh straight hold in the policy rate stood at about 94 per cent as of Monday morning, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Over the spring, Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem routinely said that if the energy price shock tied to the war in Iran started to show signs of spreading beyond gas pumps, the central bank might be forced to step in with consecutive interest rate hikes to keep inflation tamed.

He similarly warned that any tightening of trade restrictions between Canada and the U.S. might push monetary policymakers to instead ease the policy rate.

Fresh gross domestic product data from Statistics Canada on Friday showed the economy grew at its fastest pace in more than three years in the second quarter following a year of little growth.

But most forecasts, including the Bank of Canada’s outlook, expect that pace to slow somewhat in the second half of the year.

“I don’t want to overemphasize the negativity, because it is possible that both sides could de-escalate in the months ahead. But I think we do have to brace for a tough spell for a little while here,” BMO chief economist Doug Porter said in an interview.

He said it’s still possible the Canadian and U.S. trade teams reconvene to avoid further escalation in the weeks ahead.

But absent a return to the negotiating table, Porter said he’s expecting the third quarter of the year to look much like the early days of the trade war in 2025, when a lack of clarity about tariffs weighed heavily on business activity.

While Stillo believes the tariff measures themselves aren’t enough to sink the economy into a recession, he said it’s the uncertainty around the long-term trading relationship with the U.S. that might put a chill on growth.

Inflation, meanwhile, has fluctuated sharply in response to gas price volatility. The annual inflation rate has since settled at three per cent as of July, and the central bank’s preferred core inflation metrics have remained well-behaved.

Even if the Bank of Canada does assume Canadian jobs or output will take a hit from the latest U.S. tariffs and associated uncertainty, Stillo said monetary policymakers can’t afford to take their eyes off the Middle East war.

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on a range of U.S. goods could also add to inflationary pressures, though Stillo said it’s not clear whether those costs would necessarily get passed on to consumers as businesses grapple with a weak demand environment.

In Oxford Economics’ baseline forecast, Canada’s economy continues to grow through to next year, though a few tenths of a percentage point lower than the pace before the latest round of tariffs.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

In that scenario, Stillo said he expects the Bank of Canada would hold its policy rate steady through 2027.

But if the central bank starts to see later this year that the economic slowdown is more pronounced, he said a drop in the policy rate by as much as half a percentage point could be in the cards.

While monetary policymakers aren’t expected to rush to cut rates on Wednesday, Stillo said he expects Macklem will lean against market expectations for a return to rate hikes.

“We think there’s an easing bias that’s going to be signalled, because they will look at potentially lowering rates if the economy performs, let’s say, weaker than we expect,” Stillo said.

Porter said that, absent the new tariff headwinds, the strong second-quarter GDP data would have made the case that rate hikes could be on the horizon.

But like Stillo, Porter said he expects the central bank will signal a bias for easing on Wednesday as threats to growth outweigh the risks of resurgent inflation.

“The trade battle really does darken the growth outlook. Unless that’s resolved, I think that’s really what they’ve got to focus on, first and foremost,” Porter said.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press
