stories.title: Animal tranquilizer, sedatives found in Winnipeg fentanyl supply, warns expert
stories.summary: Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply.
stories.author: Kayla Rosen
stories.content:
Winnipeggers are being warned about the presence of animal tranquilizers and sedatives in the city’s drug supply.

Nurse practitioner Heidi Pharand-Joven, who works for Siloam Mission’s opioid addictions program, said her clinic is continuing to see fentanyl-related issues.

She explained one of the problems is that the synthetic opioid is often mixed with benzodiazepines or animal tranquilizers, which makes it less effective against opioid antagonists.

“Naloxone, Narcan is not as effective because it doesn’t have any effect on the animal tranquilizers or the benzodiazepines,” she explained in an interview with Your Morning Winnipeg on Monday.

“(Opioid antagonists are) still the best way. It’s still really important to educate people on how to use Naloxone and make sure that people who are using substances or who are with people who are using substances have Narcan kits available on them.”

Pharand-Joven’s warning comes on International Overdose Awareness Day — a day created to raise awareness and take action against overdoses.

According to numbers from the Manitoba government, more than 350 Manitobans died from substance-related deaths between January and November 2025.

Beyond the overdoses, Pharand-Joven said injection drug use is also contributing to the province’s high rate of HIV infection.

“When I’m working with clients at Siloam, that is definitely something that we talk about: infectious disease … You can’t treat one without the other,” she said

“We can’t have these continued siloed approaches for treating addiction and substance-use disorders. We have to consider all the other risk factors.”

In May 2026, the Manitoba government declared a public health emergency to fight the spread of HIV.

The province reported that HIV rates had been steadily increasing to a high of 328 new cases in 2025.

With files from CTV’s Rachel Lagacé

stories.title: Unifor turns focus to Stellantis after wrapping up deals with General Motors, Ford
stories.summary: Unifor says it will begin contract talks with U.S. automaker Stellantis after ratifying new collective agreements in Canada with General Motors and Ford.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Unifor says it will begin contract talks with U.S. automaker Stellantis on Tuesday.

The talks come after the union ratified new collective agreements in Canada with General Motors and Ford.

Unifor said Sunday its members at General Motors voted overwhelmingly in favour of ratifying new contracts with the automaker, with those in Oshawa, St. Catharines and Woodstock voting 80.5 per cent in favour, while members in Ingersoll were 96.5 per cent in support.

Latest updates on company news here

GM Canada president Jack Uppal says in a news release the new agreements include “meaningful improvements to wages, benefits and job security,” while making sure to “sustain good-paying jobs that have long been a cornerstone of Canada’s automotive industry.”

The three-year collective agreements increase wages for full-rate production members to $50.20 per hour and skilled trades workers to $62.71 an hour.

The union says its agreements with GM mirror the three per cent annual wage increases reached with Ford, which Unifor selected to kick off its pattern bargaining with the industry.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Lake Ontario merchandise grabs attention on both sides of the border
stories.summary: Branded hats and T-shirts are selling fast as Canadians and Americans alike spend to show support
stories.author: Arisa Valyear
paragraphs: Since U.S. President Donald Trump moved to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America , there has been a surge in interest in Lake Ontario-themed merchandise from shoppers on both sides of the border.

Google searches for Lake Ontario shirts in Canada peaked around Aug. 30, three days after Mr. Trump signed the executive order to rename the body of water, and audiences looking for Lake Ontario hats, tees and other items have reached what the search engine labels as “breakout” status – a phrase meaning interest in the search term has grown by a margin of more than 5,000 per cent compared to a previous period, such as the prior week.
Searches for Lake Ontario T-shirts are also at breakout level in the United States, with peaks occurring on Aug. 27 and 30.

Clothing retailers and e-commerce sites are taking notice. Province of Canada, a Toronto-based company offering a variety of Canadian-themed selections (including an exclusive Heated Rivalry sweater ), released a Lake Ontario quarter-zip sweater on Friday and saw strong interest from consumers.
“Customers are specifically looking for made-in-Canada products,” said Allison Piccininni, Province of Canada’s product and operations manager, in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

Like all of the company’s merchandise, the item is manufactured in Canada. It’s available for pre-order at $128, and Ms. Piccininni said they’ve already sold hundreds, with about 75 per cent of orders coming from Ontario, and the next-highest from British Columbia. The company will donate 15 per cent of each sale to Indigenous charity Indspire .

The light grey sweater, which has the words “Lake Ontario” printed in blue text on the front, has a cheeky online description that hints at the ongoing strife between Canada and the U.S. : “Some names are already pretty good.”
“We can see Lake Ontario from our office, so it feels very relevant. It’s not just a trend we’re trying to jump on,” Ms. Piccininni said.

While the retailer currently isn’t shipping to the U.S. (a decision they made in July to mitigate tariff-related cross-border shipping issues), Ms. Piccininni said they’ve fielded a number of inquiries from shoppers in America, who are either expats or Canadian supporters.

In Calgary, Connor Curran, co-owner of the Canadian-made custom apparel brand Local Laundry, said he’s already sold about 100 of his company’s Lake Ontario T-shirts . “Alberta and Ontario are where most of the sales are coming from, and then B.C. and Manitoba,” Mr. Curran said in an interview with The Globe. “Albertans are proud of the name Lake Ontario, and we’re proud Canadians as well.”

The T-shirt – a light blue offering with the words “Lake Ontario Canada” printed in white text on the front – launched on Local Laundry’s website Friday and is available for pre-sale for $55. “Lake Ontario doesn’t need a rebrand,” reads the description.

The item, which is entirely made in Canada, is an opportunity for the company to support the Canadian economy, Mr. Curran said. “Our milling facility is in Toronto, our dyeing is done in Ajax, our cutting and sewing is done in Scarborough and then the items are shipped to Calgary where we decorate and print them.”

In the United States, particularly in areas along the shores of Lake Ontario such as Rochester, N.Y., interest in Lake Ontario-branded merch is also high. A post in a Rochester subreddit titled “Where to get Lake Ontario Merchandise?” received nearly 400 interactions and more than 100 comments, with users mostly listing Rochester-based businesses that supply the requested items.

One user pointed to Pretty Apothecary , a Rochester-based gift shop and home goods store that sells Lake Ontario caps, stickers, candles, patches and more. The store’s owner, Mike Pretty, said by Saturday morning they were completely sold out of their Lake Ontario inventory. “There’s been a big surge in interest and there’s a lot of pride surrounding the lake,” he told The Globe in an interview.
Mr. Pretty said the lake-themed merchandise was always decently popular with customers, but now eager buyers are entering the shop asking: “What do you have that’s Lake Ontario?”

Given the surge in interest, Mr. Pretty said he’s already filled about 50 pre-orders, and he’s going to be restocking his collection of themed patches, stickers, candles and caps. He’s also expanded his hat offerings from one design to three to meet demand. Mr. Pretty said the restocked merchandise should hit shelves within the next few weeks, and that the patches will be available again in early October.

Lake Ontario Press , a Rochester-based screen-printing shop run by Matt Saxon, also saw an influx of customers looking to support the Lake Ontario cause. He said interested buyers have been contacting him non-stop, and that on Saturday, the shop printed some 300 Lake Ontario-themed items for patrons.
“I had customers waiting an hour out the door and we ended up staying open an hour later just to finish up,” the business owner said.

“Customers are specifically looking for made-in-Canada products,” said Allison Piccininni, Province of Canada’s product and operations manager, in an interview with The Globe and Mail.

Like all of the company’s merchandise, the item is manufactured in Canada. It’s available for pre-order at $128, and Ms. Piccininni said they’ve already sold hundreds, with about 75 per cent of orders coming from Ontario, and the next-highest from British Columbia. The company will donate 15 per cent of each sale to Indigenous charity Indspire .

The light grey sweater, which has the words “Lake Ontario” printed in blue text on the front, has a cheeky online description that hints at the ongoing strife between Canada and the U.S. : “Some names are already pretty good.”

“We can see Lake Ontario from our office, so it feels very relevant. It’s not just a trend we’re trying to jump on,” Ms. Piccininni said.

While the retailer currently isn’t shipping to the U.S. (a decision they made in July to mitigate tariff-related cross-border shipping issues), Ms. Piccininni said they’ve fielded a number of inquiries from shoppers in America, who are either expats or Canadian supporters.

In Calgary, Connor Curran, co-owner of the Canadian-made custom apparel brand Local Laundry, said he’s already sold about 100 of his company’s Lake Ontario T-shirts . “Alberta and Ontario are where most of the sales are coming from, and then B.C. and Manitoba,” Mr. Curran said in an interview with The Globe. “Albertans are proud of the name Lake Ontario, and we’re proud Canadians as well.”

The T-shirt – a light blue offering with the words “Lake Ontario Canada” printed in white text on the front – launched on Local Laundry’s website Friday and is available for pre-sale for $55. “Lake Ontario doesn’t need a rebrand,” reads the description.

The item, which is entirely made in Canada, is an opportunity for the company to support the Canadian economy, Mr. Curran said. “Our milling facility is in Toronto, our dyeing is done in Ajax, our cutting and sewing is done in Scarborough and then the items are shipped to Calgary where we decorate and print them.”

In the United States, particularly in areas along the shores of Lake Ontario such as Rochester, N.Y., interest in Lake Ontario-branded merch is also high. A post in a Rochester subreddit titled “Where to get Lake Ontario Merchandise?” received nearly 400 interactions and more than 100 comments, with users mostly listing Rochester-based businesses that supply the requested items.

One user pointed to Pretty Apothecary , a Rochester-based gift shop and home goods store that sells Lake Ontario caps, stickers, candles, patches and more. The store’s owner, Mike Pretty, said by Saturday morning they were completely sold out of their Lake Ontario inventory. “There’s been a big surge in interest and there’s a lot of pride surrounding the lake,” he told The Globe in an interview.

Mr. Pretty said the lake-themed merchandise was always decently popular with customers, but now eager buyers are entering the shop asking: “What do you have that’s Lake Ontario?”

Given the surge in interest, Mr. Pretty said he’s already filled about 50 pre-orders, and he’s going to be restocking his collection of themed patches, stickers, candles and caps. He’s also expanded his hat offerings from one design to three to meet demand. Mr. Pretty said the restocked merchandise should hit shelves within the next few weeks, and that the patches will be available again in early October.

Lake Ontario Press , a Rochester-based screen-printing shop run by Matt Saxon, also saw an influx of customers looking to support the Lake Ontario cause. He said interested buyers have been contacting him non-stop, and that on Saturday, the shop printed some 300 Lake Ontario-themed items for patrons.

“I had customers waiting an hour out the door and we ended up staying open an hour later just to finish up,” the business owner said.

stories.title: Trump ally Laura Loomer faces criticism over racist comments against Black women
stories.summary: Multiple lawmakers and rights advocates condemned Donald Trump’s ally Laura Loomer on Monday over her racist comments attacking Angie Nixon, as well as other prominent Black U.S. politicians and a U.S. Supreme Court justice.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
paragraphs: Washington - Multiple lawmakers and rights advocates condemned U.S. President Donald Trump’s ally Laura Loomer on Monday over her racist comments attacking Democratic socialist Florida State Representative Angie Nixon, as well as other prominent Black U.S. politicians and a U.S. Supreme Court justice.

“Angie Nixon is a ghetto, black, communist,” Loomer, a right-wing blogger, conspiracy theorist and Trump ally, said on X on Monday , while doubling down after previous similar comments from her sparked widespread criticism.

On Friday, she cast Nixon, U.S. Representatives Ilhan Omar and Ayanna Pressley, former U.S. Representative Cori Bush and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson - all of whom are Black women - as “ghetto, entitled, race-obsessed, destructive black Bitches who are completely unfit for the power they hold.”
Nixon recently scored an upset victory in Florida’s Democratic primary race for the U.S. Senate.
Loomer has also often made anti-Muslim comments, ranging from calling for Muslims to be banned from holding office in the U.S. to advocating for deporting and removing “all Muslims from America.”
“You attack and insult Black women because you believe peddling racism is good for your clicks and your business model,” Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said in response to Loomer.
U.S. Representative Rashida Tlaib, a Palestinian American who herself has been attacked by Loomer, said “anti-Black racism goes unchecked.”
U.S. House of Representatives Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Loomer a “stone-cold racist.”
Loomer has long been one of the Republican president’s most fervent supporters and is known to have Trump’s ear.
“Black women should Never have to endure such hateful and degrading rhetoric for daring to lead,” prominent civil rights attorney Ben Crump said on Monday.
The Council on American Islamic Relations said Loomer’s comments “are the very definition of anti-Black racism.”
Kanishka Singh, Reuters

stories.title: Judge says Smucker's lawsuit against Trader Joe's over frozen PB&J can proceed
stories.summary: A federal judge has ruled that J.M. Smucker can proceed with a lawsuit against Trader Joe’s over frozen sandwiches that Smucker claims are too similar to its Uncrustables.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
A federal judge has ruled that J.M. Smucker can proceed with a lawsuit against Trader Joe’s over frozen sandwiches that Smucker claims are too similar to its Uncrustables.

Smucker sued Trader Joe’s in federal court in Ohio last fall, claiming Trader Joe’s committed a trademark violation when it introduced frozen peanut butter and jelly sandwiches with the same round shape and crimped edges as Uncrustables.

The lawsuit further alleged that Trader Joe’s put its crustless PB&Js peanut in packaging that too closely resembled the colouring of an Uncrustables box and featured a similar photograph of a sandwich with a bite taken out of one side.

In court filings, Trader Joe’s said its frozen sandwiches aren’t round but shaped as “squircles,” or square sandwiches with rounded edges. The company said the crimped design is necessary to keep the contents inside the sandwich and Smucker, based in Orrville, Ohio, shouldn’t be allowed to monopolize it.

Trader Joe’s also said Smucker’s current Uncrustables packaging, which it only introduced in 2024, is not famous enough to meet the standards of a federal trademark dilution claim.

“Smucker reaches too far. Its sandwiches’ appearance and cartoon avatar are no Nike swoosh or McDonald’s golden arches,” Trader Joe’s said in a January court filing that asked for the case to be dismissed.

But U.S. District Judge John Adams ruled Friday that Smucker had devoted significant resources to developing Uncrustables and protecting the brand over the past 20 years. Adams said customers have come to associate Uncrustables’ design trademarks with the brand.

The judge also declined Trader Joe’s request to move the case to California, where it is headquartered and where the third-party supplier of its frozen sandwiches is also located.

The Associated Press left messages seeking comment Monday with Trader Joe’s and Smucker.

Smucker is seeking restitution from Trader Joe’s. It also wants a judge to require Trader Joe’s to deliver all products and packaging to Smucker to be destroyed.

Smucker filed its case a few months after another high-profile trademark lawsuit. In May 2025, snack food maker Mondelez International sued the Aldi supermarket chain, alleging the packaging for Aldi’s store-brand cookies and crackers “blatantly copies” Mondelez products like Chips Ahoy, Wheat Thins and Oreos.

In a July federal court filing, Mondelez and Aldi told the judge they were participating in settlement discussions.

Dee-ann Durbin, The Associated Press

A well-known bar that has been a space for Halifax’s LGBTQ2S community says it’s struggling to keep the doors open and is asking the public for help to prevent them from ever closing down.

Gerald McCowan and Jose Chiu, the owners of Rumours Cabaret, posted on Facebook on Sunday that they had approximately two months to secure a new, two-year lease and ensure it has the financial stability to continue.
“It’s not a bar, it’s a community space for everybody and everyone. Straight people, gay people, trans people, doesn’t matter,” said McCowan in an interview with Global News.
The financial issues are large, with McCowan saying the new lease that begins in November is jumping by about $6,000 per month, bringing costs to $18,000 monthly before taxes.
Those costs don’t include other expenses like security, DJs, payroll, garbage, repairs and anything else it takes to run the business.
Given the costs, the couple has now turned to the public, asking for donations to a crowdfunding campaign — something neither wanted to do.
“It’s hard for us to make this decision that we went on GoFundMe to get support from the community because we don’t want to close the bar, we want to keep the doors open,” Chiu said.
The bar first opened in 2024, financed by McCowan who invested money from a settlement from Veterans Affairs Canada.
But its opening was actually a revival, bringing it back to Halifax decades after its former location on Gottingen Street closed down in the 1990s.
The couple has a two-month window to come up with an extra $18,000 to secure a lease.
“I’m looking at our finances. Looking at everything and the numbers, they just don’t work,” McCowan said.
There’s another reason behind wanting to keep Rumours open. McCowan and Chiu pointed to the recent closure of ARIS Bar and Nightclub in Moncton as another queer-friendly space disappearing.

“There’s definitely a need for these places that have historically served as places of communion, places of protest, places of joy,” said Teri Appleby, owner of Stardust Bar and Kitchen, another LGBTQ2S space in Halifax.
Appleby told Global News it’s integral for spaces like Rumours to exist for the community.
The Downtown Halifax Business Commission also offered its support in a statement.

“‘Rumours,’ as a name, has a long history in the LGBTQ+ community in Downtown Halifax,” it wrote. “We (DHBC) were excited when Gerald and Jose opened the NEW Rumours, and we hope to see it continue in Downtown Halifax for years to come.”
The GoFundMe raised more than $4,000 in less than 24 hours.

If the bar is unable to reach its goal, McCowan warned the business could suffer the same fate as the Rumours bar from the 1990s. He told Global News it would be difficult to move the business to a new location, likely costing tens of thousands of dollars.
“We will be closed, very simple, there’s no doubt about it. Rumours will close for a second time,” he said.

Three people in Regina died from suspected toxic drug overdoses on Saturday, according to the Saskatchewan Coroners Service.

The deaths prompted the provincial health ministry to issue an alert Monday regarding the unknown substance. The alert is only in effect in the city of Regina. It noted that recent events “indicate a higher risk of overdose and death from drugs in the area.”
“Alcohol may have been a contributing factor to the suspected overdose in one instance,” the Saskatchewan Ministry of Health added in its bulletin .
Officials are unsure what the drug is being sold as, according to the ministry. In some instances, it said the drug was possibly sold as cocaine or fentanyl.
People are injecting or inhaling the substances, the health ministry said. It was described as a cloudy liquid with a white, or solid, residue at the bottom.

Cocaine, fentanyl and alcohol were among some of the substances officials believe may be in the toxic drug. The health ministry cautioned that the overdose-reversing drug naloxone is not effective against non-opioids like cocaine.
The overdose alert will expire in one week, on Sept. 7.

stories.title: Alberta's Smith says Canadians 'confused' by Trump's targeting of Lake Ontario
stories.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is pushing her message for an end to the fierce U.S.-Canada trade war directly to Americans.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton — Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is pushing her message for an end to the fierce U.S.-Canada trade war directly to Americans.

Smith, appearing on the Fox Business Network on Monday, was asked how Canadians feel about U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent move to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America.

“Canadians are confused. I think they’re disappointed,” she said.

Smith added it’s particularly confounding given the two countries’ long-standing economic and military relationship.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

Canadian troops stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Americans in Afghanistan, she said, and the upcoming 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks against the United States is a reminder of that close relationship.

“We don’t understand why the Americans would want Canada to be weaker,” Smith said.

“I think we’re stronger together.”

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports starting Aug. 22, after trade talks fell apart. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products would start Sept. 8.

When asked who will be hurt the most by the trade war — Canada or the United States — Smith said it will topple small businesses and decimate jobs on both sides of the border.

She also repeated that her province’s oil and gas exports wouldn’t be used as a bargaining chip in trade talks, despite a push from some, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford, to keep everything on the table.

Smith continued to urge the Trump administration and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to resolve the dispute.

“Canadians are really hopeful that we can get back to the table — just talk about the outstanding issues, (and) resolve them. We came very close to a deal,” she said.

Smith isn’t the only Canadian premier to appeal to American television audiences since trade talks between the two countries disintegrated.

Ford told Cnn’s Wolf Blitzer last week his war of words with Trump got a little personal but that he wants to make a good deal for people on both sides of the border.

Ford and Trump had exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford.

Sitting in the Oval Office on Thursday, near a map with the name “Lake America” over the body of water, Trump said Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country is ripping off the United States.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they are not a state,” Trump said.

When asked why he’s targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.”

“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly,” Trump said.

“They are nasty people.”

Lisa Johnson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: U.S. Treasury secretary taunts Canadian navy's lack of firepower: 'Two submarines from the Edmonton mall'
stories.summary: "We’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada?" U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said of the trade dispute.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
paragraphs: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration is “not at war” with Canada, dismissing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s concerns about the ongoing trade rift while also taunting Canada for its lack of military naval power.

In an appearance on Cnbc, Bessent laughed off any suggestion that the U.S.-Canada trade dispute amounted to conflict between the two countries, then jokingly asked whether Canada would attack the U.S. with its fleet of defunct submarines that were once part of a West Edmonton Mall tourist attraction.
“We’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? What, are they going to take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?”

Bessent, who was responding to Carney’s previous claim that Canada was now “at war” with the U.S. and fighting for its sovereignty, took direct aim at the prime minister in his comments, framing Carney’s posture toward the U.S. as being politically motivated.

The West Edmonton Mall previously had four white and yellow submarines operating at its Deep Sea Adventure ride, which opened in 1985 and took riders through the mall’s aquarium. The ride was closed in 2005 after ridership dwindled. The submarines, which continued to fall off of the tracks they travelled on, were later dismantled in 2012.

Canadian observers had long pointed out that the ride had more operational submarines than the entire Canadian military. The Royal Canadian Navy currently has just four aging submarines in its fleet, each with intensive maintenance schedules that typically keep just one or two operational at a time.

In July, the federal government announced plans to purchase a new fleet of up to 12 submarines from Germany’s ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (Tkms), with the first orders set for delivery in 2034. The entire submarine program is expected to cost around $100 billion.

The U.S. Treasury secretary is just the latest Trump administration official to throw a jab at Ottawa as they look to justify their trade fight to American voters. Carney and his trade negotiators have been in a war of words with administration officials including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who have long sought to frame the trade dispute as a result of Canada’s decision to back away from diplomatic discussions.
“I think this is very unfortunate that prime minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match,” Bessent said during the Cnbc interview.

In late July, U.S. President Donald Trump declared he would be slapping punishing 50 per cent tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian exports, including on products like alcohol and dairy, unless the two sides could reach a new trade deal. Negotiations ultimately fell through after the U.S. president added last-minute amendments that would have restricted Canada’s ability to trade with other nations, Carney and several other media reports have said. Canada responded with its own retaliatory tariffs on a range of products like home appliances and makeup, which will take effect Sept. 8.
Bessent on Monday said that Carney had won the election on an “anti-Trump” campaign, and sought to frame Canada’s trade posture as a result of the prime minister’s political interests.

“Carney “came to power on an anti-American, anti-Trump agenda. He was 20 points behind in the polls, and then he started this. And it’s unfortunate that he’s not doing what’s best for the Canadian people. He’s doing what’s best for the Liberal Party, what’s best for Mark Carney. And in the long run, the Canadian people are going to see through that.
Bessent denied that the U.S. had poisoned the trade talks by asking for too many concessions from Canada, saying that Ottawa had received a better offer than “any country on the globe.”

stories.title: Carney appoints former envoy to China Dominic Barton to lead investment promotion agency
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed high-profile executive and former diplomat Dominic Barton to lead the federal agency charged with
stories.author: Rahim Mohamed
paragraphs: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed high-profile executive and former diplomat Dominic Barton to lead the federal agency charged with promoting foreign investment in Canada.
Carney said in a press release on Monday that Barton will be taking over as chair of the board of directors of Invest in Canada.
“Mr. Barton brings extensive experience in global business, investment, and public service,” read the release.

Barton, 63, has long been a powerful behind-the-scenes figure in Liberal circles. He was appointed Canada’s ambassador to China by then prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2019 and served until 2021. Earlier, in 2016, he had been named chair of the Trudeau government’s advisory council on economic growth.

His time as Canada’s envoy to China was dominated by the “Two Michaels” diplomatic crisis. In December 2018, China detained Canadian nationals Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor on espionage charges widely viewed as retaliation for Canada’s arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. The two were held for over 1,000 days before their release in September 2021, shortly after Meng was freed.
Barton personally accompanied the two Michaels on their flight back to Canada.

Shortly after stepping down from his post as Canada’s envoy to China, Barton accepted a position as chair of global mining giant Rio Tinto. While the job change raised eyebrows over Rio Tinto’s extensive activities in China, Barton was able to avoid an ethics probe into the matter.

Barton, a former senior executive with consulting firm McKinsey & Company, was called to testify before the House of Commons in 2023 in relation to more than $100 million in consulting fees incurred by the Trudeau government.
“Carney has appointed the ultimate Liberal powerbroker to head up the government’s corporate welfare agency,” he wrote. “The Liberal Club gets rich making everyone else poor.”
Carney also announced the appointment of financier Gurinder Grewal as Chief Executive Officer of Invest in Canada.

“Dominic Barton and Gurinder Grewal have the experience and ambition Canada needs. Under their leadership, Invest in Canada will catalyse billions in new investments into Canada to build a stronger, more independent, more resilient Canadian economy for all,” said Carney.
Founded in 2018, Invest in Canada is an arms-length federal agency that promotes and attracts foreign direct investment into Canada.

content_blocks.text: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney has appointed high-profile executive and former diplomat Dominic Barton to lead the federal agency charged with promoting foreign investment in Canada.
Carney said in a press release on Monday that Barton will be taking over as chair of the board of directors of Invest in Canada.
“Mr. Barton brings extensive experience in global business, investment, and public service,” read the release.

Barton, 63, has long been a powerful behind-the-scenes figure in Liberal circles. He was appointed Canada’s ambassador to China by then prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2019 and served until 2021. Earlier, in 2016, he had been named chair of the Trudeau government’s advisory council on economic growth.

His time as Canada’s envoy to China was dominated by the “Two Michaels” diplomatic crisis. In December 2018, China detained Canadian nationals Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor on espionage charges widely viewed as retaliation for Canada’s arrest of Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou on a U.S. extradition request. The two were held for over 1,000 days before their release in September 2021, shortly after Meng was freed.
Barton personally accompanied the two Michaels on their flight back to Canada.

Shortly after stepping down from his post as Canada’s envoy to China, Barton accepted a position as chair of global mining giant Rio Tinto. While the job change raised eyebrows over Rio Tinto’s extensive activities in China, Barton was able to avoid an ethics probe into the matter.

stories.title: Ontario’s new cash bail rules on hold: judge
stories.summary: will be suspended while a court case on whether they are consistent with Canada’s constitution is decided, an Ontario Superior Court justice ruled Monday.
stories.author: Jon Woodward
stories.content:
will be suspended while a court case on whether they are consistent with Canada’s constitution is decided, an Ontario Superior Court justice ruled Monday.

In a written decision, Justice William Chalmers said that he was willing to grant an injunction against the rules created by the Keeping Criminals Behind Bars Act to avoid the possibility that someone’s chance at bail would be affected by them.

“An impact on the liberty of presumed innocent individuals is irreparable harm,” Chalmers said in his ruling, as he quoted a Canadian Supreme Court judge in saying, “Liberty lost is never regained and can never be fully compensated for.”

The ruling’s effect is to cancel, for now, the new rules, which came into effect two weeks ago and require that someone granted bail would have to produce the money within two days of being released.

Previously, someone granted bail was usually required to pledge the money, with it being given up only in the case of a breach of the bail terms. Requiring cash bail up front has been an option for judges, but federal rules have required that to be a last resort for about 50 years.

The Ford government had enacted the new rules earlier this month, arguing that the rules would better encourage people on bail to follow the rules with their own money held by the court, which could more easily seize it.

The rules were challenged on the same day they came into force by the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (Ccla) and the Criminal Lawyers Association.

Those groups said that requiring a cash deposit up front would lead to different rules for the rich and the poor, and that if every order from a judge to pledge an amount became a requirement for cash bail, that would conflict with federal law.

Chalmers said the test for an injunction was granted, saying that it was a serious issue, that there was the possibility of irreparable harm, and that the balance of convenience favoured the challengers.

“Although I acknowledge the strong presumption that the impugned legislation is for the public good, I also acknowledge that the existing bail provisions in the Code were enacted by Parliament for the public good,” he wrote.

“The legislation came into effect less than two weeks ago. I am also of the view that it is not necessary or appropriate to wait for irreparable harm to occur before an injunction May issue,” he wrote.

Shakir Rahim, the director of Criminal Justice Program at the Ccla, said he was happy with the interim rules and said this would go a long way to settling some of the disruptions they had created at bail hearings through Ontario.

One judge in Milton ruling on a bail application, for example, had ruled he would not follow the provincial rules, arguing that they conflicted with federal rules.

“We even heard situations where Crown (attorneys) had different views about what to do with this. The uncertainty was going to continue if we didn’t have the clarity of the injunction,” Rahim said.

Chalmers has yet to rule on the merits of the case. The injunction’s effect is immediate, Rahim said, which means the courts will revert to a pledge bail system.

“They will just go back to how they were operating around two weeks ago,” Rahim said.

The office of Ontario’s Attorney General, Doug Downey, said in a statement,“Our government will never apologize for the actions we are taking to strengthen the bail system. We are using every tool available to make bail more consequential to protect victims and communities. As this matter is before the court, we have no further comment.”

stories.title: Family of woman killed in Thunder Bay asking for answers after man convicted in her death granted parole
stories.summary: Family and supporters of the family of Barbara Kentner marched Monday to the Parole Board of Canada's office in Ottawa, asking for answers as to why her killer is walking free on full parole.
stories.author: Beverly Andrews
paragraphs: Posted August 31, 2026 5:33 pm.
Family and supporters of the family of Barbara Kentner marched Monday to the Parole Board of Canada’s office in Ottawa, asking for answers as to why her killer is walking free on full parole.

“Barbara was my sister, she was a mother, an aunt and a friend, she was loved, she had a family who needed her, we still need her,” said Kentner’s sister Connie. “And now we are being asked to accept a decision that allows Brayden Bushby, the man responsible for her death to return to Thunder Bay, a small community,on full parole.”

In Jan. 2017, Kentner, a 34-year-old woman, was walking along a quiet Thunder Bay street with her sister. Bushby, who was 18 years old at the time, threw a trailer hitch from a passing vehicle, striking Kentner in the stomach.
She died several months later from injuries suffered during the assault.
Bushby was sentenced to nearly eight years in prison for manslaughter in 2021 minus time served. The ruling said his unlawful act significantly contributed to the victim’s death.
He was granted full parole in August, despite previously having his day parole revoked.

“We are forced to ask ourselves the question, what kind of considerations for victims is that? Our family is left feeling that once again we have been failed by a system that is supposed to recognize and respect victims of crime,” said Connie.

The Kentner family says they were not consulted or provided any information on the condition of Bushby’s parole and they have continued to experience injustice, including having to hear the details of the crime and explain their pain over and over again.

“Barbara Kentner is another statistic of murdered and missing Indigenous women. The murder and the killing of our women must stop,” Caludent Commanda, a supporter of the Kentner family. “Bushby walks free but Barbara’s family, they will continue to live a life sentence of sorrow, of sadness, of grief, of trauma. Canada’s justice system and the Parole Board of Canada must be held accountable.”

“As we continue to experience injustice, we have to hear the details again, we have to explain our pain again, when the parole board makes a decision like this, they are not deciding in a vacuum,”added Connie.
Bushby was previously granted day parole in 2023 which was later revoked.
At the time, the board said it found Bushby had violated several terms of his day parole, including a prohibition on consuming alcohol.

Bushby had failed a breathalyzer test during a traffic stop, the board said. He also had failed to remain at the scene after he reversed a car into another vehicle, and was a suspect in a car theft investigation, it said in a report.
He was returned to custody in 2024.

“There are Indigenous women and girls watching, there are families who are asking themselves whether the justice system will protect them and whether their voices will matter if something happens to them,” said Connie.
For now, Kentner’s family will be waiting for a response from the parole board and honouring the life of their sister who was a loving mother and friend.
With files from The Canadian Press

Connie Kentner, sister of Barbara Kentner, participates in a March following the decision to grant full parole to the man who was convicted of her sister's manslaughter, in Ottawa, ON Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. Barbara Kentner, a member of Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation, died after complications to her injuries after she was struck by a trailer hitch thrown from a moving vehicle by Brayden Bushby in Thunder Bay in 2017. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

stories.title: Majority of Albertans in favour of staying in Canada and few intend to change their vote: poll
stories.summary: The majority of Albertans believe the province should remain in Canada and very few intend to change their opinion ahead of fall referendum
stories.author: Cindy Tran
paragraphs: The majority of Albertans believe the province should remain in Canada and very few intend to change their opinion ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum, according to an August Leger poll.

Albertans are set to vote on 10 yes or no questions this Oct. 19, with the most anticipated being a two-pronged question on separation. Option one asks Albertans whether they believe the province should remain in Canada and option two asks whether or not the provincial government should hold a binding referendum on separation.

Andrew Enns, executive vice-president at Leger, said Albertans seem motivated to cast their votes. According to the poll those who said they’d vote for option one are 89 per cent certain their vote will not change by Oct. 19.
“People are paying attention,” Enns said.
“Those that feel Alberta’s better off to stay in Canada aren’t really hearing anything to change their mind to any demonstrable degree.”

About 72 per cent of respondents said there is a high chance they will be voting in the upcoming fall referendum. Leger asked respondents how likely they were to vote on Oct. 19 using a scale from one to 10.

The latest August poll shows a two per cent increase in the number of people who are following the separation discussion to some degree. According to the August poll, 75 per cent of respondents say they’re paying attention to Alberta independence discussions and 24 per cent say they’re not paying as close attention.

Voting intention on the two-part separation question on the fall referendum has remained fairly steady since June. About 65 per cent of respondents said they intend to vote for option one — for Alberta to remain in Canada and 23 per cent intend to vote for option two — for the government to hold a binding referendum on separation.
In the past two months, the number of respondents who are undecided about which way to vote has increased to 10 per cent, compared to the six per cent reported in June.

About 62 per cent of respondents believe their vote will make a difference compared to the 36 per cent who believe those who will choose the same option as them will vote in large enough numbers and 32 per cent believe the vote is a “foregone conclusion.” The remaining 14 per cent say they are less motivated to vote because they expect the option they prefer to win easily.

Perception of the fall referendum and separation discussions on the economy have changed significantly since June. According to the August poll, 48 per cent of respondents perceive separation to have a negative impact on the economy — down 12 per cent from June.
About 25 per cent of respondents say the referendum and independence talks are having a positive impact on the economy.
In between are 14 per cent who say there is no real impact on the economy and 12 per cent are unsure.

Enns said the numbers were likely higher in June due to the novelty of the separation question being announced. He said commentary from the business community and political parties likely influenced public perception on the potential impacts of separation.
“I think that what some people said was going to be really bad as a result of the referendum some of that hasn’t necessarily transpired,” Enns said.

Amidst the ongoing separation discussions, Canada and the United States are currently locked in a trade war after the two countries failed to reach a deal. The result has been clashing on both sides with U.S. President Donald Trump reviving his previous statements about Canada becoming the 51st State.

According to the poll 62 per cent of respondents are concerned about the possibility of American interference and influence in discussions around the province’s independence. About 31 per cent said they are not concerned at all.
“Whether it’s the trade issues, whether it’s his 51st state comments, or now he’s renaming a lake to Lake America, so I’m not surprised that there’s this level of concern,” Enns said.
“I think everybody including Elections Alberta is right to be on their toes in terms of keeping an eye on things (related to American interference).”
The poll was conducted Aug. 21-23 in an online survey among 1,001 adult Albertans. Leger said the probability sample yields a margin of error no greater than +/- 3.1 per cent.

stories.title: Legal aid lawyers begin weeklong strike in regions of Quebec
stories.summary: Montreal - Legal aid lawyers in four regions of Quebec are on strike this week.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
paragraphs: They are asking the government to offer them the same salary as Crown prosecutors.
Cédric Bernier is an executive member of the Quebec City union.
He told The Canadian Press that the collective agreement for legal aid lawyers in Quebec expired three years ago.
Article continues below
The legal aid offices in the Quebec City, Outaouais, Estrie and Côte-Nord regions will be on strike until Friday.
Legal aid lawyers represent clients who do not have the financial means to hire a private lawyer.
The strike has already caused 230 criminal and youth cases to be delayed in Quebec City, Bernier said.
A longer strike is still on the table if negotiations don’t move forward, he said. He added that the unions hope not to get to that point, fearing the effect of long strikes on clients.
“The people who are represented by legal aid, we’re talking about the most vulnerable people in our society: people with mental health problems, students, seniors, people with low income,” he said.
Bernier said legal aid lawyers regularly have to negotiate to maintain the same salary as the Crown prosecutors.
“We always have to fight to get it, every time (the collective agreement) renews,” he said.
The government has offered the unions a 14.5 per cent increase over four years, he said.
Bernier noted that the government gave Crown prosecutors a 17 per cent increase and said it’s now up to the government to improve their offer to avoid further labour action.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.
The Canadian Press

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is pushing her message for an end to the fierce U.S.-Canada trade war directly to Americans.
Smith, appearing on the Fox Business Network on Monday , was asked how Canadians feel about U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent move to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America.
“Canadians are confused,” she said.
“I think they’re disappointed.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think they're disappointed."
Smith added it’s particularly confounding given the two countries’ long-standing economic and military relationship.

Canadian troops stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Americans in Afghanistan, she said, and the upcoming 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks against the United States is a reminder of that close relationship.
“We don’t understand why the Americans would want Canada to be weaker,” Smith said.
“I think we’re stronger together.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think we're stronger together."

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports starting Aug. 22, after trade talks fell apart. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products would start Sept. 8.
When asked who will be hurt the most by the trade war — Canada or the United States — Smith said it will topple small businesses and decimate jobs on both sides of the border.

She also repeated that her province’s oil and gas exports wouldn’t be used as a bargaining chip in trade talks, despite a push from some, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford, to keep everything on the table.
Smith continued to urge the Trump administration and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to resolve the dispute.
“Canadians are really hopeful that we can get back to the table — just talk about the outstanding issues, (and) resolve them. We came very close to a deal,” she said.
Smith isn’t the only Canadian premier to appeal to American television audiences since trade talks between the two countries disintegrated.
Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer last week his war of words with Trump got a little personal but that he wants to make a good deal for people on both sides of the border.

Ford and Trump had exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford.

Sitting in the Oval Office on Thursday, near a map with the name “Lake America” over the body of water, Trump said Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country is ripping off the United States.
“They want to be treated like a state, but they are not a state,” Trump said.
When asked why he’s targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.”
“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly,” Trump said. “They are nasty people.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is pushing her message for an end to the fierce U.S.-Canada trade war directly to Americans.

Smith, appearing on the Fox Business Network on Monday , was asked how Canadians feel about U.S. President Donald Trump’s recent move to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America.

“Canadians are confused,” she said.

“I think they’re disappointed.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think they're disappointed."

Smith added it’s particularly confounding given the two countries’ long-standing economic and military relationship.

Canadian troops stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Americans in Afghanistan, she said, and the upcoming 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks against the United States is a reminder of that close relationship.

“We don’t understand why the Americans would want Canada to be weaker,” Smith said.

“I think we’re stronger together.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I think we're stronger together."

The United States imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars in Canadian exports starting Aug. 22, after trade talks fell apart. Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on U.S. products would start Sept. 8.

When asked who will be hurt the most by the trade war — Canada or the United States — Smith said it will topple small businesses and decimate jobs on both sides of the border.

She also repeated that her province’s oil and gas exports wouldn’t be used as a bargaining chip in trade talks, despite a push from some, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford, to keep everything on the table.

Smith continued to urge the Trump administration and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government to resolve the dispute.

“Canadians are really hopeful that we can get back to the table — just talk about the outstanding issues, (and) resolve them. We came very close to a deal,” she said.

Smith isn’t the only Canadian premier to appeal to American television audiences since trade talks between the two countries disintegrated.

Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer last week his war of words with Trump got a little personal but that he wants to make a good deal for people on both sides of the border.

Ford and Trump had exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a “less charismatic, intelligent” version of his late brother, former Toronto mayor Rob Ford.

Sitting in the Oval Office on Thursday, near a map with the name “Lake America” over the body of water, Trump said Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country is ripping off the United States.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they are not a state,” Trump said.

When asked why he’s targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said “they haven’t treated us well.”

“The Canadian officials have treated us very badly,” Trump said. “They are nasty people.”

stories.title: Canadian, U.S. markets fall as oil prices rise amid geopolitical tensions
stories.summary: Canadian and U.S. stock markets fell and oil prices rose on Monday after the U.S. launched its first military action in a month against Iran.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Toronto — Canadian and U.S. stock markets fell and oil prices rose on Monday after the U.S. launched its first military action in a month against Iran.
U.S. forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates said it intercepted an Iranian drone over its waters on Monday.
The aggressive actions follow a lull in activity in the U.S. war with Iran, which has lasted more than six months.
Real-time TSX market updates here

“We’ve got renewed tensions between the U.S. and Iran around shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, and they’ve pushed the price of crude oil higher,” said Anish Chopra, managing director with Portfolio Management Corp.
“That really matters because the price of oil feeds directly into inflation expectations and into interest rate expectations.”
The October crude oil contract was up US$2.36 at US$85.76 per barrel.

The war has curtailed traffic in the strait, which accounts for about 20 per cent of the world’s oil shipments. Oil prices remain high after an initial surge earlier in the conflict and that has made everything from gasoline to shipped goods more expensive.
The S&P/TSX composite index was down 283.44 points at 36,270.48. Technology led the declines, while the energy sector was the only positive force.
S&P 500 market updates here

On Wednesday, the Bank of Canada is set to deliver its next interest rate announcement as the escalating trade war with the United States casts an uncertain light. The central bank has kept its benchmark rate on hold at 2.25 per cent for nearly a year now.
Chopra said investors will be closely watching for any comments from the central bank around inflation and the trade situation.

On Aug. 22, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on roughly five per cent of Canadian exports and Canada plans to retaliate with its own counter-tariffs starting Sept. 8. U.S. President Donald Trump has also threatened steeper levies on autos and auto parts starting Jan. 1, 2027.
Financial market odds for a seventh straight hold in the policy rate stood at 95 per cent as of late afternoon on Monday, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.
“A hold at 2.25 per cent is the near-universal call, so the story is the tone, not the rate,” Sébastien Mc Mahon, chief economist at iA Financial Group, said in a statement.
Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA
He said he doesn’t expect Canada’s central bank to raise interest rates this year.
“If the bank drops or softens that language, or nudges toward October, that’s the real headline,” Mc Mahon said.
In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 374.09 points at 53,185.90. The S&P 500 index was down 25.62 points at 7,686.14, while the Nasdaq composite was down 31.54 points at 26,370.89.
The Canadian dollar traded for 72.12 cents US compared with 72.00 cents US on Friday.
The December gold contract was down US$48.40 at US$4,481.50 an ounce.
Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press
With files from The Associated Press
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: Mother suffers burns to genitals, thighs, sides while giving birth in Prague hospital
stories.summary: A mother giving birth in a Prague hospital suffered burns during a caesarean section, the hospital said Monday, with media reporting a disinfectant caught fire during the procedure.
stories.author: AFP Staff
paragraphs: A mother giving birth in a Prague hospital suffered burns during a caesarean section, the hospital said Monday, with media reporting a disinfectant caught fire during the procedure.
The baby was not injured in the incident, a spokeswoman for the Bulovka hospital on the northern outskirts of the Czech Republic’s capital said.
But the Denik N daily said Sunday that the 24-year-old mother suffered burns to her genitals, thighs, sides and lower belly.

“The caesarean section was performed because of acute obstetrical complications,” the spokeswoman, Eva Stolejda Libigerova, told AFP on Monday, adding that the hospital was investigating the Aug. 25 incident.
“The mother is in a stable condition which does not require intensive care and... remains at a standard ward with her child,” she said, refusing to go into detail about the rare incident.
Denik N said the mother caught fire when the hospital staff administered a disinfectant, then used a surgical instrument to stop bleeding.
It added the woman was taken to another Prague hospital with a renowned burn ward for subsequent treatment before returning to Bulovka.
The Bulovka hospital also had to apologize in 2024 when it performed an abortion on the wrong pregnant woman after mixing two Asian women up.
The hospital paid compensation to the woman and police shelved the case, Czech media said.

stories.author: The Canadian Press

Toronto — When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama “The Woman King” for about $50 each.

This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106.

“That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on Tiff galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices.

While Tiff fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark.

Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” justice system thriller “Prima Facie” and the Ryan Gosling-produced “Love of Your Life” going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98.

Tiff did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing.

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during Tiff’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many Tiff fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.

“I love Tiff. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.

While Tiff typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, Tiff advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.

Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said Tiff is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.

“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.

But there’s more than demand at play.

Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. Tiff is likely no exception.

“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.

On top of inflation, Tiff is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.

In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, Tiff lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.

The federal government offered $23 million to help Tiff launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information Tiff published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1 million and more than $41.9 million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.

Its revenue was $39.6 million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2 million in expenses, its annual reports show.

Tiff’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in Tiff’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”

Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of Tiff’s stature — this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows — but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.

Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.

But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”

Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film — German historical drama “Silent Friend” — and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a Tiff diehard.

“I see it as the tail end,” she said.

This year, she hopes to see at least one movie — a Midnight Madness film — with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”

That’s a problem, said Keil, because Tiff has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping Tiff lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.

“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.

“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

The B.C. Conservatives came within three ridings of victory in the 2024 provincial election, winning 44 seats.

But since then, the party’s caucus has been thinned to 30, amid differences over its ideology, and questions about its direction under both former leader John Rustad and new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay .
Here are the 14 legislators who have exited the party, and why.
Brodie (Vancouver-Quilchena) is thrown out of the caucus by Rustad on March 7, 2025, over remarks that Rustad says mocked residential school survivors.
Armstrong (Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream) and Kealy (Peace River North) follow later that day, in sympathy with Brodie.

Armstrong briefly joins Brodie as a member of the new OneBC party before they split. Because OneBC lacks official party status, both now sit as Independents, as does Kealy, who was charged with sexual assault this year. He denies the accusation.

Sturko (Surrey-Cloverdale), a former RCMP officer, was a star recruit for Rustad’s Conservatives when she left BC United in June 2024, ahead of the election. But he fires her from caucus on Sept. 23, 2025.
She says Rustad accuses her of plotting against his leadership, a charge she denies. Sturko now sits as an Independent.
Boultbee (Penticton-Summerland) resigns from the Conservative caucus on Oct. 20, 2025, accusing Rustad of telling her to “get the F out.” Rustad questions her health and state of mind.
She sits as an Independent before joining the NDP caucus on July 3, 2026, saying that the Conservatives have swung toward “Trump-style populism” under new leader Findlay, who succeeded Rustad in May.

Chan (Richmond Centre) is removed from the Conservative caucus on March 26, 2026, by interim leader Trevor Halford, after Chan is charged with assault, assault by choking and uttering threats in a case of alleged intimate partner violence.
Chan, now sitting as an Independent, says he disagrees with the allegations dating back to 2024, and plans to defend himself in court.
Milobar (Kamloops Centre) quits the caucus on Aug. 14, citing a lack of “ideological alignment” with Findlay.

Milobar, a former leadership contender and finance critic for the Opposition, had clashed with Findlay in a debate when she accused him of having a conflict of interest because Milobar’s Indigenous wife once held paid positions with the local Indigenous band.
Gasper (Abbotsford-Mission) resigns her seat on Aug. 22 so Findlay can run in a byelection.
Gasper is appointed Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.
Paton (Delta South) quits the party on Aug. 24, saying the Conservatives’ direction under Findlay no longer aligns with his beliefs and he intends to form a new party with Milobar.
Milobar says at the announcement that he and Paton could be a party of two, but suggests there could be more defections.
Bird (Prince George-Valemount) quits the Conservatives on Aug. 25. She says she will sit as an Independent, issuing a statement warning about divisive leadership.

She says legislators “should be able to firmly reject racism, antisemitism, homophobia and hatred while still having difficult and necessary conversations about immigration, Indigenous reconciliation, addiction, crime, gender, religion and the many other issues on which reasonable people sometimes disagree.”
Wat (Richmond-Bridgeport) resigns from the party to sit as an Independent on Aug. 26.
She accuses Findlay of reneging on a promise to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” reportedly made by Findlay about Wat, calling her “CCP,” a reference to the Chinese Communist Party.

Wat says she cannot remain in a party whose leader has questioned her loyalty to Canada, while Findlay says Wat’s departure is a “betrayal of the hardworking volunteers, campaign workers and voters who helped get her elected.”
Day (Courtenay-Comox) exits later on Aug. 26, saying he no longer supports the direction of the party under Findlay.
Day says he has lost confidence in the judgment, conduct and ethical standards of Findlay’s leadership and the people she surrounds herself with. He says he will sit as an “Independent Conservative.”
Banman (Abbotsford South) quits to sit as an Independent on Aug. 27, rallying other Conservatives to join him “regardless of political affiliation.”
He says many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP is becoming increasingly likely.
Banman gave the B.C. Conservatives official party status in the legislature in 2023 when he crossed the floor to join Rustad, in a key moment on the party’s path to becoming the official Opposition.

Warbus (Chilliwack-Cultus Lake) announces on Monday she has lost faith in Findlay’s leadership, citing the sudden cancellation of a caucus meeting and the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.
Warbus, who will sit as an Independent, says the departures last week were an “implosion” and there has been a “critical breakdown” of communication under Findlay.

The B.C. Conservatives came within three ridings of victory in the 2024 provincial election, winning 44 seats.

But since then, the party’s caucus has been thinned to 30, amid differences over its ideology, and questions about its direction under both former leader John Rustad and new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay .

Here are the 14 legislators who have exited the party, and why.

Brodie (Vancouver-Quilchena) is thrown out of the caucus by Rustad on March 7, 2025, over remarks that Rustad says mocked residential school survivors.

Armstrong (Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream) and Kealy (Peace River North) follow later that day, in sympathy with Brodie.

Armstrong briefly joins Brodie as a member of the new OneBC party before they split. Because OneBC lacks official party status, both now sit as Independents, as does Kealy, who was charged with sexual assault this year. He denies the accusation.

Sturko (Surrey-Cloverdale), a former RCMP officer, was a star recruit for Rustad’s Conservatives when she left BC United in June 2024, ahead of the election. But he fires her from caucus on Sept. 23, 2025.

She says Rustad accuses her of plotting against his leadership, a charge she denies. Sturko now sits as an Independent.

Boultbee (Penticton-Summerland) resigns from the Conservative caucus on Oct. 20, 2025, accusing Rustad of telling her to “get the F out.” Rustad questions her health and state of mind.

She sits as an Independent before joining the NDP caucus on July 3, 2026, saying that the Conservatives have swung toward “Trump-style populism” under new leader Findlay, who succeeded Rustad in May.

Chan (Richmond Centre) is removed from the Conservative caucus on March 26, 2026, by interim leader Trevor Halford, after Chan is charged with assault, assault by choking and uttering threats in a case of alleged intimate partner violence.

Chan, now sitting as an Independent, says he disagrees with the allegations dating back to 2024, and plans to defend himself in court.

Milobar (Kamloops Centre) quits the caucus on Aug. 14, citing a lack of “ideological alignment” with Findlay.

Milobar, a former leadership contender and finance critic for the Opposition, had clashed with Findlay in a debate when she accused him of having a conflict of interest because Milobar’s Indigenous wife once held paid positions with the local Indigenous band.

Gasper (Abbotsford-Mission) resigns her seat on Aug. 22 so Findlay can run in a byelection.

Gasper is appointed Findlay’s deputy chief of staff.

Paton (Delta South) quits the party on Aug. 24, saying the Conservatives’ direction under Findlay no longer aligns with his beliefs and he intends to form a new party with Milobar.

Milobar says at the announcement that he and Paton could be a party of two, but suggests there could be more defections.

Bird (Prince George-Valemount) quits the Conservatives on Aug. 25. She says she will sit as an Independent, issuing a statement warning about divisive leadership.

She says legislators “should be able to firmly reject racism, antisemitism, homophobia and hatred while still having difficult and necessary conversations about immigration, Indigenous reconciliation, addiction, crime, gender, religion and the many other issues on which reasonable people sometimes disagree.”

Wat (Richmond-Bridgeport) resigns from the party to sit as an Independent on Aug. 26.

She accuses Findlay of reneging on a promise to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” reportedly made by Findlay about Wat, calling her “CCP,” a reference to the Chinese Communist Party.

Wat says she cannot remain in a party whose leader has questioned her loyalty to Canada, while Findlay says Wat’s departure is a “betrayal of the hardworking volunteers, campaign workers and voters who helped get her elected.”

Day (Courtenay-Comox) exits later on Aug. 26, saying he no longer supports the direction of the party under Findlay.

Day says he has lost confidence in the judgment, conduct and ethical standards of Findlay’s leadership and the people she surrounds herself with. He says he will sit as an “Independent Conservative.”

Banman (Abbotsford South) quits to sit as an Independent on Aug. 27, rallying other Conservatives to join him “regardless of political affiliation.”

He says many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP is becoming increasingly likely.

Banman gave the B.C. Conservatives official party status in the legislature in 2023 when he crossed the floor to join Rustad, in a key moment on the party’s path to becoming the official Opposition.

Warbus (Chilliwack-Cultus Lake) announces on Monday she has lost faith in Findlay’s leadership, citing the sudden cancellation of a caucus meeting and the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Warbus, who will sit as an Independent, says the departures last week were an “implosion” and there has been a “critical breakdown” of communication under Findlay.
