stories.title: Trump shares Christian group's proposal allowing Canadian Jews facing antisemitism to flee to the U.S.
stories.summary: Donald Trump has shared a report on a potential plan to create a legal pathway into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians facing antisemitism.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
paragraphs: As he finds new ways to poke Canada amid an ugly trade war, U.S. President Donald Trump has amplified a Christian group’s proposal to create a legal pathway into the United States for Canadian Jews facing antisemitism.

He shared on social media a news report about a letter written by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers (Nacl), which urges Trump to establish an expedited method of entry into the U.S. for Jewish Canadians “who are experiencing persecution or who credibly fear for their safety because they are Jewish.”

It points to “an alarming climate of harassment, intimidation, vandalism, threats, and violence” that Jewish Canadian families have faced since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, adding that “advocates working directly with these families report that more than 2,000 Jewish Canadians have expressed interest in relocating because of growing concerns for their safety.”

The letter continues: “Accordingly, we respectfully ask that you direct the Department of State and the Department of Homeland Security to identify and implement lawful, secure, and appropriately expedited pathways for eligible Jewish Canadian nationals and their immediate family members who face persecution.”

Nacl founder and president Jason Rapert signed the letter, alongside state representatives and religious leaders, and it was sent to the U.S. president, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and several U.S. senators and representatives on Thursday.
Trump shared a link to the report on Truth Social on Sunday evening, but did not comment on the contents.

The letter said that any potential program should maintain national security safeguards such as identity, criminal history, medical and security screening and protect family unity. It also called for the Trump administration to work with states, local governments, Jewish organizations, churches, nonprofits and employers who are willing to assist arriving families.

The letter comes a month after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year. While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.
Jewish schools, synagogues and other institutions have been shot at, firebombed and targeted by hateful graffiti in Canada since Hamas’ October 7 attacks on Israel.

Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s Chief Executive Officer, told National Post in an email: “While we have members of the Jewish community questioning their futures in Canada, make no mistake that this is our home and we are here to stay. Our community is strong and resilient and will not be made to live in fear.”

On the report shared by Trump, Wolle added: “At the same time, this should serve as a serious wake-up call for the Canadian government that immediate and concrete actions are needed to stem the tide of violence against our community.”

Meanwhile, in the U.S., the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) reported earlier in August that anti-Jewish hate crimes accounted for 63 per cent of all reported religion-based hate crimes last year, according to FBI data. It marked the third-highest year on record of anti-Jewish hate crimes in the U.S.

The letter states that an expedited pathway for Jewish Canadians would be consistent with “America’s historic commitment to stand against religious persecution,” adding, “We believe this moment presents another opportunity for America to demonstrate those principles.”

Elsewhere, the Nacl letter references Jewish and Christian leaders in Tulsa who have already offered to help receive Canadian Jewish families, and points out that Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt previously told Trump his state would welcome Jewish families who legally enter the United States .
In a July 22 letter, Gov. Stitt wrote that “Oklahoma would proudly welcome those who choose to make our state their home,” should Jewish families lawfully move to the U.S. in search of safety.

The Nacl letter concludes: “For generations, America has served as a refuge for people fleeing religious persecution. We urge you to ensure that, consistent with federal law and the security interests of the United States, that door remains open to our Jewish brothers and sisters in Canada who need it today.”

stories.title: Ontario breaks ground on longest stretch of proposed Ring of Fire road network
stories.summary: Construction on the longest stretch of a road network to Ontario's mineral-rich Ring of Fire region has begun.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
paragraphs: The provincial government announced today that ground has been broken on a road to eventually connect the remote Marten Falls First Nation to the provincial highway network.
Chief Bruce Achneepineskum says the route will strengthen connections to health care and other essential services, while helping to accelerate the community’s growth.
ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW
Toronto Island waitlist life: why one man will never give up his dream of living lakeside
The provincial government says it’s part of a plan to unlock the economic potential of the Ring of Fire region and meet global demand for minerals.
That plan has been met with pushback by some First Nations, notably in response to legislation giving the government powers to fast-track projects.
The road to Marten Falls will span about 184 kilometres, or just over a third of the total network, and is expected to open by November 2031.
In June, the province and Webequie First Nation announced the start of construction on a 107-kilometre segment of the road network to that community.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.

stories.title: London resident dies after head-on crash in Thames Centre
stories.summary: Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
paragraphs: A London resident died in hospital after a head-on crash between an SUV and a transport truck in Thames Centre last week.
Middlesex County OPP and emergency crews responded shortly before 1 p.m. Aug. 26 to the collision on Dundas Street near Fairview Road.
The driver of the transport truck was taken to hospital with injuries not considered life-threatening, police said in a Monday release.
The SUV driver, a 40-year-old from London, was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries and later died.
Members of the OPP Traffic Incident Management Enforcement team attended the scene to assist with the investigation.
Dundas Street was closed for hours between Fairview and Shaw roads for the investigation.
Anyone with information is asked to contact OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (TIPS).
Provincial police are investigating after people posing as Dorchester Fall Fair representatives collected money and information from prospective vendors for phony permits.
Middlesex County OPP responded to a fraud complaint on Hamilton Road in Thames Centre about 1:40 p.m. on Aug. 27.

The North Dorchester Agricultural Society, which manages the fair, learned potential vendors had provided information and paid an undisclosed amount of money to people posing as fair representatives to secure vendor permits, police said.
The fraudulent messages appeared on social media and in unsolicited emails, police said.
The suspects are unknown, and police believe there may be additional victims.
Anyone who believes they were victimized is asked to contact Middlesex County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (TIPS).
For more information about fraud, contact the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre at 1-888-495-8501.

content_blocks.text: OPP investigate scam involving fake Dorchester Fall Fair permits
Provincial police are investigating after people posing as Dorchester Fall Fair representatives collected money and information from prospective vendors for phony permits.
Middlesex County OPP responded to a fraud complaint on Hamilton Road in Thames Centre about 1:40 p.m. on Aug. 27.

The North Dorchester Agricultural Society, which manages the fair, learned potential vendors had provided information and paid an undisclosed amount of money to people posing as fair representatives to secure vendor permits, police said.
The fraudulent messages appeared on social media and in unsolicited emails, police said.
The suspects are unknown, and police believe there may be additional victims.

B.C. Conservative MLA A’a:liya Warbus, one of the Opposition’s most prominent legislators, has joined the exodus from the party’s caucus, saying she has lost confidence in it under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.
Warbus said in a statement on Monday morning she would sit as an Independent, becoming the seventh Conservative MLA to quit the caucus this month, including five last week.
The Indigenous MLA and former House leader cited the cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called for Monday in light of a “reasonable cause for concern” about last week’s “implosion.”
“The decision to postpone today’s caucus meeting for a month reflects the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions,” she said in her statement.
“It is one thing to ask for people’s trust, and quite another to blindfold someone and expect faith alone to substitute for transparency and accountability.”
The Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA also said she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Reann Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a byelection.

Findlay, who was narrowly elected party leader on May 30 but does not have a seat in the legislature, had said last week that suggestions a leaked audio recording showed she illegally offered jobs to MLAs, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a byelection, were “preposterous.”

Gasper has taken a paid position as Findlay’s deputy chief of staff. RCMP said they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators, but “does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who may be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid.”

The party has been in a state of upheaval over the ideological direction and strategies of the party under Findlay since Peter Milobar quit on Aug. 14, saying they had a lack of “ideological alignment.”
Findlay, who has said she will focus on “faith, family and freedom,” has since suffered the losses of Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman.
Neither Warbus nor Findlay immediately responded to requests for comment.
Warbus said in her statement that there had been a “critical breakdown” of communication under Findlay.
“Caucus members have learned of hirings, firings, critic appointments, and leadership positions through any and all channels including social media before being informed by leadership,” she said.
She said it was not just MLAs leaving, but “critical and talented members of our riding associations and staff that we rely on.”
Paton and Milobar have said they will form an alternative party.

Banman rallied other Conservatives to join him as an Independent on Thursday “regardless of political affiliation.” He said many have told him Findlay is “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP was increasingly likely.

stories.title: Canadian Nato intern facing espionage charges to remain in custody, Belgian prosecutor says
stories.summary: Prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that ‘a Canadian national of Chinese origin’ had been arrested on accusations of espionage
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Belgian federal prosecutor’s office says a Canadian facing espionage charges will remain in custody.

After a hearing today of the woman’s appeal of a July decision to keep her in detention, Belgium’s Chamber of Indictments decided to extend her pretrial custody by one month.

The prosecutor’s office announced on July 25 that “a Canadian national of Chinese origin” had been arrested on accusations of espionage and participation in a criminal organization.

The suspect, who has not been named by the prosecutor’s office, worked as an intern at NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe in Mons, Belgium.

The office said she came to the attention of the organization’s security services, who reported the matter to Belgium’s military intelligence agency.

A federal source not authorized to speak publicly about the issue said officials in Canada were proceeding on the basis the suspect is Biwei Zhang – also known as Claire Zhang – who was previously employed by Canadian government agencies.

stories.title: Ontario woman questions $500 fee to transfer family's medical records to new doctor
stories.summary: Ontario woman questions $500 fee to transfer family's medical records to new doctor CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: An Ontario woman says her former family doctor's office quoted her $100 per person to transfer the medical records of her family of five to their new family physician.
· Posted: Aug 31, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: August 31
Doctors say the new system will reduce administrative paperwork which takes time away from patients.(Shutterstock)
When Melissa Snider found a new family doctor closer to her home in Denfield, Ont., she was happy at the thought of no longer travelling to London for medical visits.
The relief turned to shock however when her former family doctor quoted Snider $100 per person to transfer her records, along with those of her husband and their three children, to a new physician.
"It was quite surprising to me that transferring medical records for a family of five would cost me $500," said Snider, whose kids are all under the age of nine.

"My kids are all healthy so it would just be vaccine records for them, and my husband and I are pretty healthy too, so our records themselves would not be very extensive. Half a grand in this economy is just not doable for something so silly."

Snider said she had previously paid around $35 for the service. She asked a Facebook group for moms if others have been in this situation. She said she received a variety of responses, with some saying their doctor did it for free, and others saying they had to pay varying fees.

Access to personal health information and related fees is governed by the Personal Health Information Protection Act and not c overed by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP), according to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO).

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, says the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.(Copyright (c) 2017 Stokkete/Shutterstock.)

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, said CPSO spokesperson Laura Zilke.

The Information Privacy Commissioner recommends a $30 fee for electronic transfers, according to the Ontario Medical Association, which sets out recommended fees in its Physicians’ Guide to Uninsured Services.

In some cases, doctors may charge $30 for the first 20 pages and then $0.25 per extra pages, but all other methods of reproducing records should be charged for at cost, the guidance states. This can include clerical labour costs, toner and paper costs, equipment, and storage space.

"Among other requirements, physicians must provide a fee estimate in advance and charge only reasonable fees that reflect cost recovery," said Zilke, adding that physicians must consider these recommendations and the patient's ability to pay.

"CPSO'spolicyrequires that fees be reasonable, reflect cost recovery, and be commensurate with the nature of the service provided, including factors such as the materials used, the time required to prepare the records, and the direct cost of sending them."
Snider wonders why there isn't a centralized system where every clinic charges the same fee, or bases fees on a patient's medical history.

The current system is "disconnected" because clinics have their own system of storing health information, with some using paper charts and others electronic records, said Dr. Jobin Varughese, president of the Ontario College of Family Physicians.
Canadian doctors say they’re losing 20 million hours a year to unnecessary paperwork

When patients move between clinics, doctors and their teams must spend hours preparing and sending those records manually, he said, adding that it contributes to paperwork and other administrative tasks that take away time doctors can spend with patients.

"It's pretty clear that we need to get to a point that patients shouldn't have to pay for their records and family doctors should be able to spend their time caring for patients rather than moving records through a disconnected system," he said.

Ontario plans to create connected primary care medical record system, minister says

"Right now it's on the patients to have to remember dates and times and so being able to reduce that burden will be helpful. It will also reduce the need for patients to repeat the same information to different providers just because their records aren't available," said Varughese.
The province is currently in a procurement phase but Varughese said officials have consulted with family physicians and he's hopeful this will simplify the process for doctors and patients.
As for Snider, she plans to provide her new doctor with a verbal medical history and not pay the hefty transfer cost.

Doctors say the new system will reduce administrative paperwork which takes time away from patients.(Shutterstock)

"My kids are all healthy so it would just be vaccine records for them, and my husband and I are pretty healthy too, so our records themselves would not be very extensive. Half a grand in this economy is just not doable for something so silly."

Snider said she had previously paid around $35 for the service. She asked a Facebook group for moms if others have been in this situation. She said she received a variety of responses, with some saying their doctor did it for free, and others saying they had to pay varying fees.

Access to personal health information and related fees is governed by the Personal Health Information Protection Act and not c overed by the Ontario Health Insurance Plan (OHIP), according to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO).

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, says the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.(Copyright (c) 2017 Stokkete/Shutterstock.)

The work involved in fulfilling a request for medical records may include locating and retrieving records, reviewing them, preparing the materials for disclosure, and securely transferring them to the patient or the receiving health-care provider, said CPSO spokesperson Laura Zilke.

"Among other requirements, physicians must provide a fee estimate in advance and charge only reasonable fees that reflect cost recovery," said Zilke, adding that physicians must consider these recommendations and the patient's ability to pay.

"CPSO'spolicyrequires that fees be reasonable, reflect cost recovery, and be commensurate with the nature of the service provided, including factors such as the materials used, the time required to prepare the records, and the direct cost of sending them."

stories.title: Leaders of China, Russia and India are among heads of state meeting to counter U.S. influence
stories.summary: The leaders of China, Russia and India are among the heads of state gathering in Kyrgyzstan this week for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
The leaders of China, Russia and India gathered with other heads of state in Kyrgyzstan on Monday for the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a group billed as a counterweight to U.S. global influence.

Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi are attending the events in Bishkek, the capital of the Central Asian nation.

Putin met separately with Xi and Modi in two of the many bilateral sessions on the sidelines of the summit. Putin affirmed to Xi Moscow’s readiness to make the visa-free regime with China permanent, and he said Russia’s relationship with India is strengthening.

Talks between Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are expected Tuesday, the day of the official SCO sessions.

Russia, now 4.5 years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and Iran, six months into a war with the United States and Israel, see the summit as an important platform to strengthen their relations with non-Western partners.

Modi told Putin through a translator that India supports efforts to end the war in Ukraine, and that “we need to move from endless war to the end of war, to the end of hostilities,” adding that “this is very important for all of humanity.”

The SCO was founded in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states as a security forum. Over the past quarter-century, it has grown in size and influence, although its goals and programs remain vague and its brand recognition low.

It now includes 10 nations: Russia, China, India, Iran, Pakistan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Many other countries have the status of “dialogue partners.”

Along with Russia, China has presented the SCO as an alternative to Western-aligned organizations like the G7, and in recent years has wanted to expand the scope and influence of the organization, pledging development and financial assistance.

China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said last week that the organization has successfully “explored a new path for regional cooperation.” Beijing has consistently promoted the idea of an alternative world order with Russia’s support.

Summit attendees have significant disagreements

For many SCO members, the summit will be an opportunity to show that they maintain strong ties on the global stage despite souring relations with the West.

The organization is not a unified political or military bloc, however, and analysts note that its members have significant disagreements and their own distinct interests.

For countries such as India, however, experts say the summit is likely to be more about optics and strategic signalling than substantive outcomes.

The forum is heavily influenced by China and includes Pakistan as a member -- both of which are rivals of India.

Dinakar Peri, a fellow in security studies at Carnegie India, said the SCO gives India a seat at the table in a region increasingly shaped by competition among the larger powers, allowing it to protect its interests, track shifting geopolitical currents and project itself as a reliable stakeholder.

“While it May not entirely shape the agenda, it gives New Delhi a first-hand view of the region and allows it to hedge its position with others,” Peri said.

Turkiye, which holds partner status within the SCO, also seeks to use the platform to strengthen its position in the region.

It views SCO membership as part of a balanced foreign policy that seeks to maintain its traditional ties with the West as a part of Nato, while strengthening its influence in Eurasia.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who brought his country into the SCO as a “dialogue partner” in 2012, has repeatedly stated that he wants Turkiye to become a permanent member. While Turkiye has close trade ties with the European Union under a 1995 trade deal, its EU membership bid has stalled for more than 25 years.

Security restrictions imposed in Bishkek

Major shopping malls, markets and other sites in the capital were closed for the duration of the summit as part of security measures, and commercial flights to and from Manas Airport were restricted.

“Traffic in central Bishkek will be regularly restricted,” said Askat Alagozov, a spokesman for Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov, urging residents to leave the city.

The start of the school year was postponed until Sept. 15, and authorities declared Tuesday a non-working day for public sector and civil servants in Bishkek.

Andrew Wilks in Istanbul, Turkiye, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok, and Aijaz Hussain in New Delhi contributed.

Yuras Karmanau, The Associated Press

stories.title: Tiff fans grapple with ticket price hikes
stories.summary: The hike they noticed this year marks the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
paragraphs: When Arjun Singh first started attending the Toronto International Film Festival in 2022, he remembers buying tickets to the world premiere of warrior drama The Woman King for about $50 each.
This year, he saw balcony seats at similar premium screenings, which often include a Q-and-A with the cast or director, selling for as much as $106.
“That makes you go, is this really worth it?” said the Toronto non-profit worker, who has cut back on TIFF galas and now mostly opts for regular festival screenings because of the prices.

While TIFF fans have grown accustomed to tickets edging up by a few percentage points every festival, the hike they noticed this year marked the first time in recent memory that films, other than the opening and closing night galas, cracked the $100 mark.

Fans reported tickets to the premieres of anticipated films like Palme d’Or winner Fjord , justice system thriller Prima Facie and the Ryan Gosling-produced Love of Your Life going for as much as $106. Others posted screenshots on Reddit of tickets in the first few rows of premieres selling for $128. Last year, screenings in the same tier went up to $98.
TIFF did not respond to multiple requests for comment on ticket pricing.

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during TIFF’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many TIFF fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.
“I love TIFF. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.
While TIFF typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, TIFF advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.
Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said TIFF is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.
“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.
But there’s more than demand at play.
Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. TIFF is likely no exception.
“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.
On top of inflation, TIFF is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.
In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, TIFF lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.
The federal government offered $23-million to help TIFF launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information TIFF published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1-million and more than $41.9-million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.
Its revenue was $39.6-million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2-million in expenses, its annual reports show.
TIFF’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in TIFF’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”
Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of TIFF’s stature – this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows – but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.
Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.
But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”
Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film – German historical drama “Silent Friend” – and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a TIFF diehard.
“I see it as the tail end,” she said.
This year, she hopes to see at least one movie – a Midnight Madness film – with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”
That’s a problem, said Keil, because TIFF has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping TIFF lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.
“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.
“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”

The increase has some diehards, who can see upwards of 30 films during TIFF’s 10 days, rethinking how many premieres they’ll attend. Others are wondering how long it will be until they’re priced out of the event once nicknamed “the people’s festival” because of its affordability and public access.

“It definitely adds up and when you’re getting tickets for friends too. You don’t really want to look at your credit card,” said Joel Chico, an actor who estimates he spends about $2,000 on up to 30 tickets to premium screenings each year.

Like many TIFF fans, he takes the grin-and-bear it approach to ticket prices because of the thrill of being in the room with the cast when a film is seen for the first time. Still, they wish it cost less.
“I love TIFF. It’s like my Christmas every year but the costs are just kind of crazy nowadays,” Chico said.
While TIFF typically releases price ranges for every kind of ticket it sells in the lead up to the festival, this year it didn’t tell attendees what seats in each category would top out at.

Regular screenings, which come after premieres and do not typically have cast members in attendance, were listed as starting at $30 for non-members. Premium screenings began at $46. When The Canadian Press browsed tickets, it found many premium seats at screenings going for up to $106.

In the lead-up to the festival, TIFF advertised a $2 discount on regular screenings for members. It also promised $15 tickets to select screenings but had yet to release more details about those seats with just over a week to go before festivities began.
Charlie Keil, a professor at the Cinema Studies Institute at the University of Toronto, said TIFF is likely increasing prices both because it can, and because it needs to.

Over its 51-year history, he figures festival organizers have more than realized film fans will pay big bucks to see a movie before anyone else and to see it with Hollywood’s biggest stars in attendance.
“If the demand is there, that, in a way, stimulates institutions to push the pricing envelope because they think people will keep coming,” Keil said.
But there’s more than demand at play.
Arts organizations are constantly turning to patrons to help them cope with strained budgets and higher costs. TIFF is likely no exception.
“Space costs more, transportation more, food more, hospitality more, accommodation more. Everything is more expensive,” Keil said.
On top of inflation, TIFF is still recovering from the COVID-19 pandemic, which resulted in online and pared back versions of the festival.
In 2023, the Hollywood strikes kept many stars from promoting their films at the event. That same year, TIFF lost longtime sponsor Bell, which had supported the organization since 1995.
The federal government offered $23-million to help TIFF launch a film market this year and Rogers stepped in to fill Bell’s void with a three-year agreement that runs through 2027.

The latest financial information TIFF published in annual reports showed it had revenue of about $45.1-million and more than $41.9-million in expenses in 2024. The bulk of its revenue came from ticket sales, followed by corporate partnerships, while salaries made up about half of its expenses.
Its revenue was $39.6-million in 2023, when it had roughly $46.2-million in expenses, its annual reports show.
TIFF’s program, administrative and fundraising costs have all risen in recent years, according to Charity Intelligence Canada, an organization that analyzes and publicizes charity finances.

“There’s just so many factors that are making it tough,” Keil said. “I would not want to be in TIFF’s position right now, just trying to make it all work financially, sustain the reputation of the festival.”
Cathy Crowe understands it’s not cheap to put on a festival of TIFF’s stature – this year’s iteration will debut almost 300 films and TV shows – but she’s still disappointed in the prices.

After filmmaker friends turned the street nurse onto the festival in the late 1990s, she started treating it like an annual staycation. She recalls seeing between 20 and 30 films a year, often paying only $17 a ticket.
Crowe avoids the ritziest galas, which typically turn Roy Thomson Hall and the Princess of Wales Theatre into a buzzy spectacle, so that kept her festival affordable.
But last year, when she logged on to buy tickets during a members’ window, she found most screenings she wanted to attend sold out.

“I only got one of my 20 choices, which was so disappointing and then, when I got it, it was a $37 film,” she said. “For a really big deal film it was OK, but how could I do 20 or 30 films at that price?”
Simply put, she didn’t. She attended the one film – German historical drama “Silent Friend” – and then started contemplating how many more years she could realistically afford to be a TIFF diehard.
“I see it as the tail end,” she said.
This year, she hopes to see at least one movie – a Midnight Madness film – with her grandson, but she’s under no illusion that the festival will feel like it once did.

“It is not a people’s festival any longer,” said Crowe. “I know it will be packed. I know people will be going. I know people will be coming from all over the country, but they’re losing a lot of regular folks.”
That’s a problem, said Keil, because TIFF has long prided itself on how many members of the public attend every year.

In fact, that broad access is a selling point, helping TIFF lure in movies from filmmakers who want to test the public’s reaction or build buzz with an audience broader than the industry buffs at competing festivals.
“The whole point is to give people access to films they wouldn’t normally see from places they would not normally see films coming from,” Keil said.
“If you price those films out of the normal, let’s say, cinephile’s reach, then the festival won’t be as successful in meeting that mandate.”

stories.title: Cami plant to remain open, hope for potential armoured vehicle production
stories.summary: Employees at the Cami Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ont. were surprised to learn of a few details in their new three-year agreement with General Motors.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Employees at the CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll, Ont. were surprised to learn of a few details in their new three-year agreement with General Motors.

At the ratification vote Saturday in Woodstock, Ont. members of Unifor Local 88 learned of the company’s intent to keep the CAMI plant open during the duration of the deal and also the potential for a new vehicle.

“It’s a three-year deal with General Motors and I think it’s an important agreement,” said Mark Gee, the plant chairperson.

There was also wage increases, extended benefits for those whose were about to expire and productivity and quality bonuses for laid-off employees.

CAMI ASSEMBLY Unifor Local 88 Union representatives speak to employees on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

“In my opinion, it is a best case scenario,” said employee Peggy Falkingham.

After Canadian auto assembly plants were hit with 25 per cent tariffs last year, auto workers were laid off.

Months later, General Motors ended production of the Brightdrop vehicle in Ingersoll. It’s been a difficult stretch since then for employees to make ends meet.

“I come from a family that is dual income from General Motors,” said Falkingham. “My husband also works at CAMI as well, so it is difficult. It’s a whole new family structure that we have to work around. And still the uncertainty of our future is definitely there.”

CAMI ASSEMBLY A ballot is cast by a Unifor local 88 member on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

Gee says it’s been tough for members going all the way back to the beginning of the pandemic.

As they attended the meeting Saturday, Unifor members were worried they were about to hear about a plant closure. Instead, they learned of a potential future.

“I’m surprised about the future opportunity for a new vehicle,” said Todd Sleeper, a CAMI employee. “If there’s a military contract, then Cami gets first crack at building that that military vehicle. That sounds positive.”

In the letter from General Motors to the union, it states that if the Government of Canada approves a Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) contact, the company will discuss with Unifor the potential allocation of GM Defence work to CAMI Assembly. If the CAF contract is awarded, CAMI will be first consideration.

CAMI ASSEMBLY Members of Unifor Local 88 vote to ratify a new three-year contract with General Motors on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Brent Lale/CTV News London)

“It’s the carrot dangling in front of us,” said Falkingham. “We’ll take it, because right now that’s what we have to take. If that is a possibility in the future, I’m sure everyone would jump on it to be able to get back in the plant.”

While employees don’t have all the answers, the do know they have a shot at returning to work and finishing out their pension.

“There is hope for a future,” added Falkingham. “They’re not closing the doors. That is that is a big thing right there.”

Today marks an important moment for GM Canada.

With the ratification of new three-year collective agreements with Unifor, we have reached an outcome that supports our employees, strengthens our manufacturing operations and provides a solid foundation for GM’s future in Canada.

Thank you to Lana Payne, Unifor National President, Trevor Longpre, Unifor General Motors Master Bargaining Committee Chairperson, Chris Waugh, Unifor General Motors Master Bargaining Committee Vice-Chairperson, our Unifor partners, and the GM and Unifor bargaining teams for their professionalism, respect and commitment throughout this process. Reaching an agreement requires collaboration and a shared focus on the future.

Recognizing the Contributions of Our People

The new agreements include meaningful improvements to wages, benefits and job security, and recognize the valuable contributions of our represented employees while helping sustain good-paying jobs that have long been a cornerstone of Canada’s automotive industry.

Our represented employees play a critical role in GM Canada’s success. Their skill, dedication and commitment to quality help ensure the vehicles we build continue to earn the trust of customers across North America.

Building on Our Commitment to North American Manufacturing

Today, we are also announcing significant new and reaffirmed investments that further strengthen GM’s manufacturing footprint in Canada. Together, planned investments in Oshawa and St. Catharines total approximately C$1.4 billion over the next three years, reinforcing the important role Canadian operations will continue to play in GM’s North American manufacturing network.

At Oshawa Assembly, an additional C$144 million investment will bring next-generation GMC Sierra Heavy-Duty production to the plant, building on the previously announced C$343 million investment in next-generation truck production and manufacturing enhancements. Together, these investments bring total planned investment in Oshawa to nearly C$500 million.

This is an important addition for Oshawa, for GM Canada and for our customers. It means Oshawa will now build both of GM’s next-generation heavy-duty trucks, the GMC Sierra HD and the Chevrolet Silverado HD, strengthening the plant’s role in one of the company’s most important vehicle segments while building more of the trucks Canadians rely on every day.

At St. Catharines Propulsion, a new C$215 million investment establishes the plant as the sole source for an important next-generation transmission. Combined with the previously announced C$691 million for sixth-generation V8 engine production, total investment in St. Catharines now exceeds C$900 million, securing high-value jobs and the plant’s future.

For our team at CAMI Assembly, we have extended layoff benefits to reflect our continued commitment to support employees while we take the necessary time to assess potential opportunities for the site.

GM’s Presence Across Canada

While today’s announcement includes important investments in manufacturing, GM Canada’s presence is built on a broad ecosystem that spans vehicle engineering, software development, sales and customer care, parts distribution, and corporate operations. That includes our Canadian Technical Centre, where more than 1,000 engineers, developers and technical experts are helping advance the next generation of vehicle technology, software and testing.

As Canada’s vehicle sales leader, our success is powered by approximately 450 Chevrolet, Buick, GMC and Cadillac dealerships employing over 20,000 Canadians and serving customers in communities across the country. Together, our people, dealers and operations contribute to local economies, support communities and advance innovation. Their contributions help strengthen GM’s North American business and underscore the important role Canada continues to play in our shared success.

Looking Ahead

The strength of GM Canada has always been our people. Their expertise, dedication and commitment will continue to shape our future and the role we play in Canada’s automotive industry.

I am optimistic about the future and confident in what we can achieve together.

President and Managing Director

The strength of GM Canada has always been our people. Their expertise, dedication and commitment will continue to shape our future and the role we play in Canada’s automotive industry.
I am optimistic about the future and confident in what we can achieve together.
President and Managing Director

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that he would meet with his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, on the sidelines of a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors, adding that the U.S. was not in a war with Canada .
“I think this is very unfortunate that Prime Minister Carney has turned this into a political shouting match. I mean, we’re not at war with Canada,” Bessent told CNBC in an interview.
He added that Carney was “not doing what’s best for Canada.”
In his interview, Bessent also called out Canada’s retaliatory tariffs.
“I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are,” he said.

Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs, a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

The poll found that 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of older boomers supported both of those positions.
— with files from Reuters and Global’s Sean Boynton

stories.title: ‘Wow!’: Video shows B.C. man’s up-close orca encounter
stories.summary: A man who went fishing in West Vancouver, B.C., Friday afternoon ended up catching a spectacular show.
stories.author: Lisa Steacy
stories.content:
A man who went fishing in West Vancouver, B.C., Friday afternoon ended up catching a spectacular show.

Jhordan Stevenson was at Sunset Marina when a trio of orcas suddenly surfaced just metres away.

“Wow,” he says, his amazement audible as he witnesses the first breach in what he told CTV News was an “incredibly special” encounter that lasted for nearly an hour.

Since posting video of what he witnessed online, it has racked up tens of thousands of views on Instagram.

Getting this close of a glimpse of the endangered marine mammals from the water is difficult without violating regulations in place for their protection.

Transport Canada issued an interim order on June 1 declaring that all vessels must stay at least 1,000 metres away from southern resident killer whales in southern B.C. coastal waters, including the Strait of Georgia, the Juan de Fuca Strait and waters off Vancouver Island.

This is up from the previous 400-metre approach distance.

The term vessel doesn’t only apply to motorized watercraft. Last year, a paddleboarder was fined for getting too close to a southern resident killer whale after a video of that incident gained traction online.

stories.title: France takes aim at ultra-fast fashion with new levy
stories.summary: France will from Tuesday impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost 20 euros per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content:
France will from Tuesday impose a fee on ultra-fast fashion items that will eventually reach almost 20 euros per garment, as the government targets major Asian e-commerce platforms including Shein.

The levy follows legislation passed by the French parliament in June to regulate so-called “ultra-fast fashion” companies, known for selling large volumes of lower quality clothing at rock-bottom prices.

It is part of a push to rein in Asian e-commerce giants including Shein, Temu and AliExpress, which have exploded in popularity in France in recent years.

“The harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion on our environment and our economy are well known and documented,” said Mathieu Lefevre, the minister for ecological transition on Friday as details of the measure were published.

Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two criteria: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.

The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.

In 2026, companies will pay fines such as a 50-cent levy on underwear falling into the ultra-fast fashion category, rising to two euros for T-shirts, nine euros for jeans and 12 euros for a jacket.

The levy could reach up to 19.50 euros (US$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50 per cent of the product’s pre-tax price.

A tool to collect data independently, rather than relying solely on companies’ own declarations, is under development, Lefevre’s office said.

Shein -- which on Monday was valued at US$26.3 billion in its long-awaited Hong Kong initial public offering -- declined to comment when contacted by AFP.

Temu and AliExpress did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The measure has faced criticism over which retailers it will affect.

In July, Lefevre’s office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European and French companies.

French officials have made repeated statements that they view Shein, Temu and AliExpress as driving the surge in ultra-fast fashion.

The European Commission had also raised questions over whether the legislation complied with EU law, but Lefevre’s office said those concerns had been “dispelled” and the measure was not expected to be blocked.

China meanwhile warned in July of potential retaliation over the French law, slamming the regulation as “discriminatory” and in violation of trade principles.

Imports of small parcels from China into the EU have already fallen by around 30 to 40 per cent since a separate three-euro EU levy on such shipments came into force on July 1, according to the French government.

stories.title: B.C. Conservative MLA Warbus leaves caucus, marking the seventh to quit this month
stories.summary: Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA cites her loss of confidence in the party under new leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay
stories.author: Chuck Chiang
stories.content:
A’a:liya Warbus says she’d be “worried” if there isn’t mounting frustration with B.C. Conservative Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay among her former colleagues, after Warbus became the seventh MLA this month to the exit the party’s caucus.

Warbus, who said she would sit as an Independent, issued a statement on Monday partly attributing her decision to cancellation of a caucus meeting she said had been called due to concern about last week’s “implosion” that saw a near daily parade of legislators depart the official provincial opposition.

She said in an interview that the cancellation of the meeting that had been planned for Monday was “a huge blow and a major part” of her decision to leave the Conservatives.

“The decision to postpone today’s caucus meeting for a month reflects the lack of value being placed on caucus members and their opinions,” she said in her statement.

“It is one thing to ask for people’s trust, and quite another to blindfold someone and expect faith alone to substitute for transparency and accountability.”

The Chilliwack-Cultus Lake MLA also said in her statement she was concerned about the circumstances surrounding the resignation from the legislature of Reann Gasper to make way for Findlay to stand in a by-election .

“Those questions and those conversations need to be happening inside of caucus, and today was our opportunity to have those conversations,” Warbus said of the cancelled meeting.

Warbus, a member of the Sto:Lo First Nation, had been one of the Opposition’s most prominent legislators as its only Indigenous MLA and as former House leader.

She said in her interview there had been an “unacceptable” lack of communication from Findlay to the caucus.

“If I’m feeling it, others must be feeling it as well,” Warbus said, although she said she wasn’t sure if others would follow her exit.

“If there isn’t frustration, I would be worried. I can only guess that it’s mounting, but in terms of direct conversations and getting a feel for how people are reacting today, I have no idea.”

But she added that she was in “daily conversations” with people still in the caucus and others who had left.

The Conservatives have been in a state of upheaval over the ideological direction and strategies of the party under Findlay since Peter Milobar quit on Aug. 14, saying they had a lack of “ideological alignment.”

Ian Paton, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat, Brennan Day and Bruce Banman followed last week, all critical of Findlay.

Warbus said she sent a notice of resignation to Findlay but had not spoken to her. She said there had not been “the same level of fluid interaction between the leadership team and the staff and MLAs” that she expected.

“I think the main example I can give is finding out from a post on X or from media that a main director is being fired, or that critical staff is being let go, or that there are important meetings and decisions being made at a party level,” Warbus said.

She contrasted that with communications under former leader John Rustad, saying he had once called a 6 a.m. caucus meeting to tell MLAs something face to face.

“That’s how that operated then. That is not the same thing, the same way, that things are operating today.”

Findlay, who has said she will focus on “faith, family and freedom,” was narrowly elected party leader on May 30 but does not have a seat in the legislature.

She did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Warbus said she had not decided whether to join any party formed by former Conservatives; Paton and Milobar have said they hope to have a new party running by the fall sitting of the legislature.

Warbus and others have expressed concern about how Gasper came to resign her seat of Abbotsford-Mission.

It is illegal under the Criminal Code to negotiate a reward or benefit related to resignation from political office. Findlay had said last week that suggestions a leaked audio recording showed she illegally offered jobs to MLAs, in exchange for resigning so she could stand in a by-election, were “preposterous.”

Gasper has taken a paid position as Findlay’s deputy chief of staff. RCMP said they were aware of the purported recording of Findlay addressing Conservative legislators, but “does not confirm or deny any investigation, or the identity of any person who may be subject to an investigation, until such time as charges have been laid.”

Banman has meanwhile rallied other Conservatives to join him as an Independent on Thursday “regardless of political affiliation.”

He said many had told him Findlay was “unelectable,” and that under her another election win by the NDP was increasingly likely.

stories.title: Trump pressures Apple to use ‘Lake America’ as Canadian, U.S. officials trade blame for tensions
stories.summary: U.S. President contacted the tech giant directly to ask that it change Lake Ontario’s name, a U.S. official said
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump contacted Apple AAPL-Q directly to pressure the tech giant to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” a top administration official said Monday.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told the Fox Business network the body of water’s name might soon change on Apple maps.

Trump signed an executive order last week to rename the Great Lake as tensions between the two countries escalated following a breakdown in trade talks.

Google Maps updated its service to identify the body of water as “Lake America” for users in the United States over the weekend. The company said in a post on its corporate website Saturday the change was made because the U.S. government’s geographic names database had formally renamed the lake.

Users in Canada will still see it displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, while people elsewhere in the world will see both names.

Apple has not yet responded to a request for comment.

In a social media post Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign declaring “Lake Ontario, now and always” lakeside on Saturday, while Trump spent much of the weekend posting on social media about the name change and making inaccurate claims about Canada.

Republicans and members of Trump’s administration fanned out across U.S. news stations Monday to make the case for the name change and Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford answered President Donald Trump’s “Lake America” decree Saturday with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shoreline — “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” — as Canadian leaders met the move with ridicule rather than outrage.

The Associated Press

When asked whether the U.S. is in a “tit-for-tat” trade war with Canada on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, “I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are.”

He accused Carney of turning the trade talks into a “political shouting match” and said the U.S. isn’t at war with Canada.

“What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?” Bessent said.

When Republican Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland was asked about trade tensions on the far-right Newsmax news service, he suggested the United States make Alberta the 51st state and said there’s “tremendous oil reserves there.”

“The socialism doesn’t work in Western Canada,” he said. “A lot of those provinces don’t want to be associated with Ottawa and the president is taking advantage of it.”

Explainer: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

But the move to change the lake’s name faced widespread pushback, even from members of the Republican party. As midterm and gubernatorial elections loom, the current tensions in the bilateral relationship could be problematic for Republican candidates in states that trade heavily with Canada.

Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The name comes from the Wendat word Ontari:io, which means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”

The Canadian province is named after the lake.

Indigenous leaders on both sides of the border have called Trump’s order blatantly disrespectful and a violation of treaties.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse said Monday that Indigenous languages, people and nations existed long before Confederation or the U.S. Constitution.

“Like the lake itself, our people will be here long after any administration has come and gone,” she said.

Over the weekend, “Lake America” popped up on maps available on the websites of Hydro One, Ontario transit service provider Metrolinx and the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, as well as websites connected to other provinces.

Hydro One blamed the name’s appearance on its power outage map on a third-party service. Hydro One did not respond to questions Monday about which service it uses for naming, but the map showed Google’s name in corner.

Google uses the U.S. Geographic Names Information System to populate its maps. The database maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey, a federal science agency, contains records for more than one million geographic features in the U.S., including lakes, streams, summits, valleys and ridges.

Bri Watson, an assistant professor in Western University’s faculty of information and media studies, said organizations in need of mapping have come to rely on the database because it’s comprehensive and cheaper than creating one from scratch.

“These companies just are using whatever free data sets are available and the freest data set is the data set the United States government developed and put out over public domain,” Watson said.

That means that when there’s a political dispute over a place’s name, it “can set off a bunch of awkwardness,” Watson said.

stories.title: John Galliano withdraws from Met Gala exhibition after antisemitism backlash
stories.summary: "I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time."
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
Top fashion designer John Galliano announced Monday he was cancelling an exhibition of his work that was to kick off New York’s Met Gala next spring, following criticism from donors and political leaders over his past antisemitic remarks.

“After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano, 65, wrote on Instagram.

“I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry,” he added.

A French court convicted Galliano in 2011 of making racist and antisemitic comments, after he hurled Jewish and Asian slurs at a Paris bar.

The Briton, famed for his flamboyant personality and daring designs, was also fired from his job as creative director of Dior after the incident surfaced.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art had planned a nine-month exhibition of his work starting with the star-studded Met Gala next May but high-profile Jewish figures, including renowned art dealer Arne Glimcher and city council speaker Julie Menin, voiced opposition this month.

“I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute,” Galliano said Monday, referencing the museum’s department dedicated to fashion.

“I also recognize and respect that an exhibition honoring my work would be painful for some,” he said.

Galliano referenced the rehabilitation that followed his conviction, noting his “deepest gratitude to all those who have guided, supported and accompanied me throughout these fifteen years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction.”

The Met confirmed that the “John Galliano: Horizons” show would not proceed as planned, and that a new exhibition would be announced at a later date.

Andrew Bolton, curator in charge of the Met’s Costume Institute, said he supported the decision.

“I believe deeply in the responsibility of museums to examine difficult histories with rigor, candor, and care. I also recognize the pain and concern this exhibition has caused,” he said in a statement.

Anna Wintour, the fashion icon and ex-Vogue editor who is a trustee of the Met, expressed her “full support” for Galliano and the museum.

“John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” she said.

After Dior, Galliano took the reins as creative director at Maison Margiela. He stepped down in 2024 after 10 years at the French label that helped repair his scandal-tainted image.

In March, he signed a two-year creative contract with Spanish retailer Zara.

Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the nonprofit Anti-Defamation League, said on X that showcasing Galliano’s work was “the wrong move at the wrong moment.”

“With antisemitism at crisis levels, the Met honoring John Galliano at this moment was misguided, and even Galliano ultimately recognized what the Met should have done from the start,” Greenblatt said.

“After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano, 65, wrote on Instagram.
“I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry,” he added.
A French court convicted Galliano in 2011 of making racist and antisemitic comments, after he hurled Jewish and Asian slurs at a Paris bar.
The Briton, famed for his flamboyant personality and daring designs, was also fired from his job as creative director of Dior after the incident surfaced.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art had planned a nine-month exhibition of his work starting with the star-studded Met Gala next May but high-profile Jewish figures, including renowned art dealer Arne Glimcher and city council speaker Julie Menin, voiced opposition this month.

“I do not want the debate surrounding me to place the Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute,” Galliano said Monday, referencing the museum’s department dedicated to fashion.
“I also recognize and respect that an exhibition honoring my work would be painful for some,” he said.

Galliano referenced the rehabilitation that followed his conviction, noting his “deepest gratitude to all those who have guided, supported and accompanied me throughout these fifteen years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction.”
The Met confirmed that the “John Galliano: Horizons” show would not proceed as planned, and that a new exhibition would be announced at a later date.
Andrew Bolton, curator in charge of the Met’s Costume Institute, said he supported the decision.

“I believe deeply in the responsibility of museums to examine difficult histories with rigor, candor, and care. I also recognize the pain and concern this exhibition has caused,” he said in a statement.
Anna Wintour, the fashion icon and ex-Vogue editor who is a trustee of the Met, expressed her “full support” for Galliano and the museum.
“John’s decision that the exhibition devoted to his work should not take place at this time is very courageous and a measure of the man he is,” she said.
After Dior, Galliano took the reins as creative director at Maison Margiela. He stepped down in 2024 after 10 years at the French label that helped repair his scandal-tainted image.
In March, he signed a two-year creative contract with Spanish retailer Zara.
Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO of the nonprofit Anti-Defamation League, said on X that showcasing Galliano’s work was “the wrong move at the wrong moment.”

“With antisemitism at crisis levels, the Met honoring John Galliano at this moment was misguided, and even Galliano ultimately recognized what the Met should have done from the start,” Greenblatt said.

President Donald Trump says he's renaming Lake Ontario to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada. (Aug. 28, 2026)
AP Video Produced by Elaine Carroll

Google Maps updated its service to identify the body of water as “Lake America” for users in the United States over the weekend. The company said in a post on its corporate website Saturday the change was made because the U.S. government’s geographic names database had formally renamed the lake.
Users in Canada will still see it displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, while people elsewhere in the world will see both names.
Apple has not yet responded to a request for comment.
In a social media post Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign declaring “Lake Ontario, now and always” on Saturday. Trump, meanwhile, spent much of the weekend posting on social media about the name change and making inaccurate claims about Canada.
"Now and Always": Doug Ford unveils Lake Ontario sign amid U.S. tariff war. (Aug. 29, 2026)
The Canadian Press
Republicans and members of Trump’s administration fanned out across U.S. news stations Monday to make the case for the name change and Trump’s tariffs on Canada.

When asked whether the U.S. is in a “tit-for-tat” trade war with Canada on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said, “I don’t think you can be in a tit-for-tat with someone who’s 13 times larger than you are.”
He accused Carney of turning the trade talks into a “political shouting match” and said the U.S. isn’t at war with Canada.
“What are they going to do, take their two submarines from the Edmonton mall and sic them on us?” Bessent said.

When Republican Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland was asked about trade tensions on the far-right Newsmax news service, he suggested the United States make Alberta the 51st state and said there’s “tremendous oil reserves there.”
“The socialism doesn’t work in Western Canada,” he said. “A lot of those provinces don’t want to be associated with Ottawa and the president is taking advantage of it.”

But the move to change the lake’s name faced widespread pushback, even from members of the Republican party. As midterm and gubernatorial elections loom, the current tensions in the bilateral relationship could be problematic for Republican candidates in states that trade heavily with Canada.
Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The name comes from the Wendat word Ontari:io, which means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big.”
The Canadian province is named after the lake.
Indigenous leaders on both sides of the border have called Trump’s order blatantly disrespectful and a violation of treaties.
Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse said Monday that Indigenous languages, people and nations existed long before Confederation or the U.S. Constitution.
“Like the lake itself, our people will be here long after any administration has come and gone,” she said.

Over the weekend, “Lake America” popped up on maps available on the websites of Hydro One, Ontario transit service provider Metrolinx and the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, as well as websites connected to other provinces.

Hydro One blamed the name’s appearance on its power outage map on a third-party service. Hydro One did not respond to questions Monday about which service it uses for naming, but the map showed Google’s name in corner.

Google uses the U.S. Geographic Names Information System to populate its maps. The database maintained by the U.S. Geological Survey, a federal science agency, contains records for more than one million geographic features in the U.S., including lakes, streams, summits, valleys and ridges.

Bri Watson, an assistant professor in Western University’s faculty of information and media studies, said organizations in need of mapping have come to rely on the database because it’s comprehensive and cheaper than creating one from scratch.

The Lake America name has popped up on maps available on the websites of Hydro One, Ontario transit service provider Metrolinx and the Liquor Control Board of Ontario. Bri Watson, an assistant professor in Western University’s faculty of information and media studies, said it's a result of companies relying on a U.S. database because it's comprehensive and cheap. (Aug. 31, 2026)
“These companies just are using whatever free data sets are available and the freest data set is the data set the United States government developed and put out over public domain,” Watson said.
That means that when there’s a political dispute over a place’s name, it “can set off a bunch of awkwardness,” Watson said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 31, 2026.
— With files from Kyle Duggan and Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa and Tara Deschamps in Toronto

stories.title: Unifor turns focus to Stellantis after reaching deals with GM and Ford
stories.summary: Union members at GM ratified new contracts on the weekend that include higher wages for production and skilled trades workers
paragraphs: Unifor says it will begin contract talks with U.S. automaker Stellantis STLA-N on Tuesday.
The talks come after the union ratified new collective agreements in Canada with General Motors GM-N and Ford F-N .

Unifor said Sunday its members at General Motors voted overwhelmingly in favour of ratifying new contracts with the automaker, with those in Oshawa, St. Catharines and Woodstock voting 80.5 per cent in favour, while members in Ingersoll were 96.5 per cent in support.

GM Canada president Jack Uppal says in a news release the new agreements include “meaningful improvements to wages, benefits and job security,” while making sure to “sustain good-paying jobs that have long been a cornerstone of Canada’s automotive industry.”
The three-year collective agreements increase wages for full-rate production members to $50.20 per hour and skilled trades workers to $62.71 an hour.
The union says its agreements with GM mirror the 3-per-cent annual wage increases reached with Ford, which Unifor selected to kick off its pattern bargaining with the industry.

stories.content:
Unifor says it will begin contract talks with U.S. automaker Stellantis STLA-N on Tuesday.

The talks come after the union ratified new collective agreements in Canada with General Motors GM-N and Ford F-N .

Unifor said Sunday its members at General Motors voted overwhelmingly in favour of ratifying new contracts with the automaker, with those in Oshawa, St. Catharines and Woodstock voting 80.5 per cent in favour, while members in Ingersoll were 96.5 per cent in support.

GM Canada president Jack Uppal says in a news release the new agreements include “meaningful improvements to wages, benefits and job security,” while making sure to “sustain good-paying jobs that have long been a cornerstone of Canada’s automotive industry.”

The three-year collective agreements increase wages for full-rate production members to $50.20 per hour and skilled trades workers to $62.71 an hour.

The union says its agreements with GM mirror the 3-per-cent annual wage increases reached with Ford, which Unifor selected to kick off its pattern bargaining with the industry.

stories.title: Rape-convicted Norwegian queen’s son let off house arrest for king’s funeral
stories.summary: Marius Borg Hoiby, the son of Norway’s queen, will be allowed to leave his house arrest for a rape conviction to attend the funeral of King Harald V, police said on Monday.
stories.author: AFP Staff
stories.content:
Oslo, Norway -- Marius Borg Hoiby, the son of Norway’s queen, will be allowed to leave his house arrest for a rape conviction to attend the funeral of King Harald V, police said on Monday.

Hoiby, born from a relationship prior to Queen Mette-Marit’s marriage to Harald’s son, King Haakon, was sentenced in June to four years in prison for two rapes, a conviction he is appealing.

He is serving his sentence under house arrest with an ankle tag while awaiting his appeals trial and was previously granted dispensation to visit Harald in hospital before the late king’s death aged 89 on Friday.

“The public prosecutor deemed that there were grounds to grant the requests for leave submitted by Hoiby in connection with the death,” police prosecutor Oda Karterud told AFP.

“Leave has been granted... for the funeral on September 9,” she added.

Hoiby, 29, was also given permission to attend the transfer of the king’s remains to the palace chapel on Monday evening.

Besides the two counts of rape, Hoiby was also convicted of 32 other charges, including violence towards a former partner.

He was acquitted of two other rapes.
