stories.title: With Canadians quietly lending a hand, a U.S. spy satellite-turned-telescope takes flight
stories.summary: Nasa’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could shed light on some of the deepest questions researchers have about dark energy and the universe
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Andrea Crespi was still a middle-school student in Italy when three American astronomers won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

Back then, the mystery of that acceleration – and the curious phenomenon called dark energy that powers it – seemed like an unsolvable problem.

Fast-forward 15 years and Mr. Crespi, now a graduate student at Ontario’s University of Waterloo, May be among those with the best shot yet at cracking the riddle of dark energy.

That exciting possibility moved a step closer to reality on Sunday morning with the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Named after Nasa’s first chief astronomer, who helped usher in the era of astronomy in space, the telescope is now poised to explore some of the deepest questions that researchers have about the universe, with dark energy topping the list.

“It feels like an opportunity,” said Mr. Crespi about the launch. “Like we’re at the turning point of the story.”

Despite concerns that weather would postpone the early morning liftoff, conditions proved favourable enough for a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket to send the telescope roaring on its way at 7:26 a.m. ET.

The bus-sized observatory is now on a 100-day journey to L2, a point in space about 1.5 million kilometres away, where gravitational forces are balanced in a way that allows objects located there to easily maintain their position relative to Earth.

After a period of testing, the Roman telescope is expected to begin its epic survey of the universe in the coming months. Astronomers in the U.S. and around the world are anticipating a trove of data from the newly launched instrument and hoping for discoveries across a range of subfields.

“It’s going to be revolutionary,” said Jason Rowe, an astronomer at Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, who is part of the team that will be using the new telescope to probe the characteristics and distribution of alien solar systems around our galaxy.

Years in the making, the 10.5-tonne, US$4.3-billion satellite is Nasa’s third large-scale astronomical observatory in space – and the most unique in its purpose and history.

Nasa's new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on Sunday on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology.

Whereas the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes were built to peer at tiny patches of sky to make their penetrating discoveries, Roman has a field of view that is roughly 100 times larger. Its forte is less about zeroing in on individual targets than it is looking at the universe in bulk – either by taking in the myriad of stars that make up the Milky Way, or by gazing out at the innumerable galaxies that lie beyond.

By seeing more, it will also have a better chance of spotting what is fleeting or rare, including supernovas and other short-lived phenomena.

“Our universe puts on spectacular cosmic displays every second, but they happen very quickly, so they often elude our telescopes,” said Julie McEnery, Nasa’s senior scientist on the project, during a press briefing on Saturday. “With Roman’s panoramic vision, we’ll not only catch these events, but we’ll see many at once.”

Fittingly for a telescope so well-suited for spying on the cosmos, the instrument’s primary mirror was originally meant to be used for spying on other countries.

Measuring 2.4 metres across, it is as large as the Hubble’s main mirror but has a much shorter focal length, which accounts for its more expansive view of the heavens.

When it was created more than two decades ago by a division of ITT Corporation, now part of L3Harris Technologies Inc., the mirror was to be used in a spy satellite. But when the satellite was cancelled in 2005, the exquisite mirror became a white elephant. In 2012, the National Reconnaissance Office, an agency of the U.S. military, officially gifted it to Nasa. (The gift originally included two mirrors, but Nasa was later asked to return the second.)

The surprise donation could not have come at a better time. Less than a year after the Nobel Prize was awarded for the discovery of dark energy, astronomers were now looking at the possibility of an instrument that could see enough of the universe to definitely measure dark energy’s effects.

The telescope that took shape around the mirror was tailor-made for that purpose. Its design ensured that it would be extremely stable, offering views of distant galaxies that would enable astronomers to perceive how mass is distributed in the universe based on how gravity distorts the light of objects in the background.

It was also geared to observing at infrared wavelengths, which are best for capturing the faint light of galaxies as the universe expands.

Other areas of interest to astronomers were also sure to benefit, including the search for exoplanets – planets around other stars.

And with the mirror already in hand, the project, then called the Wide Field Infrared Survey Telescope, or Wfirst, had a big head start on its way to the launch pad.

The trip has not been a smooth one, however. Starting in 2019, U.S. President Donald Trump tried to axe the telescope on multiple occasions during his first administration. Congress ultimately rescued the project and did so again after another attempt by the White House to cancel it last year.

The outcome was not as happy for the Canadian Space Agency, which initially saw an opportunity to partner with Nasa and build a calibration system and other hardware for the telescope’s Wide Field Instrument. This is the device that is crucial for the telescope’s dark energy measurements. In exchange, Canadian astronomers would have had a dedicated share of the telescope’s time. (Similar arrangements have earned Canada time on both the Hubble and Webb space telescopes).

Ultimately, Ottawa balked at the $100-million price tag for a Canadian contribution to the telescope , and in 2018, withdrew from the project. The decision left Canadian astronomers out in the cold.

Yet Canada has maintained a presence on the Roman telescope, even if it is not an official one. A second instrument, called a coronagraph, which is designed to spot exoplanets orbiting distant stars, utilizes cameras built by Nüvü Camēras Inc. of Montreal. The equipment was assembled and prepared for space flight by Quebec-based tech company ABB Canada.

Nasa’s Pandora is on a mission to help answer the question: Is there other life out there?

Frédéric Grandmont, an astronomer by training who is technology and business manager for ABB, has been with the project from the start. He said it was thrilling to see the Canadian-made hardware in images of the telescope’s scientific package – and sobering to realize its significance to the coronagraph.

“If our component doesn’t work, nothing works,” he said.

The coronagraph is designed to suppress the light of stars in order to reveal planets that orbit around them. Its presence on the Roman telescope is primarily to test a technology that one day could be used to ferret out Earth-like worlds in a proposed future space telescope, called the Habitable Worlds Observatory

But the coronagraph is just one of the ways the telescope is expected to shed light on solar systems beyond our own.

Starting next year, astronomers will use the Wide Field Instrument to stare at a star-rich portion of our Milky Way, looking for planets and moons that May reveal their presence when they momentarily cross in front of and distort the light of background stars. At the same time, the telescope will identify planets that orbit around some of those stars in cases where a planet repeatedly blocks a portion of a star’s light.

With upward of 100 million stars in the telescope’s field of view, it is inevitable that the new data will provide an unprecedented look at the demographics of worlds across different regions of our Milky Way galaxy.

“How do planetary systems end up like our solar system?” said Dr. Rowe. “I think that will be a key question we’ll answer with Roman.”

In the longer term, Roman will gradually amass data on galaxies that will be used to trace the expansion of the universe over a large chunk of cosmic time.

It’s this measurement that researchers hope will ultimately pin down the degree to which dark energy is causing the expansion of space to accelerate. Once that number is quantified and confirmed by other independent measurements, including Europe’s Euclid Space Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, researchers hope they can identify the physical mechanism behind the acceleration.

“Putting them all together and getting that full picture across, basically, all of the history of the universe is going to be very exciting,” said Will Percival, a professor at Waterloo who is Canada’s lead researcher on the team that will be using the Roman telescope to clock the motion of distant galaxies as the universe expands.

Both Dr. Percival and Dr. Rowe are participating in Roman science through grants from the Canadian Space Agency that were awarded last year.

For Mr. Crespi, who is a part of Dr. Percival’s team, the successful departure of the telescope on Sunday signals the start of an adventure that could define his career.

“It was really great,” he said after watching the launch. “It’s amazing to be part of this moment that is going to shape the cosmology of tomorrow.”

stories.title: Candidates talk affordability on Day 4 of Quebec's election campaign
stories.summary: Affordability and the economy took the spotlight on Sunday as Quebec's election campaign entered its fourth day, with party leaders unveiling their visions to ease financial pressures while grappling with the province's budgetary constraints.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
paragraphs: Affordability and the economy took the spotlight on Sunday as Quebec’s election campaign entered its fourth day, with party leaders unveiling their visions to ease financial pressures while grappling with the province’s budgetary constraints.

The Quebec Liberal Party and Québec solidaire promised to make housing more affordable, while the Conservatives promised more tax cuts and the Coalition Avenir Québec released its full fiscal plan. Meanwhile, the Parti Québécois emphasized protecting the French language by proposing stricter immigration policies.

According to Quebec’s auditor general, the next government will face significant budgetary constraints. A pre-election report published earlier this month highlighted that Quebec’s multi-billion dollar deficit must be eliminated by 2029-2030 under the balanced-budget law, leaving little room for ambitious campaign promises.
The Coalition Avenir Québec called on the other parties Sunday to follow its lead and release their own fiscal blueprints.

According to party leader Christine Fréchette and Finance Minister Eric Girard, a third Coalition Avenir Québec government would spend an additional $9.7 billion over five years to fulfil its promises, including more support for victims of domestic violence.
Quebec would then need to generate $6 billion in revenue to reach a balanced budget, they said. Fréchette said she would not lower taxes until the budget is balanced.
Fréchette’s party is counting on “expected revenues” from the federal government, without any formal commitment from Ottawa.
“We’re focused on balancing the budget, and we’re also facing an economic and financial climate that’s leading us into rougher waters than usual,” she said.

Opponents to the right and left of Fréchette’s party accused her of falling into the “same old bureaucratic model” as her predecessor, François Legault, who stepped down as premier in January after the Coalition Avenir Québec tanked in the polls.
“She likes big government,” said Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime. “She wants to spend instead of leaving money in taxpayers’ pockets.”
Meanwhile, the parliamentary leader of the leftist party Québec solidaire, Ruba Ghazal, accused Fréchette of being “irresponsible” and implementing “austerity” measures.
Liberal leader Charles Milliard said that it’s too early in the campaign to release a fiscal plan.
Housing affordability was a focal point of Sunday’s campaign announcements, with the Liberals and Québec solidaire both unveiling plans to address rising costs.
Milliard focused on making life more affordable for seniors, proposing to cap rents and service fees in privately managed seniors’ homes.
“A senior citizen on public housing assistance should never have to leave their home because of an exorbitant rent increase,” he said.

Québec solidaire promised 50,000 new units of social housing and a rent cap for all tenants, saying rents should not outpace inflation. Ghazal said the average rent prices skyrocketed since the Coalition Avenir Québec first took power in 2018.
Both Milliard and Ghazal took jabs at Fréchette, who claimed on Saturday that the housing crisis has been “solved” in “many regions” of Quebec with increasing vacancy rates.
“Just because homes are empty doesn’t mean people can afford them,” Ghazal told reporters on Sunday.
Duhaime emphasized tackling the cost of living through tax reductions. On Sunday, Duhaime announced that a Conservative government would abolish the sales tax on used goods.
The Conservatives have also promised what they describe as “a historic reduction in the tax burden on individuals” and to reduce government spending by $47 billion.

PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon continued to focus on immigration, linking it to the decline of the French language in Quebec, which prompted renewed criticism from his rivals who accuse him of using immigrants as scapegoats.
St-Pierre Plamondon told journalists Quebec is facing a “linguistic emergency” and a “historic decline in the French language,” which he considers to be central to Quebecois identity.
He proposed expanding French-language laws to junior colleges, limiting access to English-language schools for francophones and immigrants.

The PQ leader also suggested requiring children of temporary migrants to attend French schools and tightening French-language requirements for work permits, with exceptions for the agricultural sector. Additionally, the PQ would prioritize immigrants proficient in French.

“The CAQ has undermined control over our immigration system,” said St-Pierre Plamondon. “We will significantly lower immigration quotas, which ... is also essential if we are to tackle the historic decline in the use of French in Quebec.”

Immigration has been a central theme of the PQ’s campaign so far, with St-Pierre Plamondon arguing that current immigration levels exceed Quebec’s capacity to provide adequate housing and public services.
Quebec election Day 3 brings promises on immigration, transit, taxes and home care. (Aug. 29, 2026)
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Some Ontario websites showing Lake America after Google Maps update
stories.summary: Google Maps has updated to display "Lake America" when people in the United States search for the term.
stories.author: News Staff
paragraphs: By Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press
Posted August 30, 2026 10:40 am.
Last Updated August 30, 2026 6:08 pm.
Google Maps has updated to display “Lake America” for users located in the United States, after President Donald Trump signed an executive order this week to rename the Great Lake.
Users in Canada will still see it displayed as Lake Ontario on Google Maps, though the search engine will pull up Lake America as a result if users enter that name in their query.

However, several Canadian websites and apps, including Hydro One, Lcbo and GO Transit, are also displaying “Lake America” in their map images. This is likely due to the fact they employ third-party mapping tools that are based out of the United States.

“We are aware that Lake Ontario is being incorrectly labeled on our outage map,” Hydro One said in an online post on Sunday. “The issue originates from a third-party mapping service. We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference. We regret the error and apologize for any confusion it has caused.”

Stephen Crawford, the Ford government’s Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, acknowledged the issue by saying some government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps.
“Following recent changes by Google, we’re actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario,” he said in an online statement .
The issue appeared to be fixed as of 10 p.m. Sunday.

The search giant said in an Aug. 29 post on its corporate website it made the change because the U.S. government’s geographic names database has formally renamed the lake and that users outside Canada and the U.S. will see both names..
“It’s official! Lake America on Google Maps,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on the social media website X on Sunday.
Appearing on Abc’s “This Week” program on Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the name change won’t stick, despite Trump signing the executive order on Thursday.
“It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when (Trump) signed a document saying change it to Lake America,” Ford said.
“No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”
On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large sign in Winona, a small lakeside community part of Hamilton, Ont., which says, “Lake Ontario, now and always.”

Also on Saturday, Trump posted a video rendered by artificial intelligence where he replaces a Lake Ontario sign with another that reads “Welcome to Lake America,” then dances to the Ycma song by the Village People.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s bid to rename the lake in a social media post on Thursday. Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”
Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said after Trump signed his order that New York won’t call it that.
Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade talks fell apart on Aug. 21.
Both countries have accused each other of implementing last-minute changes to a proposed interim trade deal.
On Tuesday, the federal government unveiled upward of $27 billion in retaliatory measures, set to kick in on Sept. 8, responding to new U.S. tariffs.
Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario’s premier.
Ford had called the president a bully and a loser on Aug. 24, while Trump said the premier was a “less charismatic” and less intelligent version of his late brother Rob Ford.

The premier said during his ABC appearance on Sunday that things “got heated” between Trump and himself, but “you’ve eventually got to stand up to someone who just continuously attacks our country and insults our country.”

“It’s unfortunate that he stoops down to that level and unfortunately I did that day,” Ford said, adding he wants to see both sides return their focus to advancing a mutually beneficial free-trade deal.
Trump signed a similar executive order last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.
The orders only apply to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services and American news agencies have since called it the Gulf of America.
— With files from Kelly Geraldine Malone in Washington

Stephen Crawford, the Ford government’s Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, acknowledged the issue by saying some government agency websites pull map data directly from Google Maps.

“Following recent changes by Google, we’re actively reviewing our websites to make sure they all identify Lake Ontario by its correct name: Lake Ontario,” he said in an online statement .

The issue appeared to be fixed as of 10 p.m. Sunday.

The search giant said in an Aug. 29 post on its corporate website it made the change because the U.S. government’s geographic names database has formally renamed the lake and that users outside Canada and the U.S. will see both names..

“It’s official! Lake America on Google Maps,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on the social media website X on Sunday.

Appearing on Abc’s “This Week” program on Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the name change won’t stick, despite Trump signing the executive order on Thursday.

“It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when (Trump) signed a document saying change it to Lake America,” Ford said.

“No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large sign in Winona, a small lakeside community part of Hamilton, Ont., which says, “Lake Ontario, now and always.”

Also on Saturday, Trump posted a video rendered by artificial intelligence where he replaces a Lake Ontario sign with another that reads “Welcome to Lake America,” then dances to the Ycma song by the Village People.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s bid to rename the lake in a social media post on Thursday. Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”

Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said after Trump signed his order that New York won’t call it that.

Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade talks fell apart on Aug. 21.

Both countries have accused each other of implementing last-minute changes to a proposed interim trade deal.

On Tuesday, the federal government unveiled upward of $27 billion in retaliatory measures, set to kick in on Sept. 8, responding to new U.S. tariffs.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario’s premier.

Ford had called the president a bully and a loser on Aug. 24, while Trump said the premier was a “less charismatic” and less intelligent version of his late brother Rob Ford.

The premier said during his ABC appearance on Sunday that things “got heated” between Trump and himself, but “you’ve eventually got to stand up to someone who just continuously attacks our country and insults our country.”

“It’s unfortunate that he stoops down to that level and unfortunately I did that day,” Ford said, adding he wants to see both sides return their focus to advancing a mutually beneficial free-trade deal.

Trump signed a similar executive order last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The orders only apply to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services and American news agencies have since called it the Gulf of America.

Users outside Canada and the U.S. will see both names, Google’s post said.

“It’s official! LAKE AMERICA on Google Maps,” White House communications director Steven Cheung posted on the social media website X on Sunday.

Appearing on ABC’s “This Week” program on Sunday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the name change won’t stick, despite Trump signing the executive order on Thursday.

“It was like something out of ‘Saturday Night Live’ when (Trump) signed a document saying change it to Lake America,” Ford said.

“No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

But Hydro One, Ontario’s power utility, apologized Sunday after its outage map called the water body Lake America.

“The issue originates from a third-party mapping service. We are working with our vendor to correct the issue as quickly as possible and restore the proper geographic reference. We regret the error and apologize for any confusion it has caused,” said a statement from the utility on social media.

On Saturday, Ford unveiled a large sign in Winona, a small lakeside community part of Hamilton, Ont., which says, “Lake Ontario, now and always.”

Also on Saturday, Trump posted a video rendered by artificial intelligence where he replaces a Lake Ontario sign with another that reads “Welcome to Lake America,” then dances to the YCMA song by the Village People.

Prime Minister Mark Carney responded to Trump’s bid to rename the lake in a social media post on Thursday. Carney said Canadians know Lake Ontario will always be known by its original name, “then, now and always.”

Lake Ontario, one of the five Great Lakes, is located between Ontario and New York. The Canadian province is named after the lake.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul said after Trump signed his order that New York won’t call it that.

Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade talks fell apart on Aug. 21.

Both countries have accused each other of implementing last-minute changes to a proposed interim trade deal.

On Tuesday, the federal government unveiled upwards of $27 billion in retaliatory measures, set to kick in on Sept. 8, responding to new U.S. tariffs.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario’s premier.

Ford had called the president a bully and a loser on Aug. 24, while Trump said the premier was a “less charismatic” and less intelligent version of his late brother Rob Ford.

The premier said during his ABC appearance on Sunday that things “got heated” between Trump and himself, but “you’ve eventually got to stand up to someone who just continuously attacks our country and insults our country.”

Trump continued to take jabs at Canada on social media Sunday, urging Canadian companies doing business with the U.S. to cross the border. He also insisted he doesn’t want Canadian cars, parts or “Canadian anything.”

Trump signed a similar executive order last year to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

The orders only apply to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services and American news agencies have since called it the Gulf of America.

stories.title: London Transit seeks $2M more from taxpayers amid rising fuel costs, demand
stories.summary: The London Transit Commission is looking for more city cash as fuel prices and growth in service for the public transit agency increase.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
The London Transit Commission is looking for more city cash as fuel prices and growth in service for the public transit agency increase, a new budget report states.

The increase in fuel, driven largely by volatility in the energy sector following the U.S. attack on Iran, will cost London Transit an additional $2.6 million in 2027, and an increase in the “service hours” it provides will require more than $700,000 in additional funding.

The transit agency will dip into reserves to cover a portion of the costs but will need support from city hall to cover the balance, say city council members who sit on the commission.

“It’s understandable these increases are coming, we were anticipating that,” said Ward 7 Coun. Corrine Rahman, vice-chairperson of the London Transit Commission. “We will find a way forward.”

The city may transfer money from reserves to cover the additional cost, she added.

The budget report asks “administration to submit a budget amendment case increasing the City of London investment by $2,037,800 for 2027 to support the permanent addition of 2,400 service growth hours and the increased cost of diesel fuel.”

Service growth hours is an increase in the service provided by city buses.

In 2025, London Transit refunded more than $700,000 to city hall when fuel costs dropped as a result of the federal gasoline tax being eliminated, noted Ward 11 Coun. Skylar Franke, who chairs the London Transit Commission.

“The ongoing escalation of fuel costs fluctuates greatly,” she said.

The City of London provides $78.3 million annually to London Transit, which also generates more than $56 million in annual revenue at the farebox. It has $134.4 million in expenditures.

The 2027 operating budget represents the fourth and final year of the current multi-year budget it submits to the city.

As for diesel fuel, London Transit budgeted for a price of roughly $1.22 per litre but the recent average price is $1.65 per litre.

The report also pointed to a drop in ridership from January through July this year of 13.2 per cent. The decline is due largely to a decrease in student riders amid a reduction in immigration nationally that’s resulted in fewer post-secondary students arriving in London.

“We are aware of the decline given the reduction of students. But overall, ridership shows signs of recovering. It’s trending back up,” Franke said.

stories.title: Riders cash in on Argo miscues to post 28-24 win
stories.summary: There will be no Toronto Argonauts sweep of Saskatchewan in 2026.
stories.author: Brendan McGuire
stories.content:
Regina – There will be no Toronto Argonauts sweep of Saskatchewan in 2026.

In front of a sold-out Mosaic Stadium, where 33,350 seats were filled for the CFL’s biggest crowd of the season, the hometown Roughriders used a noisy fan base to expose a few leaks in the Argonauts’ boat en route to a 28-24 win.

Reminiscent of a 12-round boxing match, the opening quarter featured the teams feeling each other out by trading short touchdown passes. Then the bout went from jabs to haymakers when Toronto quarterback Chad Kelly connected with Damonte Coxie for a 58-yard-hookup to set up a second Tyler Kahmann touchdown catch for a 13-7 Argo lead early in the second quarter.

But Toronto had trouble holding the momentum. Botched converts were especially problematic for the Argonauts in this game, resulting in a four-point swing.

After the second Toronto touchdown, receiver David Ungerer was caught on the wrong sideline, creating an illegal substitution penalty that marched the Point-After-Touchdown back 10 yards, resulting in the kick hitting the upright and the Argos missing out on a single point.

Then later, after a third Toronto touchdown, Argo kicker Brady Lidster’s kick was blocked by Mike Rose and returned 79 yards the other way by Marcus Sayles to give the Roughriders another two points.

Argos head coach Mike Miller says it would be unfair to blame the loss on his special teams unit.

“It really doesn’t come down to one play,” Miller said. “It changes the cosmetic of the game but we still have to overcome it. We had opportunities to do that and we weren’t able to.”

Chad Kelly, who went 28-of-38 passing for 416 yards with three touchdowns and one interception for the Argonauts, took some big hits in this game, including a pair of sacks, and had to leave momentarily in the third quarter, being relieved by backup Nick Arbuckle.

Kelly, who revealed after the game that he suffered a broken toe, blamed the defeat on self-inflicted wounds.

“I think we had seven two-and-outs today,” Kelly said. “On second-and-long, you’re trying to find the hole, right? And it might take a little longer for the hole to develop and you might have to hold (the ball) a little longer. They have a good defensive line and they’re very well coached. They have great players up front.”

Trailing 24-21 just before the three-minute warning, the ‘Riders lined up for an 11-yard field goal attempt to try and tie the game when Argo Tarvarus McFadden jumped offside, sparking a roar from the capacity crowd and giving Saskatchewan a fresh set of downs to set up a Tommy Stevens two-yard touchdown run to give the hosts a 28-24 lead.

For the Roughriders, quarterback Trevor Harris and receiver KeeSean Johnson rediscovered a rhythm that had been missing in their back-to-back losses before this game, connecting 10 times for 146 yards and a touchdown. Part of a 313-yard passing night for the quarterback who credited the supporting cast of other receivers for making it possible.

“Dhel (Duncan-Busby) made some big plays tonight. Shemar (Bridges) made a couple big catches and then we had (D’Sean) Mimbs make a big catch on second-and-15 to keep a drive alive,” Harris said. “So, everybody was kind of doing their part.”

Head coach Corey Mace suggested earlier in the week his team needed this game to prevent a two-game skid from deteriorating into something bigger. He saw the urgency from his squad.

“I thought it was more visible in the second half,” Mace said. “I thought we were doing some really good things in the first half but the ball just didn’t fall our way in certain situations.”

Argonauts: Visit the Hamilton Tiger-Cats on Monday, Sept. 7.

Roughriders: Host the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sunday, Sept. 6.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 29, 2026.

stories.summary: As students prepare to head back to class next week, a Saskatchewan boy is focusing his last days of summer on sales.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
paragraphs: Martensville, Sask. - As students prepare to head back to class next week, a Saskatchewan boy is focusing his last days of summer on sales. Gus Fandrich has been serving up sweet treats and nostalgia all summer long from his Dickie Dee-inspired ice cream cooler. “I’m a big fan of ice cream,” Fandrich told CTV News. At 10 years old, the savvy businessman is too young to remember the Dickie Dee’s ice cream sellers of the 1980s. But he was fascinated by the freezer-on-wheels concept when he first saw it at a hockey game. “He was wondering what it was, so I explained to him they used to drive around neighbourhoods selling ice cream when I was a kid,” his dad Jason Fandrich said. With help from his dad, Fandrich created his own ice cream cart called Gus’ Sweet Treats, which officially took to the streets in May. “It is like a modern Dickie Dee bike,” Fandrich explained. The pair connected an e-bike to a freezer and a couple of cupboards that store ice cream treats, snacks and pop. It can hold about 200 ice cream treats and weighs about 300 lbs when it is fully stocked. “It would take me a while to just get down one street because I do not have the leg muscle to do it, so it is easier with an e-bike motor,” Fandrich said. Fandrich rolls through the streets of Martensville, Sask., a small city just north of Saskatoon, a few times every week. He attracts customers of all ages with a jingle he plays through a speaker. “Most of the adults that we come across are very excited when they hear the music,” Jason said. “It brings them right back to childhood.” Fandrich suspects he has visited every neighbourhood in the city at least once this summer. He hopes to continue sales until the snow falls. “(Customers) are super supportive and people will give lots of tips if you are a young kid,” he said. The soon-to-be Grade 6 student is saving up to buy new hockey cards, Lego sets and a dirt bike. He initially hoped to make about $300, but his dad says sales are already “well over that.” “It can definitely get him some hockey cards and can definitely get him that dirt bike if he wants it,” Jason said. This is just Fandrich’s first summer doing business and he already has plans to expand. Over the winter, he would like to build more ice cream carts to sell to other small communities in Saskatchewan and Alberta. “I couldn’t be more proud of him,” Jason said. “He is a great kid and he has always been motivated.”

stories.title: GM's idled Ingersoll plant a top priority for defence contracts: Union
stories.summary: Unifor says General Motors has pledged in new contract deal not to sell or close its Cami plant and consider it first for any military work.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
General Motors won’t sell or close its idled Cami assembly plant in Southwestern Ontario, with the automaker pledging to make the Ingersoll factory a top priority for any military contracts, according to a union report.

Unifor, the national union representing 1,100 laid-off Cami workers, won language in its latest round of bargaining with GM stating the plant will stay on the radar for future investment.

In a bargaining report released by the union Saturday after workers ratified the agreement, Unifor Local 88, which represents Cami employees, detailed the talks with GM Canada and the automaker’s commitment.

“The company has provided the union with a commitment letter, that outlines the following:

The company will continue to review and consider potential opportunities for Cami Assembly.

Should the Government of Canada approve a Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) contract, the company will discuss with Unifor the potential allocation of GM Defense work to Cami Assembly. If the CAF contract is awarded, Cami will be a first consideration.

The company will also continue to engage in good faith with the union as additional information becomes available regarding Cami Assembly.

The company stated that there is no intent to close or sell Cami Assembly during the life of the agreement,” the report says.

Local 88 chairperson Mark Gee also stated in the report the Southwestern Ontario factory is a top priority for the automaker.

“GM has committed that it will continue to seek opportunities for the Cami facility. They have provided a letter of commitment stating Cami will be the first consideration for the allocation of Canadian Armed Forces defence work if it is awarded to GM by the Government of Canada,” Gee said.

The agreement will also see some Cami workers eligible for retirement receive a one-time payment of $50,000. There are also pension and benefit improvements.

“This is good news, it keeps a lot of of options open,” said industry observer Greg Layson, digital and mobile editor of Automotive News Canada.

The contract agreement between GM Canada and Unifor covers about 4,600 workers at GM’s operations in Ontario, including in Oshawa, St. Catharines, the Cami factory in Ingersoll and at a Woodstock parts distribution centre.

It’s likely the automaker will wait until there’s a resolution to the trade and tariff dispute between Canada and the U.S before deciding the Ingersoll plant’s future, but a few possibilities have emerged, Layson said. Those options include building a new small-volume electric vehicle at the plant, assembling a Canadian military vehicle or partnering with a Chinese automaker to bring production to Canada, he said.

“It’s an attractive plant. The workforce is great, it has the ability to assemble electric vehicles. The potential for Cami is incredibly high but so are the hurdles, namely (U.S. President Donald) Trump and the trade agreement.”

Ingersoll Mayor Brian Petrie said he’s received messages of support for the local plant from GM Canada.

“This is fantastic news, especially for its workers who have been through a rough patch. We heard from GM that they love the workforce, the area,” he said. “They (GM) want to make an investment here and we welcome that. That plant is so versatile, it can pivot. I know GM has been talking about defence production.”

GM ceased operations at Cami last October, laying off its 1,100 workers.

The plant had built two versions of the BrightDrop electric cargo delivery van after undergoing a $1-billion overhaul to convert the factory for the production that began in 2022.

BrightDrop production was ended amid slow sales and the company saying the commercial electric vehicle market had developed slower than expected, the business made even more challenging by changing regulations and the elimination of buyer tax incentives in the U.S. market.

One analyst applauded the latest development affecting the Cami plant’s future.

“You can’t help but think this is good news. At the end of the day, it hinges on trade talks but they must have something up their sleeve,” said David Adams, past president of the Global Automakers of Canada.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. recently broke down, leading to a new round of U.S. tariffs slapped against Canadian exports worth about $28 billion a year and retaliatory tariffs by Canada on American imports worth roughly the same amount scheduled to take effect Sept. 8.

The auto industry is still largely covered by the continental free-trade agreement between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico, though both the U.S. and Canada have levied tariffs on vehicle sales.

stories.title: The swing of young families away from Toronto needs to stop
stories.summary: It will take a determined shift in policy, and attitudes, to stop the exodus of families with children from Canada’s biggest city
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
In May, Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow cut the ribbon on a new building that will deliver 255 rental apartments, 51 of them with below-market rents. It’s a sign of the times that this, the construction of a single midrise building, is seen as a success in a dynamic city of 3.3 million.

But it is. Homebuilding in Toronto and its surrounding region has cratered in the past few years. Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. projects housing starts this year will be roughly half of the 2023 total.

This connects to two other statistics that should give pause: Toronto is losing children at a rapid pace, and the region’s population has gone from growth into a sudden decline. Statistics Canada data shows that the Toronto metropolitan area swelled by 269,000 people between 2023 and 2024. In 2024-2025, it lost about a thousand. And in the City of Toronto, the number of children under five dropped 12 per cent in a decade from 2011 to 2021.

What does it mean when a city is losing its youngest residents? Can it have a future?

Toronto can, but that will require dramatic changes in attitude and in public policy. The region – and especially Toronto itself – must be deeply concerned with building much more housing, making the city more accessible to the young people who are its next generation.

At the moment, the story here is one of young people being pushed out.

In 2024-25, the Toronto area still took in a robust 53,000 international migrants, despite a dramatic throttling down of international-student visas and other forms of migration.

But these new arrivals were outnumbered by 77,000 residents who left the Toronto area for elsewhere in Canada.

As the economist Mike Moffatt has noted , most of these people are in their twenties and thirties. They are starting families, and moving their kids, in other places: Halifax or Calgary.

Despite all the economic and cultural factors pulling Canadians to its largest metropolis, the big city and even its suburbs are simply proving too expensive.

Fixing this must begin with a new attitude: It should be easy to build new housing in Toronto, especially housing that suits families. Today, it is not.

Where are people with kids living in the big city? Largely, in places where new homes are getting built. The fastest-growing populations of kids in the city since 2000 have consistently been in the downtown. Young families move where they can afford to buy, or to rent. A backyard is out of reach, financially.

But a condo may also be out of reach, and the rising government fees on new development are a major reason why. Governments – and Toronto is a particular culprit – have used development fees to fund all sorts of projects, many of which are only tangentially connected to the new homes. A Toronto Board of Trade report found these charges have increased 178 per cent since 2011.

An example: A decade ago, Toronto’s Spadina Subway was extended into the neighbouring city of Vaughan. The new subway stations spurred thousands of new condominiums in Vaughan, but almost zero within Toronto.

Yet new homebuyers in Toronto were paying for it. Over a decade, Toronto plans to spend $900-million on this project that it collected from development charges. There is no geographic correlation between these charges and this expense. That is typical. The same Toronto buyers – most of them young, many of them new arrivals – are funding a significant piece of rebuilding the crucial Yonge-Bloor subway station.

This attitude of dumping costs onto new arrivals has been a dead weight on homebuilding. Low-priced homes are simply impossible when they have charges and taxes of $100,000 tied to them. The conversation around such fees has been changing. For the building Ms. Chow was celebrating in May, the city is deferring all development charges . Prime Minister Mark Carney has committed billions of federal dollars to Ontario and B.C. specifically to reduce development charges. But in Toronto, that deal just takes these charges back to where they were in 2018.

The necessary changes go far and beyond money. Planning regulations of all kinds continue to make it hard to build apartments. Toronto has now legalized “multiplexes,” or small apartments of up to six units, in certain zones, and larger apartment buildings on particular streets. This is slow and incremental change. So far these policies have delivered only a few hundred new homes . And the federal government has allowed Toronto to slow-walk reforms. When the city backed off on legalizing six-unit buildings, Ottawa let them get away with it. Ottawa’s Housing Accelerator Fund – which is designed to spur growth in cities – gave Toronto almost all of the funding it had been promised.

What’s needed is much more decisive. Apartments should be legal, in a commercially viable form, everywhere. In the last 30 years, Toronto’s growth has been hyperconcentrated in a few places, largely in certain parts of the downtown.

There are models for how it could spread out more broadly. Look at history: Between the 1950s and 1970s sizeable apartment buildings were constructed in existing neighbourhoods across Toronto, and those today house hundreds of thousands of people.

In the Annex, one of the city’s most successful neighbourhoods, apartment dwellers form a majority of the population. Students, pensioners and professionals, they live in towers whose presence has not made the sky fall. But contemporary architects and planners are also looking ahead. Impossible Toronto: On The Courtyard , a report from the Neptis Foundation, puts forward a specific proposal for family-focused housing in Toronto. Designed by Studio Vaaro and Gabriel Fain Architects, these are apartments of up to six stories with green, shared courtyards. Their courtyards provide light and air, and somewhere comfortable for little kids to play. The report sets out a series of regulatory changes that would be required to allow housing on this scale to be realized. These include highly technical matters such as elevator regulations. Altering fire regulations to allow an apartment building with just a single stair could be a key to delivering bright, liveable apartments. In short, if Canada’s governments can follow the lead of their Swiss or German counterparts, city dwellers will be able to live better, in conditions that rival the lure of the suburban backyard.

At the moment, such designer’s visions are impossible in Toronto because the city’s own rules still don’t allow buildings of six storeys on side streets. Will that change?

It must. Cities make choices about who belongs. Toronto’s choice, over the past generation, has been to welcome growth while taxing and restricting the new homes that growth requires. The result is predictable: They come, drawn by the city’s opportunity and dynamism, and then they leave. A city that wants a future cannot simply celebrate the occasional new building that weaves through a system. It must instead build a new system.

In the Annex, one of the city’s most successful neighbourhoods, apartment dwellers form a majority of the population. Students, pensioners and professionals, they live in towers whose presence has not made the sky fall. But contemporary architects and planners are also looking ahead. Altering fire regulations to allow an apartment building with just a single stair could be a key to delivering bright, liveable apartments. In short, if Canada’s governments can follow the lead of their Swiss or German counterparts, city dwellers will be able to live better, in conditions that rival the lure of the suburban backyard.
At the moment, such designer’s visions are impossible in Toronto because the city’s own rules still don’t allow buildings of six storeys on side streets. Will that change?

The result is predictable: They come, drawn by the city’s opportunity and dynamism, and then they leave. A city that wants a future cannot simply celebrate the occasional new building that weaves through a system. It must instead build a new system.

stories.title: Voters head to the polls in three federal byelections in B.C., Ontario and Quebec
stories.summary: A trio of federal byelections are set for Monday in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A trio of federal byelections are set for Monday in Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia.

Two of the ridings are considered fairly safe Liberal seats, both of which were vacated by former cabinet ministers. In Quebec, where voters had elected a Conservative four consecutive times, the Tories may have a difficult time holding their ground.

Here’s a closer look at the three races.

North Vancouver-Capilano

Former Trudeau-era cabinet minister Jonathan Wilkinson resigned his seat in June, leaving federal politics for a diplomatic posting in Europe. He secured close to 60 per cent of the vote in April 2025.

The Liberals have chosen a former top-level staffer in the Prime Minister’s Office as their candidate: Braeden Caley was Mark Carney’s deputy chief of staff and a senior staff member on Carney’s election campaign who’s returning to his home province to run for a seat in Ottawa.

The Conservative candidate is Stephen Curran, a commercial lawyer who came second to Wilkinson in 2025, with just over 33 per cent of the votes. He has run attack ads on social media challenging Caley’s connection to the community.

In the most recent election, where NDP support across the country flagged as voters considered the implications of a trade war with the U.S., the New Democrats finished a very distant third, with just over four per cent of the vote. Stephen Tweedale, a party staffer for the local MLA, is carrying the NDP banner in this byelection.

Beaches-East York

Nate Erskine-Smith’s political future remains uncertain, but he has ruled out representing this Toronto-area seat in Ottawa. First elected in 2015, the frequently outspoken Erskine-Smith was a cabinet minister briefly during his time in Parliament, but stepped down after deciding to run for the provincial party leadership — a job he’s no longer pursuing after losing a provincial Liberal seat nomination contest earlier this year.

His former constituency office manager, Tanveer Shahnawaz, is running for the Liberals in this byelection.

Erskine-Smith won with more than 67 per cent of the vote in 2025, a full 23 points ahead of the Conservative candidate.

Shannon Devine, a labour leader and activist who came in a distant third in the riding in 2025, is the NDP candidate once again. Jim Sybros is running for the Conservatives.

Chicoutimi-Le Fjord

The rural Quebec riding, about 200 kilometres north of Quebec City, was a tight race in April 2025.

Incumbent Richard Martel, a former junior hockey coach who won four straight elections for the Conservatives in the area, narrowly edged out candidates from the Bloc Québécois and the Liberals.

This spring, Martel was the fifth Conservative MP to leave Pierre Poilievre’s caucus after Carney nominated him for a seat in the Senate.

Daniel Gobeil, a dairy farmer and former president of a provincial dairy association, is running for the Liberals.

Trade, Trump and the wider implications

Daniel Béland, a professor of political science at McGill University, said Chicoutimi-Le Fjord is the race to watch on Monday.

The Saguenay region of Quebec has been hit particularly hard by U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs: it’s a major producer of aluminum and forestry, and home to a significant number of dairy farmers who’ve found themselves in the crosshairs during this trade war because of the Americans’ irritation with Canada’s supply management system.

And yet it seems Carney’s decision to walk away from negotiations has not hurt the federal government in Quebec.

“Donald Trump is extremely unpopular in Quebec, and I think that most Quebecers believe Mark Carney’s explanation that the Americans were asking for too much,” Béland said.

A poll by the Angus Reid Institute after the trade talks ended last weekend suggests three-quarters of Canadians think the government made the right decision in walking away — and that number in Quebec was 85 per cent.

Shachi Kurl, the president of Angus Reid Institute, said that could impact the byelection results.

“If there is to be an impact, which there may well be, that impact is more likely to be advantageous (for the Liberals) than disadvantageous,” she said.

Béland said if the Bloc or the Liberals win in Chicoutimi-Le Fjord, it will be more bad news for Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

“If they really finish in a, say, distant third place in that riding, it will reinforce the narrative that Pierre Poilievre’s leadership is not helping the party,” he said, though he added that Martel’s personal popularity likely helped him win a tight race in the last election.

Kurl said her data shows why the issue of Trump’s tariffs continues to be a difficult one for the Tory leader.

“Conservatives are evenly divided as to whether they think that what Mr. Carney and his negotiators did was the right thing to do or the wrong thing,” she said.

Kurl warned that byelections at the tail end of summer are unpredictable, with turnouts typically low. An added complication for voters in Quebec is the provincial election campaign that is now in full swing.

The stakes are also lower than in previous byelections. In April, the Liberals secured their 174-seat majority in the House of Commons by winning three byelections, as well as courting five opposition MPs to cross the floor.

As of Sunday, there are six vacant seats in the House. The Liberals still have a majority, at 171 members, while the Conservatives sit at 139, the Bloc at 21 and the NDP at five. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May remains her party’s only representative.

Monday will fill three of those six seats, with byelections still to be called in a further three ridings in the upcoming months.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 30, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The fight for Alberta's 'soft separatists' — the conservatives who want to send Carney a message
stories.summary: Vote to Stay wants to sway the conservative soft separatists, who think they are being tactical, but are really playing with fire.
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Monte Solberg is between a rock, a hard place and a divided conservative base.

The former Conservative MP and founder of Vote to Stay wants Albertans to believe their “future is stronger within a united Canada than outside of it.” Of all the players trying to sway the Oct. 19 vote — pro-separation and pro-Confederation — his path is the most treacherous.

Champions of Alberta separation lean into a grievance culture carefully fed for a decade, especially during the Trudeau years. They have a motivated, sometimes angry base. Progressive “remain” campaigns — Thomas Lukaszuk’s Forever Canadian, Stephen Carter’s Alberta’s Voice, Anne McLellan’s Before You Vote — draw natural support in Liberal and NDP constituencies.

Solberg and his team, which includes former premier Jason Kenney, are hunting in tougher country. “We’d like to sway 100,000 soft separatists to vote on the federalist side,” he tells me over coffee in Calgary. “As far as I know, we’re the only ones in the Conservative fold.”

Those soft separatists are his people. “These are the people who say, ‘I’m going to send Carney a message,’” and choose Option 2 — forcing the Alberta government to begin the legal process for a binding separation referendum. They think they are being tactical; Solberg thinks they are playing with fire.

“I urge people not to see it as a way to send a message to Ottawa about Alberta’s ill treatment, which I acknowledge has been the case in the past. But I urge them to think about the consequence of blowing oxygen on a separatist movement.”

Sending a message divides, he says. “We don’t need to turn people against each other.” That is the real contest. The separatist campaigns need the soft separatists — the conservatives who think Option 2 is a warning shot, not a first step out the door. Solberg is asking those voters to stand down; the independence camp is asking them to use the ballot as leverage.

Solberg knows polarized politics. He chuckles recalling his youth in Saskatchewan under then premier Allan Blakeney, when the NDP partially nationalized the potash industry. “My dad was a conservative, very involved in politics, and fought against the NDP. It was a crazy time. You think democratic socialists are a thing in the U.S. now; they were way more extreme in those days in Saskatchewan.”

In Alberta, he grants the anger is often righteous. “We were really attacked by Justin Trudeau. No question.” But Trudeau is gone. Mark Carney, he says, has moved in a different direction on electricity regulations, the EV mandate and export pipelines.

“We’ll never know if we moved five people or 50,000 or 100,000,” Solberg says. The campaign’s job is to give people reasons to reconsider. “This is not a joke. Even though it’s a referendum on a referendum at this point, we could quickly be cast into a binding vote on the future of Alberta and Canada.”

Overall enthusiasm among federalists is picking up

He is at his sharpest when he leaves the atmospherics and talks specifics. The Alberta Prosperity Project recently released a draft constitution for an independent Alberta that includes elements he says most Albertans would not recognize. “Making Alberta an open-carry state is ridiculous. I say this as somebody who is a firearms owner myself. This is not what Albertans are looking for. It’s not a priority.” Albertans care about affordability and about not being swallowed by larger powers — risks, he argues, that are more manageable inside a country than as a “statelet.”

In a world now defined by an intense trade war with the United States, he would rather stay united than split off and become easy pickings. He will not go further into fear; I am surprised by the calm. These decisions are emotional, yet he remains relentlessly logical. The question hanging over Vote to Stay is whether logic is enough against people who are not trying to be reasonable.

The campaign has raised roughly $100,000 and hopes for more. It profiles prominent Albertans — Stephen Mandel, Iris Evans, Ed Stelmach, Brett Wilson, Mike Shaikh — with a civic message: you have a stake in this; spend an hour and vote.

That is a decent appeal to people who already like Canada. The voters who May well decide this thing are the ones telling Solberg they want to send Ottawa a message.

“My sense is that overall enthusiasm among federalists is picking up,” he says. Flags, online engagement, polling. “I think we saw the peak of separatism in the spring, almost concurrent with when the separatist group brought in their petition.” Maybe; but peaks do not matter if the other side is better at turning residual anger into turnout.

Solberg is a natural for this role. He was a Reform MP for Medicine Hat from 1993 to 2008, a Harper cabinet minister and an early believer in “The West Wants In.” After politics he founded New West Public Affairs in Calgary; his sons Matt and Michael Solberg are partners.

A card-carrying United Conservative Party member, he has sympathy for Premier Danielle Smith. “Politics within the UCP is very difficult these days, very elbows up.”

He credits her working relationship with Carney. “They’ve actually made great progress on things that are important to Albertans. We should celebrate that, not cheer against it.” Political courage is in short supply, he says, “and both are showing a bit of it. That should be applauded.”

Then the trade war with America made the argument more complex. Kenney — Solberg’s most prominent ally — publicly suggested that Alberta oil stay on the table as potential leverage with Washington. Keith Wilson, the Let Alberta Decide campaigner, immediately turned the remark into a separatist talking point. Vote Option 2, Wilson said, and put that leverage in Alberta’s hands rather than Ottawa’s.

Solberg’s pitch is that “sending a message” only inflames division. Wilson’s use of Kenney’s suggestion shows how fast that message escapes the conservative fold Solberg is trying to hold together.

“Canada is something more than a bunch of trade deals and it’s not an ATM,” Solberg says. “It’s actually all these relationships between people and provinces and communities and families. It’s all of that that is at stake.”

True enough. It is also the language of people who already agree with him; I know, I’m one of them.

The only frustration he shows is when I ask who has not shown up. “It’s the business community,” he says — the real one, not former premiers fronting for the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

“Who has more to lose than the business community?” he asks. He understands the reluctance: some worry they will anger customers or anger workers in Red Deer and Grande Prairie. “But you know what,” he reiterates, “it’s about political courage. You need it everywhere.”

He is right. The separatists have warriors; the conservative case for Canada still needs some.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: A Couche-Tard convenience store is seen in Montreal, Thursday, Sept. 5, 2024. The Japanese owner of 7-Eleven has rejected a takeover offer from Quebec-based Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. THE Canadian Press/Christinne Muschi
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Couche-Tard results

Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. will release its financial results for its first quarter of its 2027 financial year on Tuesday after the close of trading followed by a conference call with investors and financial analysts on Wednesday morning. The company recently made an offer for Polish convenience store operator Zabka Group.

Interest rate announcement

The Bank of Canada will make its interest rate decision on Wednesday. The central bank is widely expected by economists to keep its policy interest rate on hold at 2.25 per cent. The rate decision comes after Statistics Canada reported the annual rate of inflation rose to three per cent in July, up from 2.8 per cent in June.

Economic data

Statistics Canada will release a pair of key reports this week. It will publish its figures for international merchandise trade in July on Thursday followed by its snapshot of the job market in August on Friday when it releases its labour force survey for the month.

BRP Inc. will release its second-quarter financial results before markets open on Thursday and plans to hold a conference call with investors and financial analysts. Tariffs have taken a toll on the maker of recreational vehicles this year as its products are largely made in Canada and Mexico but find their biggest market in the United States.

Lululemon earnings

Lululemon Athletica Inc. will publish its second-quarter results after the close of markets on Thursday. The results come just days ahead of the arrival of former Nike executive Heidi O’Neill who will assume the role of chief executive of the Vancouver-based retailer on Sept. 8.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 30, 2026.

stories.title: Is it legal for cars to speed up when I’m trying to pass them?
stories.summary: If you don’t want someone passing you, you can’t hit the gas to block them, experts say
stories.author: Jason Tchir
paragraphs: When I’m trying to pass cars on the highway, they often speed up so I can’t pass them. When there’s a passing lane, it’s mostly just annoying, but I’ve also had drivers do this on an undivided highway when I’m trying to pass in the oncoming lane. That’s incredibly dangerous and I usually end up abandoning my move. Then, once I’m behind them again, they often slow down to exactly the speed limit, like they’re trying to teach me a lesson. Isn’t this illegal? – Graham, Kamloops, B.C.
If you don’t want someone passing you, you can’t hit the gas to block them, experts say.
“ It is both illegal and dangerous to prevent someone from passing by increasing your speed,” Corporal Michael McLaughlin, a spokesman for B.C. Highway Patrol, said in an e-mail.
In British Columbia, the law states that if a car is being passed, the driver “must not increase the speed of the vehicle until completely passed by the overtaking vehicle.”

If you do, you could face a $109 fine and three demerit points . From 2021 to 2025, police issued nine tickets for the offence, according to data from the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (Icbc).
The rules vary by province, but most, including Alberta and Quebec , say you can’t speed up while being passed.
Most provinces also require you to move right if you safely can so other drivers can pass you.
While Ontario’s passing rules don’t specifically ban speeding up to block a pass, you could be charged with stunt driving .

“That’s a level of aggressive driving that is simply unacceptable,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “It’s a 14-day vehicle impound, a 30-day licence suspension, a one-to-three-year driving prohibition, an up-to-$10,000 fine and up to six months in jail.”
In most provinces, you could also be charged with careless driving.
What can you do if someone is speeding up so you can’t pass?
The safest thing to do is drop back and let them get ahead of you, Shapiro said. “Let that person go.”

If it escalates to the point that you’re worried about a crash – for instance, if they’re slamming on their brakes once you’re back behind them but they still won’t let you pass – consider calling the police, Shapiro said.
“This kind of situation shows why everyone needs a dash camera,” he said. “If you don’t have it [and there’s a collision], it’s your word against theirs.”
But if you floor it to try to get ahead of a car that’s speeding up while you pass, you become a danger on the road, too.
In fact, you shouldn’t be speeding at all when you pass someone, McLaughlin said.
“The most common mistake people make when passing is to speed,” he said. “If you need to exceed the speed limit to pass … that is by definition illegal.”
The law states drivers must keep a safe distance from the car they’re passing and not pull back in front of it until they’re safely clear.
When you’re passing in the oncoming lane, you must make sure you can do it safely – and you need a clear view of the road ahead before you pull out.
In 2023, three people died in a head-on collision about 60 kilometres north of Kamloops while the car was trying to pass a semi.
But anytime you pass someone going the speed limit or even above it, consider whether you really need to pass them at all.

“Slow drivers are the source of many online rants, but slow drivers rarely cause serious collisions,” McLaughlin said. “Many, many serious collisions occur because impatient, speeding drivers are attempting to make an unsafe pass.”

stories.title: The Snowbirds are making their last flights over Toronto. Why the air show will be a bittersweet ‘ballet in the sky’
stories.summary: Labour Day weekend will be the last chance for GTA residents to catch this version of the Snowbirds, set to be grounded.
stories.author: Bruce Campion-Smith Special
paragraphs: It starts with the twinkle of nine lights on the distant horizon. Then comes the staccato radio check-in by the pilots, one through nine.
“Smoke on,” commands the team lead.

For 55 years, the Snowbirds — Canada’s air demonstration team — have brought their graceful aerial performances to North American skies, some 2,700 air displays in all for more than 140 million people.
This Labour Day weekend, the team will once more headline the Canadian International Air Show along Toronto’s waterfront for a performance that promises to be memorable — and bittersweet.
That’s because the curtain is closing on the Snowbirds, at least this version of the team.
Time has caught up with the team’s aircraft, the venerable CT-114 Tutor jet, which is now approaching 60-plus years of service.

Despite the miracles worked by air force technicians, the federal government has decided it’s no longer feasible to keep the aging aircraft serviceable. It has declared that the Snowbirds will stop flying until a replacement aircraft is ready in the early 2030s.
The grounding ends a remarkable run. The Snowbirds first appeared at the Toronto air show in 1971 — the same year they were formed — and have only missed one year since.
“They are absolutely what holds our show together,” Lori Duthie, executive director of the Canadian International Air Show, said in an interview. “Everybody looks forward to it.”

From their base in Moose Jaw, Sask., the Snowbirds — officially known as the 431 Air Demonstration Squadron — criss-cross the continent to perform at venues big and small, from mega-air shows to summer fairs, small-town displays and ceremonial fly-pasts. They dazzle spectators with their looping, rolling aerobatic display.

The U.S. demonstration teams Blue Angels and Thunderbirds, which fly front-line fighters, are impressive, but different. The Snowbirds’ Tutor jet is an older-generation trainer. It’s slower, even a little underpowered for its air show role.

But that’s a big part of what makes their performances so enjoyable. “The fact that they can go a little bit slower allows them to get closer,” Duthie said. “Having nine jets versus six certainly gives them a lot more variety than some of the faster jet teams.
“It looks like a ballet in the sky, something that you just can’t achieve with some of the other demo teams. It’s not just jets shooting across the sky from left to right.”

Thirty years ago, I flew with Dan Robinson, Snowbird 4, the first line astern position. It was a memorable flight, with Snowbird jets filling the view on either side and ahead that at times were barely a metre away. Our formation of nine jets swooped over the Ontario landscape and made a dramatic pass above Niagara Falls.
I caught up with Robinson last week. He remembers the two seasons he spent with the Snowbirds as the highlight of his flying career.

“It was the first time I’d been all around Canada,” Robinson recalled. “To go and meet people all across the country, all the provinces, all the territories, that’s what stuck with me. To be a part of that is something that I treasure forever.”
What it’s like to fly a Snowbird
From the ground, the formation flying appears effortless as nine planes fly as one.

In the cockpit though, it is hard work, demanding intense concentration as pilots constantly move the stick and throttle to maintain position, battling turbulent air and the wash from the jets around them.
Yet Robinson said that by the time air show season began, flying in tight formation had become second nature, thanks to months of practice in Prairie skies.
“It’s building blocks,” he said. “You start flying wider formations, then you get in tighter. You don’t do the big formations until you’ve done the smaller formations.
“You never lose your edge, but at the same time what seems impossible to people on the ground is actually something that you’ve worked your way to. It’s not unsafe.”
But there have been sad reminders that it’s not without risk, including a dark day at the 1989 Toronto air show.

Thousands of spectators, including myself, watched in disbelief when two Snowbird jets collided during a manoeuvre. One piloted by Capt. Shane Antaya plunged straight into the lake. Team leader Maj. Dan Dempsey managed to eject from his aircraft before it, too, tumbled into the water.
Over the team’s history, eight Snowbird members along with a passenger have been killed in flying accidents and another Snowbird pilot was killed in a car accident following a show.
Could the Snowbirds keep flying?

This day of reckoning for the Snowbirds was not unexpected. For years, questions have been raised about the age of the Tutor, which served as the jet trainer for the Air Force from 1963 to 2000, and the pressing need for a replacement aircraft.

But decisions were kicked down the road. And now, the federal government has decided to ground the team even though a replacement aircraft is still years away. While some $30 million was recently spent on avionics upgrades to the Tutor jets, the Defence Department says “engineering challenges” with the airframes, engines and escape systems pushed the decision.
Supporters aren’t letting the team go without a fight.
The Snowbirds Alumni Association has launched a “No Pause” campaign to press Ottawa to keep the team in the air.
