stories.content:
Peter Kuitenbrouwer is a registered professional forester who teaches in the Master of Forest Conservation at the University of Toronto. He is the author of Maple Syrup: A Short History of Canada’s Sweetest Obsession.

A few months ago on a Sunday morning, Gaétan Pouliot performed a ritual common among many families across Canada, including ours: He made crêpes (we usually eat pancakes and waffles), and doused them in maple syrup. At least, the label on the can from which he poured the liquid read, “pure maple syrup.”

But something tasted wrong. Mr. Pouliot, who had bought the syrup at a Montreal supermarket, just happens to be a journalist at Enquête , the flagship investigative television show on Radio-Canada. The team brought five syrup cans bought at different supermarkets, but all with the sticker of one producer, to a maple syrup testing lab, and visited the unsuspecting syrup packager in St. Chrystostome, south of Montreal, with hidden cameras. Their report revealed that oceans of “maple syrup” sold for around $5 a half-litre at all Quebec’s big supermarket chains was in fact at best half syrup, the other half being cane sugar. They titled their TV story Sirop de Poteau, the derisive Quebec term for table syrup, or literally, the syrup you would make if you tapped a fence post.

This month, a Vancouver-based law firm has asked court permission to certify a class action naming the syrup packager, Steve Bourdeau, and Quebec retailers including Loblaws, Sobeys and Metro, for allegedly selling something as maple syrup that is not the real thing. Courts have yet to rule on any of this. (Confronted by the Enquête reporters about test results that found 50-per-cent cane sugar in the syrup he canned, Mr. Bourdeau speculated that perhaps one of his suppliers in Ontario or New Brunswick sold him adulterated syrup. I have been unable to get ahold of Mr. Bourdeau for comment).

How did we get here? Quebec is after all the beating heart of the world’s maple syrup industry. A powerful cartel of maple syrup farmers, the Producteurs et Productrices Acéricoles du Québec, run out of the top floor of a kind of secular agricultural cathedral in the Montreal suburb of Longueuil, sets the price of syrup, tells Quebec farmers how much syrup they May produce, and owns three high-security warehouses – the grandly named Strategic Maple Syrup Reserve – that between them can stockpile the equivalent of 53 Olympic-size swimming pools of the liquid gold.

The Centre Acer, a Quebec maple syrup research institute, maintains a team of testers in its inspection division, who from March through September taste, and run tests on, samples from millions of litres of maple syrup, to classify it, and also to make sure it is, in fact, maple syrup.

This infrastructure and control has helped propel Quebec to global supremacy, as source of more than two-thirds of the global maple syrup supply; Statistics Canada suggests that maple syrup production has more than doubled over the past 15 years.

But now we have massive sales of adulterated syrup in, of all places, Quebec. Aren’t Quebeckers supposed to know what maple syrup tastes like? How was this subterfuge possible? One wonders: Is any of our syrup pure?

We have been here before, as I describe in my history book, Maple Syrup . At a 1916 meeting of maple syrup producers in west Quebec, John H. Grimm, maker of the famed Grimm maple syrup evaporators, praised the Inland Revenue Department in Ottawa for punishing grocers under the Adulteration Act, which read in part, “No person shall manufacture for sale, keep for sale, offer or expose for sale, or sell, any article of food resembling or being an imitation of maple sugar or maple syrup or which is composed partly of maple sugar or maple syrup, and which is not pure maple sugar or pure maple syrup.”

The current fake syrup scandal stems to a loophole in the Quebec syrup marketing framework. Each spring, most maple syrup leaves industrial sugar shacks in Quebec in 200-litre drums, about the size of a barrel of oil, and gets tested either at bottling companies or at the federation warehouses that stockpile excess syrup. But the producers’ federation permits syrup farmers to also can their own syrup, which they May sell directly to supermarkets or at the roadside, with a cut of sales paid to the federation. This accounts for about 10 per cent of Quebec syrup.

That syrup never gets systematically tested, although the Quebec syrup federation told me that it directs Acer to sample in a random way the maple syrup sold on the roadside or in grocery stores, and report any violations to the competent authorities.

This is the system that fell apart.

Making maple syrup is hard work, as the legions of Canadians who, often through grade schools, have made pilgrimages to a local sugar shack in spring can tell you: One must boil down 40 litres of the sap that drips slowly from the sugar maple tree, to get a litre of syrup. That’s why the stuff is pricey! So when one spring pyramidical stacks of cans of syrup appeared in grocery aisles for $5 a can, about half the usual price, across Quebec, everyone buys it and nobody blinks an eye? And where was the random taste-testing crew, supposedly guided by the high priests of Quebec’s maple syrup orthodoxy? They didn’t notice the flood of bargain-basement syrup?

One problem May be that Canadians (gasp!) and even Quebeckers (bigger gasp!) are forgetting what real maple syrup tastes like. The maple syrup that we make on my little Ontario farm by collecting sap with buckets hanging from metal spiles tapped into maple trees, and then boiling the sap for days over a wood fire, is dark, smoky and flavourful. But these days in big sugar bushes, vacuum pumps suck sap through plastic tubes to vats where other pumps then force the sap through membranes to take out most of the water, before the sap goes into high-efficiency evaporators fired usually by stove oil or electricity, producing a lovely syrup, sure, but a lighter syrup that, purists insist, lacks that caramelly, slightly smoky, mysterious, zesty sweet taste that reminds us of youth, wilderness and home.

At its annual meeting this May in Lévis, south of Quebec City, the syrup federation faced syrup farmers furious with the syrup subterfuge . A federation lawyer told them that the federation had taken custody of 46 totes (usually holding 1,000 litres each), 142 barrels (each holding about 200 litres) and was still trying to round up about 50 shipping pallets of cans of “maple syrup” from the suspect producer, which the lawyer described as “radioactive.”

We May not need a Royal Commission, but something tastes very sour in the heart of maple syrup country right now, leaving consumers across Canada with diminished confidence in our national condiment.

The newspaper La Presse this spring quoted Joël Vaudeville, a spokesperson for the Quebec syrup federation, suggesting to consumers to “take advantage of the next few weeks to fill up [with maple syrup] directly from the producer. This direct connection ensures quality.”

That’s easy if you live a convenient drive from a sugar bush. Others across Canada would prefer that the cartel of farmers, who maintain a rigid control over the market in the sweetener that comes from the tree represented on our flag, along with our governments, do a better job to make sure that the maple syrup we buy in a can or bottle tastes good, and is the real thing.

stories.title: The main threat to Canadian unity is not in Alberta
stories.summary: While current polling shows strong majorities of voters in both Alberta and Quebec would reject separation, one can plausibly imagine a scenario in which PQ government could sway enough Quebeckers to vote Yes in a future referendum
stories.author: Konrad Yakabuski
stories.content:
On the eve of Canada’s 150 th birthday, in 2017, the then-premier of the country’s most reluctant province interrupted the party preparations with an awkward reminder of the federation’s unfinished constitutional business. Philippe Couillard, the Liberal premier of Quebec, chose the moment to call for an end to an unofficial moratorium on federal-provincial talks to recognize his province’s distinct character in the country’s supreme law.

In making his bid to relaunch negotiations that had broken down in 1992, after Canadians rejected the Charlottetown accord in a national referendum, Mr. Couillard aimed to ensure Quebeckers no longer felt “ like exiles in their own country .” This, apparently, was asking too much. The rest of Canada, beginning with its then-prime minister, blew him off .

After the failure of Charlottetown, and its 1987 predecessor, the Meech Lake accord, the rest of Canada had given up on attempting to accommodate Quebec’s constitutional demands. The French-speaking province had objected to the adoption of the 1982 Constitution without the inclusion of enhanced protections for its language and culture. While the rest of Canada moved on, Quebeckers never forgot the “ coup d’état de 1982 .”

“The 150 th anniversary of the federation provides an opportunity to resume a meaningful dialogue on the place of the country’s different national elements, ON the role and composition of its institutions, ON the principles that guide intergovernmental relations – in short, ON the evolution of federalism,” declared the Couillard government’s 192-page proposal for renewed talks, entitled “ Quebecers, Our Way of Being Canadian. ”

Mr. Couillard’s outstretched hand was summarily snubbed by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose father Pierre Trudeau had been the architect of the 1982 Constitution and the adoption of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. “You know my views on the Constitution,” the younger Trudeau snapped . “We’re not reopening the Constitution.”

If Mr. Trudeau felt he could be so dismissive of Mr. Couillard’s proposals, it might have been because Quebec’s sovereigntist movement appeared, at the time, to have run out of steam. Support for the Parti Québécois had plummeted as the upstart Coalition Avenir Québec captured nationalist voters by promising to obtain more autonomy for the province within Canada and, importantly, to never hold another divisive referendum.

Now, as Quebeckers prepare to vote in a provincial election on Oct. 5, the PQ is back on top of the polls and potentially poised to form a majority government, based on its large lead among francophone voters. The sovereigntist party’s stunning comeback May be partly attributed to the Caq’s second-term blunders, unrelated to the constitutional file, under former premier François Legault, who stepped down in April . Regardless, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s vow to hold a third referendum – though not, he now says , while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office – has put sovereignty squarely back on the agenda.

The rest of the country is wholly unprepared for where this might lead. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has been laser-focused on countering rising separatist sentiment in Alberta. An Oct. 19 referendum asking Albertans whether they want to remain in Canada or hold a binding plebiscite on secession has stolen the media spotlight.

As a result, more than twice as many Canadians consider the possibility of a referendum on Alberta separation to be a bigger threat to national unity (45 per cent) than a future plebiscite on Quebec secession (17.8 per cent), according to a June Nanos Research poll .

This defies logic, and history.

Quebeckers’ visceral attachment to their unique culture is rooted in their 400-year-old struggle for la survivance . The Quebec sovereignty movement grew out of this quest, not out of circumstantial economic grievances toward Ottawa, as is the case in Alberta.

While current polling shows strong majorities of voters in both Alberta and Quebec would reject separation, one can plausibly imagine a scenario in which a PQ government could sway enough Quebeckers to vote Yes in a future referendum. After all, it almost happened once before, in 1995, when sovereigntists fell less than a percentage point short of victory.

Francophone Quebeckers are intrinsically nationalist. Almost two-thirds of them identify first or only with their home province, rather than Canada, according to the Environics Institute’s most recent Confederation of Tomorrow survey . Many francophones who say they would vote No now could switch sides during a referendum campaign to ensure their province does not face a third defeat that weakens its negotiating hand.

Sovereigntist support could also surge if three controversial laws passed by the CAQ government aimed at affirming Quebec’s distinctness are struck down by the courts. Two of these laws involve Quebec’s unilateral moves to amend the Canadian Constitution to declare French as the province’s only official language and to abolish the oath to King Charles III for members of the National Assembly. The other concerns la laïcité , Quebec’s unique form of secularism, which enjoys broad support in the province even though it interferes with certain Charter rights. Court rulings invalidating or defenestrating these laws could help a PQ government create the winning conditions for a Yes victory.

If another referendum is held, the PQ could well be third time lucky.

The PQ’s return to the fore of Quebec politics under Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has upended the narrative that many analysts had subscribed to after the CAQ first swept to power in 2018. In their telling, Quebeckers opted for the Caq’s “third way” after decades of feeling they had been held hostage to referendum politics by the federalist Quebec Liberal Party and the PQ, which had sought to polarize public opinion around the secession question.

Mr. Legault, an ex-PQ cabinet minister who founded the CAQ in 2011, had solid nationalist credentials. But he insisted he could protect Quebec’s culture and enhance its autonomy by seeking more power from Ottawa without threatening to break up the country. During his first term, which covered the COVID-19 pandemic, he often appeared to walk on water.

At the outset of the 2022 election campaign, support for the PQ was hovering in the single digits . Thanks to a breakthrough campaign performance by Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, the sharp-witted Oxford University-educated lawyer who became PQ Leader in 2020, the sovereigntist party managed to win 14.6 per cent of the vote – but only three seats – in the 2022 election.

It is what Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon – who is known by his initials, Pspp – did next that really caught Quebeckers’ attention and helped relaunch his party. He, along with his two PQ colleagues, refused to swear an oath to King Charles III to sit in the National Assembly.

Nationalist MNAs had long complained about having to declare allegiance to the monarch, a requirement under Section 128 of the Constitution, but had begrudgingly gone along with it. In 1982, then PQ premier René Lévesque added a second oath – proclaiming loyalty to the Quebec people – to ease the sting of having to bow before the British Crown, which remained for many Quebeckers a hated symbol of La Conquête .

“The absurdity of this ritual has gone on long enough,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon declared after the 2022 election. An overwhelming majority of voters agreed. A Léger poll found that 76 per cent of all Quebeckers, and 82 per cent of francophones, favoured conserving the oath to the Quebec people; only 15 per cent wanted to keep the oath to the King.

“Quebeckers were proud to see this resistance to the monarchical symbol,” Catherine Mathieu, a constitutional law professor at l’Université du Québec à Montréal, says of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s act of defiance. “It reinserted the PQ and its aspirations into the political conversation. Pspp and his MNAs were able to capitalize on that attention.”

This left Mr. Legault’s newly re-elected CAQ government scrambling to conserve the nationalist mantle that it had inherited in 2018. It quickly tabled legislation to abolish the oath to the monarchy for MNAs through a unilateral amendment to the Constitution to exempt Quebec from Section 128. The National Assembly unanimously adopted the bill .

Experts were divided over whether Quebec could invoke Section 45 of the Constitution, which allows provincial legislatures to “make laws amending the constitution of the province,” to abolish the oath requirement for its MNAs. But the Trudeau government did not oppose the move, suggesting its own legal opinions supported Quebec’s position.

(As with those of other provinces, Quebec’s constitution – which is considered part of the Canadian Constitution – is not contained in a single written text; rather, it is composed of provincial laws governing such matters as the electoral system and the rules of the National Assembly, the provincial human-rights code and unwritten conventions, in addition to the parts of the federal Constitution that relate to its exclusive areas of jurisdiction.)

The CAQ government had used Section 45 to unilaterally amend the Constitution once before with Bill 96 , its beefed-up version the 1977 Charter of the French Language. The law, tabled in the spring of 2021, inserted two clauses into the Constitution to state that “Quebeckers form a nation” and that French “shall be the only official language of Quebec.”

Here, too, Mr. Trudeau did not object. His muted response sharply contrasted with his reaction, four years earlier, to Mr. Couillard’s request to relaunch constitutional talks. But unlike in 2017, when he commanded a majority government, he was in a much weaker political position in 2021. Picking a fight with Quebec could have threatened his party’s chances of holding onto francophone seats in the province in that year’s federal election.

Indeed, the political salience of the issue was borne out when the Bloc Québécois tabled a House of Commons motion endorsing the constitutional amendments set out in Bill 96. The motion passed overwhelmingly with 281 votes. Only two MPs voted against it; 50 MPs abstained, including 11 Quebec Liberals from mostly anglophone and allophone ridings.

The constitutional amendments contained in Bill 96 and Bill 4, the law abolishing the oath to the monarchy for MNAs, were largely inspired by the academic work of a new generation of nationalist jurists and political scientists who had advocated unilateral action by Quebec to shatter the “constitutional inertia” of the previous decades.

A similar movement in favour of unilateralism emerged in Alberta and Saskatchewan, though one largely aimed at stymieing federal climate policies and asserting provincial control over resource development. In Quebec, unilateral action was instead promoted as a tool to affirm Quebec’s distinct identity in the Constitution without having to engage in inevitably contentious multilateral negotiations with Ottawa and the other provinces.

“We had been told in our constitutional law courses that constitutional reforms were impossible in Canada, that the fruit was not ripe, that it was too complex,” explains Prof. Mathieu, who co-edited a recent collection of essays on the new trend of constitutional unilateralism. “But it is not because it is complex that provinces can content themselves with the status quo. Unilateralism is a response by certain provinces to increase their autonomy without going through elaborate rounds of [federal-provincial] negotiations.”

It remains a matter of fierce legal debate whether the amendments introduced into the Constitution by Bill 96 are merely symbolic or create new protections for Quebec’s language and culture that courts will be required to consider in assessing the constitutionality of provincial legislation. That is because while Section 45 empowers provinces to unilaterally amend their own constitutions, many experts contend that such amendments cannot alter the overarching architecture of the Constitution, including the Charter.

Ultimately, it will be up to the courts to rule on the matter.

In a legal challenge to Bill 96 , a Quebec English-language rights group called the Task Force on Linguistic Policy argues that the amendments included in the law violate Section 133 of the Constitution, which stipulates that both French and English can be used in Quebec courts and the National Assembly. The group’s lawsuit also charges that Bill 96 “indirectly and impermissibly bring into effect the concept of ‘distinct society’ which the so-called Meech Lake and Charlottetown Accords failed to achieve” and will hence have “an interpretative impact on the division of powers” between Ottawa and Quebec.

Of course, this is exactly the effect their proponents hope they have.

“I think [Section 45] is an element of the Constitution that can lead courts to grant more autonomy to Quebec, particularly in language matters,” insists Université de Sherbrooke law professor Guillaume Rousseau, a former PQ candidate tapped by Mr. Legault to co-chair a 2024 commission on ways for Quebec to increase its autonomy within Canada.

Prof. Rousseau, who is now running for the CAQ , also advocates systematic pre-emptive use of the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause (which nationalist politicians refer to as the “parliamentary sovereignty clause”) to shield provincial legislation from Charter challenges, as Mr. Legault’s government did in Bill 96 and Bill 21, its secularism law. He concedes bilateral negotiations with Ottawa are still necessary to achieve some of the Caq’s autonomist goals, such as gaining exclusive jurisdiction over immigration and a deciding say in the nomination of judges.

“The Caq’s position is to say that we will use all the means at our disposition to secure more autonomy unilaterally, sometimes bilaterally, but more often unilaterally with Section 45 and the parliamentary sovereignty clause,” Prof. Rousseau says.

In its recent 550-page “ blue book ” on sovereignty, the PQ argues Bill 96’s constitutional amendments carry no legal weight. “The recognition of Quebec as a nation/distinct society will have no effect unless [Ottawa and all provinces] agree that this recognition should produce tangible effects,” the document says. “This means that the Legault government deceived Quebeckers with respect to this issue, unless the objective was simply to affirm something to an interlocutor that is not listening.”

The legality of Quebec’s abolition of the oath to the King is also before the courts. A lawsuit brought this month by the Public Interest Litigation Institute (Pili) argues that the move “exceeds the scope of permissible unilateral constitutional amendments” under Section 45.

Indeed, Article 41 of the Constitution stipulates that amendments related to “the office of the Queen, the governor-general, and the lieutenant governor of a province” require the approval of the House of Commons, the Senate and the legislatures of every province. The Pili, a group led by University of Ottawa law professor Lawrence David, also contends that exempting MNAs from Section 128 undermines democratic rights guaranteed in Section 3 of the Charter by “leading to the election of politicians who are not constitutionally qualified to sit in the National Assembly by refusing to take the oath of allegiance.”

The legal intricacies of constitutional law May be lost on average Quebeckers. But history has shown they are never indifferent to how courts rule on efforts by the National Assembly to protect their language and culture.

No future court ruling will be as closely followed by Quebeckers, or as potentially explosive, as the Supreme Court of Canada’s decision on Bill 21, expected in the fall .

Bill 21 prohibits Quebec public servants in a position of authority (including teachers) from wearing religious symbols on the job. The Supreme Court must decide whether Quebec’s pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clause in Bill 21 prevents a judicial review of the law, as the province contends, or whether to set limits on its use.

A ruling by the Supreme Court that censures Quebec or constrains its ability to invoke the notwithstanding clause would be a gift to the PQ, buttressing its argument that the federal system remains a dangerous threat to Quebec’s language, culture and values.

But any future concessions by Ottawa on French-content rules would play into the PQ’s hands.

Three-quarters of francophone Quebeckers think French is threatened in their province, the highest proportion since at least 1992, according to the Confederation of Tomorrow Survey by Environics. Seven in 10 feel English Canadians consider francophones inferior; half feel anglophones still dominate them economically.

If the recent past is any guide, English Canadians outside Quebec will be following the Alberta referendum campaign much more closely than the Quebec election campaign – even if the country’s future could be shaped far more by what happens east of the Ottawa River in October.

Philippe Couillard, the Liberal premier of Quebec, chose the moment to call for an end to an unofficial moratorium on federal-provincial talks to recognize his province’s distinct character in the country’s supreme law.

In making his bid to relaunch negotiations that had broken down in 1992, after Canadians rejected the Charlottetown accord in a national referendum, Mr. Couillard aimed to ensure Quebeckers no longer felt “ like exiles in their own country .” This, apparently, was asking too much. The rest of Canada, beginning with its then-prime minister, blew him off .

After the failure of Charlottetown, and its 1987 predecessor, the Meech Lake accord, the rest of Canada had given up on attempting to accommodate Quebec’s constitutional demands. The French-speaking province had objected to the adoption of the 1982 Constitution without the inclusion of enhanced protections for its language and culture. While the rest of Canada moved on, Quebeckers never forgot the “ coup d’état de 1982 .”

“The 150 th anniversary of the federation provides an opportunity to resume a meaningful dialogue on the place of the country’s different national elements, ON the role and composition of its institutions, ON the principles that guide intergovernmental relations – in short, ON the evolution of federalism,” declared the Couillard government’s 192-page proposal for renewed talks, entitled “ Quebecers, Our Way of Being Canadian. ”

Mr. Couillard’s outstretched hand was summarily snubbed by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose father Pierre Trudeau had been the architect of the 1982 Constitution and the adoption of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. “You know my views on the Constitution,” the younger Trudeau snapped . “We’re not reopening the Constitution.”

If Mr. Trudeau felt he could be so dismissive of Mr. Couillard’s proposals, it might have been because Quebec’s sovereigntist movement appeared, at the time, to have run out of steam. Support for the Parti Québécois had plummeted as the upstart Coalition Avenir Québec captured nationalist voters by promising to obtain more autonomy for the province within Canada and, importantly, to never hold another divisive referendum.

Now, as Quebeckers prepare to vote in a provincial election on Oct. 5, the PQ is back on top of the polls and potentially poised to form a majority government, based on its large lead among francophone voters. The sovereigntist party’s stunning comeback May be partly attributed to the Caq’s second-term blunders, unrelated to the constitutional file, under former premier François Legault, who stepped down in April . Regardless, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s vow to hold a third referendum – though not, he now says , while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office – has put sovereignty squarely back on the agenda.

The rest of the country is wholly unprepared for where this might lead. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has been laser-focused on countering rising separatist sentiment in Alberta. An Oct. 19 referendum asking Albertans whether they want to remain in Canada or hold a binding plebiscite on secession has stolen the media spotlight.

As a result, more than twice as many Canadians consider the possibility of a referendum on Alberta separation to be a bigger threat to national unity (45 per cent) than a future plebiscite on Quebec secession (17.8 per cent), according to a June Nanos Research poll .
This defies logic, and history.

Quebeckers’ visceral attachment to their unique culture is rooted in their 400-year-old struggle for la survivance . The Quebec sovereignty movement grew out of this quest, not out of circumstantial economic grievances toward Ottawa, as is the case in Alberta.

While current polling shows strong majorities of voters in both Alberta and Quebec would reject separation, one can plausibly imagine a scenario in which a PQ government could sway enough Quebeckers to vote Yes in a future referendum. After all, it almost happened once before, in 1995, when sovereigntists fell less than a percentage point short of victory.

Francophone Quebeckers are intrinsically nationalist. Almost two-thirds of them identify first or only with their home province, rather than Canada, according to the Environics Institute’s most recent Confederation of Tomorrow survey . Many francophones who say they would vote No now could switch sides during a referendum campaign to ensure their province does not face a third defeat that weakens its negotiating hand.

Sovereigntist support could also surge if three controversial laws passed by the CAQ government aimed at affirming Quebec’s distinctness are struck down by the courts. Two of these laws involve Quebec’s unilateral moves to amend the Canadian Constitution to declare French as the province’s only official language and to abolish the oath to King Charles III for members of the National Assembly. The other concerns la laïcité , Quebec’s unique form of secularism, which enjoys broad support in the province even though it interferes with certain Charter rights. Court rulings invalidating or defenestrating these laws could help a PQ government create the winning conditions for a Yes victory.
If another referendum is held, the PQ could well be third time lucky.

The PQ’s return to the fore of Quebec politics under Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has upended the narrative that many analysts had subscribed to after the CAQ first swept to power in 2018. In their telling, Quebeckers opted for the Caq’s “third way” after decades of feeling they had been held hostage to referendum politics by the federalist Quebec Liberal Party and the PQ, which had sought to polarize public opinion around the secession question.

Mr. Legault, an ex-PQ cabinet minister who founded the CAQ in 2011, had solid nationalist credentials. But he insisted he could protect Quebec’s culture and enhance its autonomy by seeking more power from Ottawa without threatening to break up the country. During his first term, which covered the COVID-19 pandemic, he often appeared to walk on water.

At the outset of the 2022 election campaign, support for the PQ was hovering in the single digits . Thanks to a breakthrough campaign performance by Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, the sharp-witted Oxford University-educated lawyer who became PQ Leader in 2020, the sovereigntist party managed to win 14.6 per cent of the vote – but only three seats – in the 2022 election.

It is what Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon – who is known by his initials, Pspp – did next that really caught Quebeckers’ attention and helped relaunch his party. He, along with his two PQ colleagues, refused to swear an oath to King Charles III to sit in the National Assembly.

Nationalist MNAs had long complained about having to declare allegiance to the monarch, a requirement under Section 128 of the Constitution, but had begrudgingly gone along with it. In 1982, then PQ premier René Lévesque added a second oath – proclaiming loyalty to the Quebec people – to ease the sting of having to bow before the British Crown, which remained for many Quebeckers a hated symbol of La Conquête .

“The absurdity of this ritual has gone on long enough,” Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon declared after the 2022 election. An overwhelming majority of voters agreed. A Léger poll found that 76 per cent of all Quebeckers, and 82 per cent of francophones, favoured conserving the oath to the Quebec people; only 15 per cent wanted to keep the oath to the King.

“Quebeckers were proud to see this resistance to the monarchical symbol,” Catherine Mathieu, a constitutional law professor at l’Université du Québec à Montréal, says of Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s act of defiance. “It reinserted the PQ and its aspirations into the political conversation. Pspp and his MNAs were able to capitalize on that attention.”

This left Mr. Legault’s newly re-elected CAQ government scrambling to conserve the nationalist mantle that it had inherited in 2018. It quickly tabled legislation to abolish the oath to the monarchy for MNAs through a unilateral amendment to the Constitution to exempt Quebec from Section 128. The National Assembly unanimously adopted the bill .

Experts were divided over whether Quebec could invoke Section 45 of the Constitution, which allows provincial legislatures to “make laws amending the constitution of the province,” to abolish the oath requirement for its MNAs. But the Trudeau government did not oppose the move, suggesting its own legal opinions supported Quebec’s position.

(As with those of other provinces, Quebec’s constitution – which is considered part of the Canadian Constitution – is not contained in a single written text; rather, it is composed of provincial laws governing such matters as the electoral system and the rules of the National Assembly, the provincial human-rights code and unwritten conventions, in addition to the parts of the federal Constitution that relate to its exclusive areas of jurisdiction.)

The CAQ government had used Section 45 to unilaterally amend the Constitution once before with Bill 96 , its beefed-up version the 1977 Charter of the French Language. The law, tabled in the spring of 2021, inserted two clauses into the Constitution to state that “Quebeckers form a nation” and that French “shall be the only official language of Quebec.”

Here, too, Mr. Trudeau did not object. His muted response sharply contrasted with his reaction, four years earlier, to Mr. Couillard’s request to relaunch constitutional talks. But unlike in 2017, when he commanded a majority government, he was in a much weaker political position in 2021. Picking a fight with Quebec could have threatened his party’s chances of holding onto francophone seats in the province in that year’s federal election.

Indeed, the political salience of the issue was borne out when the Bloc Québécois tabled a House of Commons motion endorsing the constitutional amendments set out in Bill 96. The motion passed overwhelmingly with 281 votes. Only two MPs voted against it; 50 MPs abstained, including 11 Quebec Liberals from mostly anglophone and allophone ridings.

The constitutional amendments contained in Bill 96 and Bill 4, the law abolishing the oath to the monarchy for MNAs, were largely inspired by the academic work of a new generation of nationalist jurists and political scientists who had advocated unilateral action by Quebec to shatter the “constitutional inertia” of the previous decades.

A similar movement in favour of unilateralism emerged in Alberta and Saskatchewan, though one largely aimed at stymieing federal climate policies and asserting provincial control over resource development. In Quebec, unilateral action was instead promoted as a tool to affirm Quebec’s distinct identity in the Constitution without having to engage in inevitably contentious multilateral negotiations with Ottawa and the other provinces.

“We had been told in our constitutional law courses that constitutional reforms were impossible in Canada, that the fruit was not ripe, that it was too complex,” explains Prof. Mathieu, who co-edited a recent collection of essays on the new trend of constitutional unilateralism. “But it is not because it is complex that provinces can content themselves with the status quo. Unilateralism is a response by certain provinces to increase their autonomy without going through elaborate rounds of [federal-provincial] negotiations.”

It remains a matter of fierce legal debate whether the amendments introduced into the Constitution by Bill 96 are merely symbolic or create new protections for Quebec’s language and culture that courts will be required to consider in assessing the constitutionality of provincial legislation. That is because while Section 45 empowers provinces to unilaterally amend their own constitutions, many experts contend that such amendments cannot alter the overarching architecture of the Constitution, including the Charter.
Ultimately, it will be up to the courts to rule on the matter.

The group’s lawsuit also charges that Bill 96 “indirectly and impermissibly bring into effect the concept of ‘distinct society’ which the so-called Meech Lake and Charlottetown Accords failed to achieve” and will hence have “an interpretative impact on the division of powers” between Ottawa and Quebec.
Of course, this is exactly the effect their proponents hope they have.

“I think [Section 45] is an element of the Constitution that can lead courts to grant more autonomy to Quebec, particularly in language matters,” insists Université de Sherbrooke law professor Guillaume Rousseau, a former PQ candidate tapped by Mr. Legault to co-chair a 2024 commission on ways for Quebec to increase its autonomy within Canada.

He concedes bilateral negotiations with Ottawa are still necessary to achieve some of the Caq’s autonomist goals, such as gaining exclusive jurisdiction over immigration and a deciding say in the nomination of judges.

“The Caq’s position is to say that we will use all the means at our disposition to secure more autonomy unilaterally, sometimes bilaterally, but more often unilaterally with Section 45 and the parliamentary sovereignty clause,” Prof. Rousseau says.

stories.title: One of Canada’s largest law libraries is on the move along with the court it serves
stories.summary: The Supreme Court building in Ottawa needs renovations. Step 1 – moving its books across the street – is far from simple
stories.author: Ian Bailey, Photography by Dave Chan
stories.content:
Canada’s highest court is nearing the end of a massive moving effort. Every piece of the operations of the Supreme Court of Canada is being shifted across the street from the building that has been its home for 80 years.

The building that housed the court has faced symptoms of physical decline similar to those that afflicted 24 Sussex Dr. – the official historic residence of the prime minister – and the Centre Block of Parliament Hill. Centre Block and 24 Sussex remain closed for renovations.

Now it’s the turn of the high court.

Its building, completed in 1941, began functioning as a court in 1946. Eight decades later, the court furnishings and records are being moved, piece by piece, to the West Memorial Building, on the other side of Wellington Street. The 1950s-era complex, which covers a city block and once housed Veterans’ Affairs, was vacated in 2008, and has been upgraded to temporarily accommodate the Supreme Court, along with one of Canada’s largest law libraries.

When the justices convene for the court’s fall session in October, they will do so in the West Memorial Building.

But it will be a massively changed version of that building. For the past six years, the government has been rehabilitating the building, making it more accessible, resistant to earthquakes, as well as preserving its heritage features. This week, the Public Services and Procurement Canada department said the cost of the upgrades totalled $671-million, excluding taxes.

As for the renovation of the original Supreme Court building, department spokesperson Michèle LaRose said the effort remains in the planning stage and a detailed timeline and costing are being developed.

“This is a significant undertaking, comparable to other major heritage rehabilitation projects managed by Public Services and Procurement Canada,” Ms. LaRose said in a statement. Previously, the renovation project had been budgeted at more than $1-billion.

In a statement, Chief Justice Richard Wagner acknowledged the court’s move is bittersweet.

“While we will miss our historic building, we recognize that the rehabilitation is necessary to preserve this important piece of Canadian heritage and symbol of our justice system for future generations.” The building will be used for the Supreme Court’s functions once again once the upgrades are completed.

From the old Supreme Court library, visitors can look up through a skylight at the historic roof. Time has taken a toll on many other parts of the building: When The Globe took a tour in 2024, staff set up a diagram of the critical problems. Justin Tang/The Globe and Mail

The move has included the Supreme Court of Canada Library, based for decades in the original building. That’s a lot of books, files and historic records.

Xuan Zhou, the director of the court library, said the exercise has not been easy. “The library move has been one of the most challenging components of the overall relocation,” she said.

The challenges include the size and specialized nature of the collection, the placement of thousands of linear metres of material, and the necessity of maintaining essential research and information services throughout the transition.

Ms. Zhou said that the library team conducted extensive research on best practices for such a move. That included discussions with staff at the Library of Parliament, formerly housed in Centre Block, which is in the midst of a renovation process expected to run into the early 2030s.

“The Supreme Court of Canada Library has one of Canada’s most specialized and authoritative legal collections, reflecting the research needs of Canada’s highest court,” Ms. Zhou said in a statement.

It has 300,000 physical volumes, 3,000 rare books and 50,000 perpetual-use electronic resources. And there are also audiovisual materials.

Artists’ renderings of the West Memorial Building’s grand hall, gallery and Supreme Court chamber give some idea of its finished form. The complex was left vacant in 2008, and reviving it has taken years of effort and hundreds of millions of dollars. Regenerate 344 Joint Venture: Moriyama Teshima Architects and Kasian Architecture Interior Design and Planning

The West Memorial rehabilitation project is a joint venture between Moriyama Teshima Architects and Kasian Architecture Interior Design and Planning. Sketches of the new court space within the building have been published online, but access for the media has been limited so far.

However, The Globe and Mail was invited to visit the interior of the temporary new home. The route to the library complex passes through a spectacular new Grand Hall, an atrium in the core of the building that echoes the grand entrance hall space in the classic building. However, the new space, engineered as a greeting area and event space, is more striking. It’s five storeys high, with office windows looking out over the space.

To get to the library, there’s the option of taking a glass-enclosed spiral staircase down into the space. Visitors can also take an elevator.

The new space, awaiting the arrival of members of the legal community seeking its resources, is smaller than the library’s space in the original building - 1,400 square metres compared to 2,029 square metres. It is slick, and spacious, with a breezy feel. It has the ambiance of a new public library in a prosperous Canadian community. There are 19th-century law books spanning the history of Canadian law on spotless shelves filling the space.

A spokesperson for the team that designed the new library space says that it was central to the overall project.

“It was strategically located near the Grand Hall in order to preserve the access for the legal community, creating a meaningful connection through the new circular feature stair/elevator, allowing the flow of natural light,” Emmanuelle van Rutten, an Ottawa-based partner in Moriyama Teshima Architects, said in a statement.

Additions to the new space include a dedicated rare-book room, printing room and meeting room as well as a microform room. “Microform” refers to microfilm and microfiche records, of which the library has more than 180,000.

Ms. Zhou noted that litigants appearing before the court can access the library on the day of their hearing. Also the library makes material available through inter-library loans.

The court was established in 1875, with a small collection that grew over time, necessitating the appointment of a librarian in 1892. The Supreme Court Library was eventually designed by Ernest Cormier in the 1952 court complex.

But Ms. Zhou says the library was physically declining, consistent with problems in the overall building, battling water leaks, temperature and humidity-control issues, and problems with the compact-shelving system.

“These issues presented particular challenges for a library responsible for safeguarding a large and valuable collection,” says Ms. Zhou. At times, items had to be moved to areas with better conditions to protect them.

The library move, planned for the last five years, was completed in early August after five weeks of work, said Ms. Zhou.

Ms. Zhou said Chief Justice Wagner has encouraged the library staff to think about how the library can continue supporting the court’s work in a changing and evolving legal and technological environment.

“As the Library settles into the West Memorial Building, we will work with Court staff to explore new approaches to library services,” she said.

Grégoire Webber, a law and philosophy professor at Queen’s University who once served as a law clerk to former Supreme Court justice Ian Binnie, said the court’s iconic art deco building has been an Ottawa landmark, and standing representation of our system of government’s commitment to the rule of law.

“It is to Churchill that we owe the thought that although we shape our buildings, in turn our buildings shape us. The Court’s justices will be shaped by their time in their new home,” he wrote.

“I hope that the court continues to be – and to be perceived by the wider public – as open to all and accessible.”

Heritage conservation is a hot topic in Canada as cities, racing to build new homes, reassess what older buildings are worth. Two years ago, City Space took a deeper look at one famous case – Montreal’s Van Horne mansion – and how its demolition in 1973 still shapes our debates about preserving the past.

“It was strategically located near the Grand Hall in order to preserve the access for the legal community, creating a meaningful connection through the new circular feature stair/elevator, allowing the flow of natural light,” Emmanuelle van Rutten, an Ottawa-based partner in Moriyama Teshima Architects, said in a statement.

Additions to the new space include a dedicated rare-book room, printing room and meeting room as well as a microform room. “Microform” refers to microfilm and microfiche records, of which the library has more than 180,000.
Ms. Zhou noted that litigants appearing before the court can access the library on the day of their hearing. Also the library makes material available through inter-library loans.

The court was established in 1875, with a small collection that grew over time, necessitating the appointment of a librarian in 1892. The Supreme Court Library was eventually designed by Ernest Cormier in the 1952 court complex.

But Ms. Zhou says the library was physically declining, consistent with problems in the overall building, battling water leaks, temperature and humidity-control issues, and problems with the compact-shelving system.

“These issues presented particular challenges for a library responsible for safeguarding a large and valuable collection,” says Ms. Zhou. At times, items had to be moved to areas with better conditions to protect them.
The library move, planned for the last five years, was completed in early August after five weeks of work, said Ms. Zhou.

Ms. Zhou said Chief Justice Wagner has encouraged the library staff to think about how the library can continue supporting the court’s work in a changing and evolving legal and technological environment.
“As the Library settles into the West Memorial Building, we will work with Court staff to explore new approaches to library services,” she said.

Grégoire Webber, a law and philosophy professor at Queen’s University who once served as a law clerk to former Supreme Court justice Ian Binnie, said the court’s iconic art deco building has been an Ottawa landmark, and standing representation of our system of government’s commitment to the rule of law.
“It is to Churchill that we owe the thought that although we shape our buildings, in turn our buildings shape us. The Court’s justices will be shaped by their time in their new home,” he wrote.
“I hope that the court continues to be – and to be perceived by the wider public – as open to all and accessible.”

Heritage conservation is a hot topic in Canada as cities, racing to build new homes, reassess what older buildings are worth. Two years ago, City Space took a deeper look at one famous case – Montreal’s Van Horne mansion – and how its demolition in 1973 still shapes our debates about preserving the past.

stories.title: Why this expert on severe weather risk is leaving the U.S. for Western University

paragraphs: Q&A CBC News | Posted: August 29, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 29
Steve Guikema leaving Michigan amid federal push to attract global scientific talent
America's brain drain is London's brain gain.
Western University is among the Canadian universities benefitting from the federal government's $541 million effort to attract top research talent, including from the United States.
On Thursday, the government announced it had brought in 64 professors to lead scientific research at universities across Canada, 48 of whom are from south of the border.
Seth Guikema is one of them. He's leaving the University of Michigan to join Western University as the first Eddie Goldenberg Research Chair of Canada in Climate Risk and Resilience Analytics.

The civil and environmental engineer is receiving $8 million from Ottawa, with his research focusing on using data, AI and risk analysis to help communities prepare for severe storms, wildfires and other natural hazards, university officials said.
Guikema spoke with interim Afternoon Drive host Nav Nanwa a short time after Thursday's announcement.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Nav Nanwa:What made you decide to leave the U.S. and come to Canada and Western University at this particular point of your career?

Well, when looking at where things are going in my future career, I think Western offers an incredibly strong environment for doing this sort of research. It's already a world leader in natural hazards risk analysis and wind engineering, and I think the opportunity to come there and be part of this super strong team and move to Canada was very attractive.
NV: How significant is it for Canada to make this kind of investment in attracting researchers such as yourself?

It is an incredibly large and powerful investment, and also a statement of the level of support that research has in Canada and the willingness to invest in that research, and in turn to invest in furthering the Canadian economy.
LISTEN | Seth Guikema on why he's continuing his research in Canada:
NV: You specialize in looking at the impacts of severe weather rather than simply predicting the weather itself. What does that distinction mean?

I look more at, when that weather happens, what will happen at the household scale? Loss of power, loss of access to essential services like food, childcare, education—the things households need to go about the patterns of daily life, and when disrupted, to be able to recover quickly from those disruptions.

NV:We've seen increasingly destructive storms over the last recent years ... How much more difficult is it to assess future risk when climate change means the historical data we're relying on May no longer tell us what to expect?

It becomes a very interdisciplinary and challenging problem, and this is why we tackle it with teams. I've done quite a bit of work in the U.S. looking at hurricanes and how they'll change in a changing climate. We team up with climate scientists, with meteorologists, to look at those changes and project the impacts. I look forward to continuing to do this with a variety of different sorts of hazards in Canada.
NV:Where do you see AI making the biggest difference when it comes to helping governments, utilities, and communities prepare for severe weather?

I see AI as a tool that can help us provide good information faster. I don't see AI as a tool that we are going to let autonomously make these decisions. I view it as a way that we can process these very large, complex data sets faster and get better predictions of what these impacts are going to be.
NV:If we know these risks are increasing, what do you think governments and communities should be doing differently right now to best prepare for this?

Some of what we've looked at is, can we get down to a fairly fine scale? Like the household scale—which neighborhoods, which households are most at risk of losing access to different services—so that we can design policy responses to try to help those communities be better positioned before the event, so we're not scrambling to help them recover after.

Like the household scale—which neighborhoods, which households are most at risk of losing access to different services—so that we can design policy responses to try to help those communities be better positioned before the event, so we're not scrambling to help them recover after.

stories.title: Donald Trump has imposed himself as the X factor in Quebec’s election
stories.summary: The question from Gaspé to Gatineau is which party leader will be the U.S. President’s most effective foil
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee
paragraphs: He’s not on the ballot. He’s certainly not Québécois, although he does proclaim to “love French Canadians.” But Donald Trump is currently the most influential politician in Quebec.

As the province embarks on a high-stakes election campaign, with a separatist party leading in the polls, emergency rooms overflowing and infrastructure crumbling, the U.S. President has imposed himself as the X factor.

With his escalating trade war against Canada, ratcheted up days before Quebec’s writ drop on Thursday, the question from Gaspé to Gatineau is which prospective premier will be Mr. Trump’s most effective foil.

It was not supposed to be this way. Until the Trump administration threatened to impose 50-per-cent tariffs on $28-billion worth of Canadian goods, then apparently scuppered the talks with last-minute demands, this was a provincial campaign about change, or holding a third independence referendum, depending on who you asked.

The Coalition Avenir Québec, unpopular after eight years in power, was struggling for viability under new leader Christine Fréchette. The Parti Québécois was riding high in the polls by hammering her government’s scandal-plagued record, but was vulnerable over its insistence on holding a separation vote in its first mandate.
It was, in other words, a fairly conventional Quebec pre-election season. But nothing about Canadian politics is conventional in the second Trump presidency.

Ms. Fréchette, like Mark Carney in 2025, so far looks to be the winner from the Trump effect. As Premier, she has had the good fortune of standing next to Mr. Carney at the unveiling of several major industrial and infrastructure announcements in recent months. That includes the federally facilitated hydro deal between Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, and a massive icebreaker contract for the Lévis, Que.-based Davie shipyard unveiled this week.

Both projects were pitched by the Premier and her federal counterpart – still the most popular politician in Quebec after riding the province’s support to an election victory last year – as insurance against Mr. Trump’s hostile trade policies.
On Monday in Lévis, across the St. Lawrence from Quebec City, Ms. Fréchette was clearly relishing her role as Carney ally and Trump opponent.
“I’m getting more and more used to our Monday meetings,” she beamed at the Prime Minister.

Sure enough, a Synopsis poll on Friday showed the CAQ virtually tied with the PQ, a seven-point jump for Ms. Fréchette’s troops since the imposition of U.S. tariffs. It is little wonder she began the campaign by describing Mr. Trump as her “real opponent.” The incumbency advantage and a perception of Ms. Fréchette as steady and economically minded make her likeliest to reap the rewards of American aggression.

In turn, her rivals have accused the outgoing Premier of “instrumentalizing” the crisis to her political advantage, in the words of Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, and using it to “save her skin,” as Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard put it.
PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who seems to have the most to lose from the Trumpian turn of events, pleaded with Quebeckers not to let U.S. tariffs “confiscate” their election.

It may be too late. Already some observers are drawing parallels to the 2025 federal election, when a moribund governing party was saved by a fresh-faced leader and the anxiety produced by economic warfare.

The PQ stands to play the role of the federal Conservatives, led by Pierre Poilievre. He lost an imposing lead by “resisting the pivot at all costs,” said Dimitri Soudas, who was prime minister Stephen Harper’s spokesperson and chief Quebec aide.
“The ballot question was very different seven days ago,” Mr. Soudas added. “The ballot question has become who can protect Quebeckers against Donald Trump.”

The U.S. President will continue to loom unpredictably over the campaign. At any point, a reporter in the Oval Office could ask him if he supports the separatist party running in Quebec, noted the former PQ leader Jean-François Lisée.
“If he says yes, that will be a tough week for St-Pierre Plamondon.”

The wild card influence of Mr. Trump could cut many ways. His administration has already complicated matters by publicly denying Canadian claims that French-language labelling rules were a sticking point in trade negotiations – which Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has used to suggest the Premier and Prime Minister misled the public.
“That’s a bit of a problem for the Fréchette-Carney team,” Mr. Lisée said.

Ironically, the trade war could also help the PQ by pushing its promise to hold a referendum further onto the back burner. The party’s polling lead has obscured the fact that support for separation in Quebec is historically low. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has tried to square his commitment to a referendum with the current mood by promising to push such a vote until after Mr. Trump leaves office. The recent escalation will allow the PQ leader to talk even less about independence.

The staying power of the Trump factor is another unknown. This is not the first time the President has slapped Canada with tariffs, so the shock may wear off faster now, pollster Jean-Marc Léger said.
“The question is whether Quebeckers are immunized against this.”

It will also be harder for Ms. Fréchette to convince voters that she can protect them as a mere provincial leader. Mr. Carney won his election by credibly claiming he could take a tough line against the U.S. in negotiations. The Premier of Quebec can’t say the same.
“Madame Fréchette is not the decider,” Mr. Léger said. “Quebec is still a province; it’s not at the negotiating table.”

At the moment, at least, Quebeckers seem unconcerned with such nuance. The Trump trade war is front of mind, and Ms. Fréchette seems poised to benefit. Confronted with the CAQ’s apparent leap in support on Friday, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters he would like to wait for other polls before believing in such a sudden turnaround.
On the other hand, he wouldn’t be the first Canadian politician to underestimate the Trump effect.

stories.title: Strong support for Canada axing U.S. trade talks, retaliatory tariffs: poll
stories.summary: The Ipsos poll for Global News suggests the Liberal government still enjoys broad backing from Canadians, but that support dips among younger voters.
stories.author: Sean Boynton
stories.content:
Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs , a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and Millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

“These people are living in what we like to call ‘the endurance economy’: they’re just getting by from day to day, and they’re enduring economic life right now,” said Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada.

“I think one of the takeaways here is that while Canadians are generally supportive of the idea of pushing back hard on the United States … if any of those things could bring a personal risk, if you’re somebody who’s living in that endurance economy, you’re less likely to support it.”

The poll found 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of Millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of Millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of elderly boomers supported both of those positions.

Bricker said the disparity points to economic realities for those different age groups.

“The people who were the ‘elbows up’ crowd in the last election campaign, who voted for the Liberals and continue to vote for the Liberals, they’re older, they’re more economically established, they tend to have higher degrees of education, they tend be more affluent,” Bricker said.

“So as a result of that, there’s less risk for them. So they can be all ‘elbows up,’ but it doesn’t cost them as much as it’s going to cost the other people they’re asking to have their elbows up.”

The age gap also extends to who Canadians said they would vote for if an election were to be held tomorrow.

While the Liberals maintain a healthy lead of 44 per cent support overall among those surveyed, compared to 33 per cent for the Conservatives, 40 per cent of Millennials chose the Conservatives over the Liberals, who see just 30 per cent support in that age group.

The Liberals’ support is down by just one point since April, while the Conservatives saw no change. The NDP at 10 per cent and the Bloc Quebecois at eight per cent nationally are each up one point since April.

“I have not in my consciousness recalled as tumultuous a week, or couple of weeks, or couple of months, in Canadian politics since probably 1995, when we went through the sovereignty referendum,” Bricker said.

“You would expect that you would see a lot of change in terms of political support, and we’re seeing virtually none (since the federal election). … I would say a lot of what’s going on right now is basically baked in, in terms of how it relates to federal politics.

Bricker added Canadians are likely not anticipating another election anytime soon, meaning they’re not thinking hard about their vote intentions right now.

Asked if they felt Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and his party would have done a better job handling the trade issues with the U.S. than Carney, 37 per cent overall said yes, with 67 per cent of Conservative voters agreeing.

A sizeable 62 per cent of respondents said they would like to see Parliament recalled before it’s due to reconvene in late September in order to debate and vote on Canada’s response to the U.S., which Bricker said could pose a vulnerability to an otherwise politically strong Carney.

“Canadians know their institutions actually matter to them,” he said. “Not recalling Parliament and not having a conversation through our political institutions is something that does represent a little bit of a vulnerability … (but) I would say, at this stage of the day, a mere crack.”

The poll also found strong support for a slew of other retaliatory measures that Canada could take against U.S. trade actions, from imposing tariffs on critical minerals and energy (both 73 per cent) to limiting those exports south of the border (71 per cent for critical minerals and 69 per cent for crude oil, natural gas and electricity).

Two-thirds said they would like to see an “aggressive” tax on U.S. tech giants operating in Canada, while 64 per cent were supportive of logistically slowing down U.S. imports by tightening border inspections on incoming goods.

The least popular option presented — letting the Canadian dollar weaken naturally to make Canadian exports more globally competitive — saw 45 per cent support.

On “Buy Canadian,” 80 per cent said they supported government purchasing and infrastructure projected prioritizing Canadian materials and contracts, with 60 per cent saying they will make an effort to prioritize Canadian products, services and companies themselves.

Between two-thirds and 80 per cent of respondents were supportive of other possible government support measures in the trade war, such as helping businesses expand to markets outside the U.S., providing job training and retraining programs for affected workers, and offering loans, emergency aid, extended Employment Insurance, or financial incentives to businesses.

Sixty-seven per cent of Canadians said they would like to see a major COVID-era subsidy program put in place to support Canadian workers affected by tariffs by both countries in the trade war, up eight points since last July.

And while 52 per cent overall said they are personally willing to undergo some “significant” economic pain to help Canada weather the storm, that number once again was lower among Generation Z (41 per cent) and higher among boomers (67 per cent).

“I thought the numbers would be stronger,” Bricker said.

“As you start going down the list and people start considering things that might be a little bit more onerous, or things that they’re really not that certain what it means, you start to see things get a little bit more wobbly. On the side of support right now, but definitely not as baked in and strong.”

These are some of the findings of an Ipsos poll conducted between August 26 and 27, 2026, ON behalf of Global News. For this survey, a sample of 1,001 Canadians aged 18+ was interviewed online. Quotas and weighting were employed to ensure that the sample’s composition reflects that of the Canadian population according to census parameters. The precision of Ipsos online polls is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the poll is accurate to within ± 3.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all Canadians aged 18+ been polled. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. paragraphs: Strong majorities of Canadians support the federal government walking away from U.S. trade talks and hitting back with retaliatory tariffs , a new poll suggests, which is translating to persistent support for Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Liberals.

However, the Ipsos polling conducted exclusively for Global News and released Saturday also shows that support varies by age, with fewer Generation Z and Millennial adults backing the Liberals and their approach to the growing U.S. trade war.

“These people are living in what we like to call ‘the endurance economy’: they’re just getting by from day to day, and they’re enduring economic life right now,” said Darrell Bricker, chairman of Ipsos Canada.

“I think one of the takeaways here is that while Canadians are generally supportive of the idea of pushing back hard on the United States … if any of those things could bring a personal risk, if you’re somebody who’s living in that endurance economy, you’re less likely to support it.”

The poll found 63 per cent of Canadians surveyed feel Canada was right to stand firm in the trade negotiations, “even if it meant higher costs and job losses,” while just 18 per cent said Canada should have made additional sacrifices to get a deal.

An even larger majority, 73 per cent, said they back Ottawa’s “dollar for dollar” counter-tariffs on $28 billion worth of U.S. goods, matching the up to 50 per cent tariffs imposed by U.S. President Donald Trump last week after trade talks collapsed.

But those numbers fall to 48 per cent of Gen Z adults and 57 per cent of Millennials who support Canada standing firm, and 59 per cent of Millennials who were happy to see Canada’s retaliatory tariffs. By comparison, about 80 per cent of elderly boomers supported both of those positions.
Bricker said the disparity points to economic realities for those different age groups.

“The people who were the ‘elbows up’ crowd in the last election campaign, who voted for the Liberals and continue to vote for the Liberals, they’re older, they’re more economically established, they tend to have higher degrees of education, they tend be more affluent,” Bricker said.
“So as a result of that, there’s less risk for them. So they can be all ‘elbows up,’ but it doesn’t cost them as much as it’s going to cost the other people they’re asking to have their elbows up.”
The age gap also extends to who Canadians said they would vote for if an election were to be held tomorrow.

While the Liberals maintain a healthy lead of 44 per cent support overall among those surveyed, compared to 33 per cent for the Conservatives, 40 per cent of Millennials chose the Conservatives over the Liberals, who see just 30 per cent support in that age group.

The Liberals’ support is down by just one point since April, while the Conservatives saw no change. The NDP at 10 per cent and the Bloc Quebecois at eight per cent nationally are each up one point since April.

“I have not in my consciousness recalled as tumultuous a week, or couple of weeks, or couple of months, in Canadian politics since probably 1995, when we went through the sovereignty referendum,” Bricker said.

“You would expect that you would see a lot of change in terms of political support, and we’re seeing virtually none (since the federal election). … I would say a lot of what’s going on right now is basically baked in, in terms of how it relates to federal politics.
Bricker added Canadians are likely not anticipating another election anytime soon, meaning they’re not thinking hard about their vote intentions right now.

Asked if they felt Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and his party would have done a better job handling the trade issues with the U.S. than Carney, 37 per cent overall said yes, with 67 per cent of Conservative voters agreeing.

A sizeable 62 per cent of respondents said they would like to see Parliament recalled before it’s due to reconvene in late September in order to debate and vote on Canada’s response to the U.S., which Bricker said could pose a vulnerability to an otherwise politically strong Carney.

“Canadians know their institutions actually matter to them,” he said. “Not recalling Parliament and not having a conversation through our political institutions is something that does represent a little bit of a vulnerability … (but) I would say, at this stage of the day, a mere crack.”

The poll also found strong support for a slew of other retaliatory measures that Canada could take against U.S. trade actions, from imposing tariffs on critical minerals and energy (both 73 per cent) to limiting those exports south of the border (71 per cent for critical minerals and 69 per cent for crude oil, natural gas and electricity).

Two-thirds said they would like to see an “aggressive” tax on U.S. tech giants operating in Canada, while 64 per cent were supportive of logistically slowing down U.S. imports by tightening border inspections on incoming goods.
The least popular option presented — letting the Canadian dollar weaken naturally to make Canadian exports more globally competitive — saw 45 per cent support.

On “Buy Canadian,” 80 per cent said they supported government purchasing and infrastructure projected prioritizing Canadian materials and contracts, with 60 per cent saying they will make an effort to prioritize Canadian products, services and companies themselves.

Between two-thirds and 80 per cent of respondents were supportive of other possible government support measures in the trade war, such as helping businesses expand to markets outside the U.S., providing job training and retraining programs for affected workers, and offering loans, emergency aid, extended Employment Insurance, or financial incentives to businesses.

Sixty-seven per cent of Canadians said they would like to see a major COVID-era subsidy program put in place to support Canadian workers affected by tariffs by both countries in the trade war, up eight points since last July.

And while 52 per cent overall said they are personally willing to undergo some “significant” economic pain to help Canada weather the storm, that number once again was lower among Generation Z (41 per cent) and higher among boomers (67 per cent).
“I thought the numbers would be stronger,” Bricker said.

“As you start going down the list and people start considering things that might be a little bit more onerous, or things that they’re really not that certain what it means, you start to see things get a little bit more wobbly. On the side of support right now, but definitely not as baked in and strong.”

These are some of the findings of an Ipsos poll conducted between August 26 and 27, 2026, ON behalf of Global News. For this survey, a sample of 1,001 Canadians aged 18+ was interviewed online. Quotas and weighting were employed to ensure that the sample’s composition reflects that of the Canadian population according to census parameters. The precision of Ipsos online polls is measured using a credibility interval. In this case, the poll is accurate to within ± 3.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all Canadians aged 18+ been polled. The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls May be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to coverage error, and measurement error.

stories.title: Fire wrecks B.C.'s historic Little Red House, beloved by painters and photographers
stories.summary: A historic home popularly known as the Little Red House has been destroyed by fire after standing in the Township of Langley for almost 140 years.
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A heritage house, shown in this Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026 handout photo, that stood for more than 130 years in Township of Langley, B.C., has burned down. THE Canadian Press/Handout — Ken Baber (Mandatory Credit)

A historic home popularly known as the Little Red House has been destroyed by fire after standing in the Township of Langley for almost 140 years.

The township’s archives say the home properly known as Mclver House burned down early on Thursday.

It says the home was built by Murdoch and Annie McIver between 1887 and 1890.

While the Langley Heritage Society says in a social media post that the house in the Glen Valley area had fallen into disrepair, its location in the middle of a turf farm helped make it “one of the most photographed and painted” homes in the area.

It says the Gothic-style farmhouse, which also served as a backdrop for photo shoots and videos, “evoked memories of simpler times.”

Rob Rindt, a Township of Langley councillor, shared videos of the house being engulfed in flames, saying its destruction was “incredibly sad.”

“So many people photographed, painted and stopped to admire this house over the years, and now these images capture its final moments,” he said.

A description of the house in the Township of Langley’s archives, held by its heritage facility known as salishan Place by the River, says the house was built by the McIvers to replace an earlier log cabin, “which was most likely too small to accommodate the McIvers’ growing clan of nine children.”

It says the house was still occupied until the early 1990s “but by 2010 it had been surrounded by a turf farm and was uninhabited and falling into disrepair.”

The heritage society said in an online post Friday that it was “sad and unfortunate” the home was never preserved.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 29, 2026.
