stories.title: Luxury London mansion listed for record-setting $5.5 million
stories.summary: A London home that sold for a record price of $5.3 million is up for sale again with an asking price of $5.5 million.
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
A London home that sold for a local record price of $5.3 million four years ago is back on the market with an asking price of $5.5 million.

The property at 2-756 Riverside Dr., west of Wonderland Road in London’s Oakridge neighbourhood, previously sold at a record price for a publicly listed property in London in 2022.

Shahin Tabeshfard, the Century 21 broker of record for the sale, says the luxury housing market, which he describes as homes over $3 million, is stronger than it has ever been in the London area.

“People are getting more comfortable with this price point,” he said. “If you rewind about 10 years ago, it was very rare to see homes over $3 or $4 million switching hands.”

Tabeshfard said that the previous sale of the Riverside home still holds the record for a publicly listed sale in the city, meaning it would break its own record if sold for its asking price.

The London housing market previously experienced its worst start in five years from January to April, with March being the only month where home sales were higher than one year prior. The market did bounce back in May and June, with a slight increase in home sales compared to the same months in 2025, before dropping again in July.

Tabeshfard says that, for the luxury market, most are sold off the market, with sellers typically valuing confidentiality more than most people. So far this year, the luxury market is stable, with him even selling a $4-million home off the market just two weeks ago.

“The high-end home market in London is more active than the data might show, and this sale would be on par with market value,” he said.

Sitting on more than half an acre next to the Thames River, the Riverside Drive home was custom-built in 2014 and designed by Bradley Skinner of Skinner and Skinner Architects Inc. The home offers 7,664 square feet of total living space, including a heated exterior driveway and soundproof theatre room, among other features.

Tabeshfard says there’s been some aesthetic updating and maintenance since it changed hands back in 2022, but overall, the property has the same components. He confirmed that, since it was built, this will be just the second time it has changed hands.

Back in 2022, the property was originally listed at $5.5 million. Tabeshfard says the asking price is the same this time around, because he hasn’t seen a significant increase in the market but believes the house has not lost any value.

“We’re priced accurately for where the market sees it. Ultimately, the market will dictate the value. $5.5 million, we felt, is a good starting point to market the property for sale,” he said.

The house, Tabeshfard says, is a one-of-a-kind property in the London area, especially being built with concrete, steel and a glass curtain wall.

Tabeshfard says the current owner of the property has been building their dream home over the last few years and is near completion, which is why the home is changing hands again after just four years.

In 2022, the house sold after just three days on the market, but Tabeshfard does expect it to take a little longer this time around.

“(Friday) will be the third day on the market, and we’re not expecting it to sell by then,” he said. “Properties of this value, they don’t typically fly off the shelves. Last time we were lucky, where the buyer was ready to go right away.”

rgoodison@postmedia.com

stories.title: Watch: Pickup truck towing camper rolls over on Highway 401
stories.summary: Dramatic video submitted to CTV News shows the single-vehicle collision happened in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people suffered minor injuries after a pickup truck towing a camper trailer rolled over on Ontario’s Highway 401 on Wednesday afternoon.

Dramatic video submitted to CTV News shows the single-vehicle collision happened in the eastbound lanes of Highway 401, just east of Kent Bridge Road in Chatham-Kent, at about 12:30 p.m.

Police said the pickup truck, which was hauling a camper trailer, lost control and entered the highway median before rolling over.

The driver and passenger were taken from the scene with minor injuries.

One eastbound lane of Highway 401 was closed for a short time while emergency crews worked at the scene.

Police thanked motorists who stopped to assist following the collision.

stories.title: Hot Stuff: It's hard turning an airport runway into a concert venue. But it's worth it
stories.summary: London International Airport as a concert venue? For the second straight year, yes. Part 13 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
London International Airport as a concert venue? For the second straight year, yes. Part 13 of our series on people and things that make summer sizzle here

Got a suggestion for a Hot Stuff story about a person or thing that makes summer special in Southwestern Ontario? Email us at curiouslondon@postmedia.com or read our entire series so far right here .

A year ago, Rock the Runway turned the London International Airport into something it had never been before – an outdoor concert venue.

More than 25,000 people showed up on opening night of the inaugural two-day festival, the biggest concert in the city’s history.

But how did a commercial airport become the place to bring this massive concert to life?

Scott McFadzean, London International Airport’s chief executive officer, says the idea for a concert was born nearly two years ago. McFadzean says the airport is always looking into giving the community other reasons to come out, like Airshow London, beyond just getting on a commercial flight.

The idea for a music festival came about as a fix to a problem: London not having a large enough venue space to attract some major bands, though Rock the Park in Harris Park and Canada Life Place do attract some big-name performers.

“I kind of looked at the vast amount of open space we have here at the airport, and thought there could be potential to really take London’s music scene to the next level,” McFadzean said.

McFadzean soon reached out to Brad Jones, president of Jones Entertainment Group, and invited him to take a look at the grounds. He says the Jones family’s history with hosting Rock the Park seemed like a natural fit and the first place to start.

Jones says that when he first saw the airport grounds, he immediately could picture what the London airport was pitching to him. “We literally walked out on that runway, and I just sort of saw the vision,” Jones said.

But to make it come together, they needed the right act.

Jones says he gets calls every year from musicians’ agents asking if there are things he’s working on that are bigger in scale to host them. It just so happened that Noah Kahan’s agent mentioned he was playing in Louisville, Kentucky, in early September 2025 and wasn’t going to be making a trip to Toronto.

“When Noah Kahan was brought to us, one of the biggest stars in the world, we thought the runway was the right place,” Jones said.

But to host a concert on airport grounds is easier said than done.

McFadzean says the most important thing leading up to the concert was prioritizing aviation safety, because the airport would continue to operate on other runways while the concert was held.

He says the airport had to work closely with Transport Canada and NAV Canada throughout the process, not only to get the proper approvals, but to ensure they could keep surfaces for the airport active.

“We worked very closely with all the authorities and regulators, including both federal and municipal,” McFadzean said. “It was a great collaboration between everyone, including London police, EMS and fire. A great way to bring us together and prepare for various scenarios that can result from large crowds being in one location.”

The first edition of Rock the Runway drew 25,000 people for the first night to see Noah Kahan – which Jones says is the largest concert in Southwestern Ontario ever. About 10,000 showed up the second night to see American DJ Marshmello.

McFadzean believes that Rock the Runway is likely the first-ever concert to be held on active commercial airport grounds in the country.

Jones credits the timing of the festival with much of the success. He says hosting it in mid-September prevented them from competing with themselves and Rock the Park, and it has the advantage of London’s post-secondary students returning.

“You’ve got 40,000 or so students that attended Fanshawe and Western, and not a lot of them are in London in July,” he said. “You’ve got a whole new audience that’s coming back to London. So to capture that, that’s a big part of why we picked mid-September.”

The first year wasn’t without its lessons, however, with traffic and parking problems occurring throughout the festival and the need to bring in their own power to run the concert, Jones says.

The organization is capping attendance at 15,000 people for this year’s concert set for Sept. 17 and 18, a 40 per cent drop from last year’s record crowd. Limp Bizkit is the main headliner on a bill that also features Cypress Hill.

“We just want to get it perfect this year, so we’ve scaled it back,” Jones said. “Once we get everything perfect, then we will look at scaling it back up for future years.”

Jones says he doesn’t want to make any commitments that the festival will be around as long as Rock the Park, which has lasted more than two decades, but he does see it going for a number of years at this point.

“We certainly have an interest to continue to make the experience better every year,” he said.

stories.title: Body of missing swimmer recovered at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: The search remained underway Thursday, with two OPP vessels, the OPP Underwater Search and Recovery Unit and OPP Aviation Services.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say the body of a swimmer reported missing in Lake Huron at Pinery Provincial Park has been recovered.

Lambton County OPP said officers were called to the park shortly after 1 p.m. on Aug. 26 after receiving a report that a 28-year-old person from Scarborough had gone missing in the water.

Police said beachgoers located the swimmer’s body on Aug. 27.

OPP thanked several agencies and organizations that assisted in the search, including the Joint Rescue Coordination Centre, the Anishinabek Police Service, the Walpole Island Police Service and staff at Pinery Provincial Park.

No further details were released.
paragraphs: Ontario Provincial Police say the body of a swimmer reported missing in Lake Huron at Pinery Provincial Park has been recovered.

stories.title: Champagne touts deepening economic ties in visit with Indian counterpart
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said he’s looking at ways to streamline payments between Canada and India as part of a broader effort to deepen ties with the world’s fast-growing major economy.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said he’s looking at ways to streamline payments between Canada and India as part of a broader effort to deepen ties with the world’s fast-growing major economy.

Champagne hosted Nirmala Sitharaman, India’s minister of finance and corporate affairs, in Toronto on Thursday where the two announced a new economic and financial dialogue between the nations. The pair also sat for a fireside chat at the Canadian Club Toronto in the afternoon.

Champagne told reporters the economies of the two countries are “uniquely complementary” and positioned Canada as a reliable supplier of food and energy for India.

“Canada can provide energy security and food security to India. And India can provide to Canada scale, talent, and technology,” he said.

Financial services was one of the primary areas where Champagne spoke about deepening co-operation with India.

He said Canada wants to facilitate easier payments between the two nations. That would help the families of the thousands of Indian students studying in Canada to save on fees and exchange costs when sending money internationally, he said.

Champagne also suggested Canada could be critical in supporting India’s high-tech ambitions, such as a rapid build-out of data centres for artificial intelligence.

“Critical minerals, energy, are going to be essential to the growth of India. And that’s what I think Canada can offer,” he said.

Canada has broadly been trying to position itself as a trusted supplier of key commodities as war and shifting trade flows upend the previous global order.

Asked whether Canada was ramping up its efforts to build out trade with India given the re-escalating trade war with the United States, Champagne said it was always Ottawa’s “plan A” to diversify Canadian trade.

Sitharaman said bilateral relations between countries are increasingly important in a period of geopolitical instability.

She credited prime ministers Mark Carney and Narendra Modi with bringing “fresh momentum” to the partnership.

“The economic and financial dialogue reflects this broad ambition to move beyond traditional trade and goods and services and build a deeper economic partnership, encompassing investment, finance, capital markets, and regulatory co-operation,” Sitharaman said.

Champagne joined Carney on a trip to India in late February — the first official visit by a Canadian prime minster since Justin Trudeau’s visit in 2018.

Modi is expected to visit Canada in the coming months.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu said on Wednesday that he intends to lock down a trade agreement between Canada and India before the end of the year.

Canada and India are looking to more than double two-way trade between the nations to $70 billion by 2030.

Canadian investment in India was more than $110 billion in 2024. Champagne pointed out Thursday that Canadian pension plans are major investors in India’s infrastructure agenda.

Canada and India have worked to improve relations over the last year, after that relationship frayed over Canadian allegations that Indian government agents were involved in violence targeting Canadian citizens.

The allegations included involvement in the murder of a pro-Khalistan activist in British Columbia in 2023.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 27, 2026.

— written by Craig Lord in Ottawa

stories.title: It's Groundhog Day at London hospitals as rodents burrow, chew wires underground
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
Groundhogs drawn to good soil, plants and safety from predators, experts say
Amid an ongoing fraud investigation and costly infrastructure problems, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) has a new – and much furrier – challenge on its hands: groundhogs.

In a memo sent to staff, which was reviewed by CBC News, the centre’s Support Services department said groundhogs have begun burrowing at multiple LHSC locations, such as Victoria Hospital, Children’s Hospital and University Hospital.
“Groundhogs have high potential to injure themselves and damage critical infrastructure at LHSC by burrowing through or chewing on systems like electrical networks,” the email said.
Evidence of groundhogs started popping up within the last two weeks, said LHSC’s director of facilities operations Chris Askew.

“We’ve had similar situations at a couple of our sites. It happens,” Askew said. “We have large sites so nature does tend to find locations of where they want to create their homes and sometimes it’s around our sites.”
Askew said his main concern with groundhogs on the property is the risk of them interacting with the plumbing and electrical systems that run underneath the LHSC grounds.
“If they were to come in contact or connect with them, that can have an impact on our operations. We want to make sure that doesn’t happen, and we also want to keep them safe at the same time.”
It’s not unusual for a groundhog to chew through a wire, according to Jared John Pineda, who works with Forest City Wildlife Removal.
“They chew through anything in their path,” Pineda said. “They might also confuse an electrical wire for a root because they probably don’t really know what an electrical wire is.”
The hospital is working with an external wildlife removal company to relocate the groundhogs with traps, Askew said.
“We are doing this for the safety of the groundhog as well as everybody else,” he said.
The memo sent to staff specifies Abell Pest Control is relocating the animals. The company was not available for an interview before publication.
While Askew did not specify the exact locations groundhogs were spotted, he said the animals tend to burrow in more isolated areas with less foot and vehicle traffic.

Pineda said he typically encounters groundhogs in large fields on the outskirts of the city or in residential backyards. There, they are often digging underneath homeowners’ porches, decks, sheds and gazebos, he said.
“It gives them a place to hide where they’re not being hunted by predators,” he explained.
Groundhogs are likely attracted to LHSC properties for the same reason, in addition to the soft soil and maintained greenery around the buildings, Pineda said.
“There’s a lot of shrubs and gardens that they have around the hospital. It gives them a nice little place to hang out and eat food,” he said.
Nearby construction at the intersection of Wellington and Commissioners may have also pushed groundhogs further into the Victoria and Children’s hospital grounds, Pineda added.
Both Pineda and Professional Wildlife Removal owner Patrick Blewett said they are receiving more groundhog-related calls in the city.
Blewett said it’s not necessarily that there are more groundhogs, but that the rodents are living differently.

“If the city grows and a lot of farmland around the city is now being developed into houses, the groundhogs aren’t actually going anywhere. They’re starting to live and adapt to the urban environment,” Blewett said. “When they used to just live in tunnels under the ground, a lot of them are now utilizing structures as protective spots.”

Blewett said it’s unlikely that burrowing groundhogs are capable of damaging the structural integrity of large-scale buildings at LHSC, but it is a risk for homeowners with groundhogs in their own backyards.
“If a groundhog is digging and creating tunnel systems, they’re excavating. Anywhere that dirt is displaced, then potentially all the surrounding dirt could start to cave in.”
Blewett and Pineda both advise reaching out to a reputable wildlife removal company if groundhogs are causing damage to property. Otherwise, they recommend enjoying them from afar.
“Just be respectful and observe it. They’re pretty mild creatures,” Blewett said. “They’re not interested in attacking. They’re just interested in doing their thing.”

stories.title: Londoners will be able to file noise complaints online starting next week
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 28, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 28
Service London portal replaces existing process using police non-emergency line
The London city councillor representing Old North and student-heavy neighborhoods near Western University is praising an upcoming change to the way residents make noise complaints.
Starting on Sept. 3, Londoners will be able to file noise complaints directly through the city’s online Service London portal, instead of through the London police non-emergency phone line.
The change will benefit both residents and London police, who will no longer have to triage complaints and forward them to city staff, said Sam Trosow, the councillor for Ward 6.
“Sometimes it’s very difficult to get through on the police non-emergency phone, depending on what their current demands are,” Trosow said.

“To have it initiate with the police seemed like a poor use of police resources, and it created a lot of frustration, so I’m very happy about this change because it’s something I’ve been talking to code enforcement and police about for a long time.”
Amanda Pfeffer, London’s director of municipal compliance, said the city had received feedback about the current process, and found the experience could be made “a little more seamless.”
“This way, residents will know that the report has been received immediately, and our noise and parking enforcement officers will be dispatched immediately upon receipt of those noise complaints.”

Trosow says he’s heard from some in his ward that voicemail messages left on the non-emergency line May not be returned, and responses May differ based on who answers the phone. He says some residents have reported being told to contact the city instead.
“I know that’s not what their policy is … but this is just what I’ve been hearing,” he said.

“All in all, I’ve been hearing a very frustrated and unhappy response from people who live in the near-campus neighbourhoods, particularly areas where you’re close to houses that might be considered party houses.”
Noise complaints that May be dangerous, including those that involve weapons, an altercation or a domestic situation, would still see police respond, Pfeffer said.

Londoners can already report other issues through the portal, including road and sidewalk problems, broken traffic lights and streetlights, needles, parking infractions, and lot and yard maintenance violations.
Starting Sept. 3, Pfeffer says Londoners can also use the portal to report noncompliance for nearly all bylaws investigated by municipal law enforcement officers.

stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
The article Trudeau receives RCMP protection on trips: report (Aug. 21) begs the question does former prime minister Stephen Harper similarly receive RCMP protection when he sojourns in his dubious role heavily funded by the Republican Party as the chair of the International Democracy Union?

For example when Harper appeared at a Mar-a-Lago gala in 2018? Or when Harper travelled to Budapest in 2023 seeking closer ties with the authoritarian autocratic Viktor Orban?

Michael Luce, London

We are witnessing the decline of the competitive spirit of America.

The demolishing of the standard of truth was the first indication of the American fear of losing competitiveness. Destruction and bullying came next.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is here to build a better country with positive values. Anyone with any sense at all will follow him.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

When buyers in Ontario drive their new $50,000 EV into the garage of their new $1.5 million home, taxpayers, many of whom are working several jobs to make ends meet, must contribute to the $135,000 rebate to which these affluent buyers are entitled.

Bill Caldwell, London

stories.title: Missing Person - Cole Rioux
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
UPDATE - LONDON, ON (September 1, 2026) – The London Police Service continues to search for missing person Cole Rioux and has received additional information.

Cole is believed to be driving a 2001 Volkswagen Jetta with Ontario licence plate AVXM 279. The vehicle is described as missing the Volkswagen emblem on the front and may also be missing a muffler. A photo of the vehicle has been included.

Police and family remain concerned for his welfare.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

ORIGINAL - LONDON, ON (August 28th, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 19-year-old Cole Rioux of London.

He is described as male, White, approximately 5’8”, 155lbs, slim build, with blue eyes, light brown buzz cut hair. He was last seen wearing a black T-shirt, with pink or green shorts, and operating a black Volkswagen Jetta.

He was reported missing yesterday and was last seen yesterday at approximately 3:40 a.m., in the area of High Street and Moore Street.

Police and family are concerned for his welfare.

For media inquiries, contact: Media Relations Officer T. 519-661-5410 Email. Media Officer

stories.title: Wellington Gateway enters final phase as Rapid Transit construction progresses
stories.summary: The Wellington Gateway project is entering its final phase of construction, with work beginning Monday, August 31, weather permitting, ON the
stories.content:
The Wellington Gateway project is entering its final phase of construction, with work beginning Monday, August 31, weather permitting, on the remaining section of Wellington Road between Watson Street and south of Base Line Road East.

Phase 2B will complete the remaining major construction work needed to build out the Wellington Road Rapid Transit corridor. This includes widening the road, installing two centre-running transit lanes, building new transit stations, and replacing underground infrastructure.

This milestone comes as other sections of Wellington Gateway near completion. Phase 2B is the final phase of the project, with construction continuing through 2029 and some final restoration work carrying over into 2030.

Crews have begun mobilizing the Phase 2B area, including temporary road construction and traffic control setup.

Starting Monday, August 31, one lane in each direction will be closed between Frank Place and Wellington Court.

Enbridge Gas is also moving gas infrastructure to make room for the project. Drivers may see occasional lane closures while this work is underway.

Access to Victoria Hospital, local businesses and properties will be maintained throughout construction. Pedestrian access will remain available on at least one side of the road, and the City is continuing to coordinate with the hospital to maintain access for emergency services.

Drivers should follow posted signs and detour routes, use caution, allow extra travel time and plan ahead.

Wellington Road will remain open throughout construction, with at least one lane in each direction. Traffic will shift as crews move through different parts of the project.

Work in 2026 and 2027 will focus north of Whetter Avenue, with construction shifting south towards Base Line Road East by late 2027.

As Wellington Gateway moves into its final phase, other parts of London's Rapid Transit network are also taking shape.

This summer, crews have continued to make progress across the network.

Clark's Bridge is now widened and complete. The bridge between Grand Avenue and South Street now has two traffic lanes, dedicated transit lanes and a new multi use path for people walking and cycling. Asphalt, red transit lane markings and permanent pavement markings were completed this summer. Landscaping and other finishing work will continue through 2026.

Wellington Gateway Phase 3 is nearing completion. The road between Wilkins Street and Harlech Gate has been paved, centre-running transit lanes have been painted, and transit shelters and new traffic signals are in place. Remaining work includes final station work, landscaping, cleanup and restoration.

Wellington Gateway Phase 4 is also nearing completion. Underground infrastructure between Harlech Gate and the Wellington Commons entrance is complete. Crews are completing transit stations, permanent traffic signals, the multi use path, landscaping, surface asphalt, and red centre-running transit lanes.

Construction continues on Phase 2A of Wellington Gateway, from Wilkins Street to Base Line Road East. Crews are continuing work on underground infrastructure, road widening and other improvements needed to accommodate the new centre-running Rapid Transit lanes.

Visit the Wellington Gateway project page for updates on construction timelines, traffic impacts, and project progress. Residents can also subscribe to receive email updates.

For the latest transit updates and detour information, visit the London Transit Commission website or follow @LTCLdnOnt on X.

stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (August 28, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 11-year-old Aadila Kochai, of London.

The missing person is described as a female, slim build, shoulder length red hair, and hazel eyes. She was last seen wearing black pants, a grey sweater, and blue flip-flops.

The missing person is believed to be in the area of Boullee St and Victoria St. She was reported missing on August 25, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for her welfare.

stories.title: Woman stabbed during early morning break and enter
stories.summary: Suspect arrested, remains in custody London, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence…
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: UPDATE – LONDON, ON (August 28, 2026 ) – The victim a 73-year-old woman of London, has died in hospital. Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section in collaboration with the Chief Coroner’s Office, continue to investigate.
The death has been deemed a homicide.
As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has additionally been charged with second degree murder.
Investigators are asking anyone with information about the accused, or any interactions with him, to contact police.
The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 31, 2026, in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .
LONDON, Ont. (Aug. 24, 2026) – A London man is facing multiple charges after police were called to a break and enter at a residence in the south end of the city over the weekend.

On Saturday, August 22, 2026, at about 6:10 a.m., an elderly woman was woken by a loud noise and found a man entering the residence in the area of Wellington Road and Base Line Road East. The victim was assaulted and stabbed before she was able to call 911.

Multiple officers responded. As officers attended the residence the accused began throwing broken glass at police. One officer sustained minor injuries. Officers entered the residence, and arrested the suspect.
The victim was transported to hospital by paramedic services with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. The suspect was transported to hospital by paramedic services with minor injuries.
The suspect and victim were not known to each other.
As a result of the investigation, Nelson Enrique Cornejo, 40, of London, has been charged with the following offences:
Aggravated assault;
Break and enter with intent;
Assault a peace officer with a weapon; and
Obstruct peace officer.
The accused remains in custody and is expected to re-appear in London court August 27, 2026, in relation to the charges.

stories.title: Expanding critical care where cardiology patients need it most
stories.summary: August 28, 2026
stories.content:
Members of the CCU team are pictured at the bedside in a Level 3 inpatient room.

August 28, 2026

The addition of critical care Level 3 beds within the Coronary Care Unit supports patients and families, strengthens critical care capacity, and improves patient flow across London Health Sciences Centre

For patients arriving at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) with complex cardiac needs, care can move quickly from the Emergency Department or Catheterization Lab to the critical care unit for monitoring and ventilation, and then onto recovery in an inpatient unit. Now with the opening of three net new Level 3 beds in the Coronary Care Unit (CCU), LHSC is helping to smooth the care journey for cardiology-focused patients and their families.

The new beds, made possible through provincial funding from Ontario Health, add ventilated care capacity within the CCU at University Hospital. They are designed to support critically ill cardiac patients who previously may have required care in a traditional critical care unit before transitioning to a cardiology-focused unit as their condition improved.

"We didn't have the physical space needed to add beds within the critical care unit at University Hospital, so we started to look at what other centres were doing to support level 3 care for this patient population and found an example where they had incorporated advanced care within their CCU," says Rachel Rushton, Director, Cardiac Care at LHSC. "We were confident that a similar model could work here and the benefits that we've seen to-date have been threefold, with benefits to our patients and their families, to our CCU team members, and to our broader patient flow."

Benefits to our patients

With this new model, patients can be cared for by a cardiac-focused team from the most acute phase of their illness through recovery and, in many cases, discharge to home with appropriate supports in place. For patients and families, remaining within a familiar care environment and being supported by many of the same team members can bring comfort and confidence during a stressful and uncertain time.

"Being managed by a team that specializes in cardiac care in one location is important," says Dr. Daniel Durocher, Cardiologist and Critical Care physician at LHSC. "Ultimately, we can provide advanced critical care support for patients while keeping their care journey focused within a cardiac centre."

Benefits to our people

To make these new beds possible, CCU nurses who were already trained to care for Level 2 patients received additional education and hands-on preparation, including classroom learning, simulation labs and buddy shifts in the ICU. Clinical educators, respiratory therapy educators, Critical Care Outreach Team members, respiratory therapists, dietitians, physiotherapists and ICU nurse mentors have all helped support the transition.

That deep collaboration has also created new opportunities for staff development. Nurses working within cardiology can build from foundational skills to Level 2 and Level 3 care, supporting some of the hospital’s most complex cardiac patients, while also following patients through a broader portion of their recovery journey.

For CCU team members, that continuity has been especially meaningful. Rather than caring for patients only during one stage of illness, staff can see the progress patients make as they move from critical illness to recovery. The result is a less siloed experience for both patients and care teams, with a stronger sense of connection across the full inpatient journey.

Benefits to our capacity

The new beds also support improved patient flow across LHSC by adding critical care capacity for cardiac patients at University Hospital. By caring for appropriate ventilated cardiology patients within the CCU, the hospital can better preserve traditional critical care capacity for patients with other urgent needs, including medical and surgical critical care. The model helps better ensure patients receive the right care, in the right place, at the right time.

From a regional perspective, the Level 3 CCU beds strengthen access to advanced cardiac support at LHSC, a tertiary care centre that serves patients from London and across southwestern Ontario. The expansion helps advance the organization’s broader goal of increasing critical care capacity by leveraging existing space and expertise in a new way.

stories.title: From Fun Ride to Emergency Department Visit: Children's Hospital warns of e-scooter related injuries
stories.summary: August 28, 2026
stories.content:
August 28, 2026

E-scooters have become a common sight zooming around neighbourhoods and city roads. For many riders, they offer a fun and convenient way to get around, but over the course of the spring and summer months, emergency physicians at Children's Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) have noted an alarming increase in the number of patients seeking care for injuries related to unsafe riding.

Between April and June of 2025, Children's Hospital treated approximately 22 injuries related to incidents involving e-scooters. During the same time period in 2026, that number has increased to 58, a 164 per cent increase. Physicians believe that trend has continued through the summer months.

Dr. Sheena Belisle, Paediatric Emergency Medicine Physician and Assistant Professor for the Department of Paediatrics at Schulich School of Medicine and Dentistry at Western University, says she and her colleagues are growing more concerned as the number and severity of injuries continues to climb, with many of them preventable.

"We've definitely seen an increase in the number of children and teens coming to the emergency department with e-scooter-related injuries," says Belisle. "While some injuries are relatively minor, we're also seeing patients with broken bones, significant cuts, facial injuries and concussions. What's particularly concerning is that many of these injuries involve children who are younger than the legal riding age. When we see a child seriously injured on an e-scooter, it often means the crash should never have had the opportunity to happen in the first place.”

Some patients are lucky with their tumbles only leading to cuts and bruises that heal relatively quickly. However, other injuries are so severe that they require surgery and lead to recoveries that stretch for weeks or even months, putting a significant damper on summer fun.

"The injuries that concern me the most are head injuries. My main concern is the potential for intercranial bleeds which can be life threatening or life altering," Belisle explains. "Even concussions can have long term consequences as they are more at risk for future concussions and it can take them longer to return to regular activities and routines."

Dr. Belisle hopes that by sharing the impact these injuries can have on children and families, more people will understand the importance of following safety rules and taking steps to prevent serious injuries.

"Many of the injuries we see share common factors. Riders may not be wearing helmets, there may have been more than one person on the scooter, or they are riding distracted."

Belisle also comments that families are often surprised that some of the most serious injuries occur during short, routine rides close to home.

"The length of the ride isn't what determines the risk. What matters is whether a child has the physical coordination, judgement and awareness needed to safely operate the scooter and respond to what's happening around them," says Belisle also noting the importance of following provincial regulations which prohibit children under the age of 16 from riding the devices. To help address the growing number of injuries, LHSC has partnered with community organizations including London Police Service , the City of London , the Middlesex-London Health Unit and Western University to raise awareness about e-scooter safety and local bylaws.

Throughout the summer, medical students from Western University’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry engaged with community members to better understand what residents know about e-scooter safety and regulations. Their findings helped inform the safety messages being shared by Belisle and her colleagues.

Belisle encourages families to have ongoing conversations about road safety and responsible e-scooter use, particularly around the importance of wearing a helmet and following local regulations. More importantly, she wants families to know that if an injury does occur, they should never hesitate to seek medical care.

"We would always rather someone come in to get checked if they're worried about an injury," says Belisle.

For Belisle, the message is ultimately a simple one. "E-scooters are not toys. Our goal isn't to take the fun away from riding them, but to help children and families stay safe. If sharing what we're seeing in the emergency department helps prevent even one serious injury, then these conversations are worth having."

In an effort to inform the general public and families about E-scooter safety, Dr. Belisle has provided some additional information surrounding misconceptions and common questions she’s asked as patients and their families come into the Emergency Department.

Myth: "They're just toys."

Reality: These are motorized vehicles capable of causing significant injuries. According to the City of London, the speed limit for E-scooters is set at 24 km/hr and they should only be ridden on roadways posted at 50 km/hr or less, in bike lanes, and on multi-use pathways.

Myth: "I don't need a helmet for a short trip."

Reality: Many serious injuries occur close to home and during leisure rides. Helmets help protect against serious head and brain injuries and should be worn every time you ride, regardless of the distance. Riders aged 16 or 17 must wear a helmet when using an electric kick-scooter, and no one under the age of 16 should be riding an E-scooter.

Myth: "It's okay if my child just rides for a few minutes."

Reality: Length of time isn't what determines risk. Children need physical coordination, judgment, and awareness to safely operate an e-scooter and react to traffic, pedestrians, and obstacles. Age restrictions are in place for a reason, and younger riders may not yet have the skills needed to safely navigate unexpected situations. As per the City of London bylaw, parents are responsible for ensuring their child under the age of 16 does not ride an e-scooter.

Myth: "One extra rider isn't a big deal."

Reality: E-scooters are designed for one rider. Adding a second passenger changes the scooter's balance, steering and braking ability, making it much harder to control. Multiple riders increase the likelihood of a crash and can lead to more serious injuries when a fall occurs. As part of the provincial regulations, no individual operating an E-scooter is allowed to carry any additional people.

Myth: "Most e-scooter injuries are just scrapes and bruises."

Reality: While some riders walk away with minor injuries, emergency physicians are also seeing fractured bones, significant facial injuries, and head trauma. What starts as a fun ride can quickly become an emergency department visit, making prevention and safe riding practices critical.

stories.title: Federal government assures farmers of support amid trade war concerns
stories.summary: Federal government representatives are conducting outreach across the country, hosting events designed to reassure Canadians about the impacts of the ongoing trade war.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Federal government representatives are conducting outreach across the country, hosting events designed to reassure Canadians about the impacts of the ongoing trade war. A recent stop brought MP Wayne Long to Forbesvue Farm in St.

Clair Township, east of Sarnia, to emphasize the government’s commitment to financial support for farmers. The Forbes family, who have operated their dairy farm for three generations, manage approximately 350 head of cattle, including 200 milking cows.

While they have witnessed numerous U.S. administrations target the Canadian supply management system, Kevin Forbes stated their focus remains firmly on the domestic market. “We’re not really looking to export. We’re not trying to get into that game,” Forbes said.

“Our primary focus is strictly Canadian consumers and a fair and equitable quality product for them.” During the visit, Long, the Secretary of State responsible for the Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions, stressed the federal government’s dedication to providing funding to help farmers navigate economic challenges.

“Canada is taking action for defense workers, businesses and communities,” Long stated. Earlier this week, the federal government announced an additional $7.5 billion in funding for tariff impact relief. This package aims to help farmers offset increased costs, particularly on equipment purchases.

Long highlighted the government’s commitment to rapid deployment of these resources. “There’s a sense of urgency here. We’re going to make sure the regional development agencies, obviously, the Business Development Bank of Canada, are funded.

So these programs will go out literally within weeks.” The Secretary of State explained that working with regional development agencies (RDA) like FedDev Ontario and the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) is key to the effective distribution of funds.

“The RDAs are going to actually manage the funding, especially through the rapid response initiative,” he noted. “So applications are actually actively going in there now. They’re being evaluated. We’re going to turn those around really, really quickly.” Forbes expressed his continued dedication to running the farm and supporting local businesses, adding a message of confidence in the government’s broader strategy.

“I think you have to filter out the noise a certain amount and have faith in our government that they’re going to continue to do what’s right for Canadians,” he said. “And not just the dairy farms, but negotiating trade deals that are mutually beneficial for all Canadians, Canadian families, consumers and businesses.”

stories.title: Resale housing market, already sluggish, could take hit from Trump tariffs
stories.summary: "If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while . . . that can certainly slow things down."
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Ontario’s sluggish resale housing market could face some headwinds from renewed trade tensions between Canada and the U.S., but the impact is unlikely to completely derail its ongoing recovery – at least in the short term, industry watchers say.

Uncertainty and low consumer confidence resulting from the trade war, which entered a new chapter after trade talks collapsed between the two countries last week, have been some of the driving factors behind slower-than-expected home sales in the province in 2026.

Last month, for example, 16,276 homes were sold in Ontario, a 1.3 per cent decline from July 2025, while year-to-date sales also remain below 2025 levels, according to the latest figures from the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA).

However, on a month-to-month basis, July also marked the fourth straight month of gains in home resale activity at the national level, with upticks also seen in recent months in provincial markets such as Toronto, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, London and Ottawa.

“This latest round of the trade war with the U.S. puts at risk the confidence gains we’ve seen in recent months,” said Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada.

“It certainly raises the risk of being derailed once again. But still, our base case is that the recovery will remain on track. It’s going to be gradual. It’s going to be uneven, and it’s probably going to be bumpy but, overall, it’s still likely to be sustained going forward.”

After talks collapsed last Friday, the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian products on Aug. 22, with Ottawa announcing on Tuesday a dollar-for-dollar counter-tariff response, slated to come into effect starting Sept. 8.

Hogue, however, said that while the latest tariffs will hit certain sectors and businesses hard, from a larger perspective, “this is unlikely, in our view, to push Canada’s economy into a recession.”

He said that despite the uncertainty of recent months, the Canadian economy has shown signs of resiliency. Canada’s jobless rate, for example, went down to 6.4 per cent in July, its lowest level over the past year. Interest rates have also remained steady after peaking in 2024.

And while sales have been far from spectacular, Hogue also said there’s a lot of pent-up demand in the market from people who would’ve otherwise already purchased a home.

“So, we’re not quite at the point of saying the housing market is about to fall off again,” he said. “We think there’s a bit of momentum there.”

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Place Centre economic think-tank at the University of Ottawa, said the impact on the housing market will depend on how long the U.S. tariffs remain in place.

“If these kinds of tariffs stick around for a while, and we start seeing job layoffs, particularly in the manufacturing sector, that can certainly slow things down,” he said. “But I think, overall, we’ve just had this uncertainty for so long that I think we’ve grown kind of numb to it.”

Moffatt also said there are other barriers impacting the market, including people’s ability to afford a home, even if prices have been trending upward in recent months. Demand has also been impacted by changes in immigration targets, which have slowed population growth, particularly in Ontario.

“The housing market, over the last five to 10 years, has had to adjust to so many big changes, whether it be population growth or COVID-related migration, big swings in interest rates, and I think we’re dealing with the effect of that right now, where a lot of the market is just locked up.”

Kevin Barry, owner and broker at Thrive Realty Group in London, said it’s still too early to gauge whether the latest trade-war developments are having an impact on buyers, given August is traditionally a slow month for sales.

“Whenever anything big like this shifts, changes, or moves, there’s a moment of pause in the market, which I think we are seeing right now,” he said.

“But people are also focused on going back to school, getting back into routine, getting the kids ready for the fall, so we normally see a bit of a lull in the market right now, so it’s tough to measure it against the reality of what’s happening south of the border.”

Barry, however, acknowledged worries about the economy have been an issue for many buyers over the past several months, keeping some on the sidelines of the market.

“The big conversation is need versus want,” he said. “If you need to move, you’re still going to do it. If you want to move, you’re going to pause and maybe be a little bit more considerate, a little bit more deliberate with your decision-making process.”

stories.title: Multilingual volunteers help patients navigate St. Joseph’s Health Care London
stories.summary: St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
St. Joseph’s Health Care London is introducing new tools to help patients and visitors who face language barriers communicate when they arrive at the hospital.

Multilingual volunteers are now wearing buttons identifying the languages they speak, making it easier for patients to find someone who can communicate with them in their preferred language.

In the first two weeks of the initiative, volunteers have helped more than 25 people communicate in another language.

There are currently 14 languages represented, including Arabic, Mandarin, French, and Hindi, with more expected to be added as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

Monica Naskret-Reyes, a volunteer who speaks Spanish, said seeing someone who speaks their language can provide relief for patients who are already dealing with the stress and uncertainty of being in hospital.

“When people come to the hospital, the concern they have about their health, the uncertainty, what is going on and not speaking the language is a lot of pressure,” said Naskret-Reyes.

“But when they see someone speaking their own language it’s like, ‘oh my God’, what a relief. At least I can communicate a little bit with this person.”

According to Statistics Canada, more than 20,000 new immigrants moved to the London region between 2016 and 2021. About 22 per cent of Londoners identify as immigrants.

Tracy Drenth, manager of Volunteer Services at St. Joseph’s, said the program reflects the diversity of the community.

“Patient population is becoming a lot more diverse much like the community. So, we have had several patients come into the hospital who have limited English proficiency. So, we want to provide the best customer service as possible as patients enter our buildings,” she said.

The initiative also supports people who communicate using sign language. Melissa Fowler, a sign language volunteer, said she has helped patients communicate where they need to go within the hospital.

“I’ve had quite a few people come in that don’t know how to speak to somebody, so I’ve let them know that I know sign language and then able to finger spell to me where they need to go and then can take them there,” said Fowler.

For languages that aren’t represented by an on-site volunteer, trained volunteers can use an iPad equipped with an interpretation service that provides access to an additional 200 languages.

The live interpretation service is intended for general information, such as finding a department, getting directions or locating the cafeteria. It is not intended for clinical information.

St. Joseph’s says more languages could be represented at hospital entrances as additional multilingual volunteers join the program.

stories.title: International Overdose Day marks 25 years in Oxford County
stories.summary: International Overdose Awareness Day was recognized this week in Oxford County, with a series of events to mark 25 years of remembering those lost to addictions.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
International Overdose Awareness Day was recognized this week in Oxford County, with a series of events to mark 25 years of remembering those lost to addictions.

In Tillsonburg, resident Gary Graham was on hand to check out an awareness campaign by the Oxford Mental Health and Addictions Action Coalition (Omhaac) Thursday. He pulled no punches when describing the situation in the downtown.

“Every day there’s ambulances out here looking after overdosed people,” Graham said.

He said the addiction crisis is also contributing to homelessness in the community.

“They’re pretty much all in the underground, or they’re spread all over the place. The town should be doing something about it,” he remarked.

Members of Omhaac had a display set up in front of the Tillsonburg mall in the heart of downtown. They were spreading awareness of the ongoing crisis, handing out naloxone kits, and even training people how to use them to save lives. Omhaac member Patti Monaghan says street drugs appear to be getting stronger.

“We are noticing that one naloxone kit isn’t enough. We need to do multiple, sometimes up to like five or six kits of administering naloxone, because the substances that are out there are a lot more serious than prior years,” she explained.

According to Ohmaac, the rate of opioid-related incidents resulting in ER visits in Oxford County peaked in 2021 during the pandemic.

While it declined through 2024 (44.2 per 100,000 population), it remained more than five times higher than 10 years earlier in 2014 (7.2 per 100,000 population).

Opioid-related deaths also peaked in 2021, before declining by 2024 (15.5 per 100,000 population).

But the rate was still more than one and a half times higher than in 2018, pre-pandemic (9.3 per 100,000 population).

Joanne Beresford, Administrator at the Tillsonburg BIA, says the ongoing opioid crisis shows little signs of waning, and is being felt most in the downtown.

“This is where the hub is. Unfortunately, things happen at night-time and sometimes during the day as well. It’s a sad state apparently when they come in sometimes in the morning and everything’s turned upside down and graffitied on and whatever,” she said.

Ohmaac hosted awareness events this week in Woodstock as well. Patti Monaghan asked that people have compassion.

“Nobody wants to live this life. Nobody wants to be stuck in these cycles of addiction,” she said.

stories.title: Missing swimmer found dead at Pinery Provincial Park
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 4:13 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Beachgoers found the missing 28-year-old's body on Thursday, police said
Provincial Police in Lambton County say they have recovered the body of a missing swimmer who was last seen at a Pinery Provincial Park beach on Wednesday afternoon.

Police say visitors to the beach located the body of the individual on Thursday. They did not share any details of the person's identity, other than specifying the deceased as a 28-year-old from Scarborough.
OPP say the search began when police were called at 1 p.m. on Aug. 26, about the missing swimmer who was last seen at a beach in the park.

Two OPP boats, as well as the underwater search and recovery unit, and OPP aviation services, were helping with the search. Anishnabek Police Service, which operates a detachment at Kettle and Stony Point First Nation, also helped.
It's unclear why it took almost 24 hours for OPP to notify the public about the missing swimmer.

stories.title: ‘Dream come true’: New Muslim community centre opening in London
stories.summary: Fourteen years in the making, Noor Gardens brings worship, education and recreation under one roof in the city’s southwest.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
A 14-year effort to build a new home for London’s Muslim community will culminate Friday with the opening of Noor Gardens in the city’s southwest.

The mosque and community centre at 457 Southdale Rd. W. combines worship, education and recreation under one roof. It features a prayer hall, gymnasium, youth lounge and classrooms for educational and social programs.

“This is truly a dream come true,” said Dr. Nabil Sultan, chair of the Noor Gardens centre committee and a physician with London Health Sciences Centre.

The Muslim Association of Canada bought the 13-acre property near Wonderland and Southdale roads in 2012, Sultan said. The organization placed the total project cost at $14.3 million in a fundraising update last year, up from the $12-million estimate reported when plans were presented to the city in 2017.

Sultan said the project was funded by London’s Muslim community throughout the years from donations ranging from $5 and $10 to much larger amounts.

“There’s probably thousands of individual donations that have been made to this project by the community here in London,” he said.

The centre arrives as existing mosques face growing pressure for space, particularly during Friday prayers and Ramadan. About 35,000 Londoners identified as Muslim in the 2021 census , representing 8.4 per cent of the city’s population.

London’s Muslim roots stretch back generations. Families began raising money for a mosque in the 1950s and bought a house at 151 Oxford St. W. in 1956. After fire destroyed that building in 1961, the current London Muslim Mosque opened in 1964. It is recognized as Ontario’s first mosque and Canada’s second.

Sultan, who has lived in London since 1989, recalled growing up with cramped worship spaces and few of the recreational and educational services Noor Gardens will offer.

Its name means “gardens of light” in Arabic, a theme carried through the large windows, lighting and traditional Islamic architectural details inside the building. The property was once home to Wally World, a water park remembered by many longtime Londoners.

“As the community grew, the needs and the aspirations and what we wanted to achieve started to grow with the numbers of people,” said Dr. Munir El-Kassem, Imam of the Islamic Centre of Southwest Ontario.

El-Kassem, marking his 50th year in London, said Noor Gardens marks the community’s evolution from modest beginnings to a new generation of Muslims in London.

He believes the centre will be a place of reflection, peace and dialogue for people of all backgrounds.

A ribbon-cutting ceremony for the public is scheduled for Friday at 11 a.m., followed by tours of the facility.

Organizers also envision Noor Gardens hosting open houses, interfaith events and conversations intended to connect Muslim and non-Muslim Londoners.

“Our doors are wide open for any visitors to come,” Sultan said.

paragraphs: A 14-year effort to build a new home for London’s Muslim community will culminate Friday with the opening of Noor Gardens in the city’s southwest.

The mosque and community centre at 457 Southdale Rd. W. combines worship, education and recreation under one roof. It features a prayer hall, gymnasium, youth lounge and classrooms for educational and social programs.
“This is truly a dream come true,” said Dr. Nabil Sultan, chair of the Noor Gardens centre committee and a physician with London Health Sciences Centre.

The Muslim Association of Canada bought the 13-acre property near Wonderland and Southdale roads in 2012, Sultan said. The organization placed the total project cost at $14.3 million in a fundraising update last year, up from the $12-million estimate reported when plans were presented to the city in 2017.
Sultan said the project was funded by London’s Muslim community throughout the years from donations ranging from $5 and $10 to much larger amounts.
“There’s probably thousands of individual donations that have been made to this project by the community here in London,” he said.

The centre arrives as existing mosques face growing pressure for space, particularly during Friday prayers and Ramadan. About 35,000 Londoners identified as Muslim in the 2021 census , representing 8.4 per cent of the city’s population.

London’s Muslim roots stretch back generations. Families began raising money for a mosque in the 1950s and bought a house at 151 Oxford St. W. in 1956. After fire destroyed that building in 1961, the current London Muslim Mosque opened in 1964. It is recognized as Ontario’s first mosque and Canada’s second.
Sultan, who has lived in London since 1989, recalled growing up with cramped worship spaces and few of the recreational and educational services Noor Gardens will offer.

Its name means “gardens of light” in Arabic, a theme carried through the large windows, lighting and traditional Islamic architectural details inside the building. The property was once home to Wally World, a water park remembered by many longtime Londoners.

“As the community grew, the needs and the aspirations and what we wanted to achieve started to grow with the numbers of people,” said Dr. Munir El-Kassem, Imam of the Islamic Centre of Southwest Ontario.
El-Kassem, marking his 50th year in London, said Noor Gardens marks the community’s evolution from modest beginnings to a new generation of Muslims in London.
He believes the centre will be a place of reflection, peace and dialogue for people of all backgrounds.
A ribbon-cutting ceremony for the public is scheduled for Friday at 11 a.m., followed by tours of the facility.
Organizers also envision Noor Gardens hosting open houses, interfaith events and conversations intended to connect Muslim and non-Muslim Londoners.
“Our doors are wide open for any visitors to come,” Sultan said.

stories.title: Kincardine wants more municipal input on potential data centres
stories.summary: The Municipality of Kincardine believes municipalities should have to give formal support to a data centre before it can be built in their community.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
The Municipality of Kincardine believes municipalities should have to give formal support to a data centre before it can be built in their community.

That’s just one of several recommendations Kincardine is making to the Ontario government as they put together Ontario’s plan on how to deal with prospective projects.

The large projects have been divisive across the country and world as they use large amounts of electricity and water.

Kincardine says closed loop water systems and clear standards for electricity usage should be laid out before any data centre project can proceed.

Council directed town staff to submit their recommendations to the province advocating that stronger municipal involvement, cost recovery, environmental protections, community benefits, transparency, and emergency planning are needed for responsible investment, while ensuring host communities share in the long-term benefits of potential growth.

The public has until Sept. 12 to share their comments with the provincial government about data centre development.

stories.title: Bruce County warns of “fraudulent emails” that appear to come from them
stories.summary: Bruce County officials are warning residents of fraudulent emails that appear to originate from Bruce County email accounts.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Bruce County officials warn residents of fraudulent emails that appear to originate from Bruce County email accounts.

They say they are actively investigating where the emails originated from, and asking residents to share any suspicious emails that look like they’re from Bruce County with them.

In one instance, a fraudulent e-mail was seeking an e-transfer payment. Bruce County say they do not use e-transfers as payments.

Officials say some of the fraudulent e-mails contained invoices, County logos and branding to appear legitimate.

If you suspect you’ve received a fraudulent email from Bruce County, officials ask you to send it to them at https://www.brucecounty.on.CA/whats-news/contact

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream pledges no price increase as Ontario company shifts away from U.S. suppliers
stories.summary: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: , Isha Bhargava | CBC News | Posted: August 27, 2026 1:32 PM | Last Updated: August 27
Company says it will replace 70% of U.S. ingredients with Canadian, other suppliers by 2027
An Ontario ice cream company says it will replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and won't increase prices for two years.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is shifting away from American suppliers as the trade dispute between Canada and the United States continues. The family-owned company also says it won't raise prices for its ice cream until March 2028.
It began looking for alternatives to U.S. suppliers in March 2025, when the first round of tariffs from the Trump administration was announced, CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“We made a statement at that time that we weren’t raising prices and we were going to start this journey. And here we are. We have not been sitting idle. We have been working very hard,” Chapman told CBC's London Morning on Thursday.
The company said it's on track to replace more than 70 per cent of its American ingredients and components with Canadian or non-U.S. sources by mid-2027.
One of the biggest changes involves sugar cones.
There are no producers of industrial sugar cones in Canada, so the company partnered with Original Foods, a Dunville, Ont.-based company, to bring in a cone oven, Chapman said.
“We are going to be the only company in Canada who has a 100 per cent Canadian cone line."
Original Foods Limited will produce the sugar cones for Chapman's. The manufacturer tapped the ice cream retailer a few months ago when trade talks with Canada and the U.S. intensified.

"We knew there will be opportunities for customers who are currently buying in the U.S. to look for local manufacturing and we approached Chapman's to discuss if they would be interested to buy locally," said president Steeve Tremblay.

"It's very rewarding to keep the jobs in Canada. It makes our economy stronger and we're not being dependent outside the country, especially when there's a country that tries to make our economy and our lives more difficult. It's nice to see that we can collaborate and give somewhat of strategic response that’s good for Canada."

The two companies have already signed their agreement and equipment has been purchased in Germany. However, Tremblay said, there have been delays due to Canada's electricity registration requirements and other red tape.

"Sometimes [the requirements] are really unique to Canada and not aligned with European manufacturers, so it causes extra costs and delays and is a perfect example of something that can be reviewed," he said.
Tremblay said he plans to contact other Canadian companies to encourage more local partnerships.
Chapman's is also moving production of wafers used in its ice cream sandwiches to Canada, and is sourcing ingredients such as almonds from Australia and cherries from Chile.
The trade dispute has prompted Canadian companies like Chapman's to reconsider what they produce domestically, he said.

“The first round last year of tariffs really opened the eyes of a lot of industry in Canada. Companies that we’ve known for years that would never consider producing certain products, suddenly they were saying, 'You know what, maybe we should look at this.'”
He said some of the changes have also proved to be more affordable than expected.

“It’s crazy what this has done for businesses in this country. Almonds from Australia, are you crazy? How is that possible that we could get an even better price, plus freight, from Australia instead of the United States? So we’re finding a lot of opportunities out there.”
Chapman said some of the changes are long-term commitments, including the five-year contract for Canadian-made cones.
Chapman’s is also working to make its production more efficient to help control costs, he added.
“I am fully confident that we are going to make it to the other side of this."
The company said it will continue to use 100 per cent Canadian dairy in its ice cream.

stories.title: Chapman’s Ice Cream ditching U.S. ingredients as trade war escalates
stories.summary: The Southwestern Ontario company is replacing U.S. ingredients and vowing no price hikes until March 2028.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
A Southwestern Ontario ice-cream maker whose products are sold across Canada is ditching U.S. ingredients as the Canada-U.S. trade war escalates.

Chapman’s Ice Cream is replacing American ingredients with Canadian and other non-U.S. alternatives, while pledging not to raise prices until March 2028.

The family-owned company began exploring other suppliers in March 2025 to avoid “future headaches,” CEO Ashley Chapman said.

“In March last year, we released a statement saying we would not raise our prices due to the aggravation from the tariffs, and that’s kind of what started us on this journey,” Chapman said.

By mid- to late 2027, the company expects to have replaced 70 per cent of its American-sourced ingredients with Canadian or other non-U.S. alternatives, he said.

“This is a perfect story of Canadian companies cooperating,” Chapman said. “… No interest in using any American dairy or any American products that we can source other places.”

Chapman’s has signed a five-year deal with Original Foods, near Hamilton, to supply sugar cones, with the switch expected to be completed by the end of the year, Chapman said.

“And we will be the only ice cream company in the country that has 100 per cent Canadian ice cream cones,” he said.

While Chapman’s will continue using 100 per cent Canadian dairy, producing entirely Canadian ice cream is “impossible” because Canada does not produce cocoa, sugar cane and other key ingredients, Chapman said.

But “the reliability of the United States is in question, to say the least,” he added.

“That’s what we want for our business. We want able trading partners that are not emotional, and whenever there’s a dispute, we can just sit down and have an adult conversation and get to the end,” Chapman said.

“With the Trump administration interfering in the business world worldwide, it really has changed our view and a lot of other companies’ views on who we should be making long-term deals with.”

New supply deals include almonds from Australia by mid-2027 and cherries from Chile.

“Shockingly, they’re slightly less expensive than the American almonds, even when you factor in the transportation,” Chapman said. “There are some companies out there that really want to deal with Canadians and really want to ship their product here, and when you get to the economies of scale that we have, it just works out.”

Chapman said the company is also working internally to improve systems, cut costs and find suppliers that can provide high-quality products at lower prices.

“It’s a really nice time (for Canadian companies), shockingly, considering the trade war, because we’re finding new partners that we can rely on,” he said. “This is a time to think outside of the box and set us up for success in the future.”

“Shockingly, they’re slightly less expensive than the American almonds, even when you factor in the transportation,” Chapman said. “There are some companies out there that really want to deal with Canadians and really want to ship their product here, and when you get to the economies of scale that we have, it just works out.”
Chapman said the company is also working internally to improve systems, cut costs and find suppliers that can provide high-quality products at lower prices.

“It’s a really nice time (for Canadian companies), shockingly, considering the trade war, because we’re finding new partners that we can rely on,” he said. “This is a time to think outside of the box and set us up for success in the future.”

stories.title: Clouds, cooler air move into southwestern Ontario, but fair weather ahead
stories.summary: Mainly cloudy skies are expected today as temperatures rise into the afternoon, despite a cold front moving through the region.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A cold front moving through southwestern Ontario is bringing cooler temperatures and increased cloud cover Thursday, but a stretch of pleasant late-summer weather is on the way.

According to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison, the front ushered in cooler air from Lake Huron, leading to mainly cloudy skies with occasional breaks of sunshine across the region.

“We have had a cold front come through the area and that is generating a bit of cloud cover with the cool air coming in off Lake Huron,” Atchison said.

Temperatures varied considerably across southwestern Ontario Thursday afternoon, with cooler conditions closer to the lake. Atchison said temperatures near the Bruce Peninsula remained between 16 C and 18 C, while London reached about 23 C and Windsor climbed to 26 C.

A few lingering showers were also possible, particularly north of London. Light rainfall was reported in parts of northern Huron County, while London faced only a slight chance of precipitation through the late afternoon.

“The probability through the late afternoon is just a 30 per cent chance,” Atchison said.

Overnight temperatures are expected to fall to about 14 C in London as a weak backdoor cold front moves through the region. Atchison said the system will usher in cooler, drier air ahead of the weekend.

“High pressure is forecast to build into southwestern Ontario overnight, clearing skies and setting up what forecasters describe as an extended period of comfortable weather.”

Conditions on Friday are expected to be mainly sunny, with only a few fair-weather clouds and a daytime high near 23 C.

The favourable pattern is expected to continue through the weekend, with sunny skies and temperatures around 26 C on Saturday.

Sunday is forecast to bring a mix of sun and cloud, with temperatures remaining in the mid-20s. Atchison said there is a 40 per cent chance of showers Sunday night, although any rainfall is expected to hold off until after sunset.

“The next few days are looking good with lots of sunshine in the forecast and some comfortable conditions,” said Atchison.

Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast

Thursday Night: Partly cloudy. 30 per cent chance of showers this evening. Fog patches developing overnight. Wind northwest 20 km/h becoming light this evening. Low 14.

Friday: Clearing in the morning. Fog patches dissipating in the morning. High 23. Humidex 26. UV index 7 or high.

Friday Night: Clear. Low 10.

Saturday: Sunny. High 26.

Sunday: A mix of sun and cloud. High 27.

Monday: A mix of sun and cloud with 40 per cent chance of showers. High 29.
