stories.title: St. Thomas’ eye-catching red barn wins international design awards
stories.summary: The sculpture’s Gold certification puts it in the running for the competition’s Grand Winner title.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
The sculpture’s Gold certification puts it in the running for the competition’s Grand Winner title.

Drivers heading south from London on Highbury Avenue are greeted by a red barn that seems to break apart before coming back together. Now, the St. Thomas landmark has earned international recognition.

Fading Memories, installed in the roundabout at Highbury Avenue and Ron McNeil Line, received Gold certification in the Art and Photography category at the 19th Grands Prix du Design awards.

Gold-certified projects received an average jury score of between 80 and 100, qualifying them as finalists for the competition’s Grand Winner title.

The Montreal-based Grands Prix du Design competition, created in 2007, recognizes work in fields including architecture, landscape design, art and photography. Its Grand Winners will be announced at two galas scheduled for Oct. 8 and Nov. 19.

St. Thomas Coun. Steve Wookey, council’s representative on the city’s public art committee, called the award “fantastic validation” of the city’s efforts in recent years to encourage arts and culture.

The sculpture reimagines the traditional red barns that once dotted the countryside around St. Thomas and Elgin County. From one direction, it appears solid. As motorists circle it, the familiar shape separates into open cross-sections meant to evoke a barn weathering and fading with time.

“For me, it’s very important that many years from now where it sits, you’ll say, that’s where the country was. That’s what was here, and that’s what’s important,” Wookey said.

The city selected the submission by Shift Landscape Architecture in 2024 from 13 proposals. The sculpture was built by Lafontaine Iron Werks and cost $220,640 before HST, within the project’s $250,000 budget. Wookey said the money came from the roundabout’s construction budget.

“This piece draws attention to barns and hopefully stands as a monument as more are lost through development,” said Mike Barker, landscape architect and principal at Shift Landscape Architecture.

Barker divided the barn into sections of varying openness, allowing its appearance to change depending on the direction from which a driver enters the roundabout. The effect draws from his memories of working barns and others left to deteriorate.

“The award highlights the value of art in the public landscape,” Barker told The Free Press. “Many people question the value but it is critical we continue to tell stories of the past, present and future.”

mdaldalian@postmedia.com

stories.title: SUV driver killed in collision with commercial truck east of London, Ont.
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 PM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 PM | Last Updated: August 26
Crash happened just before 1 p.m. along Dundas Street west of Fairview Road
One person has died, and another person was injured after an SUV and a commercial truck collided Wednesday afternoon in Thames Centre, just outside of London, Ont.
Ontario Provincial Police say the collision happened just before 1 p.m. along Dundas Street just west of Fairview Road, a short drive outside of the London city boundary.
The driver of the SUV was transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries, where they were later pronounced dead, police said in a social media post on X.
The driver of the commercial truck, described as a straight truck, suffered minor injuries.
Dundas Street was closed from Shaw Road to Fairview Road, and Fairview was closed from Dundas to Evelyn Drive as of late Wednesday afternoon.
Police ask anyone with information or dashcam video to contact them or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Driver dies after two-vehicle crash in Middlesex County: Police
stories.summary: The driver of a straight truck suffered minor injuries, OPP said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The driver of a straight truck suffered minor injuries, OPP said.

A driver died and another was taken to hospital after a two-vehicle crash in Thames Centre on Wednesday afternoon, police say.

Middlesex OPP responded shortly before 1 p.m. to a crash involving a straight truck and a sport utility vehicle on Dundas Street.

Both drivers were taken to local hospital, OPP said.

The driver of the SUV suffered life-threatening injuries and later died in hospital, police said in a video posted on social media at 3:46 p.m.

Police did not identify the driver who died.

Dundas Street was expected to be closed for “some time” between Shaw and Heritage roads. Fairview Road was also closed from Dundas Street to Avalon, OPP Const. Jeffrey Beaumaster said in the video.

“Please do not go around the barricades,” Beaumaster said. “…Updates will be provided when they are available.”

Police said the roads would remain closed for an undetermined amount of time as the investigation continued.

Anyone who witnessed the collision or has footage is asked to call OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can be made at 1-800-222-8477.

A Windsor man facing charges related to kidnapping, assault and extortion has surrendered after allegedly evading police since 2024.

Windsor police said Alwassi Al Latif, 29, who was named to their Wanted in Windsor list earlier this year, turned himself in Monday.

In July 2024, Al Latif and another person allegedly abducted a man by forcing him into a vehicle in the 2300 block of Howard Avenue and taking him to another location. Police said the victim was then assaulted, threatened and robbed.

Police state on their Wanted in Windsor website that the victim’s money and jewelry were taken before he was released. The abductors also allegedly threatened the victim and his family while demanding additional payment.

At the time, police said Al Latif was serving a conditional sentence requiring him to remain in Ontario and comply with electronic monitoring. In October 2024, he received permission to travel outside Ontario without the monitoring device. Police said he had evaded apprehension since then.

Investigators added Al Latif to their Wanted in Windsor list in April.

With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: FC London escapes relegation with dramatic late-season turnaround
stories.summary: A late coaching change and a group of young call-ups helped FC London earn seven of nine points in its final three matches.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
We independently select everything we recommend. Buying through us May earn us a commission, which supports our work.

It was the best rescue in franchise history.

The FC London men’s team used a late-season coaching change and a bunch of green teenagers to vault from the basement and save itself from relegation. The local soccer club went 2-0-1 under interim boss Michael Silvera in its final three matches and will remain in the second tier of the Ontario Premier League in 2027.

“We made the change from (first-year skipper Stiven Mikhail) to our reserve coach and Michael did a phenomenal job,” FC London general manager Dave DeBenedictis said. “He’s been doing the reserve team the last three years. We moved him up and he got seven of nine points for us.

“We had a bunch of under-16s and U17s who got called up because a lot of players were gone and they pulled it off. They were amazing.”

FC London finished with a 5-13-4 record, good for 10th place in the 12-team circuit. Its 19 points were three more than Hamilton United, which will drop to the third division and switch places with Kingston.

London beat Pickering FC 2-1 on Aug. 8, tied Inter Toronto II 2-2 on Aug. 15 and slipped past Whitby FC 2-1 on the road this past weekend. The young squad handed Whitby only its third defeat in 22 games this season.

“That was the toughest of all the games,” DeBenedictis said. “There were six minutes of injury time and they went close to 10, so that was four minutes of my life taken away. It was stressful but we’re still on track. We want to be back in the premier league and, in 2-3 years, we will be in contention to try to win a national championship.”

The club acknowledges it expected to finish higher in the standings and should have won more games, especially early in the season. The optimism is buoyed by organic growth at the academy level and a culture the club hopes will entice players to stay in the program.

“The 2008s (birthdates) just started playing this year (in men’s division) but they needed a year of maturing in dealing with adults,” DeBenedictis said. “We didn’t want to go down (to third tier) because we wanted our 2009s to blend with those ’08s and ’07s and that would be our core for our future. We believe in our academy and the progression we’re seeing.”

Dylan de Melo, the club’s top prospect, started at the senior level two years ago and recently signed with the Canadian Premier League’s Pacific FC. He made his debut at age 17 with the basement-dwelling crew this past weekend.

“He’s the prototypical player we like having in our club,” DeBenedictis said. “High IQ, he thinks the game and finds space. Attitude-wise, he’s a 10 and to play in a CPL game at that age is pretty impressive.”

On the women’s side, Sofia Martins joined Sporting Braga’s U17 roster in Portugal, while FC London grads continue to bolster Northern Super League rosters. Julia Benati and keeper Samantha St. Croix are in Halifax, Lauren Rowe and Kaila Novak play for AFC Toronto, Sadie Waite is in Ottawa and Claire Monyard suits up for Montreal.

Earlier this summer, Charlotte Cromack moved from Wexford to Polish side GKS Gornik Leczna for the upcoming European campaign. Her father, Will, just coached the FC London women to an 8-8-2 record and fifth place in the OPL premier division.

The club plans to wait until the academy season winds down before announcing coaching staffs for the men’s and women’s teams ahead of next year. The U17 girls recently fell to Burlington in the 96th minute of the Ontario Player Development League Cup final and will now push for playoff seeding into the fall.

There are four FC London youth teams, including three boys squads, expected to earn post-season spots in the province’s top minor circuit. That alone is reason to hope another late-season rescue won’t be needed anytime soon.

stories.title: St. Thomas faces $167M debt as it builds wastewater plant for growth
stories.summary: The $440-million Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility is considered crucial to supporting industrial and residential expansion.
stories.author: Brian Williams
paragraphs: A $440-million wastewater treatment facility under construction in St. Thomas is crucial to unlocking major industrial and residential development in the growing city and surrounding region, even as the city expects to take on about $167 million in debt to help finance it, Mayor Joe Preston says.

Projected to be “substantially” completed by 2030, the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility is being built in the city’s north end and is the largest project associated with Yarmouth Yards, the roughly 610-hectare (1,500-acre) industrial park where PowerCo’s $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant and synthetic graphite manufacturer Vianode’s facility are under construction, according to a recent report to city council by treasurer Adam Boylan.
Preston called the wastewater treatment project “imperative” to the development of Yarmouth Yards and the city’s continued growth.

“We sat back and wrote a strategic plan that caused us to start building Yarmouth Yards, and then our second strategic plan now is about the growth of St. Thomas,” Preston said. “That includes really unsexy things like the growth of wastewater treatment, or water itself, or more electricity or better roads. So, it’s all in the plan.”

Yarmouth Yards is a “generational” investment by St. Thomas that has created the potential for “significant growth and opportunity,” Boylan’s report stated. Its $1 billion in “associated infrastructure” represents the largest such expenditure in the city’s history, the report added, providing roads, water and wastewater infrastructure needed to support regional residential, commercial and industrial expansion.

But with $833 million anticipated to come from “new and external” sources, St. Thomas does not have sufficient funding on hand to complete the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility without borrowing, resulting in an estimated $167 million in debt, Boylan’s report said.
The report estimates that debt will cost the city $9.7 million annually to service after 2030.

“Based on staff’s cash flow analysis and revenue forecasting, the City will be unable to fund its annual debt obligation of $9.7 million entirely through development charges and related development revenues and therefore must redirect portions of new industrial revenues from Yarmouth Yards towards annual debt repayment obligations in the interim,” Boylan’s report said.
Preston said there are still several years to explore ways to help pay down the debt, including funding from other levels of government and revenue generated by users.

“Lots of time to continue to work with the federal (and) provincial governments to help us with it,” Preston said. “We needed a much larger wastewater plant so that we had the capacity to grow both industrially and residential, but the users whose wastewater goes through that plant also helps pay for that plant in the long run.”
Preston said attracting large industries that generate substantial revenue could help cushion potential residential tax increases.

“Our treasurer gave us a very detailed report with a lot of risk analysis in it that said this will not have to be on the backs of the residential taxpayers because we’re doing it and planning it right, and we’re doing it over a long period of time,” he said.

The report provides several recommendations aimed at reducing financial risk and improving the city’s ability to respond to future uncertainty, including continued diversification of industrial growth, maintaining an adequate supply of developable land and adopting a new development charges bylaw.

Boylan concludes the financial modelling presented in the report shows St. Thomas is well-positioned to support the financing requirements associated with Yarmouth Yards and the Dalewood Water Reclamation Facility.

“While the outlook remains positive, the scale of the investment and the pace of growth anticipated over the coming decades requires continued monitoring, regular reassessment, and disciplined long-term financial planning,” Boylan’s report said.
Preston said St. Thomas’ investment will help attract “large industry” to the city and create “generational jobs for the future.”
“There’s lots of servicing and cost that come with developing an industrial park like Yarmouth Yards, but boy, is it ever worth the cost and effort,” he said.

stories.title: Man charged after person sprayed in face with animal deterrent: Police
stories.summary: The other person suffered minor injuries, police said.
stories.author: Beatriz Baleeiro
stories.content:
The other person suffered minor injuries, police said.

A St. Thomas resident is facing several charges after a person was sprayed in the face with animal deterrent spray during a brawl on Tuesday afternoon.

Officers on community patrol spotted an altercation between two people near Talbot and William streets. During the altercation, one person pulled out a concealed can of animal deterrent spray and sprayed the other person in the face, police said.

Officers immediately intervened and took the individual into custody, police said.

Through the investigation, police said they learned the accused was bound by a court order prohibiting him from possessing weapons.

A search following the arrest turned up approximately 2.3 grams of suspected methamphetamine.

A 33-year-old St. Thomas man is charged with assault with a weapon, assault causing bodily harm, carrying a concealed weapon, possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, disobeying a court order and possession of a Schedule I substance – methamphetamine.

The man was taken to police headquarters, where he was processed and kept in custody to attend court.

Windsor police are asking for the public’s help to identify an alleged burglar and persistent prowler accused of repeatedly targeting the same west-end home over several days.

Police said the incidents happened between July 26 and 29, typically between 5:30 a.m. and 7 a.m., at a home in the 2300 block of University Avenue West.

The man was allegedly captured on video and seen by bystanders entering the property and the home on multiple occasions.

On one occasion, investigators said the man forced his way through a door before the homeowner found him standing in the foyer. Police said he fled after being discovered.

Police said the man is white and about 40 to 50 years old. He has short ginger and grey hair and a mostly grey beard.

Windsor police released two photos of the man wearing a backpack. In one, he is pushing a dark-coloured bicycle. In the other, he is riding a red bike.

Anyone with information that could help identify the suspect is asked to contact the Windsor police’s Target Base Unit at 519-255-6700 ext. 4350. Anonymous tips can be made to Windsor & Essex County Crime Stoppers at 519-258-8477 (Tips) or catchcrooks.com .

With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: Scattered thunderstorms expected across southwestern Ontario tonight before cooler, drier weather arrives
stories.summary: Expect warm, humid conditions today before a cold front moves through the region tonight, bringing the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Expect warm, humid conditions today before a cold front moves through the region tonight, bringing the risk of scattered showers and thunderstorms, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Temperatures are expected to climb into the upper 20s this afternoon, with increasing humidity making it feel more like the low 30s.

“We’re starting to see the cloud cover build in advance of a cold front that will be pushing into the area late tonight,” Atchison said. “You can see the rain developing out over Lake Huron, so we’ll bring in the risk for scattered thunderstorms this afternoon through the Bruce Peninsula, with the rest of the region seeing that risk through the evening.”

Atchison said the atmosphere will become increasingly unstable as the cold front approaches, creating conditions favourable for showers and thunderstorms overnight.

“Scattered showers and thunderstorms will develop tonight,” she said, noting London could see storms move through around 10 p.m., with activity also expected in Huron and Perth counties, as well as parts of Sarnia and Chatham-Kent.

The frontal system is expected to move eastward overnight, bringing a shift in wind direction and slightly cooler conditions for Thursday.

“That front will push through the area and the winds will come in out of the northwest as we head into tomorrow,” Atchison said.

Despite the change in weather, temperatures will remain mild overnight, with lows settling in the upper teens.

For Thursday, northwesterly winds off Lake Huron are expected to generate some lingering cloud cover, although sunny breaks are anticipated throughout the day.

“We will see a bit of cloud cover hanging on, but some peaks of sunshine and not a bad Thursday setting up with the forecast high at 26 degrees,” Atchison said.

The outlook improves further heading into the weekend.

Friday is expected to be mainly sunny with a high of 23 C and lower humidity, while Saturday is shaping up to be sunny and dry.

“A beautiful day and a great weekend is setting up,” Atchison said.

Cloud cover is forecast to increase again on Sunday, accompanied by rising humidity. Temperatures are expected to remain in the mid-to-upper 20s, but humidex values could make it feel closer to the low 30s.

stories.title: London airport unveils new flights to sunny spots in Florida, Mexico, Jamaica
stories.summary: London International Airport officials on Wednesday announced the addition of four new non-stop, seasonal flights to warm-weather destinations starting this fall.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
London International Airport officials on Wednesday announced the addition of four new non-stop, seasonal flights to warm-weather destinations starting this fall.

Porter Airlines will be flying direct to the following spots from London’s airport:

Four weekly flights to Fort Lauderdale

Three weekly flights to Orlando

Four weekly flights to Cancun, Mexico

Two weekly flights to Montego Bay, Jamaica

The Florida flights will start in November, the Cancun and Montego Bay flights starting one month later. Tickets for these flights are available for booking.

The airport already provides seasonal travel to Toronto, Calgary, Winnipeg, Cancun, Punta Cana and Puerto Plata on WestJet, Air Canada and Air Transat flights.

“The fact that Porter Airlines has chosen London speaks volumes about the strength of our market,” said Scott McFadzean, chief executive of London International Airport. “It reflects confidence in our region, confidence in our passengers, and confidence in the future of Southwestern Ontario.”

McFadzean said a partnership with Porter has been in the works since before he became CEO four years ago.

“As long as they’ve been an airline, people from London have been trying to get them here,” McFadzean said.

Porter has also committed to adding additional connections across Canada starting next summer.

No destinations have been announced, but McFadzean said to expect connections to major cities across the country, particularly “major markets that people love to travel to during the summer months.”

Michael Deluce, chief executive of Porter Airlines, attended Wednesday’s announcement at the airport. He sees potential for more growth from London-area travellers.

“We believe that there is a lot more potential out of London. That means we are committed to expanding our service from London with year-round domestic flights next year,” Deluce said.

There are about two million residents within an hour’s drive of the airport, making it an “incredible market,” Deluce said.

“Over the last five to 10 years, it’s been significantly under-served by our competitors and people from London and the surrounding population want to travel in a more convenient way, not driving two hours to the closest airport,” Deluce said.

stories.title: London landlord to city council: I kept my word to tenants amid renovations
stories.summary: An Old South landlord is pushing back against accusations of reneging on commitments to accommodate displaced tenants as city council looks for an explanation for what happened and what recourse it has.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
An Old South landlord is pushing back against accusations of reneging on commitments to accommodate displaced tenants during renovations as city council looks for an explanation for what happened and what recourse it has.

The project at 145 Base Line Rd. W., near the intersection of Wharncliffe Road South and Commissioners Road West, involves five existing triplexes having their basements turned into new units – which spurred fear of so-called “renovictions,” or booting out long-term tenants for renovations before relisting the units at a higher rent.

In a letter to city politicians , Carlos Afanador, the principal of the numbered company behind the project, rejected suggestions he went back on promises to the remaining three tenants – saying they were offered units before later withdrawing their alternate unit acceptance.

“I committed to offering temporary alternative accommodation to affected tenants during the renovation process. Alternative units were subsequently offered. The tenants initially accepted the units and later withdrew their acceptance near the end of the applicable timeline,” Afanador wrote, adding he paid the tenants the required three months’ rent as a result, and the issue remains before the provincial Landlord and Tenant Board.

“I take pride in honouring my word and am concerned that council has been presented with an incomplete account suggesting that I failed to honour commitments made regarding temporary accommodation for tenants.”

Under Ontario law, tenants can be evicted from their units to allow for major repairs or upgrades, but they are entitled to first right of refusal to return once the work is done at the same rent they had been paying. Provincial law also requires tenants to be paid three months’ rent as compensation or be offered another unit acceptable to them.

City staff initially recommended refusing the planning application in 2024 for being too intense for the site, but council did approve it, partly based on the commitment from Afanador that existing tenants could be shuffled into other open units while work progressed.

The issue was raised by Neighbourhood Legal Services, which represents the remaining tenants at the site. Kristie Pagniello, its executive director, referred to the three months of compensation as a “red herring,” saying the tenants were entitled to the compensation anyway, and the tenants all expressed their desire for an alternate unit but were not offered a habitable one.

“The tenants in the three remaining units will require the temporary accommodations promised by the landlord (where they will be paying the same rent) if they are evicted at the next hearing of this matter. They will need a place to go to, in the same complex, pending the completion of their units,” Pagniello wrote in another letter to politicians.

“We look forward to hearing the outcome of the review of whether the developer has satisfied all applicable conditions and representations made through the planning and site plan approval processes, and what authority the city has to ensure compliance.”

Council voted 13-2 Tuesday to approve ward councillor Skylar Franke’s motion asking city staff for just that: the status of commitments made on temporary accommodation, whether all other commitments made through the planning process are being upheld and what recourse the city has to ensure compliance. Councillors Susan Stevenson and Steve Hillier voted in opposition, all others were in favour.

Stevenson pointed to the city having little legal authority to mandate alternate accommodations through its planning application process, they can only recommend them, saying she was wondering if the endeavour was “worthwhile.”

Franke said she tried reaching out to the developer for documentation mentioned in his letter, and did not hear back before the Tuesday council meeting. She expressed her desire to investigate what recourse the city has in the future for similar situations.

“Some of the information I’d be interested in is if there is any recourse for the city having been given any kind of incomplete or false information that influences project submissions,” she said.

“In the same way we have a list of businesses that we won’t procure from if they violate contracts, is there something similar for developers who do not meet commitments?”

stories.title: Sports briefs: Knights open training camp, Spence defends WBA title, Majors to wear purple
stories.summary: As the weather turned cooler this week, it feels a lot more like hockey season.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
As the weather turned cooler this week, it feels a lot more like hockey season. The London Knights opened training camp Monday with 80 players vying for either a crack at the OHL roster, or to make an impression on ownership for a spot on an affiliate club.

“I couldn’t wait to be here, honestly,” said Cooper McAslan, who played four regular season and four playoff games for the Knights last season.

“It’s really fun seeing all the guys again and meeting new faces as well. It is a battle here with a lot of good skill, a lot of good guys out here.”

“I’d say I’m a 200-foot player who is very skilled and I like to play hard,” said Barch, the son of former London Knight Krys Barch (1997-2000).

He says his game is like his father’s but “maybe not the fighting part.”

Barch says he’s heard several stories from his dad about the city and the fans, and is excited to be in London

“I mean, we have so much young talent here,” added Barch, whose rights were acquired from Kitchener in the Sam O’Reilly and Jared Woolley trade last year.

London opens its exhibition season with a two-game series with the Erie Otters on Friday and Saturday.

Friday is at Canada Life Place and Saturday they’ll play in Watford, Ont. in a rink with a capacity of 650 people.

“I’ve got a lot of friends and family coming, and it was cool to bring the Memorial Cup there, but now to play there it’s even better,” said Evan Van Gorp, a Watford native.

The game is acting as a fundraiser for the renovation of the Alvinston Arena’s floor. Tickets are sold out but they are selling additional tickets to watch the game from the gymnasium hall and there are activities planned outside as well.

“I think we’ve got a meet and greet after for all the kids to come and meet us,” added Van Gorp.

“Just to play there again, I haven’t played there since I was like 10 or 11 years old. It’s going to be really cool.”

Spence defends WBA title in Richmond, VA

Natasha Spence is now riding a four-fight win streak. The champion – who trains out of Boomerz Boxing Club in London, Ont. – defeated Precious Harris-McCray by a unanimous decision to defend the WBA International Super Welterweight title.

“We went in and we did exactly what we said we would do,” said Spence Tuesday after returning to London.

After the bout, she called out two-time Olympic Gold Medallist and 20-time world title holder Claressa Shields.

“We want Clarissa Shields,” said Spence.

“That’s been the goal ever since I realized that I could hang with these big girls. She’s naturally much bigger than me, but when I realized I could hang with these girls, I was like, okay, she’s the top, that’s what I want. She’s back at 160 (pounds), I’m at 160 and I’m strong at 160. I’m on an undefeated four-win streak, so why not? She’s complaining that there’s no competition out there for her, but I put on a fight, put on a good show every time. So, hey, I’m here! I’m here, Clarissa!”

London Majors to Shine the Light on women’s abuse

It’s a busy week for the London Majors as they try to clinch the pennant in the inaugural season of the Canadian Baseball League.

The Majors hold a two-game lead on Welland with four games left in the standings.

London will be at Guelph Wednesday, Thursday in Kitchener, and return home Friday to meet Brantford.

The next home game will revive the Purple in the Park game which supports the London Abused Women’s Centre.

The Majors will wear purple jerseys and are encouraging fans to also wear purple to raise awareness on the issue of men’s violence against women.

He went deep in the third and ninth inning to tie Sean Reilly for the most homeruns in a season in league history with 21.

paragraphs: As the weather turned cooler this week, it feels a lot more like hockey season. The London Knights opened training camp Monday with 80 players vying for either a crack at the OHL roster, or to make an impression on ownership for a spot on an affiliate club.
“I couldn’t wait to be here, honestly,” said Cooper McAslan, who played four regular season and four playoff games for the Knights last season.
“It’s really fun seeing all the guys again and meeting new faces as well. It is a battle here with a lot of good skill, a lot of good guys out here.”
“I’d say I’m a 200-foot player who is very skilled and I like to play hard,” said Barch, the son of former London Knight Krys Barch (1997-2000).
He says his game is like his father’s but “maybe not the fighting part.”
Barch says he’s heard several stories from his dad about the city and the fans, and is excited to be in London
“I mean, we have so much young talent here,” added Barch, whose rights were acquired from Kitchener in the Sam O’Reilly and Jared Woolley trade last year.
London opens its exhibition season with a two-game series with the Erie Otters on Friday and Saturday.
Friday is at Canada Life Place and Saturday they’ll play in Watford, Ont. in a rink with a capacity of 650 people.
“I’ve got a lot of friends and family coming, and it was cool to bring the Memorial Cup there, but now to play there it’s even better,” said Evan Van Gorp, a Watford native.

The game is acting as a fundraiser for the renovation of the Alvinston Arena’s floor. Tickets are sold out but they are selling additional tickets to watch the game from the gymnasium hall and there are activities planned outside as well.
“I think we’ve got a meet and greet after for all the kids to come and meet us,” added Van Gorp.
“Just to play there again, I haven’t played there since I was like 10 or 11 years old. It’s going to be really cool.”

After the bout, she called out two-time Olympic Gold Medallist and 20-time world title holder Claressa Shields.
“We want Clarissa Shields,” said Spence.

“That’s been the goal ever since I realized that I could hang with these big girls. She’s naturally much bigger than me, but when I realized I could hang with these girls, I was like, okay, she’s the top, that’s what I want. She’s back at 160 (pounds), I’m at 160 and I’m strong at 160. I’m on an undefeated four-win streak, so why not? She’s complaining that there’s no competition out there for her, but I put on a fight, put on a good show every time. So, hey, I’m here! I’m here, Clarissa!”

stories.title: Pedestrian struck on Southdale in London
stories.summary: Southdale was closed to traffic in both directions for a time while officers combed over the scene.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
London Police Service says it continues to investigate a collision in south London Wednesday morning involving a pickup truck and pedestrian.

It happened around 9 a.m. at Southdale Road East and Verulam Street.

Southdale was closed to traffic in both directions for a time while officers combed over the scene.

A white pickup truck could be seen in the intersection surrounded by several traffic cones.

Police told CTV News the pedestrian suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, but could not comment on specific circumstances of how the incident happened.

Police are expected to provide further updates when more information becomes available.

stories.title: Jerome Rancourt ready to lead Western Mustangs as starting QB
stories.summary: When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
When 6-foot-5-inches Western Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt rolls out of the pocket, it’s a nightmare for defensive backs.

“It’s definitely not the corner’s first choice to tackle when he rolls out,” said Dasani McIntosh, Mustangs wide receiver.

The fifth-year quarterback from Quebec City, Que. is the new starter after Evan Hillock graduated.

His transition from backup to starter comes at new head coach and quarterback guru Michael Faulds installs new schemes.

“We have him as a head coach, but most of the time he’s our quarterback coach,” said Rancourt.

“We spent a lot of time including a couple of days before the camp started, we had a little retreat. All the quarterbacks went over the playbook threw some balls and it’s been very good.”

Rancourt has been used in third-down and short-yardage situations over the past four seasons which has resulted in him racking up 25 rushing touchdowns.

🏈 Touchdown Mustangs!! Jerome Rancourt takes it in from short range to give @westernufb the first points of the game. 1ST Quarter - 6:20 remaining WLU l 0 WES l 7 #RunWithUs #WesternMustangs #WLUvsWES pic.twitter.com/rlr0ygZhLG — Western Mustangs (@WesternMustangs) October 21, 2023

His size has made him the perfect player in those scenarios.

“I think everyone knows he’s a bruising runner,” said Faulds.

“He can throw the ball a mile, but he’s really worked on his accuracy and his touch. I think it’s going to present some challenges for opposing defensive coordinators. Is he going to take off with his legs? Is he going to drop back and throw it? He always has a stable of running backs behind him, led by the nation’s leading rusher Ethan Dolby last year.”

For the receiver group like McIntosh, it opens up the passing game when a quarterback is a dual threat.

“Just more second chance plays,” said McIntosh.

“Anytime the play breaks down, we know Jerome’s going to keep it alive. Guys like me with a little bit of speed; we’re definitely going to try to either take the top off or come back to the ball and try to make things happen.”

He’s also seen Rancourt develop the mid-range passing game.

“When Jerome throws the ball, you have to be ready,” added McIntosh who had two receiving touchdowns in 2025.

“He definitely has a ton of arm strength, but he’s just working on those intermediate throws. He could run the ball. He could throw the deep ball. Just having a bit more touch is something that he’s added to his game in the summer.”

In a season of change, Rancourt is set to take on the leadership role. He’s been grinding all offseason to handle the workload.

“I was also prepping for the CFL combine as a tight end, but I knew there was a possibility of me coming back,” said Rancourt.

“Eventually I decided that was going to be the way. So, I was working with the guys a lot in the winter and then came back a couple of weeks earlier in the summer to make sure we were ready before camp.”

One more week of work, then Western will open their season against York on Sept. 6.

“Now it’s just about getting the boys ready,” said Rancourt.

stories.title: Expert insight: Burnout isn’t new – 18th‑century farm records show the same exhaustion
stories.summary: Western researcher Nathan TeBokkel argues workplace exhaustion is a longstanding structural issue, dating at least as far back to 18th-century farm workers.
stories.author: Special
paragraphs: Nearly 40 per cent of Canadian workers say they feel burnt out often or always, according to a 2025 survey by Mental Health Research Canada and Canada Life. The term has become part of a broader lexicon of modern work, alongside quiet quitting , hustle culture and grindset and “taskmasking.”

But burnout is older than this current moment of concern suggests. The World Health Organization first classified it in 1990, in the International Classification of Diseases , defining it as “a state of vital exhaustion.”

The WHO later redefined the term as a syndrome “resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed” characterized by feelings of exhaustion, detachment and a lack of accomplishment.

The Oxford English Dictionary dates the word itself to 1937, but the term is even older than that. More than 200 years ago, agriculturalists and workers used the phrase “burnt out” to describe fertilizer kilns , fuel , matches , fires and the consequences of excessive work.

Writing in his 1771 travelogue The Farmer’s Tour Through the East of England , agriculturalist Arthur Young documented farmers pushed to physical and emotional collapse by relentless work. For instance, he tells the story of a sub-tenant farmer, William White.

White worked hard to master new techniques of irrigation and climbed from “a day labourer to a little farmer” despite having been “twice burnt out, by which accident he lost a hundred pounds, notwithstanding the uncommon industry of repairing his buildings with his own hands.”

In other words, White’s barn burned down twice. He couldn’t stop farming while rebuilding it, which meant he was working much harder than before, to the point where he lost 100 pounds. In Young’s account, “burnt out” joins material destruction with “vital exhaustion,” and “uncommon industry” with accomplishment.

Here, burnout has both a material and a social basis – material because a barn burning down necessitates extra work, and social because workers were expected, if not compelled, to do extra work and were supposedly rewarded for it with status and stories.

Burnout’s meaning shifted from literal to figurative over time. It began as a description of candles burning out or fuel being used up, then shifted to a barn burning down and a worker’s energy or body being depleted in the rebuilding. Eventually it came to simply describe a worker’s exhaustion.
This change makes an analogy or even an identity between objects and workers. This change is figurative because this kind of identity is a metaphor: “Workers are fuel.”

We typically associate metaphor with imagination or rhetorical flourish. But philosophers George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argue that “most of our ordinary conceptual system is metaphorical.” Metaphorical concepts structure “what we perceive, how we get around in the world, and how we relate to other people.” Because we rely on them for everyday activities, they aren’t necessarily obvious.

In “burnout,” the metaphorical concept within the term is something like “workers are fuel.” This metaphor suggests that what’s true about fuel is true about workers. Both can be extracted, bought and sold, and used to power machinery. Using more of them produces more power or commodities.

Burnout referred, and still refers, to people’s response to certain conditions, not just to personal choice or poor stress management. It was, and still is , the consequence of a social structure that normalizes and compels excessive work.
The material and social bases of burnout have been generalized over time. It soon became normalized that workers always work extra , regardless of cause or result.

Consider the term “moonlight,” meaning “to do paid work in addition to one’s regular employment; to take on a subsidiary job in order to supplement one’s income.” This term May date to same period as burnout, much earlier than the Oxford English Dictionary’s first attestation in 1957 .

In A Six Months’ Tour through the North of England (1770) , Young writes of a coal miner and farmer named James Croft, “a genius of peculiar cast” he praises for receiving no “assistance either of money or labour” nor skimping on his work in the mine to work on his farm. Croft worked tirelessly:

“Since his beginning he has never had more than four hours sleep, and, of moon-light or bright star-light nights, seldom so much. The regular severe fatigue of the colliery has not been sufficient to bow down the spirit of this poor fellow; – he applies the remainder of the day, and even steals from the night, to prosecute his favourite works of husbandry – that is, to make up his hours of work twenty, out of the twenty-four.”

Young figures Croft was working 12 hours at night in the mine and then at least eight hours more on his farm. He adds that Croft had “inward complaints, that are, in all probability, the consequence of repeated strains.”

Writing like Young’s is often cited by historians for its statistics and stories , but these aren’t value-neutral. They were intended to advance the transition to capitalism, in part by using characters like Croft and White as models to encourage complaint-free, excessive work.
The period’s georgic and pastoral writing accomplished much the same task, often by obscuring or redefining agricultural labour.

In my forthcoming book, Whistling at the Plough: Poetic Infrastructure from Improvement to Romanticism , I argue that we need critical histories that examine how concepts like burnout have built our world.

Poor wages compelled Croft to “moon-light” on his farm so he could produce enough food for his family, and fires compelled White to “burn out” by rebuilding his barn twice while operating his farm. This history casts burnout in a new light.

Today’s version of burnout is often framed as an individual mental or emotional state to be managed with therapy, time off or better coping strategies. But the personal mental or emotional nature of today’s concept belies its social, material basis. This structure hasn’t changed since the 18th century. Burnout is built into capitalism, not a problem capitalism is motivated to solve.

Yet for those 40 per cent of Canadian workers who feel burnt out often or always, a temporary solution might be structural rather than personal; a seaside retreat, like the Victorians prescribed for “overwork,” perhaps, or a four-day work week , which has shown promise in Australia.
Nathan TeBokkel , Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography, Western University

stories.content:
Nearly 40 per cent of Canadian workers say they feel burnt out often or always, according to a 2025 survey by Mental Health Research Canada and Canada Life. The term has become part of a broader lexicon of modern work, alongside quiet quitting , hustle culture and grindset and “taskmasking.”

But burnout is older than this current moment of concern suggests. The World Health Organization first classified it in 1990, in the International Classification of Diseases , defining it as “a state of vital exhaustion.”

The WHO later redefined the term as a syndrome “resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed” characterized by feelings of exhaustion, detachment and a lack of accomplishment.

The Oxford English Dictionary dates the word itself to 1937, but the term is even older than that. More than 200 years ago, agriculturalists and workers used the phrase “burnt out” to describe fertilizer kilns , fuel , matches , fires and the consequences of excessive work.

Writing in his 1771 travelogue The Farmer’s Tour Through the East of England , agriculturalist Arthur Young documented farmers pushed to physical and emotional collapse by relentless work. For instance, he tells the story of a sub-tenant farmer, William White.

White worked hard to master new techniques of irrigation and climbed from “a day labourer to a little farmer” despite having been “twice burnt out, by which accident he lost a hundred pounds, notwithstanding the uncommon industry of repairing his buildings with his own hands.”

In other words, White’s barn burned down twice. He couldn’t stop farming while rebuilding it, which meant he was working much harder than before, to the point where he lost 100 pounds. In Young’s account, “burnt out” joins material destruction with “vital exhaustion,” and “uncommon industry” with accomplishment.

Here, burnout has both a material and a social basis – material because a barn burning down necessitates extra work, and social because workers were expected, if not compelled, to do extra work and were supposedly rewarded for it with status and stories.

Burnout’s meaning shifted from literal to figurative over time. It began as a description of candles burning out or fuel being used up, then shifted to a barn burning down and a worker’s energy or body being depleted in the rebuilding. Eventually it came to simply describe a worker’s exhaustion.

This change makes an analogy or even an identity between objects and workers. This change is figurative because this kind of identity is a metaphor: “Workers are fuel.”

We typically associate metaphor with imagination or rhetorical flourish. But philosophers George Lakoff and Mark Johnson argue that “most of our ordinary conceptual system is metaphorical.” Metaphorical concepts structure “what we perceive, how we get around in the world, and how we relate to other people.” Because we rely on them for everyday activities, they aren’t necessarily obvious.

In “burnout,” the metaphorical concept within the term is something like “workers are fuel.” This metaphor suggests that what’s true about fuel is true about workers. Both can be extracted, bought and sold, and used to power machinery. Using more of them produces more power or commodities.

Burnout referred, and still refers, to people’s response to certain conditions, not just to personal choice or poor stress management. It was, and still is , the consequence of a social structure that normalizes and compels excessive work.

The material and social bases of burnout have been generalized over time. It soon became normalized that workers always work extra , regardless of cause or result.

Consider the term “moonlight,” meaning “to do paid work in addition to one’s regular employment; to take on a subsidiary job in order to supplement one’s income.” This term May date to same period as burnout, much earlier than the Oxford English Dictionary’s first attestation in 1957 .

In A Six Months’ Tour through the North of England (1770) , Young writes of a coal miner and farmer named James Croft, “a genius of peculiar cast” he praises for receiving no “assistance either of money or labour” nor skimping on his work in the mine to work on his farm. Croft worked tirelessly:

“Since his beginning he has never had more than four hours sleep, and, of moon-light or bright star-light nights, seldom so much. The regular severe fatigue of the colliery has not been sufficient to bow down the spirit of this poor fellow; – he applies the remainder of the day, and even steals from the night, to prosecute his favourite works of husbandry – that is, to make up his hours of work twenty, out of the twenty-four.”

Young figures Croft was working 12 hours at night in the mine and then at least eight hours more on his farm. He adds that Croft had “inward complaints, that are, in all probability, the consequence of repeated strains.”

Writing like Young’s is often cited by historians for its statistics and stories , but these aren’t value-neutral. They were intended to advance the transition to capitalism, in part by using characters like Croft and White as models to encourage complaint-free, excessive work.

The period’s georgic and pastoral writing accomplished much the same task, often by obscuring or redefining agricultural labour.

In my forthcoming book, Whistling at the Plough: Poetic Infrastructure from Improvement to Romanticism , I argue that we need critical histories that examine how concepts like burnout have built our world.

Poor wages compelled Croft to “moon-light” on his farm so he could produce enough food for his family, and fires compelled White to “burn out” by rebuilding his barn twice while operating his farm. This history casts burnout in a new light.

Today’s version of burnout is often framed as an individual mental or emotional state to be managed with therapy, time off or better coping strategies. But the personal mental or emotional nature of today’s concept belies its social, material basis. This structure hasn’t changed since the 18th century. Burnout is built into capitalism, not a problem capitalism is motivated to solve.

Yet for those 40 per cent of Canadian workers who feel burnt out often or always, a temporary solution might be structural rather than personal; a seaside retreat, like the Victorians prescribed for “overwork,” perhaps, or a four-day work week , which has shown promise in Australia.

Nathan TeBokkel , Banting Postdoctoral Fellow in English and Geography, Western University

stories.title: Booming Toronto-based burger joint Rudy expands into London, St. Thomas
stories.summary: "What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that's what we do."
stories.author: Ryan Goodison
stories.content:
Rudy, a Toronto-based burger shop that opened in 2016, has been steadily expanding into Southwestern Ontario this year, with a restaurant at London’s White Oaks Mall and another set to open in St. Thomas on Sept. 11 at 985 Talbot St. Luke McCann, owner of the growing chain, spoke with Lfp’s Ryan Goodison on their recipe for success.

Q: For those who might not know you, what is Rudy and how did it start?

A: A buddy of mine and I started it over 10 years ago in Little Italy on College Street in Toronto, and it was a very simple concept. We were both burger fans growing up, and did a lot of travelling trying to figure out what we wanted to do. But the idea was basically just a simple griddle burger. I remember my mom making them in the frying pan when I was a kid, and then the idea was to keep the menu very simple. It’s a scratch kitchen, so everything is made in house.

Q: Where does the name come from?

A: Rudy comes from when my former late business partner and I were kids. You go to a party or something like that, and somebody’s acting a little out of hand or obnoxious or a little full of themselves. We would quietly say that guy’s being a “rudy,” he’s being rude. It’s sort of just an inside joke that we had when were kids.

Q: You’re now expanding into St. Thomas, what made it the next step for you?

A: We went down and we looked around, we spoke to a lot of places, businesses in the area, and they all seemed to be doing really well, and it was a growing area of the province. We found an amazing location on Talbot with great signage, and it’s a standalone. It reminded us of our place on the Queensway in Toronto. So when you find a special location like that, it’s hard to pass up.

Q: You recently expanded into London in January, what made the city the right place for you?

A: London is a big city outside of Toronto and when you head in that direction you can see it’s growing. You’ve got colleges, universities, and it’s a big population, so we figured it just made sense. I’ve also got some friends that lived down there that would always message and say “Hey, when are you going to open up in London?” It had been on the radar for a while.

Q: Why was the location at White Oaks Mall the right fit?

A: We just sort of liked that area. It’s right off the highway, and I think the mall is under construction right now as well as the road construction. We feel that once all that’s done, it’s going to be booming. You have the Ronaldo soccer Footlab and the Ikea going into the same mall, so it just seemed like a good fit for us.

Q: The St. Thomas location will be your 19th across the province, what do you think is behind the success so far?

A: What we aim for is a very simple menu, simple food done right, and that’s what we do. We’re not as fast as McDonald’s, but we think it’s worth it. I think what really has helped us expand is attracting the right people to come work with us. If you have great people, you can do great things.

Q: Are you planning any further expansions into Southwestern Ontario?

A: This is a far southwest as we have on the books right now, but we’d like to get eventually to Windsor, and maybe Sarnia.

Q: If you could recommend one thing on the menu, what would it be?

A: My go-to is the double cheeseburger, which is called the Rude Dude. I usually get a side of our thin fries that we cook in beef tallow, and that’s another thing we do a little different from most places, although it is becoming more popular again.

stories.title: Motorcyclist killed in Norfolk Country crash
stories.summary: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 11:39 AM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 11:39 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Part of 10th Concession Road was closed for several hours but has since reopened
Police are investigating after a motorcyclist died in a crash with a vehicle southeast of London early Tuesday evening.
Just after 5 p.m., emergency crews arrived to 10th Concession Road between Forestry Farm and East Quarter Line roads in Norfolk County, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).
There, officers responded to a serious crash between a motorcycle and sport utility vehicle.
The 34-year-old Norfolk County motorcyclist died at the scene, police said.
The driver and passengers in the vehicle were not injured, OPP added.
Police closed a stretch of 10th Concession Road for several hours, but reopened it overnight.
OPP investigators are asking anyone who witnessed or has video footage of the collision to contact the Norfolk County OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

Police are investigating after a motorcyclist died in a crash with a vehicle southeast of London early Tuesday evening.
Just after 5 p.m., emergency crews arrived to 10th Concession Road between Forestry Farm and East Quarter Line roads in Norfolk County, according to Ontario Provincial Police (OPP).
There, officers responded to a serious crash between a motorcycle and sport utility vehicle.
The 34-year-old Norfolk County motorcyclist died at the scene, police said.
The driver and passengers in the vehicle were not injured, OPP added.
Police closed a stretch of 10th Concession Road for several hours, but reopened it overnight.
OPP investigators are asking anyone who witnessed or has video footage of the collision to contact the Norfolk County OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or call Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Loss of Strathroy hospital's obstetrics unit forces pregnant moms to travel long distances
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:48 AM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:48 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Hospital closed unit in 2024 following low birth volumes, and to refocus on other aspects of women's health
More than two years after Strathroy closed down its obstetrics unit, some mothers are describing the challenges they've faced travelling out of town to London or St. Thomas to give birth.

For Melbourne, Ont., resident Tamia Chicas, SMGH is only 20 minutes away, but the lack of an obstetrics unit meant she had to travel twice that distance to London several times throughout her pregnancy for her prenatal appointments, ultrasounds and delivery.

"It was stressful," said Chicas, who had her son in 2024. "When you're pregnant and you know you need to go that far, sometimes you wonder to yourself, if there are any complications ... driving that far is really scary."

The hospital announced in March 2024 that it would transition obstetrical deliveries to its regional partner hospitals, London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital, as it re-envisions women's health care. Its last delivery was
Julie McBrien, president and CEO of Middlesex Hospital Alliance, which includes SMGH and Four Counties Health Services, said the decision followed record low births at the hospital.
"In our last year of providing obstetrical services, we did 59 deliveries so when you factor that over a year, that's just a little over one each week and that's challenging," she said.

"I think what it told us when we did our review of the situation was moms were choosing to deliver in London or St. Thomas anyway. Hence why we had lower volumes because we were a low-risk birthing centre."

However, for some new and expectant mothers, the trip away from their home community has been a logistical challenge. Chicas worries this can have a negative impact on women's health care outside of larger urban centres.

Chicas said she had a miscarriage before she got pregnant with her now two-year-old son and that made her worry about any possible complications and how difficult it would be to travel all the way to London for medical attention.

"I was just scared the entire time during my pregnancy. If something went wrong, we would have to go so far out of the way. Even if they had an ambulance or something come out here, it would still be quite the drive going all the way to London," she said.

Veronica Marchuk gave birth to her older daughter at SMGH, which was walking distance from her parents house. However, for her now seven-month old daughter, she had also had to travel to London, which made for a lengthy and tiring experience.

"With the first, I was able to labour on the couch and we basically just went [to SMGH] to deliver her and it was amazing. It was such a good experience because I was able to let my body do what it needed to. But with the second, we had to go into London for an actual induction and I had to do the whole labour in the hospital rather than being in the comfort of my own home," she said.
Transportation is also not readily accessible for many families in rural communities, so driving a long distance for the hospital can be a major inconvenience, added Marchuk.
"It makes it harder with the prices of gas too. A lot of people in Strathroy would have to take the bus, schedule an Uber or find somebody to drive them."

McBrien said SMGH has instead focused its efforts on other aspects of women's health care, such as advancing its breast health program through mammograms, breast ultrasounds, a new MRI service at the hospital, and breast cancer and reconstruction surgeries. These initiatives resulted from community feedback, she added.

"Those are things that now women don't have to travel to London for, they can get that care close to home. So we are focusing on the areas where we feel that we can excel, provide high quality care, that we can do lots of activity and really be an area of excellence in," said McBrien.

However, both Chicas and Marchuk believe that with Strathroy's population rapidly growing, an obstetrics department close to home would benefit the entire community and provide more incentive for young couples and families to live in the municipality.

stories.title: Old South neighbours fed up with traffic, trucks cutting through residential streets
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 26
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: August 26, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: August 26
Residents say commercial trucks have ripped down internet and cable wires and tree branches

Residents living on one street in London’s Old South neighbourhood say they are frustrated with the number of cars and large commercial trucks using the area as a shortcut while construction continues on Wellington Road.

Several residents on High Street, located between Commissioners Road East and Grand Avenue, say there has been increased traffic since phase two of the Wellington Gateway bus rapid transit project started in May.
Construction has caused lane closures and slowdowns at Commissioners and Wellington roads — one of London’s busiest intersections — that are expected to last into 2028.

“The trucks come over, and they shake my entire house,” said High Street resident Margaret Dow. “They’ve taken down internet lines and cable lines. Speed is also an issue because it’s just been very noisy to the point where I can’t even have my windows open on nice days.”
Dow has lived on High for 20 years, and said she’s never seen as much cut-through traffic as this summer.
Despite three signs on Commissioners indicating that no heavy trucks are permitted down High, Dow said she has seen transport trucks, cement mixers and dump trucks travelling down the street daily.

“I recognize that with the construction, we’re going to have increased traffic … It is annoying that it takes me about 5 minutes to get out of the driveway in the morning, but that’s the cost you pay to have additional infrastructure in the city,” Dow said. “So cars are not the issue. It’s the trucks.”
Two doors down, Narek Papian said he is fed up with traffic on High, especially because he and his two young children like to bike in the area.

“There’s just too many cars. You don’t leave your house around 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. because you know you’re going to get stuck behind everything,” he said. “So, you wait for your errands or you just make sure you go around the block.”
Papian said he’s also noticed a “speeding culture” on the street, with people driving at what he thinks is about 50 km/h.
The speed limit on High Street is 40 km/h, with yellow 30 km/h advisory signs near speed cushions.
“I don’t understand why they would do that. It’s just so fast, and there’s kids,” Papian said.
Both Papian and Dow said they think the solution is a mix of increased truck traffic enforcement and general calming measures.
“People won’t drive better. You can’t teach people, so you have to create obstacles so they have to slow down,” Papian said.
Doug MacRae, the city’s director of transportation and mobility, said the city considers setting up temporary calming measures before major construction projects even begin.

“We identify early during planning any potential routes that we anticipate will be subject to increased traffic. Then, throughout the construction season as conditions change, we adjust and redeploy measures as necessary and based on neighbourhood feedback,” MacRae explained.
However, MacRae said the strip of High between Base Line Road and Commissioners – where Papian and Dow live – already has permanent speed cushions, so no additional obstacles were installed.
“That section was deemed already traffic calmed,” he said, adding that the city is continuing to analyze resident feedback.
North of Base Line Road, there are several temporary traffic-calming measures on High Street, including speed bumps, posts and hazard signs.
Patrick Clancy, who lives on that side of High, said despite the obstacles, large commercial trucks continue to barrel down the street and have torn branches off the tree in his front yard.

“They put in some calming measures, but it’s not enough to solve the whole problem,” he said. “I’ve yet to see anyone set up on the side of the road to control any speeding or any trucks or anything like that, so it’s a lot of words, not a lot of action.”
MacRae said the city has requested London police enforcement of trucks on non-truck routes and there are plans to install additional no truck signage.
Clancy, Dow and Papian all said they reached out to the city about traffic issues, while the former two also reached out to Ward 11 Coun. Skylar Franke and London police.
"The Road Safety Section has reviewed the issue and conducted targeted enforcement in the area," said London Police Const. Gavin Dell.
"Drivers who fail to comply may be subject to enforcement under applicable traffic legislation. The London Police Service will continue to monitor the area and address violations as appropriate.”
Franke did not respond to CBC News before publication.
Not satisfied with the response so far, neighbours along High Street have been sharing their woes with one another through front lawn conversations and Facebook posts.
Papian said that inspired him to start collecting signatures from neighbours who want to see change.
MacRae said the best way for residents to share their traffic concerns is through the city’s online Service London portal.
He said residents can also use the portal to request a front lawn sign that reminds other drivers to “respect the limit.”

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: August 26, 2026
stories.summary: Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Isn’t it sad our mayor is going to be rewarded for a 28 per cent tax increase during three years? There does not appear to be any serious contender for the position.

Working in business for many years, I have never seen a person submit a budget request like the police department did and get everything they wanted. We need someone to stand up for the taxpayer and challenge budgets like it was their own money.

Maybe in another four years people will see the light.

Gary Rogers, London

I drive on Dundas Street at least once a week. It appears that the vagrancy situation and all its ills is not being addressed. Sorry, but a person lying face down on the sidewalk is not acceptable.

With the London election coming up on Oct. 26, 2026, I would challenge all candidates to state their position on homelessness and what they promise to do if elected.

I can’t think of a more important issue facing Londoners at this time, so let’s demand that candidates address it.

Dogs frequently ingest corn cobs whole or in pieces, resulting in a bowel obstruction. Please, keep corn cobs out of reach.

Paul Francis, Thorndale

stories.title: Victoria Park enhancements to brighten visitor experience year-round
stories.summary: Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features, enhancing community e
stories.content:
Victoria Park is set to become even more welcoming with upgraded lighting and accessible viewing features , enhancing community events and everyday park use throughout the year. Improvements include new multi-colored LED lighting surrounding the concrete pad and the interior of the bandshell, along with a portable raised seating area that will feature railings and a wheelchair-accessible ramp.

The improvements are made possible through a $165,000 donation from Canada Life, recognizing the company's deep roots in London as it celebrates 100 years at its downtown location. Coinciding with the City's Bicentennial, the investment will enhance one of London's most cherished public spaces while improving accessibility and the visitor experience.

The upgraded lighting will help create a more vibrant atmosphere for festivals, community gatherings and public skating, while the new accessible viewing area will allow more Londoners to comfortably experience performances and events.

"Victoria Park has been bringing Londoners together for generations, and these improvements will ensure even more people can enjoy everything this important community space has to offer," says Cheryl Smith, Deputy City Manager, Neighbourhood and Community-Wide Services. "We're grateful for Canada Life's generous donation, which will create a vibrant and accessible destination for residents and visitors alike."

"Having spent nearly 40 years working in downtown London, I know firsthand how Victoria Park has long been at the heart of community life in London, bringing people together to celebrate, connect and create lasting memories," says Jeff Van Hoeve, Senior Vice-President, Business Integration, Canada Life. “As Canada Life marks 100 years in downtown London, we're proud to support improvements that will help make this treasured public space more accessible and enjoyable for residents and visitors for years to come."

The improvements support Victoria Park's role as one of London's premier gathering spaces, creating a more accessible and welcoming destination for residents and visitors for years to come.

stories.title: Ice unit investigation
stories.summary: Update - London, ON (August 26, 2026) – A London man is facing additional charges after members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit (ICE) located additional evidence on seized electronic devices.
stories.author: London Police Service
paragraphs: UPDATE - LONDON, ON (August 26, 2026) – A London man is facing additional charges after members of the London Police Service Internet Child Exploitation Unit (ICE) located additional evidence on seized electronic devices.
On August 21, 2026, the accused, who was out on bail, was arrested on the additional charges.
As a result of the investigation, Isaac Higgs, 23, of London, has been additionally charged with the following offences:
Possession of child pornography;
Print/publish/possess to publish child pornography;
Import/sell/distribute, etc. child sexual abuse material;
Luring a person under 16 years of age by means of telecommunication;
Making available sexually explicit material to a person under or believed to be under 18 years of age; and
Obtaining sexual services for consideration.
The accused remains in custody and is scheduled to appear in London court on September 1, 2026, in relation to the charges.

ORIGINAL - LONDON, ON (May 21, 2026) – A London man was arrested last week by members of the LPS Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit in relation to possession of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (CSAEM).

In October of 2025, members of the London Police Service commenced an investigation after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) made them aware of information involving a London man.
On Friday, May 15, 2026, a search warrant was executed at a residence near Elias Street and Adelaide Street North.
A male suspect was arrested, and electronic devices were seized. Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (CSAEM) were located.
As a result of the investigation, Isaac Higgs, 23, of London, has been charged with one count of possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
The accused is scheduled to appear in London court on June 11, 2026, in relation to the charges.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to Protect Children from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation on the Internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Uncertainty about temporary winter homeless shelter’s location sparks debate about clustering in core business districts
stories.summary: City Council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
City council has supported the latest version of London’s Winter Response to Homelessness, but tensions resurfaced during the debate about the location of a temporary shelter that will be operated by Ark Aid Street Mission.

The updated plan will see homeless shelters open a total of 235 overnight spaces every night between Dec. 1, 2026, and March 31, 2027, plus an additional 29 overnight spaces when temperatures drop below -15C or -20 windchill.

Most of the spaces will be within existing shelters, but Ark Aid Street Mission is looking to secure a yet-to-be-determined location for 40 spaces that would operate nightly from 9 p.m. to 9 a.m.

Concerned about the clustering of frontline agencies in the Old East Village (OEV) BIA, Coun. Susan Stevenson proposed requiring council approval of the location before it receives municipal funding.

“To say that there are no other locations [but the main street of core area BIAs] is counter to our whole objective of 12 to 15 [homeless] hubs around the city,” she asserted.

Coun. Hadleigh McAlister expressed similar concern about the Hamilton Road BIA in his ward, “We need to recognize that we have repeatedly asked two areas of the city to shoulder the responsibility and that is grossly unfair.”

Downtown London Coun. David Ferreira acknowledged, “I understand the capacity that we have is really within these [core] areas, however, I also see that there is a reality that we do have service providers within a small area.”

Stevenson pressed staff about a previous council decision not to fund shelter spaces on the main streets of BIAs, but council supported a “not withstanding” amendment essentially exempting this decision from the previous restriction.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis rejected the notion that council continues to cluster frontline services for homeless Londoners in OEV, Downtown London, and along Hamilton Road.

“The core is not the only location where we have homelessness services,” Lewis stated. “On Clarke Road in the east end I have the YOU (Youth Opportunities Unlimited) youth shelter. I also have the Anova Women’s Shelter. South of [Highway] 401 is where we put the micro-modular shelter.”

The deputy mayor emphasized that The Ark and Unity Project own their buildings on Dundas Street in the OEV BIA and receive private donations to fund some of their operations.

“So if you want to talk about moving them, then you better talk about a multi-year budget business plan for property acquisition, to then do land swaps with them, because that is what you’re talking about,” he added.
